Now it's all about making different objects. Indeed, times have changed. I was thinking about teaching kids about it if I was still childminding. Do think the young ones can't keep up with all these new technologies though. It's all about exposure, right? If we can familiarize them early in school, it really helps. I tried to introduce some basics in my classroom and they were surprisingly receptive. That's good to hear. My grandkids... well, the eldest one, Ben, he's always glued to his phone. I worry if he's getting enough fresh air. Oh, same thing with my nephews. Always gaming and not moving. But funnily enough, when they visited this summer, we had a bit of shabby workmanship and they actually took an interest in fixing things around the house. It was quite surprising! Reminds me, I was looking at some old houses around here. The new ones are often so poorly built compared to what they used to be. And it's not just shabby workmanship either, it's the lack of character. Agreed. Where's the craft in building like there used to be? Nowadays, it's all about knocking up cheap houses. It's a shame really.

Ah, dear, it's so exciting that you're bringing your daughter from abroad to live with you. It must be quite an adjustment for her, especially after being away for so long. Yes, it certainly is! She's been living in Singapore with her mother for most of her life, and while she's excited to be closer to me and learn more about her European heritage, I can tell she's also a little nervous about the move. I would be. I had similar experiences when I went to university in Aberdeen. There was an initial culture shock, but then you start to find your footing and before you know it, you've grown into the new environment. I hope that's true. She's very smart, just like her mother, but she was always the type to prefer the familiar places from her childhood. That's natural. And she's coming here at a great time of the year, isn't it? Summer is so vibrant here, and we have so many local events and traditions to celebrate. Absolutely. We've been discussing how best to ease her transition, especially considering the academic year starts soon. I don't want her to feel overwhelmed, both at home and at school. You’re doing well to think ahead. You must remember what it was like when you began at university. It wasn’t all smooth sailing, was it? No, it was a bit of a struggle at first. I came from Brighton, so it wasn’t a huge cultural shock, but I missed my family and friends from home. It’s all part of growing up and finding your place in the world. Exactly! And now you're the one helping your child through this. It's a kind of full circle, isn’t it? I hadn't thought of it that way, but yes, you're right. She'll be fine. Brighton is a wonderful city to grow up in—vibrant, diverse, and really welcoming. And you're here to guide her through it all. That’s very reassuring to hear. But sometimes I do worry. I'm sure she'll experience a bit of homesickness, and I don't want her to feel like she doesn't belong here. Homesickness is a normal part of moving to a new place. And she almost certainly already has a sense of connection here, right?

Ah, James, welcome back to my home in Brighton! It's been ages since we've caught up over a cuppa. How are you after the holidays? Oh, thanks for having me, Simon. It's lovely to relax here for once. Things are going all right, though the Scottish referendum has been on everyone's minds. I don't think many people expected the outcome, eh? Absolutely! It's shaken up a lot of things. I was speaking with some colleagues about it just the other day. The implications for the job market are quite interesting, particularly how it might affect our profession. Yes, I've been reflecting on that too. It just had me thinking about some upcoming interviews I've got lined up. Might just highlight the added importance of preparation. You're right about that. It can't hurt to be over-prepared. Though sometimes you just hope for a certain level of understanding from the other side of the table. Indeed. I've been applying for a spot in the sociology department of the local university. It's a bit of a step up, but I've been feeling the need for a change. That sounds interesting. We certainly need more professionals like you in the field. Speaking of which, has any news on your daughter come while you’ve been away? Last I heard, she was at university... Ah, Emily? She's doing well, thankfully. Just finished her first year and seems to be really enjoying it. She's been quite involved in the Scottish independence discussions in her university, really opened my eyes to another side of the debate. Shows how relevant and impactful they are in a broad range of academic fields. Well, that's the nature of good education - contextualising and broadening understanding, especially in these times. We can learn a lot from the next generation. Seems like the young people are quite engaged and passionate about the issues. She said she's considering doing a year abroad next year, perhaps to Scotland. She's very interested in the cultural and political landscape there after what's happened. That would be quite an educational experience. Where do you think it might take her, do you think? Well, I suppose it just depends on what direction her studies take her. She's always been keen on understanding global political trends and social movements. I could see that.

Alright, I remember my first trip to the States. It was like no other experience. The food, the people, the noise... it was overwhelming. You mean overwhelming in a good way or bad? I once had this friend who spent a month in New York City and his main complaint was the noise. Everywhere, all the time. He was surprised how much silence means to him now. I had a similar experience when I spent a few weeks in LA. I thought I was used to crowds in London, but LA's crowd noise was a different kind of beast altogether. It was hard to get a quiet moment anywhere. But the food, though.. is it as weird as they say? I've heard tales of big burgers and sweet treats making people wobbly. Oh, you'll love it. The portions are huge and very sweet. But there's a catch, you know? Behind the sweetness, there's a whole world of healthy food too. My cousin worked in a vegan café in LA and I was really surprised. Exactly. I think most tourists just hit the usual spots but the variety is incredible. From food trucks to fine dining – and the quality varies so much, you learn quickly where to look. Do they really call all soft drinks 'soda' across the US? I find that in Britain, we really have regional dialects for things like that. No kidding. That's one of things that really stood out for me from Netflix shows and such. Here we'd have 'pop', 'fizzy drink', or regional variations. It’s interesting how language changes, isn't it? Even across the Atlantic, our shared English language can vary so much. It's quite fascinating but also can be a bit disorienting sometimes. Definitely. I remember my time in New Orleans, for instance, people would use words that were old English to me. It was like stepping back in time but in a real, modern city. And the kids! Speaking of Americans... what’s it like raising children in the States? I've heard it’s quite different. Yeah, I've watched a few documentaries on American kids and they seem to be more... adventurous, perhaps? More individualistic. Oh, I think that’s generally the case. Independence is encouraged from a young age. In England, we're a bit more... well, the system's quite strict till quite late.

Oh, did I find bargains or what? I've just today returned from a shopping spree around town. Right! What did you get? Well, let's see... Go on, I can't wait! I found this beautiful set of silk blouses that I think would be perfect for work. They were almost 70% off, I couldn't resist. I can see why you couldn't resist. Silk blouses like that don't come around often. Yeah, and the designs are really making a statement, too. I think they'll pair beautifully with most of my work trousers. That sounds great. What else did you get? I also got this beautiful shift dress - it's both simple and elegant. It was a total impulse purchase, but it looks and feels amazing. It is rather nice. What's the label? It's by this relatively unknown British designer, actually. The quality is superb, and the price was surprisingly affordable. Less known labels can often be a fantastic buy. Exactly. Plus, doesn't it feel good to support the local kind? Absolutely, and if it’s as good as the first two items you bought today, I reckon it’s a great find, too. On that note, I also got another pair of boots. They’re from a great shoe store I found online. Oh, these are nice. The build quality looks solid, and the design is quite versatile. Yeah, I think they'll fit well with a range of outfits, and they're very comfortable. Good choice. Did you meet any other British expats while shopping? I know you often spot other English speakers around these parts. You know I always do! In fact, there was another British woman there, too. We ended up chatting about... pretty much everything. I bet you did. You always make friends with the locals, too, which is great. It's amazing how quick bonds are formed over shared experiences or common heritage. Indeed it is. We found that when we first moved here. Now, are these clothes all new additions to your rotation or replacing old items? A bit of both. I've been looking to refresh my work wardrobe and, to be honest, I had to replace a few items that didn't survive the move here. The dry air does weird things to fabric, doesn't it? It sure does. I've had to replace a few of my own shirts due to the same issue.

Ah, lads and lass, did any of ye catch the Six Nations match today? Yeah, dad and me watched it after dinner. It was pretty exciting. Ireland beat Wales by quite a bit. Aye now, the match was a drama! Ireland's performance was grand. Oisin, don’t you think it was a good game? It certainly was. I loved seeing the young players perform so well. Indeed. Rory Best was excellent out there. You know, I’m actually organising a small gathering for Oisin’s birthday, and I thought we could have a bit of a screening of the match if anyone’s interested to watch again. That sounds cool, but would you prefer the whole match or the highlights? Highlights would be better. We don’t need to spend the whole evening watching it again, but it would be nice to recap and chat about it. And possibly discuss similar sports in school. Oisin enjoys sportsball. Perhaps we could even play some backyard games if the weather permits this weekend. That's an idea. I’ve been meaning to set up a little net in the garden for him. For a rugby ball, you mean? Exactly. Speaking of sports, did ya see the qualifying match for the under-16s? I heard it was quite a spectacle. Haven’t had a chance, but that’s definitely something we should plan to watch together sometime. Speaking of the lads, how about this; we could get them balls for playing, and maybe some stargazing later in the week. Ballincollig’s sky’s decent for that, isn’t it? We could do. The clear evenings are perfect for stargazing around here. That’s a great idea, but let’s make sure Oisin doesn’t sit up too late staring at stars. True. He needs his sleep for school. How about setting a time? Like, say, 7 or 8 pm? It’ll still be light enough for sports and still allow some stargazing if the weather agrees. I like that. 8 pm sounds good. We can set up the nets and maybe even light some fairy lights or a bonfire if we're allowed. Awesome! Can we also sign these birthday cards? I never thought Oisin’s birthday would turn into a mini rugby-world-cup-celebration. Indeed! We should get everyone to write a little message. Let’s get these cards signed and give Oisin a sense of community around his birthday.

Oh, so many topics! I can barely keep up. Exactly! It feels like years since we last caught up properly. I know, isn't it? I've recently been doing research on baby talk and how it varies across different cultures and languages. Fascinating stuff! That sounds really interesting! I wish I could have spent some of my early childhood language development research on baby talk. Our older nephew is just starting to babble, it's adorable. I bet it is! And, speaking of babies, have you heard about the new nursery near the campus? Apparently, it's really popular and getting good reviews. Might have to consider moving to that area. Really? That's big news. I've been thinking about moving as well. My flat share is getting too small with the new baby on the way. Oh, congratulations! How far along are you? And do you know where you're planning on moving to? Just past 10 weeks or so. We're still deciding, actually. I don’t know if we should stay close to work or find something different. The debate of convenience vs. 'ideal' location. Always tough. But the university area can be so nice to raise a family, lots of park space and whatnot. Absolutely. Honestly though, right now, it's all about functionality. I just need something really practical. I hear you. And with the baby, you're going to need plenty of storage space and stuff. Oh, definitely. And then there's the whole thing of sharing or not sharing clothes... More logistics! How are your siblings? Have they offered to share anything yet? They've offered quite a bit, which is lovely, really. But honestly, it's more emotional than practical - the thought of passing on their things is quite sweet. Definitely. I've had friends start doing this for me before I had my baby, it's always a bit sentimental. And speaking of siblings, how was your brother last time you spoke to him? He's doing okay, thanks for asking. Actually, he just started learning Spanish. I swear, he's taken to it like a fish to water. That's great! Language acquisition really can vary so much between different individuals. Exactly. I mean, I recall that time... Oh, don't remind me. My um, early language learning experiences weren't quite as smooth. I really struggled with German, if I'm honest.

Right, so here's a thing I've always wondered. We've all got our own accents; how do you think that affects the way we interact with people?      That's a great question, actually. There's quite a bit of research on that now, and it’s quite interesting. We do tend to stereotype based on accents. You hear a certain accent and automatically assume a certain social status or background. And that can influence how we treat someone.      Absolutely, and it isn’t very helpful. But I've got another question: Are there still certain places in Bedford where certain dialects are really prominent? I mean, I've heard there's quite a bit of variation even within just the county.      Yeah, that’s true. I mean, even here in Bedford, you get different dialects based on places like village or town. I'm from the north of Bedfordshire, so my accent's a bit different to some of the people I've met from Luton, for example.      That’s right, regional variations are still pretty strong. And it's funny because it's not just between districts or villages, sometimes within the same town you can hear different accents. We've got a bit of a melting pot here.      Speaking of melting pots, how about those photographs of Luton? You must have seen some of the old architecture around there. Did it used to be much more industrial than it is now?      Oh, yes! Definitely. I mean, look at Dunstable, it's got old mill buildings and factory remains all over. But they're slowly being converted into apartments and all that. And there’s some really cool projects now revitalizing the area with art and stuff.      That’s true. The influence of industry is still visible but it’s all changing now. I worked at one of those factories for a side job, and it was incredible to see just how much they were focused on keeping that history alive while updating the buildings. ---      Changing industries reminds me of something else. Have any of you got into any hobbies or changing professions? Accents sure, but what about things like music or sports?      Well, I’ve always been into languages. I mean, besides just teaching English, I take classes in Spanish and French. I find it really fascinating how different languages shape thought patterns and culture.      That’s interesting.

I've decided I need a new car. The one I have is still reliable but it's old and uses a lot of fuel. Do you think it's worth getting a new one? Hi there! Yes, I think now is the right time. If you've had your current car for a while and it isn't fuel-efficient, then definitely. A new car can be more environmentally friendly and cost-effective in the long run, right? Exactly! That's what my dad always says. Plus, I get a bit anxious in it sometimes. You know, it's a bit shaky on the motorway. Fair enough! I used to have a similar car. Sentimental value aside, it's nice to upgrade sometimes. Do you have any in mind? Yeah, I've been looking at a few models. I like the Hyundai Ioniq, it's supposed to be good value for money and also quite eco-friendly. But, the problem is, buying a new car is such a big investment. It's not just the initial cost, you know, but also running costs like insurance, fuel, and maintanence. That's true. But you can always consider electric or hybrid models. They might be more expensive upfront, but they're cheaper to run overall. And with the government incentives to buy eco-friendly cars, it might be more affordable than you think. I'd love to go electric but, you know, range anxiety isn't in my favor as I have to commute quite a bit. You're right, but modern electric models have a much better range than they used to. You could consider a hybrid if you're not ready for full electric just yet. Plus, many places offer charging points now, so it's less of a worry than it used to be. That's a point. Maybe I'll look at hybrids initially. What about the cost of insurance? It's quite high for young drivers and it's supposed to depend on a lot of factors. It can be expensive, yes, but insurance does vary a lot depending on the model of car, your location, and a few other things. If you're willing to do some comparison shopping, you might find a better deal than your current insurer is offering. Again, it's about doing your research and comparing prices. I've been put off by how time-consuming it feels.

Ah, so many of you here today. It's wonderful to see the whole family together. How's every one doing, then? I'm good, thanks for asking. We just got out of school for the summer. Ah, young folks just getting a break from school, eh? Yeah, they need their rest. Haven't had the chance to plan out everything yet, though. That's all right. Take your time, enjoy the summer before school starts again. What've you been up to, Bob? Just the usual, pottering around the garden. Sue and I went on a nice little walk along the River Hull the other day. Really? My dad sometimes talks about that area. Is it as nice as he says? Yes, it's lovely. Quite peaceful. You should try it out sometime. And how about you, dear? What do you and the others plan on doing during these summer months? Well, I assumed we'd have a bit of a family get-together here, at our place, to catch up, you know? Maybe a BBQ or something like that. A BBQ sounds great! Yeah, I thought we'd make some burgers and have some nice English food. Plus, I've got plenty of room for a few friends and family if you'd all like to come over. That sounds lovely. I might even bring the secret family recipe for Yorkshire Pudding. Oh, good on you! You know how to warm up a family gathering. Well, it's all part of the fun. You know how it is with Yorkshire folk. What’s the secret recipe for Yorkshire Pudding, Grandma? Well, let's see... first, you need to make sure the batter's nice and light. No heavy stuff. Then, you pop it in a hot oven. The real trick is getting the temperature right and making sure it rises nicely. And of course, it all happens when you've just made all that other food and everyone's hungry. Exactly! And don't forget the leftovers. Yorkshire Pudding is perfect for soaking up all that lovely gravy. That sounds delicious. Well, we've got all summer to plan. Let's start setting some dates. Yeah, how about next weekend? It's a Sunday, everyone's usually free. Sure, that works for me. I'd like that. Just need to make sure I've got the recipe, and all the essentials.

Alright, kids! Let's pretend we're pirates for our today's activity during Shakespeare week. You boys are my trusty crewmates, and we're sailing the high seas for treasure. You two can be first mate and lookout, okay? Yarr! I want to be the lookout! I'll keep a sharp eye for the treasure, Captain! And I be the first mate! I'll help navigate and set the sails! That's great. Well, lookout, keep your eyes sharp. We're headed for the Caribbean Sea where we've heard there's a treasure island. I see the island, Captain! There be palm trees and mountains! And what about the treasure? Is it hidden under the sand? That's a good question, first mate. It could be hidden under the sand, or perhaps in a cave on the island. We'll have to explore carefully. Can we use this treasure map on the table to find it? That's a good idea! Let's use this treasure map. It's written in old English – just like Shakespeare used – to make it more fun and challenging. Arr, I can decipher this map, Captain, it reads 'At the tallest palm, turn northwest, for the treasure waits.' "Yarr, First Mate! Let's follow the map! But where's the northwest?" That's a great understanding of the map, matey. Turns out, we have to go towards that big tall vase in the corner of the kitchen. Oh, I see it! The treasure must be there! Indeed! But first, let's set up our treasure. I know where we can hide it, Captain! In the treasure chest! That was a lot of fun, didn't it? You two were great pirates and navigators. Can we do more pirate activities during Shakespeare week? Maybe make DIY pirate costumes? Absolutely, and why don't we draw our own treasure maps as a further activity? We can share them tomorrow at school during the week's activities. Ooh, I like the idea! Maybe we can even do some pirate-themed writing! That sounds like a great idea too. We could create stories about our pirate adventures. That would be a fun task for the acting and storytelling part of Shakespeare week. And Captain, will we get to go to the circus workshop next week? It sounds so fun! Yes, indeed. We have the circus workshop planned after this week's activities.

Oh, let me tell you first about the time I was arrested. It was during my stint teaching English in Saudi Arabia. I had this crazy idea to sail a small yacht from Jeddah to Cyprus. You must have had a touch of madness to attempt such a journey alone! But go on, what happened? Well, I had prepped this boat of mine, named Daisy, I'd purchased in Jeddah. It was a bit rusty, but I thought, “Why not?” Didn't you have any... um... appropriate documentation, sailing experience? Not like you'd expect, no. I was young and reckless, but my big mistake was trying to "sail" from inside Saudi waters without clearance. So, you were basically breaking international laws and Saudi ones too? What a fine mess you got yourself into! I was stopped by the Saudi coast guard within hours of leaving. I'm pretty sure they were more amused than angry. The photographs of Daisy must have been quite the sight. A tiny boat with English lady and her dreams to explore the sea. Indeed they did. I had to explain my story, why Daisy was named as such and in return, they really did get quite interested in my "experience" of sailing. And they didn't know it at the time, but they were probably more fascinated by your story than serious about arresting you, weren’t they? I reckon that’s a fair assessment, yes. The local police confiscated Daisy and I had to sort things out with the British consulate. It was a bit of an adventure really. While you were dealing with the coast guard, did you find out much about life in Jeddah? Yes. The experience of living and working in Saudi Arabia was quite enriching. As a foreigner, I was aware of the strict rules, of course. Didn’t they almost blow your mind with the sudden change from... well, let’s say "normal" life, to observing the local rules and customs? Oh, absolutely. The rules regarding alcohol were particularly strict. I remember one of my students had warned me that if I was caught with a bottle of wine... Because, if anyone knows anything about alcohol, it’s the British abroad, right? Right. But it wasn’t just about drinking—it was the idea of being "caught" that was at the heart of it. The local customs around that were what really stuck with me.

Oh, did I ever tell you about's Dad's latest bathroom catastrophe? He's trying to install that new heated floor he bought, but it's been a week and the whole bathroom is still out of commission. That sounds like a drama fit for a sitcom. I've seen his efforts at home improvement before, but heated floors, eh? Exactly! He's been right at the center of a never-ending chaos. All he says is “this will be so cozy in the winter” but right now, it's just cozy chaos. That does sound funny. Do you think I can have a say in my future bathroom design if we ever move to a new house? Absolutely! You can have a say on everything. And speaking of future plans, what are you thinking about for a career path? You're going to be an adult soon, you know. Honestly, it's all a bit overwhelming. I'm interested in coding and tech but also wanted to try my hand at refereeing sports this summer. That's interesting! Refereeing's a good way to learn leadership and responsibility, while the coding job will need problem-solving skills. It’s a good idea to try things to figure out what you like. Absolutely, and while you're exploring jobs, perhaps look into some work experience. Almost every tech company offers work placements or shadowing for young people interested in coding. That's a great idea! Maybe I could email some companies in Fradley that work in tech and see what the possibilities are. You should. Plus, if you can get some work experience, it will look good on your CV, and it’s also a great way to learn more about a career. And remember, teenage years are all about trying things out. You're figuring out what you're really interested in, so keep trying new things. Yeah, I guess you're right. It does make things a bit clearer. Remember what Mr. Smith said at school? 'There's zero shame in not knowing what you want to do right now. The majority of people don't have it sorted until they're in their 20s or even 30s.' That’s true. We all took our time. And look at our careers now, it’s not just about the immediate but also about what you enjoy doing. That's reassuring.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that truffle dish we had in that fancy restaurant in London? It was like nothing I'd ever had before, so rich and earthy. Yes, you've mentioned it before! You were practically salivating at the questions you were asking the chef. You do have a way with asking people about food, don't you? Careful, right? Yeah! And can we even get truffles here? Does Istria have them too? Actually, yes – Istria is famous for its delicious truffles, very similar to the ones in Italy. It must be down to the same kind of terrain and climate here. And the best of all, the prices are generally a bit more affordable. Well, that's a piece of information I'd be interested in. Our friend Mark is a big foodie, he'd love to hear about that. Have any of you seen this? It's our favorite chef, this is actually on his menu – truffle pasta dish. He uses different types of truffles depending on the season too. Wow, that looks amazing! Do we have time to go and find truffles while we're here? Is there like a truffle-hunting expedition you can do? Ah, I see where you're headed, lad. Alright, I'm all for it. But bear in mind, it's not likely we'll come across truffles in the wild. These are usually preserved and sold, or grown specially. You'd have to be super lucky or hire a professional hunter. Still, it could be an adventure. And then there's another chef in America who uses quite a bit of truffles in his dishes and it's always a hot topic on food channels. You know, these guys could sit on these jewels and sell them for a pretty penny, but instead they spoil us with these extravagant dishes. And speaking of America, what's up with people smoking in movies? We saw one on TV the other day and one character was always lighting up almost every scene. It just seems so odd. Ah, I suppose it’s just the culture, or the sense of drama perhaps. Though, thinking back, it’s really just about when that film was made. I know that was often the case in the past, but... Not so much now. Yeah, I remember that about old movies. It’s always so surprising when you see it now how it was just a normal part of life back then.

Oh, did I just choose the table's most awkward seat? Am I blocking your view of the clock tower? Not at all, just enjoying the view myself. It's lovely out today isn't it? Yes, absolutely! Aylesbury can't compare to this , even if it's home. I feel like a kid in a candy store just walking around Cambridge! I couldn't agree more. I love how much history is here. As a Projects assistant, it's always fascinating to learn about the origins of the industry, especially in a city like this. I used to be a language student here too. It just felt right to end up working with the Press. The sense of tradition and expertise in language is really unique here. That's interesting! What aspect of language did you study? And aren't you worried sometimes about the creative part of marketing in a place like this? Well, I studied English Literature, which I think actually helps in my job. As for the creative side, it's quite challenging. We're a bit more traditional here at the Press, focusing on academic and educational materials. However, the 'marketing' label is quite broad; it often means explaining complex topics in a clear way, which is actually quite creative. Ah, I see. Like making 'high-brow' concepts accessible to 'regular folk'. I could see that as really satisfying. I'm more on the administrative and project management side. I don't have to worry about the creative part as much, but I enjoy how every project kind of tells a story behind the scenes. Whether it's a new textbook or a digitisation project of some less known text from our archives. You mean the more obscure texts? That's really cool. I did some research on regional dialects as part of my postgraduate studies and it really makes me think about how language changing over time. It's fascinating but also heartbreaking in a way—so much history and identity tied to language. Sounds like we're all quite interested in language from different angles. I've always found regional dialects fascinating too, especially how they are often tied to social class and education. Yes, and sometimes job too. As Projects assistant, I’ve been part of several projects that deal with language access for different communities. It's amazing to see the impact language can have.

Right, so I think we've got everything figured out for our visit to Natalka's. The address, the GPS, even the spare change for the parking meter. Everything seems set. Are you sure? Let me just check our route one more time, make sure we're not missing anything important on the way. Oh, I'd totally forgotten about the border crossing into Poland. Do we have all the necessary documents? I believe we're good there. My passport is checked up to date, and as far as I know, most of us don't need visas to visit Poland, especially for a short time like ours. Great, just making sure. And did we confirm that Natalka is expecting us to bring anything specific for the dinner party? Ah, yes - she mentioned we should bring some drinks to share. Nothing too fancy, just something to help with the celebration. Ron also said we should bring some English tea if we have any, similar to last year. Since we're coming from England, it's a nice gesture, I think. For sure. We can pick it up on the way. Now, let's talk about accommodations. We're assuming Natalka has space for all of us for the night, but have we confirmed? I think so. She mentioned we can all stay at her place. Well, at least for those who can't or don't want to camp nearby. Camping in Poland sounds fun actually. But I wouldn't mind the comfort of a bed after this drive. Agreed. But would it be rude if some of us didn't want to stay? Just wanting to make sure we're understanding the situation correctly. As far as I know, the invitation was for those who can stay to stay, and for the rest, there's space at the campsite nearby. Seems like they're prepared for all contingencies. That's reassuring. Because I know changing plans last minute can be tricky especially when we're visiting. True. I'm sure Natalka would want to accommodate any of our needs and make us feel welcome. Anyway, I think we've covered all the essentials. It'll be great to catch up with everyone. Absolutely. It's been too long. And speaking of catching up, I've got so many stories to share from my part-time TEFL adventures. Hopefully, the others will be interested in hearing.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you seen these new Nike shirts for the World Cup? Jeez, I mean, they've resurrected the red and white stripes for England! Yeah, I saw. It's bold, isn't it? I kind of like it, though. I just hope they bring back a bit of the glory days. I know, right? But actually, I've been thinking, what's the deal with football strip designs these days? So many money-grabbing sponsors. Remember when strips were simple? Well, it's all about marketing now, dear. I mean, even McDonald's had a deal with football, right? Oh, good Lord, yes. “Pizza Soccer” even sponsored Manchester United for a bit. Exactly. But it's not all bad, though. I mean, the money from these deals often goes towards player wages or training facilities. It's just... it seems like the soul of the game has gotten a bit lost. I'm not sure about that, but at least McDonald's did give good deals. Remember the time they had that huge deal for 'Pizza Soccer'? It was peak '90s, wasn't it? Absolutely. But while we're on the subject, have you noticed how much more prevalent sports sponsorship is becoming? It's everywhere, really. It’s all about brand recognition. I mean, just look at the Olympics - doesn't matter what sport, it's always sponsored. True. And it's not just global, even local teams get sponsored. But the problem is less about who the sponsors are and more about how much dependence the sport has on them. That's a good point. Like, football can't be just about the game, it has to be a bonanza of advertising, too. You'd think after all these years of professionalization, the purity of the sport would still be valued more. But I guess it's just the way the world is now. Still, as long as the match is exciting and the team plays well, I suppose we can compromise on the commercials. Definitely. Speaking of which, who do you think is going to win this year? I've got a soft spot for Germany. I wouldn’t bet against them. Their team is solid every time. But I’ve always liked France, they have a good blend of experience and talent. What can I say, a French bias in our very own youth?

Oh, so many topics! You know, I have to admit today's eBay order was super frustrating. The company clearly messaged me that my order wouldn't arrive until next month! Aye, I know what you mean! But have you heard about the new policy regarding job seekers allowance and benefits? I'd totally hit the jackpot if I could get some help with the bills while I'm struggling to find work! Erm, yeah, it's a complex topic... So, is that what's on your mind most? Yeah, pretty much. I mean, it’s not like I want to stay on benefits forever, but right now, it’s just so hard to find work in Chatham. I feel like I’m just in a rut. I get it. It’s tough. But you know you’re not alone, right? And there are resources out there. You could visit your local job centre, there are job clubs and things like that. I know, I know. I’ve been to the job centre multiple times. They just keep sending me to these training sessions and it's all about making a great CV or presenting myself well. Where are the actual jobs while I'm upskilling? It’s a vicious circle sometimes, isn’t it? They want you to have the skills, but how do you get the job to gain the experience? A bit Catch-22. Exactly! It’s funny actually. I swear, some days I feel like they just want to throw a training manual at us unemployed folk and expect it to solve everything. Oh, I've been there too when I was in uni. The job applications. Seems like the CV's and covering letters are a black hole, never to be read by a human. Right! But at least we were in university, figuring out what we wanted to do. While I’m trying to make something happen in my late 30s after a string of jobs that all fell through. I often think about just hopping on a train and taking a day trip somewhere, just for a change of scene. Can’t afford it right now, but maybe it’s good for the soul. I've had days like that! There was once, I grabbed a cheap ticket and got stuck on a train for hours. Totally worth it though – we had to figure out each other's lives while there was literally nothing else to do.

Ah, marvellous weekend. I managed to finish the job I was working on. It wasn't an easy one, but it was satisfying to complete it. Yes, I had quite an interesting experience myself this past weekend. I had to clean up after a family gathering, but the company was fantastic. Oh, isn't that lovely? But my weekend was quiet. I've been watching a lot of documentaries about planes and this one of a plane crash caught my eye. Have you heard about that Morrow Crash? Yes, I've heard about it. It's quite fascinating, but also quite tragic. The advancements in aviation have come a long way since then, thank goodness. Absolutely. But let’s switch the topic to something more uplifting. Tell us, Speaker_1, what did you make for dinner last night? Well, it was a bit of an experiment. I was trying out this new recipe for an Indian stew. It was very nice, quite spicy, but well balanced. Oh, that sounds wonderful. I love a good spicy meal. So, do you often cook that? I’m more of a stick to the basics person, pasta and pies. I try to mix it up often. I love experimenting with international cuisine. But my family tends to stick with more traditional British meals. Do you have a favorite? Oh, for me, it has to be a roast dinner. Nothing beats Sunday roast. But I do enjoy trying new things as well. Your stew sounds delicious, by the way! I always used to make Sunday roasts for my family myself. It's a lot of work but the satisfaction when everyone sits down together... Absolutely, family time is precious. And let’s not forget about good side dishes, right? How about you, Speaker_3, do you keep up with cooking even now that you're retired? Not quite as often as I used to, but I still try to make some traditional English dishes for myself. You know, warming hearty stews and such. Speaking of shopping, I was thinking about stocking up for another Sunday roast. Either I can go to the convenience store downstairs or make a trek to the bigger supermarket across town. The convenience store would be easier, but the supermarket might be better for variety. Your thoughts? As an account manager in sales, I have to say, I believe in convenience and value. Use the convenience store for the basics and if you need more variety, use the bigger stores.

Yo, how was your week? Mine was super stressful, we've had like two big tests this week and I'm super nervous for the next one. Oh, wow, that sounds intense! I had one test this week and it was pretty manageable, but I know what you mean – the stress can be overwhelming. Totally! But on a happier note, have you heard about the new art teacher? She’s pretty cool, right? Yeah, she’s great! Really enthusiastic and actually helps us understand the techniques and concepts. It’s not just about “drawing pretty pictures” like some others might assume. Exactly! She's also very kind and supportive. And even though she’s fairly young, she seems really experienced. Yeah, I overheard her talking about some of her own art projects and exhibitions! She did mention that she used to be a student-teacher, which is how she started. Cool, innit? Very cool! You know, it's interesting how those student-teachers or trainee teachers often bring a fresh perspective to the class. True, their passion is often infectious. I just hope we’re lucky enough to have them for more than one term. Speaking of which, I saw one of the trainee teachers trying to connect with the class using humor – like jokes and stuff – which is a bit unusual, right, for a lesson? But it was actually pretty effective, really kept everyone’s attention. Shows there are different ways to engage students! But I don’t think all teachers appreciate that. But it proves that there is more than one way to teach, doesn’t it? Definitely. And let’s not forget about science – the new lab experiments are actually fun. We’ve been exploring circuits recently and it’s so cool seeing how everything works. Oh, I know! It's one of my favorite subjects and it really makes me think about science and art being interconnected. You know, especially when we do projects that combine both. Exactly! Like in that project we did last term where we had to design a sustainable city. We had to consider everything from engineering to ecology, which sorta tied in to biology and such. That was such a great project. It was one of the most fun things I've done all year. Yeah, plus it got us thinking critically about real-world issues. And English? How’s that going?

Yo, Dad, did you hear about that strict nun teaching school's film? I thought it was pretty cool how they were teaching religion through movies. Oh yeah, that one? I've not really understood it. It seems like people are using movies to portray religious teachings in a more accessible way. Nuns, Mommy? Ah, yes, Baby, nuns are like... I don't know, they live in a special place called a convent and they help people and they believe in something called God... I heard about the Matrix at school today, Dad. I don't really get what it has to do with religion, though. Ah, the Matrix is a movie about a simulated reality. Some people, though, draw parallels with religious ideas about the nature of reality and free will. Wait, so basically, the Matrix is like if our reality wasn't real and we were just in a big simulation? Exactly! It's quite deep, really. Some people even use it to discuss concepts of creation and free will. Nuns make fun drinks? No, Baby. They make sure people follow rules and behave, not make fun drinks. But, Dad, what about Scientology? We were talking about it at school today. It seemed pretty weird. Well, there are many different beliefs and practices in the world. Scientology doesn't come from the same traditions as the ones we talked about, but it's a system of beliefs that some people follow. But the school said that lots of people think it's a cult? Yes, that's a common view. Some people argue it's a unique faith or philosophy, but others are more critical. It's important to be respectful of all beliefs and traditions, even if we don't agree with them. Friends? Ah, yes, friends. We were also talking about how friends can help us learn about different religions and beliefs. They can share their own experiences and traditions, and it's one way we can learn about the world. Yeah, I guess. I don't really have friends who are into these things though. That's okay. You don't need to be friends with someone for them to help you understand these topics. There are lots of books and documentaries that can also help. Gooby friends like Max? Yes, like Max! Though we mostly talk about other things, like toys and games. You know what, though, I was thinking about how some people use religions to tackle problems in life, right?

Yo, mate, did you finish reading that paper we've been assigned? It was so long. I swear, they write like nobody speaks at university. Oh, yeah, I did. Found it pretty interesting actually. The bit about ageism in the workplace really caught my eye. You know, how questions are asked in interviews and so on. Yeah, I read that too. It's like they're trying to guess our birthdays right there and then. Haha, true. But even worse is how backwards it still feels. You'd think with all the training and regulations, ageism wouldn't be such an issue. Exactly. It's like we're back in the 80s or something. Makes me wonder what was the point of all that training in places of study if it doesn't translate directly to the job market. Exactly, and it's not just that. We've been talking about football, and how the press still lingers on players over 30 like they're done. It's madness. Yeah, I hate it. The press is so stereotypical sometimes. Like it's news when a player over 30 has a good game. Makes you think the game of football should actually label the players with their ages at the bottom of the screen to make it easier for us. Can you imagine? "Age: 32, Still Playing Like He's 25." Exactly! Anyway, did you get a chance to watch that new "Dancing with the Stars" episode? Not yet. Last night I was working on my university work until late and this morning, we jumped on the car straight off. Maybe during the drive? More like during those podcasts I just added to my queue. One of them talks about fun facts around Old English. Curious to hear more about that. Oh really? There must be some quirky stuff. Like the word "none" used to mean "all of something". Or maybe it's a bit more complex? More or less. The podcasts usually explain these things in easy terms. But speaking of fun facts, have you ever tried to convert 5 feet 8 inches into metric for someone who only uses imperial? Good grief, yes! I've had to do that so many times with work. Do you remember that time I converted a temperature from Fahrenheit to Celsius during our holiday plans? Oh yes! We were planning that trip to Norway, and I wanted to know what the hottest summer temperature feels like in Celsius.

Oh, Dad, remember when you took me to that music festival? It was like two years ago. I still remember how the noise was so loud, but at the same time, it felt so free. Yeah, wasn’t it a blast? We heard rumors there was going to be a performance by The Arctic Monkeys, and you were going to get into them weren’t you? And I was, and I did! They played “Do I Wanna Know?” and even though it was packed, I managed to sneak to the front for a bit before we had to leave. Music festivals are so cool! Have you ever been to Sentenza near Pula? It’s happening soon. Oh, yeah! Sentenza, that’s going on next month. I’ve heard great things about it, but its size compared to a festival like Glastonbury, for example, might be smaller but the vibe is similar, right? For a festival of this size, Istrian ones certainly have a charm of their own. I’m sure the atmosphere will be relaxed and intimate, which can be quite nice if one prefers it to the chaos of the larger events. Yeah, it’s about experiencing music without the madness, isn’t it? Although I always love a good mad rush at festivals as well. Exactly! We might have to check it out then! But speaking of music, doesn’t anyone else love that new album from Arctic Monkeys? I do! Their concerts just bring so much energy. I’m more of an old rock fan myself. I do appreciate good music though, no matter the genre. There’s also been some great local bands emerging from the North. You’d be surprised at the talent hidden in the small towns of Lancashire and Yorkshire. Really? I know a few from when I was in school, but I haven’t really followed them since. Did anyone else notice how green everything is out here? It’s just...different from England. Yes, and the smells! This morning, we stopped at this little market, and the scent of fresh olive oil and herbs was incredible. Reminds me of my grandma's cooking. Speaking of which, have you all tried Istrian prosciutto? It’s really good, and they make these wonderful oil tasting kits too, which are quite a treat. Oh, let’s do that! We need to try local cuisine while we’re here.

Yo, lads and lasses. What's been goin's? All good, love. Just about to start this new book for my course. Had the hardest time decidin' but I'm thinkin' it's time for somethin' a bit more chill after all that theoretical stuff we've been through. You'd think they'd have some actual "normal" reading material instead of all this fancy academic language right? Hehe, very true. But I've got another keeps me busy. I've been organising our routine for game nights this week. Oooh, game night! I need to set up some more pub games from my village. You know, like Spin the Bottle or Truth or Dare. Ah, that sounds like old times. I'm not sure I can compete with your Yorkshire razzle-dazzle there, but I might bring along some card games or something. That's a good idea! Maybe we can even set up a little recording for the funniest moments. I'll bring my old camera. Oh, that could be hilarious! Yeah, let's do that. We could even write a little fun script for it, while still keeping it spontaneous. Scripted? As if we need one for anything! Though, it might make it extra funny. Like, perhaps we could have a topic for each round? Maybe something a bit risqué... like if we ever tried anal, or the weirdest game we've played. Whoa, nice idea! But let's not make it too explicit for now. Maybe we can have it be a general 'weirdest thing you've done in a game' sort of topic. Yeah, just keep the blurred lines. We don't want to offend anyone. Fair enough, but secretly, I love confronting those blurred lines. It's all part of the fun. It might be a good idea to lay down some rules beforehand. What do we want to reveal, for sure? Agreed. I mean, we're all close, but we don't want to dive into anything that might be uncomfortable for someone. Totally. Just keep it fun and light-hearted. As long as we agree we're not gonna be overly serious. How about we discuss our 'weirdest memory' during each game night? That way we can get a bit of variety while still maintaining the surprise element... and we can all share the best/funniest bit? I like that. I bet though, everyone's thinking of that time we tried to make it a rule to make it across the youth club room without stepping on any cracks...

Right, so I'm starving. I need some advice from someone who knows these parts. You lot have any good recommendations around here for a place to grab a bite? Ah, well, Salford University library here. We've got a nice canteen just down the road, but honestly, for something a bit more... interesting, you should try the Revolution Hotel. They've got a decent food hall and it's a great spot to get some variety. Now, don't get me wrong, but if you're looking for something truly local, you have to try a proper northern pub fry-up at The Salford Curator, just off the high street. They've got great staff and the ambiance is brilliant. A fry-up sounds perfect to me. You know, proper British comfort food. Thanks, mates. That's a great suggestion. And if you're looking for something a bit more modern, Hotel Pelaw, just near your old stomping ground, Speaker_1, has a nice brasserie with a range of dishes. But if I'm being honest, the fry-up will always be the best option! Yeah, nothing beats a fry-up after a long day. Now that's what I'm saying. I just hope The Salford Curator's bacon isn't too much of the good stuff, as you know, we've got the right to protest if it ain't up to scratch, right? Aye, Pelaw, always defending the bacon. Hey, it's a tradition. What's wrong with defending the culinary arts? Absolutely, it's about maintaining the standards of northern cuisine. We're proud of our heritage, aren't we, lads? Definitely. Now, let's get back to the day's schedule. Sorry for the digression. Do we need to discuss anything specifically for today? Ah, just that next week's workshop could do with some technical tweaks. We're changing the topics and I want to make sure we've got all the right resources lined up. I've been putting together some of the handouts. Let me just send them over to you both for review. Might be a good idea to review them over lunch today if we can. That'd be great. Got any pop-in times or just general recommendations for breaks? I swear, this place seems to have a way of sucking you in. Well, I can tell you our thinking time usually gets spent well during break when we grab a cuppa and catch up like this.

Right, so I've been reading about how social networking is changing job recruitment. Apparently, today's companies are more likely to look at your online profiles than they are to read your CV. Makes you wonder doesn't it? Are we all just one bad tweet away from losing out on our next job? Ha! Very true. I had an awkward situation once where a colleague and I were going for a part-time job and we both had the same idea – to ruin each other's chances with some preemptive online slander. Luckily, we got there before it went far and managed to laugh it off. Oh dear. That must have been a tense few hours waiting for the interview. Social media can be a minefield in our line of work, I think. Absolutely. But it can also be a powerful tool. As librarians, we might be using it predominantly for outreach and educational purposes, but it's also a way to connect with our communities and promote our services. Like last year when we ran a digital literacy campaign. It got a lot of traction on Twitter and really helped reach people who wouldn't normally engage with us. We even got featured on the BBC! That's brilliant! Social media can certainly cut through traditional boundaries and get our voices heard in new ways. Speaking of voices, do either of you follow the infamous 'Librarians of TikTok'? It's amazing how they've managed to make what many people see as a quiet profession seem so dynamic and engaging in just a few seconds. Yeah, they are fantastic. It’s so refreshing to see librarians leading the charge on social media in such a creative and humorous way. Actually, that reminds me of a bit of banter I had during an inter-library meeting. One of the guys was complaining about his day and I quipped, “Well, we are the ‘last bastion of entertainment for those who still value books over streaming services’, so you should appreciate your job more and write a TikTok about it.” [laughs] Good one! Reminds me of a joke I heard. Why don’t librarians like social media? Because it's just so much easier to take notes by hand. Haha! Speaking of notes, I recall when I was a student. I once almost lost an essay because the library's copy machine caught fire and I was using it.

Good morning, I hope you're doing well today. I've been thinking about our project today and I have quite a few queries to discuss with you. Good morning, yes, indeed I am. It's always a pleasure to discuss our plans. Carry on, please. First of all, I was thinking about the tape. We're talking about the tape for the consultation process, right? I just want to make sure we're all on the same page. The tape is indeed for the consultation process. We plan to use it to record the feedback and inputs we receive, and then to create a clear business case. Exactly, that's what I thought. Now, let's discuss the business case itself. I noticed that our proposed location in Tunbridge Wells has a lot of potential. However, how well does this location align with our rationale for the project? Does it offer the best value for service delivery? Our rationale for the location in Tunbridge Wells is twofold. One, there's a clear need for additional healthcare services for the end-of-life care in this area, especially considering the ageing population and the relationship this hospice would have with local healthcare services. I understand the need, but how specifically does Tunbridge Wells align with this need? Was it just the demographic data that suggested this location, or were there also other factors like workforce availability or existing infrastructure to support the project? Well, apart from the demographic data, one of the primary reasons is the relatively under-served population in this area. Additionally, considering we’re planning to integrate this hospice with local services, Tunbridge Wells’ proximity to several community hospitals and the existing network of healthcare workers plays a significant role. We've also established good relationships with the local hospices and the borough council here who are very supportive. That definitely makes sense. As we're planning the project, I'm particularly interested in understanding how we'll organise local health services to support this project. Will we have to work closely with existing healthcare providers, and if so, what's the plan for changing the current landscape? Definitely, collaboration will be key. We plan on establishing a close relationship with the local healthcare providers. Our proposed hospice will not only provide end-of-life care but also run health education programs for the local community. This should not only improve the health outcomes for the patients but also could have positive spill-over effects in reducing healthcare costs in the long term.

Oh, look at this! Is this you and your mates at that crazy hen party in Southport? Oh God, yes. We rode around the town center in those ridiculous fancy dress costumes. Yo, I was browsing Rotten Tomatoes yesterday and came across this film's review. "The Conjuring 2" was described as one of the most terrifying movies ever. You ever seen it? Yeah, I've seen it. I was practically hiding behind the cushion, though! The whole London case, it freaked me out so bad. The house where they'd been investigating, the paranormal activity, and then that ghostly nun... I'm right behind you as far as I'm concerned! Really? That scene with the nun is indeed bone-chilling. I mean, it's just this eerie, ominous feeling. It's not about the gore or the jump scares, it's the psychological horror. Exactly! So what about the original Conjuring, have you seen that one too? They say it's as scary as the sequel. Yes, the The Conjuring is a favourite of mine. The room full of possessed dolls... my god, even now it gives me the chills. But the whole case of the Perron family, it's both scary and really tragic. For me, it's the eeriness and the suspense more than the outright gore. Indeed, it's the fact that it's based on real-life cases that really adds a layer of horror to it. It's unsettling because you know it stems from reality, right? Like, it's always creepier when it feels 'real', isn't it? Like, I mean, you never feel safe even after the credits roll. True, but sometimes it doesn't even need to be a 'real' case for it to affect you. Just last weekend, I watched "The Babadook" and I had nightmares the entire week. No way! Yeah, that's a great point. So often the scariest parts are the ones that you can relate to almost too well. It's like the movie taps into our deepest fears or insecurities. Absolutely. And what about films like Hereditary or mother? Have you checked either of those out? No, I haven’t. But I’ve read... a lot of people say they're pretty intense.

Evening, Dad. How are you feeling today? Evening. I'm feeling quite alright, thanks for asking. It was a nice day, talked to old mates over tea and had some TV to watch. That can vary, but for most things it's pretty quick. Some sites offer next day delivery or can even deliver within hours. You'd have to check per product. That's useful. Ah, lads, it's been ages since we last got together. I've been meaning to share these books with you. I've recently finished "Trainspotting" by Irvine Welsh. What are your thoughts? Are you still into his writing? Actually, the novel, though a classic, hasn't aged well for me. I prefer his later work, "Skagboys". But have you read "Lanark" by Alasdair Gray? It's one of the most impressive Scottish novels I've read in a while. Ah, indeed, Alasdair Gray. "Lanark" is an intricate, intricate beast. It's a challenging read, but deeply rewarding if you persist. It's similar to another Scottish classic, "The Master and Margarita" by Bulgakov. Exactly! Dialogue-heavy, philosophical, making you question reality. And what about modern Scottish writing? Have you read "The Women" by Charles Martin or "The Ten Thousand Things" by John Burnside? "The Women" is good. It's explores this blackout incident in Glasgow's history. I really enjoyed how the author used it to portray different societal aspects. Sure, but it's a bit of a different vibe from "The Ten Thousand Things". That one is rather poetic, isn't it? Indeed. Burnside has a way with words, bringing us closer to nature. Reminds me of how travel can also serve as a form of literature. Absolutely. Speaking of which, I've been thinking about doing a bit of traveling around the Highlands later this year. Any tips on the best places? Well, I would say that it depends on what you enjoy. There's always the stunning scenery and the lochs. But if you're into history and architecture, you should consider visiting Eilean Donan Castle or Urquhart Castle by Loch Ness. I've heard good things about them. And perhaps a couple of hiking trails? Definitely. There are some fantastic trails like the Cuillin Ridge on the Isle of Skye or the Trotternish Ridge trails on the same island. Fantastic. And what about local food and drink? Any hidden gems? Oh, you can’t go wrong with a real Scottish breakfast and an oatcake or two. But if you want to try something unique, pop into Glenmoriston in the Cairngorms. They have great local beer and some really innovative dishes using traditional ingredients. That sounds perfect! I love thinking about the food as well during planning. You're right, it makes a huge difference to the trip experience.

Mum, I've been going over my resume for this architect position I've been wanting to apply for. It's been open for ages and I really think I've got what they're looking for. But I've been stuck on the personal statement. Can you give it a look over and tell me what you think? Of course, love. I'd be glad to. But first, can you tell me a bit more about the position and the company? Sometimes understanding the right keywords or tone can help shape the statement to fit perfectly. Well, it's for a big firm in central London. They do a mix of residential and commercial projects. The job description seemed quite open about wanting someone with a strong design sense and ability to work well in a team. They also mentioned something about wanting to bring new ideas. Right, so they're looking for a creative mind who can work well with others. That’s quite specific. It also sounds like they might be looking to bring in some fresh thinking. Exactly. That's why I'm concerned about my statement. I want it to reflect my ability to be creative, detail-driven, and collaborative, but also not sound too generic. We've talked about this before, right? About how sometimes it's easier to write when you're focusing on how your skills fit specific criteria rather than general job benefits. Absolutely, we have. It really helps if you can illustrate your skills with specific examples. Right, but my issue is I feel like all my examples are from academic projects in architecture or internships. But they never fully capture the ‘me’ of it all. I know what you mean. It's hard to articulate the 'you' in a professional setting. But have you ever considered including any personal hobbies or interests that might reflect your design skills or ability to work in teams? Oh, I hadn't thought about that. I do love photography and I've even done some photography projects on architecture and city landscapes. That's brilliant! While you might not directly link it to architecture, it could show an understanding of light, space, and composition, which are all key in your field. Plus, any team or collaborative work you've done on those projects would show off your ability to work with others. That makes sense.

Ah, marvellous to see you both again, Alan's place looks just as it always has, welcoming. How's the garden doing, Margaret? You haven't talked about whether it's still bearing well this year. Ah, isn't it just now, the old place. The garden? Well, it's doing alright considering we don't do a lot of maintenance anymore, you know. Still blossoming but a bit wild, I suppose. Oh, it's lovely, really. The flowers still set off the front so nicely. I've heard it's a bit of a task keeping it tamed though, seeing as you two are a bit lazy in the garden department now. Well, we've certainly let ourselves go downhill since retirement. I suppose that's what happens after years of being in a job that tells you when to do things. Speaking of which, have you caught up with the latest political scandal? I sometimes wonder if any of them actually want to fix things, or if they're just in for the free lunch and the grand speeches. Indeed, I have. It's the same old story really. All talk, no action. Our generation promised plenty but left their kids with a mess. I often wonder how Margaret here manages to still have hope. It's the politicians we've got, not the people. There are still good folk around, aren't there? But yes, to your point, perhaps cynicism does feel like a rite of passage with age in Britain nowadays. I'm not so sure. I always believed in a better future for my children and theirs, but it seems the younger ones are the ones that have to deal with the consequences of our naivety. But the future isn't all doom and gloom. Look at the improvements in, say, the local housing. I used to regularly visit sites as a civil engineer and while it's had its challenges, there's been some really good work done in providing affordable housing. Affordable housing? You mean they've actually managed to do that? Or was that just a politician's pipe dream? Well, it depends where you are. Some areas indeed have made strides, others not so much. But the principle is good, and it's about time government and developers started putting people over profits. We could talk about that all day. I recently read an article about how certain pockets of the country are doing much better than others.

Good morning, I hope you've had a good weekend. I've been thinking about our space over the weekend and realized we really need to utilize it better. Do you think we could convert the unused area on the first floor into a community center where we can host various activities? That's an excellent idea, Sheila. I've seen so many spaces in Manchester where they do similar things. But we've got to consider the upfront cost and maintenance cost as well right? Absolutely, budget is a major factor here. Plus, it could also help with our fundraising efforts. Definitely, but we need to make sure the space we're planning to convert is going to be attractive to potential tenants. What type of activities did you have in mind? Anything we can host - book clubs, art workshops, even corporate events. And it would also be possible to rent it out for private functions, which could be a lucrative source of income. That makes sense. Also, when we’re planning income-generating activities, we need to ensure that they fit with our charity's mission and values. We don’t want to alienate our community or other users of the building. Well, we could certainly work out a balance. The Brix prides itself on community, so it's about finding activities that bring people together, really. But you're right, we should also be mindful of our mission and values. Speaking of mission, have you seen the redesigning the lounge area into a café? If we can get that off the ground, it could be a fantastic way to engage with locals and raise additional funds. Oh, I saw the designs for that. It looks stunning! And it's a space we use quite often. But before we dive deep into that, I'd like to discuss another topic - arrangements for holiday cover. We've had some issues in the past where we've been understaffed. Ah, staffing for sure. I know it's always a struggle, but we need to make sure we've got adequate holiday cover. Maybe we should also look into hiring some temp staff or even strengthening our volunteer base.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I made my own bread for the first time? You would've thought I was about to open up a bakery! No, you never did. That must have been interesting. How did it go? Well, let's just say my first attempt didn't quite look like the bread pictures in cookbooks. But actually, it tasted quite nice. Just had to work on the consistency. Right, let me guess... it was either like a rock, or a puddle. Well, something in-between. I bet the kids loved it. They always do, don't they? "Mummy made bread!" Exactly! They were all excited. I recall when my son tried to bake his first cake. It was more like a sheet of chocolate than anything else. But he was so proud he nearly cried. Yeah, it's all about the effort, right? Definitely. Kids in particular think the most about the love that goes into the food, not the chef's techniques. Ah, love. Speaking of which, I always love how you all still manage to bring a new level of passion into everything you do. It's fantastic. That's because it's family! No matter what we do, we do it together. Well, food and family, you say? I've got a joke for you then. What do you call cheese that isn't yours? Nacho cheese! Oh that's terrible. But it's kind of clever and it got a laugh! Speaking of jokes, my favorite is one my granddad used to tell... Funny, because just yesterday I taught my class a joke about a cheese. Alright, alright, I'll share. So, why did the chef quit his job? He just couldn't cut the mustard! That one's good too! You guys really have a thing for food puns, don't you? We do. There's something about food that just brings out the humour in all of us. Well, speaking of food, have we decided what we're going to do for dinner tomorrow? Let's do a BBQ, it seems like the perfect way to enjoy each other's company and some good old-fashioned British food. I love BBQs, especially if someone else is doing the cooking! Ha! That's usually the case. Oh, and can we have some Welsh sauce as well? It’s like no other!

Yo, mate, did you seen any of that new advert from Weetabix? On the telly? Yeah, it's been talked about a lot. Got some of the TV presenters in it. Is it better than the old ones though? Nah, I don’t think so. It’s missing the charm and quirkiness of the original ads. I get what you mean. I think I grew up with those ones. Really? Me too! I remember those jingles. Crazy how much ads can influence childhood stuff, eh? Definitely. I think ads form a big part of pop culture. Even the worst ones can stick in your head. Tell me about it. Like when I was a kid, "Two all-beef patties, special sauce, lettuce, cheese, pickles, onions – on a sesame seed bun." Ronseal... Brilliant! Even now, that's stuck in my head. And those Cadbury's or McDonald's ads from the 90s. I mean, they were so catchy! Absolutely. Music has a lot to do with it I think. Certain jingles just stick with you. True. Have you seen the new MacBook Air ad? It's quite minimalistic compared to some current car or phone ads. Yeah, I saw it in between a YouTube video. I think they’re trying to go for a different vibe with it. Yeah, definitely a different approach. Coming from Harpenden, I’ve seen my fair share of car ads, but I do find some of them rather over-the-top. Totally, they do go overboard sometimes. I saw one recently about a new Aston Martin – way too much CGI for my money. Yes, that's a great example of overkill. But some car ads, they’ve got a certain class to them. You know? Like the old Jaguar ads with advanced sound design and shots of some stunning scenery. Yep, that's what I mean. There’s a balance they need to strike. Speaking of balance, what’s your favorite place you’ve ever been to in England? I’d say Newcastle. Clearly biased! There’s something about the architecture and the riverside. Totally makes sense. I’ve been to Newcastle during St. James' fair and had a blast. Oh yeah! I was born and raised there, so it holds a bit of a soft spot. I bet though, Sunderland too, has its own charm from what I’ve read. Absolutely, although I never got to attend a Sunderland match because my family wasn’t that into football.

Ah, thanks so much for inviting me over to your place, I've been meaning to catch up. It's been ages. Not at all, it's lovely to see you. You look a bit tired. Is everything okay? Yes, I'm fine really. It's just been a bit of a tough week at work and then there's the hospital appointments and things... But actually, I've been thinking a lot about it and I wanted to talk to someone about it. Oh dear, what's happened? You can tell me anything. Well, my mother passed away two weeks ago. It was quite sudden. She had been fairly well apart from a few health issues, but then she just deteriorated very quickly. Oh dear, I'm so sorry to hear that. That must be incredibly difficult. It is. The funeral is next week and it's all been a bit overwhelming. I've had to handle all the arrangements as well. Sure, I can imagine. It must be especially hard when the process doesn't give you time to process everything properly. Exactly. And then within the family, there's been a bit of tension. My sister and brother keep arguing about the funeral arrangements. One of them thinks we should have a traditional service, but the other isn't in favour of it because they're both atheists and mom didn't really have strong religious beliefs. I see. But it's tough when everyone has different expectations. Yes, it is. On top of grief, dealing with family disagreements... it's just too much. You know, losing a parent can really expose existing family dynamics. But whatever you and your family decide to do, it's important that it feels right for mum and for all of you. You're right. I suppose it just takes time for us all to adjust. And it's surprising how much we see our family members in a different light when such a major event like this happens. It's like... you're all trying to cope with your own personal grief and everyone's got their own way of doing it. That's it. We're all grieving differently but finding a common ground is difficult. If you need to talk about it, remember I'm here. Not just now but any time. Thank you, that means a lot. You know, the other day, one of my coworkers came in, she's lost about 20kg over the past six months through exercise and diet.

Right, so I had a fascinating day today at work, running through some final proofs for a new client's marketing campaign. You know, it's the little things that can make or break a campaign, and I've learned to be meticulous over the years. Speaker_2 : Yeah, mum always says you need to be careful with those little details, doesn't she? Exactly, and this campaign had a lot of those.
