Still, every time I see this river, I'm always surprised by how much it's bustling with life and yet still manages to retain such a serene atmosphere at times. True. It never fails to impress me, even though I've walked along it so many times. I've heard loads of stories about medieval times when cargo ships would crowd this river, bringing goods from all corners of the world. Indeed, it's been a lifeline for London in more ways than one. Though nowadays, I wish we didn't need the docks so much. Rising property prices making life even harder for ordinary folks. Exactly! My heart goes out to all those displaced by gentrification. It's not very nice to see the local character being erased just to make room for another overpriced coffee shop or fancy apartment block. So true. But on a different note, have you noticed there are no cars around us right now? That's because neither of us owns one! We both decided years back to go without; it's much better for the environment and also means we can't mindlessly drive anywhere. Well, at least for short journeys, we're forced to take a walk or cycle, like this. Yeah, sometimes it's inconvenient, but it has its moments. Like this walk through a part of the city doesn't feel overwhelmed with traffic and the constant hum of the city that you kind of grow numb to behind a windscreen. Right. And speaking of getting around without a car, I just booked our holiday for next month. I suggested a car-free destination. Where are you planning to go? We're thinking of heading to Scotland. It's been on my bucket list for a while to see Loch Ness, but more importantly, some of the smaller towns like Oban or Fort William. Either way, it means we're all about trains, buses, or cycling if we're feeling adventurous. That sounds excellent! Scotland's got some of the most breathtaking landscapes in the world. I've had a few relatives over there and I can vouch that there’s no place quite like it for sense of peace and space.

Oh, did you see the weather forecast? It looks like we're in for a proper South East English shower all day. Hopefully, it won't ruin little Teddy's sports day at school. You two remember what a right old mess it was last time it rained? Oh yes, I do. You were a bit of a madwoman rushing around trying to get his waterproofs on before the gates closed. Now, with Tammy, it'll be very different. That's true. Well, she's already mastered those new 'build a bear' skills. Remember when we made that bear together? I swear that bear looked more like a scarecrow than a cosy companion. Oh, we've had our share of fun with those build-a-bear workshops. But they sure did help with Tammy's potty training. Every time she used the potty, the bear got a new item of clothing. Worked surprisingly well. Now, though, she's all grown-up and capable of joining Teddy at sports day. Really? Build-a-bear for potty training is a bit unexpected. You’re inventive with these parenting things. Necessity is the mother of invention, right? What about those kitchen appliances though? I swear technology is moving so fast, I need a manual just to heat up some porridge. Can relate. One time, I couldn't even get the coffee machine to turn on properly and ended up making a mess. Luckily, it was just a small spill and not the giant one I feared. Yes, technology’s great until it decides to have a meltdown, isn’t it? But I just tried to get Tammy to watch a video on her phone and it ended up freezing. She looked at me with those big eyes, “Mum, what's happening to cartoon cat?” I was trying not to laugh. It reminded me of my own confusion with these new mobile phones. Kids of this generation will never know the frustration of waiting for dial-up internet. Oh, the sweet innocence of it all. And yet, it still frustrates me. I mean, almost gone swimming at Stone Ness over the weekend and then I realised I'd left my phone in the car. Felt like I'd left half my world there. I just about went into a frenzy when I left mine at the grocery store this week. The thought of needing to ask any of the checkout chaps to borrow theirs was just too mortifying.

Alright, I think we've got a bit of time before today's task, so let's catch up. How was the weekend for you, Helen? It was quite relaxing, to be honest. Spent most of it reading a new book and enjoying the peace this beautiful Australian home offers us. That sounds perfect. Enough rest makes all the difference, doesn't it? Now, shall we start talking about the future and set some goals for ourselves? We've been discussing this alongside this whole house-sitting scenario, right? Absolutely. I've been reflecting on our careers quite a bit since we got here, despite the lovely distraction of our surroundings. It just seems like a bit of a natural time to review where we are and where we want to be. I completely understand. Hence my idea. I’ve been thinking, we should perhaps set some more defined personal goals, career wise and also, we need to start discussing family planning, don't you think? We’re both on the right side of 40 and I think it’s a good time to start making some more concrete plans about our future. Interesting, I’ve been considering that too. Honestly, I’ve felt kind of stuck in the profession of teaching. I love what I do but the work environment can be so stressful at times. Have you ever thought about changing careers or pursuing another passion? Yeah, I’ve had that thought too. Sometimes I wonder if I should really be more involved in another field, maybe something I'm more passionate about. However, running my own business has its own set of challenges and responsibilities. That makes sense. I think we both need to do some soul searching here. Maybe we could start by creating a list of the things we love doing, and a list of the things we're good at. Then we can see if there's a way to align those more closely with our current roles or perhaps something new. That's a great idea. As for family planning, do you think we should discuss it with a bit more intensity? I mean, we've talked about having kids but it's just always seemed so far down the line. I'd say that's fair. But it's definitely something we should be thinking about. We should almost schedule this discussion, just to make sure we both are on the same page and agree on a way forward.

Right, so I'm clearly from the North, anyone else notice any other northern accents around today? Oh, clearly! I've got a bit of a Wigan accent, you'd definitely pick that up. Aye, I'm from Warrington too, so we're all quite local here. I'd definitely say my Leeds accent's very noticeable, even up here. Warrington born and bred, so yeah, local accents are definitely evident. Yeah, nothing beats a good northern accent. So you guys ever see any of those Pokémon hunts that had been going on? Like, you've seen people chasing Pokémon around just like in the game? Oh yeah, when that first came out, you'd see people all over Wigan chasing them. It was kind of hilarious, but also, I didn't understand why anyone would be so invested in catching virtual animals. Right! And in Leeds we had this massive Pokémon hunt at the old market area. I mean, hundreds of people, all staring at their phones. Weird, but interesting. Yeah, I noticed it in Warrington too. Where did you all catch the most? Was there a particular hotspot? I found a few interesting ones around the park by the river. But honestly, it was more about the fun and adventure than catching specific Pokémon. Hey, speaking of fun and adventure, any of you folks done any camping recently? Haven't done that in ages. I don't think anyone here has in a while. I kind of went last year with some mates but it was all a bit... chaotic. Never again. Yeah, I went a few years ago and it was... eventful. To be honest, I couldn’t wait to get back home to a solid roof and running water. I love camping but it's a pain changing the tent and having to cook everything. It’s a workout in itself. True but there’s nothing like waking up surrounded by nature. It’s something else, isn't it? Yeah, but animals are the worst. [laughs] Agreed! Last time we camped, we had a persistent squirrel trying to steal our food. I ended up having to stand guard. And don’t even get me started on the bad manners of some campers. Sharing a site with people who don’t respect the space or quiet hours can be infuriating. True that. We had that once, and it just ruined the tranquility of the whole thing.

Right, now I know this weekend might've been a first for coordinating this family dinner but I must say, it was quite enjoyable. The roast beef was a hit, wasn't it? Oh absolutely, Alison did a wonderful job. It reminded me of the old days when mum used to do the cooking. It certainly did make us feel at home. Cooking at home has a way of bringing us together, doesn't it? Definitely. I especially enjoyed the homemade apple pie. You must get the recipe from Alison sometime. She's always willing to share her recipes. I've been meaning to ask for that shepherd's pie recipe of hers too. Might just do that then. So, what about the upcoming cricket match? Was anyone able to catch the highlights yesterday? Yeah, I managed to catch most of it. The team played really well, especially with that sixth-wicket partnership. It's always fascinating to watch these matches. I must say though, it's quite concerning the state of the local cricket team. Don't you feel that? Very much so, it's all about the youngsters nowadays isn't it? You hardly see anyone older still playing. True. But think about it, the retired players could be the perfect guides for training and coaching. That's a good point. Like we had Aunty Brenda, who still plays in her local league in Harrow, really kept the team spirits high. Brenda, love that woman. Always had a bat in her hand doesn't she? But it proves the point, the experience that these older players bring is invaluable. We should perhaps look into volunteering in some capacity. Maybe the local cricket association could use some help? I'd be happy to look into it. Seems like a couple of weekends a month wouldn't be too much of a commitment and it would be good to get a bit of fresh air and exercise. Good on you, though, you've got enough on your plate with lectures these days. True, but I think we all need to give back a bit. Besides, it would be an opportunity to show our kids the value of community work. Exactly. It's the same with food and cooking - passing down traditions and skills. Speaking of traditions, did any of us catch the news earlier this week about the new government policy regarding food markets and independent food sellers?

Oh, Lena, remember when we used to play in the mud? You'd come back to my grandma's and your shoes would be so dirty, she'd insist on scrubbing them clean. Aye, I remember! You'd always end up chasing me around grandma's garden and I'd end up covered in mud and stains. But honestly, that was our favourite pastime, wasn't it? Definitely! And look at us now, discussing whether or not to drop out of uni... life really blunders, doesn't it? Yeah, I guess it does. But in our case, let’s not go there too much. Yeah, let's not. Anyway, what's this bout dropping out you're chewing over? Just... you know, the pressure, the boredom, feeling like it’s all just not for me. I feel ya, Lena. I've been on and off about giving it up myself, but my parents would kill me. Mine too. But in all honesty, I just can’t see myself doing the career stuff that my course is leading towards. Honestly though, I think it’s good that you're thinking about it. If it's not making you happy, what's the point? But maybe there's other routes that can get you to where you want to be? I was thinking about that, but I'm not sure if I should be so open about it or less... Lena, we're family. You can tell me anything. Besides, even if we drop out, there's always room to bounce back. Yeah, but that sure doesn't sit easy with me. Well, if I'm completely honest, there’s been times I just wanted to throw in the towel too. And I thought I was going into something I loved! Really? What about? Just the general satisfaction and maybe job security that came with being a doctor or something. But halfway through first year, I realized medicine wasn't for me. Too much pressure and I didn't connect with it. But that doesn't mean I'm not involved in the medical field now. I work part-time at a local clinic and it's pretty cool. That's really good to hear. How did you make the transition then? You know, I did some volunteer work in my first year, realized I enjoyed the practical side of it more. Then, I joined a health society on campus and made some contacts, did a summer placement, and basically seized opportunities.

Oh, it's been ages! I almost didn't recognize you today. The Northern twang is still as distinct as ever! Neither have you. Project co-ordinator at Oxford isn't the most physically demanding job, but you seem to have lost some questions back! Indeed, I have. But I've been keeping busy with that and the normal struggles of balancing work and life as a singleton. How about you? All good in the world of Pearson marketing? Pretty much. Lots of new schemes and stuff to sell, keeps me on my toes. I have to keep up with all the new developments and products, it's been a challenge. But then again, I love my job. That's good to hear. I feel like I've been making the rounds of new relationships since moving back to Oxford though. It's been interesting. Oh, really? What's it like, then? Well, it's all about balancing vulnerability and stability isn't it? Sometimes I feel like I'm taking one step forward and two steps back. But on the whole, I've met some great people. You’re always so positive, I admire that about you. How's the food? It's really nice here. I do love an Oxford pub for lunch. The atmosphere is fab, nice and bustling but also relaxed. Absolutely! There’s something really special about this place. I used to come here all the time with my mates back in the day. I wonder what they’re up to now. That reminds me, we should catch up with some mutual friends soon if you're free. Maybe the next time you're down here? Would love to. Work is keeping me busy at the moment but I've got a few days off next month. How about we plan something for then? That sounds great! We'll pick something up soon. You know how much I love planning things, though... I do know. You're always so thorough. It’s all for the best though. I've found that it helps to have something to look forward to. True that. Speaking of which, any job plans or life plans in the pipeline? Well, I've been thinking a bit about doing a bit of freelance work on the side. Something that can use my project management skills while also giving me a bit of freedom.

Right, now I'm going to show you how we've been doing online shopping these days. It's mostly done through Amazon and eBay. They're so convenient, aren't they? Are you still using eBay that much? I thought it was more used by, like, people selling collectibles and stuff. Oh, certainly, there's still that. But eBay has really expanded its range. I've even bought clothes and electronics from there. I bought a new pair of smart light bulbs that connect to Wi-Fi and change color and all. Crazy stuff. Whoa, smart light bulbs! That sounds amazing. But isn't it just expensive? They're not that pricey, surprisingly. And Amazon sells them as well. The whole point of places like eBay and Amazon is that you can find things that might be cheaper than in physical stores. Plus you can compare prices from different sellers super easily. That's true. How do you spot if something is good or if the seller is reliable? Well, that's what you have to be careful about. Always look at the seller's ratings and read their feedback from previous customers. For eBay, anything significantly lower than 90% positive is a red flag. Amazon's rating system is in stars; 4 stars or more is usually good, but you can also look at individual feedback to see if there were any issues reported. That makes sense. What about all these 'new listings' and 'on sale' deals? Are they usually worth it or are they just a trick to get you to buy something? Hmm, good question. Sometimes it's a genuine deal, especially if you're planning on buying the item anyway. But often it's just a marketing trick to make things seem more attractive. You should compare prices, try looking at different sellers and see if they're matched elsewhere. For example, if you're looking at a new game console, check multiple sellers before committing. So you have to do quite a bit of research before making a purchase. Absolutely, though over time you get a sense for what reasonable prices are for different items. If something seems too cheap compared to everywhere else, there might be a reason for that. Always double-check the description and look for guarantees. I could use practice. I've almost gone ahead and bought things just because the price seemed right without really thinking.

Ah, lovely to see you over. I hope you've been keeping well. I've been meaning to reach out to you. There's been a lot going on since I talked to you last. Of course! I've missed our chats. What's new? Well, you’ll never guess what happened to me last month. I received a letter from the government. They've decided to give me some sort of allowance, a minimal income of sorts, as I've never worked and been unemployed for so long. That’s great, actually. Many people have been discussing this new policy, isn't it? Yes, it's all very sudden. I hadn’t been expecting it at all. Sent me into a bit of a spin, to be honest. That’s understandable. Change can be overwhelming. Indeed. It's a bit scary, you know? Having to go through all the paperwork and such. They want me to get some training, too, which is a bit daunting. Well, that's a positive though. You could see it as an opportunity to learn new skills. You never know what might come of it. That's the perspective I'm trying to keep, but the system is so complicated. I find it quite intimidating. Especially after so long without having to deal with such things. Perhaps we could look into it together? I might be able to help, especially with the paperwork part. And in terms of the training, there are plenty of online courses available, and they might even help with the confidence and learning part. That would be marvellous, indeed. Thanks for offering. It does sound quite helpful, to have some guidance, doesn’t it? Of course. I’d be more than happy to help. Plus, I've always enjoyed learning new things so we could probably both gain from this. Yes, that's a great point. There's always something new to learn, no matter the age. Speaking of which, my granddaughter mentioned something about her wanting to learn a new language. What do you think about that? Learning a new language is always a brilliant idea. It can be a fun challenge too. And given that she's young, it's definitely easier for her. Yeah, young minds pick things up so quickly. She mentioned Mandarin or Spanish. I was wondering which one you think would be more useful for her in the long term?

Yo, mate, got your Christmas plans sorted yet? Yeah, nearly. I've got to sort out the celebration at my flat. It's gonna be pretty simple though. Got some food on my mind. Want to come over and help cook? Sounds good. I was thinking of doing something similar. But I've also got this bizarre thought of flying on Christmas day. Is that even possible? And, like, how would I wrap presents... right before takeoff? Oh, come on! Can you imagine trying to get through security with a tree strapped to your back? Actually, there are chartered flights that operate Christmas day. It's a niche service, but yes, people do that to travel. But, yeah, securing your presents would be quite the challenge! And the food, that's going to be stellar. I’ve already planned out the menu, but I do need some more help manning the oven. What’s everyone’s favourite English Christmas food? For me, it’s gotta be the roast. Potatoes, carrots, parsnips, the whole works. But, I'm curious, what’s weird or unique from your baker perspective? Well, I love the traditional mince pies. But my mum always made this strange dish with sprouts and bacon, really weird, but oddly delicious. She said it was a traditional Midlands thing. In Birmingham, we have, like, this bizarre tradition where we eat cheese on toast on Christmas Eve. It’s meant to bring good luck. But, honestly, it’s just an excuse to have cheese on toast whenever I want. That’s fair. Any cheese is a good cheese, right? You guys are strange with your food traditions. We usually have roast lamb and veggies. But since living in England, I think I’ve become more open to trying out English food. Speaking of roast dinner, does anyone else worry about roadkill making an appearance? I once saw a fox dragged out of a store when I was working late in the city. Oh god, no! Though, if anyone does see some roadkill deer or foxes, we’ll have to make some use of it. Got any skills in that department? I swear, if I ever see a fox, I’m going to faint. I’ve actually seen a roo [kangaroo] on the road once. Here, it wouldn’t surprise me... True that. We're also talking about DIY taxidermy, right?

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new car that's been making waves these days? It's like an engineering masterpiece. Oi, talked about that recently. Got all the latest tech but I still can't quite voice my opinion. Still researching though, the tech, the design, everything. Yeah, I've heard a bit about it too. I mean, the design part fits my fancy quite a bit. I'm working on a game right now, and I'd love to get inspiration from it for my next level design. True. That's why I'm thinking of maybe checking it out, see if it lives up to the hype. What's with the design though? It's pretty out there in your opinion? Oh, design, yes. I read that the company uses 3D projections and modules which can change the form and function of the car while it's running. On one hand, it's cool and all innovative, but on the other, I'm not entirely sure if it's practical. That's a great point. As a game developer, I love those kinds of innovations or even concepts. They add that extra layer of interest to a game and make it more immersive. But as a car user, the practicality is key. The car needs to be safe, reliable, and efficient. Perfectly put. It's like the balance between art and function. Well, technology-wise, it's a marvel. The car can change its aerodynamics in real-time to suit the driving conditions. It's like something out of a science fiction book. That's fascinating. I'm curious about how it affects the engine doesn't it? Does it mean the engine redesign is the real gem here? Yeah, but then you'd wonder if it’s worth it. The extra tech means extra cost and potential complications for warranty and service. Plus, the fuel efficiency question comes in. Do we need that level of tech for our city driving? It's a fair point. But then again, it's like you said, changing the car's wings or shape on the fly might mean saving fuel by avoiding wind resistance, right? Exactly. But I've also seen it can potentially increase the production cost, which could be added to the final price tag. Speaking of costs, does anyone know how the production costs compare with other high-tech cars in the market?

Yo, anyone hear that new album from Arctic Monkeys?? It's sick. I discovered it when I was listening to some old songs and my phone suggested it to me. It's got a really cool vibe going on, you need to check it out. Yeah, I saw a review of it in NME. It's supposed to be their best work yet. But have you tried the new One Direction album? I know it's not exactly their best, but it's got a couple of tracks that are surprisingly catchy. One Direction keeps coming out with new albums. It seems like they're stuck in this phase of trying to mature but still not quite there yet. But yeah, Idk, I heard their single 'What Makes You Beautiful' was actually written by Ed Sheeran. So, there's that. Ah, that's true. Anyway, I was listening to a mix of old and new tunes this week and it made me realize how music has evolved over the years. I mean, how did we get from Arctic Monkeys to that? And now there's this new wave of music with so much electronic and hip-hop elements thrown in. For sure. We're living in interesting times, musically speaking. I mean, if you told someone in the 90s that electronic and rock could melt together like they do now, they'd think you were crazy. Exactly. I mean, physics plays a huge role in music too, right? The way beats work, frequencies, vibrations, all that. It's actually pretty fascinating when you think about it. Yeah, I know. But it's not just music, I mean, doesn't electronics and physics have a hell of a lot to do with movie special effects too? Like, how they make movies now, with all these CGI and what not. Totally, and it's evolving so fast too, isn't it? Who knows what we'll see in movies in 10 or 20 years? I heard recently that there's talk of using AI to create whole scenes now. It's scary and exciting at the same time. Yeah, that kinda scares me. Makes you think of all these Sci-Fi movies where AI ends up taking over the world. Reminds me of that film 'Terminator'. Heh, definitely. But the thing is, while there are these ups and downs, the essence of the art remains.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that Balanceability class we're doing with the kids? They love it! They're practising all sorts of balance exercises and it's so funny to see them try. Yeah, it's so cool! They even have these little balance beams and things. I just wish they could do it every day! I wish they could, too! But actually, I've been thinking... what if we could create a mini balance course in the garden? You know, that's a great idea. We've got plenty of space behind the shed. We just need to set it up safely. Can we, can we, please? And can we do somersaults on the grass? Somersaults, huh? I think that might be a bit too much, but we can definitely work on some safe tumbling exercises. I've been practicing my somersaults at school, Mom! But I was thinking... this balance course would be perfect for us to practice at home. That's a great idea, but we still need to make sure it's safe. Balancing is all about control and being aware of your body in space, isn't it? Yeah, like succeeding at something. You have to practice and not give up. Exactly! Just like in our assessments at school. And that's why we do these tests, to practice and see where we need to work harder. But what if we don't succeed? You know, succeeding doesn't always mean doing something perfectly the first time. It's about understanding where we made mistakes and getting better. Just like when we were discussing homeschooling versus traditional school. Each has its pros and cons, but the important thing is the learning and growth. Oh, did you talk about that at school? Our friend Emily's house is being renovated just like that! All the builders and stuff. Oh, yes! It's been quite the topic of conversation around the playground. Some kids think it's cool, others find it noisy and annoying. Did you know, Emily's dad came in and told us all about the manmade waterfall they're building in the garden? Really? That sounds incredible! But I suppose it makes sense given that they're a bit of a fan of swimming pools already. But isn't it dangerous to dive into water without knowing how deep it is? We learned at school that it's very important to swim only in areas where it's safe to dive in.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my new gym routine? I signed up for this crazy crossfit class and let me tell you, it's been quite a challenge. No, you never did. That sounds intense! You're a brave soul for tackling something like that. How's it going so far? Honestly, it's been a struggle, but I'm determined to stick with it. I need to get in shape for this conference that I'm organizing in a few months. It's going to be huge and I want to be able to keep up with the contestants. That's a great goal. Is it any good for mental health too? I suppose the endorphins can't hurt, can they? They definitely help. It's almost therapeutic after a long day of stressful project coordination. It's a different kind of challenging, you know? Distracting me from work. That makes sense. I've found that lately for me, running helps me clear my mind as well. But then again, I’m more of a creature of habit, so sticking to a routine is easier for me. I wish I was. I've always struggled with routine, but this conference has certainly been pushing me out of my comfort zone. It's forced me to develop some discipline, at least in this area of my life. That can only be a good thing for your future, considering your growing responsibilities in the industry. What's been the hardest part of organizing it so far? I'd say finding the right venue. There were so many options in Cambridge, but everything I liked was already booked for future events. And then of course, ensuring that the content matches everyone's expectations. That can be tough. I've dealt with similar issues while working as a production controller. It's all about balancing what you want to achieve with what you can actually deliver. You've certainly got a knack for coordination, though. I try. But honestly, I often rely on my team. We've got a great team at work, they're incredibly supportive. That's so important, and it's one aspect of your job that almost makes it worth the stress. Definitely. Speaking of stress, how's your relationship going? You ever discuss this with your partner, or do you tend to keep work stress separate? To be honest, I can get a bit introverted when it comes to sharing my work stress.

Alright, James, you've decided on pizza again for our weekly Domino Drive? Yeah, Auntie Sylvia! Can't go wrong with a good pizza, right? That's right, lad. There's no need to change a winning formula, eh? Speak for yourself, Uncle John. You never pick anything else. Well, I get a certain satisfaction from not having to make a choice. Uncle John, you need to learn how to have fun with food sometimes! I think that's a lesson we can all learn from our boy here - variety is the spice of life. Hence your stellar taste in music. Is that an announcement, or a request for an impromptu performance? Let me stop right here. I can't carry a tune in a bucket, but maybe next time? Maybe. Alright, alright. Not enough for me to listen to your singing over this pizza. Alright, alright, we get it, you two can't compete with your own music taste. It's all about compromise, right, John? Indeed it is. What's been going on over at your farm, Uncle John? Any interesting stories lately? Oh, you know it. Just the usual, trying to keep on top of everything. Late harvest has been the biggest challenge. Seems spring just got tired and handed the baton to autumn, blurred the seasons right out. Oh, Harvest is always a challenging time. I've taught and led several bonfire nights over the years - the corn and log gatherings especially are always chaotic but rewarding. I've never been to a bonfire before. Is it something like a picnic, but with fire? It's a bit like that, but without the picnic. More of a community gathering around a giant fire, toasting marshmallows, reminiscing about the year. I've got some great stories about certain years and the crazy things that happened. I bet. You know, I had to help organize the school fire this year. The kids... Let's just say the adults handle the fire, the kids handle the excitement. Kids and fire can be a perfect storm. What about other holidays? Like Easter? Got any cool plans for that? We're planning a successful Easter Egg hunt for the family this year. Last year was such fun, everyone had a blast finding all the eggs. And it's a nice way for us to get everyone together, enjoy some good food and laugh.

I've decided I need to get back to making proper cups of tea. The accelerated GCMs and water temperature control and all that noise don't make much of a difference. What really matters is that you're doing it right! Ah, yes, the art of making tea. It's something my grandma taught me. She always said the trick is in the water, and you can ruin a good pot by brewing it too long. And always remember to keeps it loose. You wouldn’t want it to be too tight would you? I mean, you wouldn’t want lazy tea – that’s just not done. Exactly! And just like the way we both got into our chosen fields, there’s a bit of technique involved. Speaking of fields, have you seen The Graham Norton Show lately? Yeah, that bit about the celebrity vegetarians was funny. You know, for all the talk about quinoa or kale, it's amazing how many of them don’t stick to it! I know, innit? All this talk of the 'gluten free' and the 'low-carb' but then they’re seen eating chips or pizza on the red carpet. Ah, but have you tried any of those hipster cafes in Cambridge? They have the best vegan treats, really good. One place even has a ‘vegetable butcher,’ which I found quite quaint! Well, I’m more of a pub kind of girl. There’s nothing like a good pint with some proper pub grub. And let’s not forget about those side of chips, they’re the best part! I know. Although, another funny thing about this new wave of health-conscious celebrities is they often endorse healthy food, but then they get photographed at McDonald's. It’s almost as if we’re stuck in a cycle of hypocrisy – preaching one thing but living another. Well, isn't that the way of the world? We all have our contradictions. Still, it's funny to watch. And it’s good for a laugh. You know what else I find funny? How much everyone raves about certain vegetables now. People talk about kale and avocados and all this fancy stuff, but honestly? Give me a good old plate of roast potatoes, or this humble cabbage any day. My partner bought some fancy jar of "vegetable purees" the other day. They were all things like beetroot and ginger and such.

Right, let's start this game. I'm pretty sure I've played Articulate before. The aim is to explain words to your team without using certain buzzwords, right? Exactly. It's all about clarifying without mentioning the actual word, the word’s synonyms, or part of the word. Sounds simple but it isn't. It gets pretty tricky and can lead to some hilarious moments! True. I played it once at a family Christmas. My dad had to explain 'allergy' and it ended up being a whole medieval history lesson. That brings back a memory. I remember playing with the boys and having to explain 'sedimentary' without using any geological terms. Finally, I had to mention the Rocky Mountains just to give a context. LOL. And what about 'mnemonic'? My grandkids had to explain that one during a game. They described it as a memory trick you use in school but barely avoided saying 'memory aid'. That was a close call. Heh, I hope we don't encounter any that tough today. But, it would be fun to see how well we all do. You’re right, it’s the challenge of it. Plus, it’s good bonding time. Who gets to go first? Should we just decide or have a quick word game to determine the order? How about we play a mini game for that? The first one of us to correctly guess a Welsh word that’s harder to explain gets to start. How about "cawl"? Is that like a soup or stew? A traditional Welsh stew made of meat and vegetables. No, I wouldn’t call it a soup exactly. But it can be quite mild. So, it’s not really soup and it’s not really stew… a very vague description. Right. I’d say that's a fair attempt but I know a better one. How about 'Caws pobi'? Is that like a type of cheese? It’s actually cheese on toast. A classic Welsh dish. Ah, so it’s a food item. A good one then. How can we describe it without mentioning cheese, toast, or eating? You could say it's this... Welsh comfort food... often served with any type of... baked bread... topped with something... yellowish, soft, usually... enjoyed in cold weather? Not bad but it sounds like a menu from across the world! I'd say that's harder to guess at.

Right, let's get this party started then! As first move's initiator, I'd suggest we start with simple rules and maybe something like UNO or Blackjack to get everyone comfortable. Are you sure, Alison? I remember our family disputes over UNO as kids, maybe a more complex card game like Bridge or Canasta would encourage some strategic brain activity. Besides, Tom's got this thing for his new deck and wants to use it. I'd be all for a more traditional game, maybe Cribbage keeps it simple yet still requires a bit of strategy. You game for it, Tom? Cribbage’s a good choice, boys and dear Alison. It's perfect for a lazy Sunday afternoon. Might just sneak down to make myself a cuppa before we start, shall I? Sounds like we've got a consensus. Cribbage it is then. Tom, can we see the new deck you've been bragging about? Hold on, I've got it somewhere here. There we are! Well, that's a quality deck. Where did you pick it up from, while on holiday maybe? Stunned at the quality, wasn’t it, Tom? What's next, a bespoke gaming table? perhaps one day, but for now, this is more than sufficient! Alison, as the host, you should deal first. That's right, deal away! But before we start, is the prize still the person who loses gets to do the dishes? We could make it interesting and whoever wins buys the tea and snacks for the rest of the day. I'd consider that quite a prize indeed. I think that's fair, and it ensures everyone's interest stays in the game. You never want to underestimate the power of a bribe to improve playing style. I'm sure we can all handle a few losses if it means getting out of cleaning duties. Ah, Tom, care to explain that move to everyone? Oh, Alison, you didn't execute your hand correctly. Here, let me show you... We're all here to learn, Tom. You've got to admit, this beats arguing about what to watch on TV. And it's a more pleasant way to start a Sunday, playing cards and enjoying family. It’s moments like these that remind me why we love holidays together. Whether it’s just playing cards or reminiscing about old times, it’s these shared activities that count.

So, I hear everyone is planning for university applications? Yeah, I am. It's been super stressful but I've got my Sixthform to help me out. Mine are all sorted. I've applied to a few places and I'm waiting for the response. I've already got my place sorted for next year, but I have to get into the swing of University life now. I've been thinking about whether to go straight to university or try an apprenticeship. It feels like loads of pressure. I know what you mean. I've been thinking about it too. But I've just had a bit of a setback health-wise. Oh, sorry to hear that. Is everything okay? Was it from your recent illness? Yeah, it was a pretty rough time. I had to take time off school but I'm on the mend now. Make sure you get all the rest you need, you won’t get anything done if you’re not well. That or you end up not enjoying the course so much if you’re too tired or stressed. I’ve heard some good things about apprenticeships too though, while earning and learning. It’s a good idea if you want to be hands on and learn by doing. Yeah, but then I'd have to weigh up the benefits against potentially missing out on a university education. Well, we're all different. Some achieve more with formal education and some get more out of practical work. Just remember the goal is to do what you enjoy and end up in a job you're passionate about. Exactly. It’s also okay if your path changes later too, no one has to have it all figured out now. That’s true. My cousin did an apprenticeship first and then went on to university for a bit more theoretical work. You know, after all this talk of future plans, does anyone know what’s for dinner? I hope it’s something festive because so far, it doesn’t feel much like Christmas does it? I was thinking maybe we could start some Christmas traditions. Like we almost never do that as just being friends and wider family. Yeah, like exchanging small gifts. It always adds to the sense of being together at this time of year. Someone’s got a bit of a festive spirit going on.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I drove from Essex to Glasgow? No, you didn't. What happened? Well, I was young, reckless, and thought the M1 was a fairy tale highway. Took me days to complete the journey and I was exhausted by the time I reached the Highlands. I'm sorry, but I've always wondered, how did you manage to set off for a long drive without properly planning it? That's a good question. I guess I thought I could just wing it. These days, I wouldn't dare attempt something like that. So, what happened when you got there? Was it worth it? Oh yes, it was definitely worth it. The scenery was incredible, and the people were very friendly. It was a real adventure. But, next time, I would plan better, that's for sure. You know, I've always wanted to take a driving trip around the country. For me, though, the planning would be quite involved. Right. You’re kind of relying on the bus system where you need to. It’s more convenient for you. Yes, it is. I think one of the things that's changed a lot in transport over the years is the cycle routes. I used to cycle a lot when I was younger and working in London. Really? London is the last place I thought would have good cycle routes. Yes, it’s improved a lot since then. They have bike shares, cycle lanes... it’s a lot safer now. So, do you think we could take a cycling tour round Cambridge next time? That would be brilliant! We could plan a route, pick a time... I think I would need to get used to cycling again and make sure my bike is in good shape. Well, that's a project for both of us. We could even plan a little driving tour too. I love that idea, but I think we should start with cycling. Driving is more tiring, especially if we're not familiar with the routes. But yes, it would be lovely to explore this way too. All sounds great to me. We should make a little tour plan. I think that would be a lovely activity. Maybe next weekend? Yes, let’s do that. And we could make an evening of it. Get some dinner somewhere nice afterwards. That's a great idea.

Ah, what a lovely day for an Alumni Day. I'm Sarah, by the way. Nice to meet you, Sarah. I'm Emily. Lovely to meet you too. Ah, just what I needed - a chance to make some new friends. I'm Professor Williams, a history lecturer here. Pleased to meet you, Professor Williams. I'm Sarah, language research co-ordinator. And I'm Emily, language research administrator. It's a pleasure to meet you, Professor. Professor Williams: The pleasure is mine. I wasn't sure if I'd find anyone to share a conversation about languages. It seems we're a good fit then! Absolutely! I've spent some time researching various dialects and accents across Europe. That sounds fascinating, Sarah. And you, Emily? Any particular language interests? I've always been intrigued by languages that are often overlooked, like Basque. I mean, it's so different from Spanish, even though they're spoken in the same region. Ooh, that's interesting! I've studied the influence of Basque on Spanish language structure. It's quite remarkable how distinctively it's influenced local colloquialisms. Indeed. And then there's China - so many dialects, from Mandarin through to Cantonese. What's been your experience with these? Actually, I've had the chance to work on a project looking at the Mandarin dialect spoken in London. It's fascinating how these languages adapt in the diaspora. That's incredible, Sarah! And, speaking of adaptations, have you noticed any interesting changes in English dialects while you visited Wales? Oh, absolutely! From slight changes in pronunciation to entirely new words. It's really interesting to see how close geographical locations can develop such distinct linguistic features. Professor Williams: I used to play rugby when I was younger. I always found it so interesting how different sports can influence language. For example, some of the terminology in rugby is so unique, and it's influenced even the way players from different backgrounds communicate. Oh, we could definitely talk about sports and language all day! I'm sure we will, Emily. But now, to sum up where we're at, we've got a group that's interested in languages, any type - from dialects across the UK to global languages like Chinese, and we're tying sports in there too! Perfect! It sounds like an alumni group across several fields of interest. We might just get along.

Oh, mates, it's been ages. I have to say though, seeing these Facebook posts about the ice bucket challenge is quite bizarre when you think about it. Right? I mean, I get it's for charity, but who really thought that dumping ice water over themselves would become so popular? Well, it's quite a brilliant idea from a marketing standpoint, actually. And it's done wonders for ALS awareness. That's true, it must be. Though, would it still be as popular if it were some other, less 'cool' cause? Idk, dear. I think it's just the novelty of it. And who says it has to be 'cool'? Fair point. What's new with you all? Anything interesting happening? Actually, I've been going back and forth with a university application. Oh, that's exciting! What are you thinking of studying? English Literature, I think. For a Grad school application, I'm assuming? Yep. It's a bit of a change for me, but I've always been passionate about literature. That's great to hear! It's always good to pursue what you love. I agree. A university education can open all sorts of possibilities. Indeed. Though, I must admit, the thought of filling all those forms and stuff is pretty daunting. True, but the reward is worth it. Just focus and you'll be fine. Oh, or you could always just give me your info and I'll fill in the forms for you? Alright, alright, but only if you're sure you know what you're doing! Yes, and we might just end up sending her to university too – on disciplinary grounds! If I must, I must, but truly, I mean it. I've filled plenty of forms for the dental practice. Again, only if you don't mishandle any of this. There's already enough going around in this house with all these new pictures we're trying to post of us. Oh, funny thinking you can hide from us just because you now work at a dental practice! You know I'll take any excuse to help. That's what I like to hear. Anyway, did anyone else catch the new food trends from over the Atlantic? I saw something about avocado on toast again, and all these fancy sandwich shops popping up. I've tried it. It's actually quite good, I'd say.

Ah, I can't believe we're having to discuss the price of things again. This coffee machine; it's been giving us trouble all morning. You'd think that after all these years you'd know better than to get into these DIY projects, Máire. It's not her fault, Joyce. She's been taking initiative and trying to fix the machine instead of just ordering new things all the time. I'd say that's commendable for a retired maths teacher keeps coming up with creative solutions. Well, I suppose, but sometimes you've just got to call a spade a spade. It's just that the cost of getting someone in is through the roof. And even then, there's no guarantee they can actually fix it. True, but that's the market we live in. Removal and storage services are particularly pricey these days. We've decided to temporarily store some of your mum's things in the attic over the house. But even that's a cost. And those costs keep climbing. I remember when my job was still active, this wasn't such a concern. But now, being long-term unemployed... These types of expenses just cut through our already tight budgets. It's the politicians who let us down really, isn't it? They talk about making things better, but nothing changes on the ground for people like us. Politics is a can of worms, as always. But have you all heard about the new Labour leadership contenders? I've been following it fairly closely. But it seems like they're the same old faces with the same old promises. Except for maybe Emily Thornberry. She's got some fresh ideas. She might, but do you think a single person, no matter how idealistic, can actually change the system from within? Seems like they all get bogged down by the bureaucratic nonsense once they get there. Maybe not, but that's no reason to stop believing in idealism. I mean, without people who believe in something better, we'd never have any change at all. Idealism doesn't pay the bills though, Joyce. True, but perhaps if more of us invested in it, things could change. Maybe if we could all find ways to work together and actively engage with local politics... but I suppose that's idealism for you. Indeed. Well, for now, maybe we should focus on this coffee machine.

Oh, what a lovely day! And an even lovelier place to catch up. It certainly is, wouldn't you say? The Seven Stars never disappoint. Indeed. Especially now, as Christmas draws near. I've always loved this time of the year, don't you? Absolutely, but sometimes the preparations can be a bit stressful, I'm right? Oh, so right! I keeps coming across new recipes and decorations online and suddenly I'm thinking, "Wasn't Thanksgiving just a few weeks ago?" I know exactly what you mean. This year, we decided to keep things simple. No big parties, no complicated turkey recipes. Just a quiet dinner with the family. That sounds perfect. I think sometimes we overdo it. True. But, there's something special about those simple family gatherings. You get to catch up on everyone's news and what's new in their lives. For me, Christmas this year is going to be particularly special because both our boys are coming home from university for the holidays. It'll be lovely to have the whole family reunited. That must be so exciting for you, really nice for us too. It'll certainly make for an interesting conversation – I'm curious to know what they're thinking about their futures, especially after this year of unrest. True, life is quite different now compared to when they were younger and "back in my day" . But it's good to keep the lines of communication open. Absolutely, and if one of them has any career questions or worries, I'm sure I can help as much as I can, as a former trainer. I've seen a lot of young people facing uncertainty. That's really kind of you, and it's always good to have a perspective changing. You've always been good for that, really. I suppose habits stick after all these years of consulting. Either way, it means I get to keep up with all the current trends and ideas too. Speaking of careers, how's freelancing been for you? I know it's not always predictable... There are ups and downs, but generally it's been good. Flexibility is fantastic. Especially with your TEFL job, which I've heard can be quite demanding at times. It can be, but it’s also very rewarding. And don’t get me wrong, I love the flexibility too. Sometimes I wonder what a traditional office job would feel like, though .

Oh, did I ever tell you lot about the time Grace discovered that she'd been snoring super loud every night and was slumped out after a deep sleep? No! Is that true Grace? Only you'd questions if this kind of revelation would be shared publicly or not! Ah, but I thought we were all of a very close family and friends here! Well, that's a new one. I've known her my whole life, and that's new to me! Does she wake up questioning her mortality then? Is that a typical morning for you, Gracie? Grace : Oh god, even my husband says that. He started noticing it before I did. I remember one night, I'd dozed off with the TV on and he said he could hear me snoring over the sound of the TV! Well, that's one way to keep a noise down! For once, the snoring was louder than the TV. That's actually kind of impressive, while the rest of us struggle to even turn the TV on at all... Yeah, well... ...it's a bit embarrassing when you're awake though, right, especially if it's happening in a shared flat or something. I'm sure you're used to it now? Grace : Yes, yes I am. Though now I kind of know what it's like to be on the receiving end if one of you lot starts the snoring. Sorry, sorry! I'll keep it in mind for whenever we all decide to crash in one room or something. Speaking of crash places, has anyone tried the new place Waterfields on Golden Square? Ah, Waterfields! Yeah, I went there last week. Their bread is amazing, but I was a bit disappointed with the service. Though the sausage roll was to die for. Really? I almost gone there yesterday after the lecture. Maybe I should give it a go. The sausage roll wasn't Richmond, then? No, but it was surprisingly good nonetheless. I know! And don't you just love the old-fashioned feel of a handkerchief? I mean, like really using it and not just as a souvenir? Oh, definitely! I've kept the one from my Grandma for years. It's more sentimental value than practical use, admittedly. We're all just a bunch of nostalgia lovers here then. Yeah, and I think that's lovely. It shows we care about our roots a bit.

So, how was your weekend? It was good actually. The markets were quite busy, and we sold a few more varieties of our heirloom vegetables compared to last week. Made some decent profit. That's great, the produce looks so fresh and vibrant at your stall. Glad you think so. Speaking of market days, I took my granddaughter with me on Saturday. She's been learning about the different types of produce, and it was amazing to see her excitement when we got to the fruit stand. She wanted to try every single kind of apple there was! That must have been fun. Children can always bring so much enthusiasm and curiosity to these things. Absolutely, it was a rewarding day. She also helped me count the change and sort the fruits - she even helped me with the organization bit. She's a bright young lady. It's important she sees and learns about where food comes from. Exactly, I couldn't agree more. And it's amazing how these little things can light up their world. I wish I could have seen it. Now tell me, how was your weekend? Well, I had the usual family dinner on Sunday. My daughter and her family came over, so it was the usual chaos, but in the best way. Sounds lovely. I had been planning to visit my friend, Sarah, but we decided to cancel in the end as it started to rain heavily towards the late afternoon, and all plans went out the window. How disappointing! But that's life. At least you didn't get too wet? No, I didn't. I just stayed in the house, tidied up the garden, and caught up on a few episodes of my favorite series. That's a good use of rainy time. I personally like to read a bit, or maybe finish off some paperwork if it's a work-from-home day. I can do that too, though I sometimes prefer to unwind with a book or podcast. Ah yes, podcasts are brilliant. I've been listening to a fascinating one on the history of 20th century farming techniques and it's been really interesting. That sounds intriguing. I've been getting into more fiction lately. I recently finished a book about a mystery in a rural English village. It really drew me into the world. Sounds good! You might enjoy this one - I know it's not fiction, but...

Hi Sarah, I'm so glad we could catch up! It's been ages since we've had a proper conversation. How's life treating you? It's great, thanks for asking! Life is life. It's got its usual ups and downs. But now, the biggest challenge is probably keeping up with the questions from my kindergardeners! Ha, I can imagine! I've been doing that for years, and I'm right there with you. Speaking of which, how's your French coming along? I've got a keeps coming up with new verbs at home! Oh, I've dabbled a bit. I have to say, it's been tough sticking to it with everything else going on. Yes, I know what you mean. It can be really challenging when you've got a full-time job and other responsibilities. But you know, even just a little bit of practice each day makes a difference. It's a bit like how you need to keep up with the new English grammar when it changes over time, right? You're so right! I really need to make time for it. But it's hard, especially with this new baby on the scene! Ah yes, I understand the baby dilemma. It's like you're in survival mode for the first year or so! But think of it this way, your baby is also learning a new language. So, you're both in it together! That's a brilliant way to look at it, isn't it? Maybe I could try incorporating some really basic vocabulary with her? For instance, when I'm changing her nappy, "Up! Down! Wet! Dry!" Or something simple like that. Absolutely, that's a perfect idea! You could even start with simple phrases or rhymes in English and then start doing them side by side in French together. It could be a nice bonding experience, and it’s so easy to learn when it's informal and fun. Yes, that's a great idea! I will definitely try that. But first, changing the nappy in peace would be a welcome novelty after these last few weeks of sleep deprivation. I'm sure you're doing wonderfully and it just takes getting used to. I remember when my little one was that age, it felt like the end of the world at the time, but it passes so quickly.

You know, it's remarkable how complex these nests can be. It's almost like they're constructing miniature buildings. I've always been fascinated by that. Indeed. I've spent countless hours watching the little varmints, as a retired civil engineer, I'm always interested in structures. Though I'd never say any bird is a "varmint". Oh, I couldn't agree more. I used to make puppets out of wood and fabric for the kids. It's amazing how similar it is to building a nest, actually. Absolutely. It's similar in the sense of instinctive construction, I suppose. Speaking of instinctive construction, have we got a well-placed nest here? Anything that could serve as a makeshift puppet theatre for its occupants? You're quite the joker, aren't you? Maybe we could get some carpentry done. Someone should make a few birdhouses while we still have energy! We could, it would be quite the project though. I'm retired now, no more civil engineering for me. Though, I might be up for a bit of amateur carpentry to make some nice birdhouses. Honestly, as long as we still can, we should. It keeps the mind active, which is important considering we’re no spring chickens anymore. I entirely agree, and who would say no to the chance to keep the birds entertained? Speaking of "no spring chickens", have we thought about what to do for the local bird’s pudding tray? Oh, for heaven's sake! While you’re at it, why not start baking bird pies and cakes? Well, if I recall correctly, most of the birds here like seeds, fruit, and insects. But I'm sure a cake might go down alright too. You could even bake bird-friendly cake... but this cake is just for us, folks! Ta, Dee. It's always wonderful to sit down and have a piece of cake with you all. Yes, it’s good to have these breaks from... other things. Health issues, for instance. Absolutely. I've been rather concerned about my blood sugar levels since retirement. Had to revise my diet, cut back on sweet things. That's true for me too, I've had to cut back on sugar quite a bit since being diagnosed with diabetes a few years ago. Same here. We've both become quite the cognizant of what we put in our mouths now.

Ah, marvellous to see you again, John! We've not had lunch together in ages. How have you been since we last met? Very well, thank you for asking. You know how it is with the usual work-life balance. But now, the sunshine, the sea, and a bit of a break are just what I needed. "Pleasure in simple things," as we often say, isn't it? I couldn't agree more. By the way, have you got a keepsake for Oscar alongside with you today? Oh, yes. His favourite toy. I've just had to learn how to clean them properly from my wife. She's just been dealing with ... ... Otitus, in the middle of her own hearing aid adjustment. Oh dear, hope she's alright now. My dad, God rest his soul, he had that and it didn't do him any favours. But, let's not focus on the gloom. Excuse me, could you perhaps recommend something or point us towards the daily special? We're open to suggestions and quite enjoying the local culture here, even if we're not quite comfortable with counting in Turkish yet! Actually, while we're in good spirits, I was intrigued to learn about the local treatments for hearing loss. They have some quite interesting traditional remedies over here, like the use of olive oil perhaps? I've heard dowsing rods are used to find the best olive groves for oil quality, much like we used to use a forked hazel twig over in Sussex! Well, I'll believe dowsing when I see it work! But, intriguing as it all sounds, I rather stick to things the NHS or my postgrad studies recommend, you know? More a fan of evidence-based practise than ... shall we say shamanism. Absolutely! Though I do have respect for people who seek out a more holistic approach. It's not about dismissing it outright, but I suppose I'm a bit of a skeptic when it comes to seeking phantom oil for phantom ears. However, there is something quite spiritual about truly soaking in one's surroundings, isn't there? Indeed, the atmosphere here does have something special about it. It's like almost every table has a story to tell. I've just been trying to figure out who's on honeymoon and who's celebrating a birthday. Always a fun game, particularly during peak season.

Mum, Dad, and everyone else. I'm so glad we've all managed to make today. I've just been super busy at work and it feels like ages since we talked. You're quite right, darling. We've missed you, though! But tell us, questions are waiting! What kind of projects are you co-ordinating now? Anything exciting that makes you hardly sleep? Oh, I'd love to tell you all about it! At the moment, I'm handling a big charity event in support of disadvantaged children. It's quite a challenge, but really rewarding. It's tough to balance everything at such a young age but I'm really enjoying it. Sounds like you're taking after your mother in the organisational skills department. We never thought you'd make an official 'project co-ordinator' so quickly after graduating! Well, sometimes you need creative solutions to manage complicated situations. But it's good that it's going well. I also wanted to ask, how is the house preparations for next year coming along? We were thinking maybe we could do a small renovation before Christmas and make it feel more like our home. That's a great idea, but we still haven't decided where to start. We might need your expertise as a project co-ordinator to make it happen! Well, I'm happy to help. Honestly though, I think it'd be lovely for the family to all contribute as well. It'll be a fantastic chance for us to all spend time together and it's something we can all be proud of. Yes, that sounds great. Though we need to consider the budget and timelines, but I do agree, if we're planning to make the house feel more like home, why not try together as a team? I'd like that. It's been ages since we did something like that together. That reminds me, I was thinking of inviting some friends over next month for a big meal. Anyone interested in helping with that? I like the sound of it. We always manage to pull together for events at the end of the year. We can all contribute in different ways. You could perhaps handle the food and invitations this time, just to make things easier for you all. Perfect, thank you! I'll start planning soon. We'll get involved when you need us.

Yo, lads and lasses. You remember that first year's film studies class? We watched that documentary on Catfish. It was about how people create fake Facebook profiles to trick other people. Yeah, totally! That documentary had me on the edge of the seat, wasn't it? It's questions how easily we just believe what we see and read online. Absolutely! It links back to the Jeremy Kyle show, right? They often have guests there who have been catfished. It's so sad that people keeps coming backwards due to this. Exactly! And those reality TV shows like Jeremy Kyle – they seem to always try and sensationalize these stories for ratings. But in reality, it's just like, so cruel. It's actually really scary when you think about it - the lengths people will go to deceive others purely for attention or whatnot. It also shows how gullible we are, doesn't it? We might be barely out of school and we're already trusted entirely in this black box of the internet. I mean, I recently saw a documentary about this guy who created a ton of fake profiles online and literally made people fall in love with him for years. I think it's because these platforms are designed to make it easy for people to create false realities, right? It's like the perfect storm – social media technology allowing for anonymity while creating a hunger for validation. It's also about the pull of the drama, isn’t it? People get drawn into these situations because they want to see love stories and "proving a point" on TV doesn’t come close to the emotional hell these people go through in real life. And to make matters worse, these catfishers often prey on the vulnerable or less tech-savvy, right? Older people or people with lower socioeconomic backgrounds who are less likely to be skeptical online. It does seem to affect certain groups disproportionately. And it's insidious, you know? Because it's changing the way we communicate and interact on a fundamental level. I mean, I know some people who’ve been in these situations. They often have a hard time talking about it, because so much of it is rooted in shame or vulnerability. So true! And yet, it still happens. Maybe if we could somehow turn this into a bigger conversation in society, maybe we could discourage more people from doing it, or at least help the victims recover better.

Mum, I've been meaning to ask you - you've got experience with foreign languages, right? Considering your background, what language would you say is the most beautiful? Ah, my dear, that's a difficult one. As you know, I was born and raised in Vienna, but I spent a part of my youth in Italy. I must say, though, I find French and Italian to have quite a melodic sound to them. I was just thinking about that. I studied French at university. It was quite difficult, but it felt right somehow. I think it's because, like Italian and Spanish, French originates from Latin. It's got that classical ring to it, very similar to the Greek I used to study when I was a bit younger. That's true. I actually tried to learn a bit of Italian during my summer break. It was fun, but I didn't get the chance to do more than a few conversation classes. Hmm, maybe it's time to pick it back up again. It'd be nice to share a common ground language next time we or your father plan a trip to Italy. We could practically apply what we've learned. That is a lovely thought. You know, I assumed we'd visit Paris eventually. I've always wanted to see the Louvre and the Eiffel Tower, not to mention the food! Ah, yes! Paris. The food, the culture, the language, all so rich. I remember visiting in my early twenties. It was quite life-changing. I'm sure it was. I'd likely feel the same way. But it's not just about the city itself, it's the whole experience of being in a new place, speaking the language, eating the food, really immersing into the culture. Absolutely. And speaking of culture, have you noticed how different our family's background is? Your father's side is quite traditional British, while mine is . . . well, you could say multicultural! That's very true. It’s actually quite interesting. I think that's part of what makes our family so unique. I completely agree, my dear. And speaking of unique, did you know that honey bees are a symbol of hard work and diligence? I was reading about apiculture and found it quite fascinating. Really? Bees as symbols? I didn't know that. Do you think that has anything to do with the sense of community and collective effort?

Oh, did you see that?? That's bravery or stupidity. The driver just cut us off and almost side-swiped us! Well, that's one way to squeeze time. Still, though, the road’s getting awfully flooded out. Why does this always happen when it isn’t a day off? Yes, and then we end up right behind the wagon fracturing out nails! And we even got an MOT done on this car a couple of weeks ago. Wonder if we’ll be stranded on the side of the road today. You two are just a pair, aren’t you? Always thinking about the worst case scenario. At least we’re all safe now - oh, and the rain isn’t going to stop anytime soon, is it? You know, we should have taken the train. It would’ve saved us the headache. And it would’ve been less stressful on the journey - especially with the Sat Nav or as I like to say, Sat Navitude this morning. I remember when I first started driving, no Sat Navs of course. Just a paper map and directions from a kind stranger at a petrol station. Now we can't even park a car without it. Aye, right, no Sat Nav? Good luck getting in and out of Dorset with that! True, but sometimes it doesn’t help much - like when the signal drops and the directions are just as lost as you are. Except, nowadays you're not lost if you're on your phone. Yeah, and weren’t we, just yesterday, sitting in a puddle because our Sat Nav led us to think this place was a building site? It's next to impossible to get directions right in these areas! It’s like these new developments. They’re building so fast that the old towns are disappearing. Soon we’ll forget what it was like to walk without tripping over a new hotel or shopping center! That's true and it’s the same with some of the bad estates we pass by. It’s like they've just put up buildings without any thought for the livability of the area. I remember when Dorset was just quaint villages and wide open fields. Now it’s like every bit of green has been clogged up with buildings. Like when I was a boy, we’d hang out in the woods till sunset, without a care in the world.

Ah, martha, it's so lovely to have you round. We don't get many visitors these days, you know. Oh, thank you old chap. It's always a pleasure to be here, you know that. Just, you know, sitting here on the sofa, it's so quiet isn't it? I find myself reminiscing more often these days. You and I have had some good times, havent we? Indeed we have. Norwich, Costessey, keeps coming back to me, how would I forget? You know, it's funny, those memories. It's nostalgic, isn't it? The simplicity of things. Though, let me tell you, even then, there were issues. The whole unemployment issue, for instance. It never let up even when we were younger. Exactly, Richard. It was a struggle. We both decided not to work out of... frustration maybe. Frustration, I suppose. But also a lack of opportunities. I mean, I left school quite young, didn't have any qualifications, so jobs were hard to come by. Oh, I understand. I managed to go a bit further than you with the 'A' levels. Still, employment was scarce. And we can't blame the system entirely. Well, perhaps we could, but that wouldn't solve anything, would it? We made do, however we could. You're right, life is what we make of it. Even in our 'retirement'. Despite the lack of formal work, we've found ways to keep ourselves busy and the years fruitful. Indeed we have. I started doing some voluntary work at the local library, that helped me keep my mind sharp. And you weren't too bad with the children either. I've seen some of the kids you looked after. It's one of the joys of life, you know. Seeing a young mind grow. It's rewarding even without a paycheck. Definitely. Though some times I do wish... well, I often think about what it would be like to truly be back in the employment pool. To be needed, to be of use to society in a more... measurable way. I understand. Even as a childminder, job or not, you are needed. I believe every individual inherently wants to feel like they matter. That's a profound thought, Martha. I suppose that's one reason why I enjoy playing this game of backgammon with you... because we feel needed, however small the game is.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you listened to that new album from The 1975 yet? It sounds so different from their usual stuff but I think it really works. Oh, isn't it great though? The creativity, the depth... I do love questions like this coming from you. You always have your finger on the pulse of the best music out there. And have you seen that there are live recordings? They announced it for their upcoming tour... So keeps changing right before our eyes. Crazy how quickly things shift in the music industry, isn't it? True, it's such a dynamic field. I used to write articles about it for my PhD, and it's even happening more among the UK bands we love. The indie scene in particular has such a unique dynamic. That's what I find so interesting! The way The 1975 decided to step out of their comfort zone. It's like they're reinventing themselves, which I totally respect. It's got me curious for whatever comes next. Absolutely! Now that you've started this, it would be quite rude of me not to ask about your own gardening adventure. How is the plot doing? It’s a daily struggle, to be honest, but it’s also become such a joy. Well, most of the time at least. I ripped my nails out last week dealing with the silly weeds. I’d be all about that if it were me, but I’m afraid my green thumb is… well, it’s not exactly green is the problem. I kind of struggle keeping anything alive inside, let alone on the plot. Don't worry, we all have our strengths! And, hey, at least you are not experimenting with our living room as a green house. Point taken and it’s been quite educational! I’ve learned a lot from you about gardening and sustainability. Like how do you do it all while working full time? Well, I have a bit of help from my assistant and so much automation now doesn’t hurt! And weekends are for the garden, 100% for the garden. Automation and an assistant, two things all the beginner gardeners dream of. Yes, but don't worry. Gardening ain't all about tech and help. It's about being out there and getting your hands dirty. I like to think of it as meditation... except with better results than my meditation practice.

Oh, so many topics we've got to cover. Let's start with the big one - what's going on with your PhD study? Ah, it's all good. Just really diving into this new research now, and it’s quite fascinating. We're on questions around the kind of jobs that are most likely to be automated and what the impact might be on society. And the funding, how's that looking? I mean, it can't be fun going through all that admin can it? Oh, you have no idea! Even with my funding secured for the next couple of years, it's still a nightmare. But yes, very grateful for that, nonetheless. And the life of a graduate student never really seems to change, does it? Always on the edge of financial stability. Exactly! But you know, we chose this path, so no complaints. That's true. Though between us, I've heard quite a bit about the ever-rising university fees. We really need a more affordable system, surely? Absolutely. It pushes so many eager minds away from this world of academia. And then on the other side, think of all the people stuck in low-paid jobs, can't afford the time or the money for further education. Yeah, right, it feels like an old system that's just stuck, really. But unemployment is another thing we should chat about. I've noticed a rise in that in some of the manufacturing towns doesn't it? Yes, it's a major issue, especially in areas that have traditionally relied on certain industries. But the problem is less about the sector itself, and more about retraining and the lack of support to do so. Oh absolutely, retraining is key. But it's also about the kind of jobs available. We're changing so quickly. With automation, there are some jobs that just won't be around in a few years. What’s your take on that? Well, my take so far is that we need to focus on adaptability rather than just re-training. The job market will always change, the key is to teach people how to keep learning, to be nimble. Yeah, sounds about right. But it still pains me to see so many fine people struggling. And all that could be avoided if the government invested more in these retraining programs, right? Exactly. Though, it's a bit of a chicken and egg - should the government fund this, or should industry step up to make it a requirement?

Mum, I was thinking that we might want to include more photos in this kids' book. You know, like pictures from when we were at Tower Bridge or when Uncle Liam took us to the Science Museum. Oh really? That's a great idea, sweetie. But remember, we want to keep it simple and easy for little kids to understand. What kind of pictures do you have in mind? Any big landmarks or things they can actually see in the pictures. Maybe we can even show them how different siblings can look even if they're related. You know how Thomas is blond and Alex has dark hair but they're both from dad? Even though they have different dads... Ah yes, that's a lovely idea to show different relationships among family members. It can be really educational for little ones to understand the variety we have in our little family here. Exactly, and it also helps to normalize all types of family dynamics. It also shows how we can still have strong bonds despite being from different pairings. Yeah, like Auntie's ex-husband and her new partner, he's really nice and so is this new guy on the scene from Poppa's side, even if they're not the same as most families. Children can learn so much from understanding the complexities of families. And it's so important to make them feel like their own family configurations are valued and normal too. I agree, but I think we should also talk about the tricky parts. Like, how do we address the fact that your Poppa and I couldn't work out but we're working hard at being good parents to both our children? True, and the feelings that come with it. Perhaps we could use a simple storybook style to explain it. Maybe something like the different pieces making up one whole picture, where together, we're still a family. That sounds fun! So it's like, we're all different pieces making one awesome puzzle. That’s a great analogy, actually. We'll definitely want to make sure to weave in these themes appropriately. And for our own children, for sure. But it might also help other children who are going through similar situations. It can be reassuring to see real stories of such adjustments in a family. That would be so helpful! Like, this book could be for them

Yo, how's studying going? It's alright, you know. Just trying to get through the week and then it's the weekend. Yeah, that's about right haha! Did you hear, though, about that new study about students shaving their body hair? No, I didn't. What's that about? Apparently, there's been a rise in people, especially women, shaving for their own comfort during lessons. Really? That's interesting. I suppose it's kind of a personal choice. Exactly, and I think that's the most important thing. If it makes you feel more comfortable or makes you feel more confident, then there shouldn't be any criticism about it. Agreed. But what about razors, bru? It's expensive and all. Yeah, it can be. But there are some affordable options out there. And it's not like you need to shave everything all at once. You could start with whatever makes you the most uncomfortable. True, that makes sense.
