But do you think it's because of the extra heat we're getting this summer or the pressure to look a certain way in lessons? I think it's a bit of both, probably. Everyone wants to keep cool in the heat, but also I'd say there's some pressure, especially in physical education classes or gym-based study areas, to be more 'presentable'. And that 'presentable' look usually means no body hair, right? Yeah, that seems to be the case. It's kind of disappointing. I mean, body hair is natural and the fact we have to go through all this trouble just to feel comfortable just because of societal expectations is a bit ridiculous. Absolutely. But it's quite complex, innit? On one hand, it's about comfort and personal choice, but on the other hand, it's influenced by societal norms. Definitely. I think for me, personally, it's about what makes me feel good. If shaving my legs makes me feel better, then that's what I'm going to do. Same here. Though, I've heard some people say that body hair being natural and all that can also be quite liberating. I don't know, maybe it just feels more liberating not to worry about shaving. I get that. But at the end of the day, whatever makes you feel more confident and comfortable with yourself... that's the important thing.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that strict new drug policy's been enforced at our university? I mean, it's good to keep students safe, but don't you think it could backfire if unrealistic? You know how it can drive the consumption underground? Ah, you're questions are always kind of like conversations in themselves. Yeah, I'd totally agree. But you've got to remember, it's not just about keeping students safe, but also about the unintended consequences. And how about that fight coming up at the local pub gym? You planning to watch it? Actually, I have to check on some readings for my thesis today, but I might squeeze in a visit. You know, I find boxing is like a weird kind of performance art, in a way. The mix of athleticism and strategy... Ah, so it's not just brute force? Definitely not. And besides, it's good for stress relief. But yes, it's mainly brute force. I’m more of a spectator, to be honest. Though, I’ve tried training before, but it was just fun. Well, don't worry, you won't be missing much if you don't go. It's mainly the die-hard fans who spend hours debating about tactics and all. Speaking of stress, how's the PhD in political philosophy coming along? It’s a wild ride. There’s always something new to learn, but it doesn’t come without its challenges. I’ve been debating how to tackle my next chapter; it seems like every time I think I’m getting somewhere, it spirals into a new topic. The labyrinth of academia. We’re kind of in the same boat, but mine is more about data analysis and research projects. Last week, I was trying to figure out a way to make complex data easier to understand for my team. You know, that’s something I’ve been struggling with for my own work too. It’s about simplifying complex ideas so that anyone can understand, while also not losing the detail. Exactly! It’s about those anecdotes, like... once this one time at a conference, I compared our research to drinking. You want to get the buzz of learning without going overboard, right? I love that analogy. You know, for some people, they get too drunk on the data and lose sight of what’s important.

Ah, marvellous weekend. I hope you've had a chance to relax after that exhausting exhibition at the Old Jefferies Estate. It was quite something, wasn't it? I still can't quite believe the proportion of the crowd that was concentrated around the Georgian wing. Exactly! You handled it all with such poise and expertise. I've been thinking a lot about our own proposed restoration project – the ruin at Shotover Hall. I'd really value your input on how to approach this. Of course, I'd be happy to help. It's always fascinating, isn't it? Even with my years of experience, I still find each project unique. Absolutely. Shotover Hall is quite a bit larger than what we've worked on before. We're hoping to create a home for the community to use, perhaps even a museum or tour space. That's ambitious but completely doable. Before we get into the how, though, let's start with the funding. Have you done any research into grants available for heritage projects? Only what I could find online. But I suppose that's where advice from someone with your level of experience would be invaluable. I think most funds specifically for heritage buildings would come from the Historic England lottery fund or the Lottery Heritage Fund. However, they do have tight criteria, and often prefer projects that can demonstrate community engagement or educational value. I see. A community project would likely boost our chances then. We can definitely highlight that as part of our application. Exactly. Another aspect to consider is that these projects usually receive better support if they come with a well-researched and detailed business plan. A business plan? I hadn't thought of it from that angle before. It's more than just being required by the funders. It helps keep you on track with costs and timeline. Plus, it can be a solid foundation if you're considering leasing out parts of the building or setting up exhibits with entrance fees later on. That's an excellent point. I suppose I should start outlining a draft. Definitely. If you'd like, I can take a look at your draft at some point and give you feedback. That would be most kind of you. No problem at all. It's the least I can do given how many times you’ve helped me with my projects.

Right, so I've been reading about this fascinating piece on linguistic variability within UK dialects. Did you know there are actually more than 30 distinct dialect varieties in the north east of England alone? Really? That's really interesting! I've always found the Midlands' dialects quite distinctive too – do you have any preferred kind of research methods for studying these dialects? Well, personally, I think phonetic analysis works pretty well, right? It's scientifically sound, and it doesn't rely too much on personal interpretation which can sometimes be subjective. But, at the same time, it's really dependent on good, representative data. Absolutely, collecting and analyzing data's a crucial part of any research. Though, let me tell you, even then, there can be so many nuances in dialect variations from village to village that it's hard to capture everything. True, you can't capture the full range of dialectal variations with data alone – also, how you conduct field research matters a lot. Exactly. It's also interesting to study the socioeconomic factors influencing dialectal changes, especially in urban centers. For example, this trend of urban dialect blurring regional lines. That is a really good point. Where I'm from, the accent of Sunderland can vary so much in just a few miles. Social status, education, even local industries can all influence the way people speak. Definitely. Like, my home city, Birmingham, has always had strong regional accents but in recent decades, because of the universities and corporations, we've also seen a shift towards more neutral English forms – partly due to perceived professionalism. Yes, that plays into the prestige theory of language change, doesn't it? People adapt their speech to fit into or aspire to higher socio-economic groups. Exactly. It's similar to the question of whether a certain dialect is seen as 'better' than another. Though personally, I think all dialects are valid and reflect cultural identities and histories in their own way. Absolutely. We should always respect and value these differences rather than trying to over-standardize language. Right. Anyway, before we delve too much into our research, how about we take a break? It's going to be such an intense year for me with the PhD. Definitely. There's always time for breaks. You know what, I was thinking we might head off on a holiday next year. Somewhere with a completely different linguistic landscape – perhaps the Outer Hebrides or maybe even Canada.

Alright, kids, who first wants to tell me about your school dinners? What have you been having for lunch these days? Oh, Miss Emma! We’ve got a really nice new cook at our school, and she’s been making all sorts of tasty things! Yeah! Today we had pasta and a salad. It was really good! That sounds lovely! I hope I get to try it too someday. You could get a visitor’s pass and eat with us. Yeah! But your food probably comes from a fancy shop, not our big kitchen in London. I bet the food here in the countryside beats London big time though! More fresh and delicious! Yeah, Granny says the best food comes from where it's grown. London’s too busy and polluted, she says. Well, it's true that's what makes their food quite unique. For me, the best is when we eat at Granny's. She makes such nice different dishes. Indeed, Granny’s cooking is always a treat. But sometimes she asks if we want pudding, and I’m always unsure. I always want pudding. She makes the best sticky toffee pudding! Alright, I think we should help Granny make that pudding together when she comes over next. Yeah, can we? Can we? Please, please, please? Of course, that sounds like a fun plan. But first, let’s talk about the school tennis tournament. How's that going? I’m in the team! And Julie and Tom are too. We’ve been practicing a lot. Oh, I was on the basketball team for a while but got taken off. I really like playing basketball. It doesn't mean you can’t still enjoy the tennis tournament, and who knows, perhaps you’ll find something else you're just as good at. Maybe even join the cheerleading team! Maybe... How about all that other fun stuff like clowns and circuses? Any of you seen any good shows lately? Oh, I loved the circus at the town fair! The clowns were so funny and the acrobats so brave! Though sometimes clowns can be a bit, well, cheeky and scary for me if they're too close. That’s perfectly okay! Everyone has different things they find amusing or a bit worrying. Some people are just like that about clowns. You know, I wish I could be in a circus. The one at the fair had a clown who was, like, really good at playing tennis.

So, I thought "The Last Watch of the Night" was quite intriguing. I'd never seen anything like it. The director did a wonderful job of blending fantasy with deep social commentary. Right! Right! Specially the way they portrayed the old, ancient magic kind of being on the backburner just like traditional skills are these days. But then, the ending... quite abrupt, don't you think? I didn't mind the ending. Sometimes, leaving things open to interpretation is a good thing. keeps it in your mind, lets you think about it for a while before we start looking for more. Absolutely, I had a lot of food for thought after watching it. Though, let me tell you, even though I was thoroughly entertained, there was something about the way they glossed over the making of the magic that left me a bit... unsatisfied. It's as if they're saying, "Well, this is the way it is, deal with it," which might be a little too convenient. As for the film itself, it reminded me of a lot of the debates that are happening around this town about history and its relevance. Remember when there was that big debate at Cambridge the other week? Oh, that one. I didn't get to go but I saw the reports. It's really unsettling, isn't it, how some people are so eager to rewrite history to suit current political interests? A bit like in the film where they dismiss old skills and in practice, the really old history that is key to understanding the present and the future. Exactly! And doesn't it show in the current curriculum? I keep saying how we need more emphasis on critical thinking and understanding the socio-economic context of historical events rather than just listing dates and events. And, as a former teacher, I noticed how that way of teaching history really misses out on so much. It's like teaching history without giving the students any room to question it or think critically about what they're being told. I do think that's a problem. I try to do that with my students, encourage them to question and look at it from different perspectives, but it's getting harder with the current curriculum. It seems so focused on standardized testing that there's little room for actual learning or debate. Exactly! It's like the job market these days - they want you to have all these specific skills that are industry-relevant but don't want to give us time to develop a well-rounded understanding of the subject.

Right, so I was going over some of these old family photos the other day. Got me thinking; how did we turn out so different from where we started? You mean we all rode different paths in life, don't you? I remember growing up in Harrow – acres of open space, kind of like Costessey where you came from, Tom. Harrow’s changed so much! And yet, despite all that change, there's still a lot of history here. Speaking of keepsakes, I still have my grandfather's old armchair. Wonder what war it saw, if anything? Even thought I have to keep it at the top of my store's storeroom now. Ah, what about the police? Did we all have our share of troubles with the law when we were younger? Troubles? More like tangles with lawful order! But, no, we were quite the well-behaved lot. But you’re right, it did get me thinking about the police these days. Ever thought what the world would be like without them? That's a sobering thought. I remember when I first started childminding, the biggest 'police' problem was the kids wanting the TV remote. And yet, for families like mine, the law was less about TV remote management and more about dealing with the hardships of life. My grandfather was involved with some community work around the time of the war – never said much about it but I remember the way he’d look at his badge. My father served during the war, you know. I don’t think I fully appreciated what he went through until much later. The weather was probably his biggest enemy weren’t it, as much as the enemy. Constant rain and mud were far from the pleasant Norfolk countryside we knew. That's a really important point, Tom. I think the younger generations don’t fully grasp what we've lived through or what our parents went through – wars, famines, unrest. Our everyday struggles of today often pale in comparison, but it's invaluable learning from the past. It does bring to mind, though, the kind of furniture we grew up with. Solid stuff. Chairs almost as old as my grandfather's. Nothing disposable or 'throwaway' back then. I wonder if that's part of why we still hold onto these generational items, out of respect and a desire to connect with our roots.

Alright, Dad. So, we're still heading to your place before I head off to Manchester then? Yeah, just down the A428 here. We can squeeze in a quick chat now, then you can chill a bit before you head back off. Yeah, I have about a half hour before I need to get out of your hair and onto the M6. And how's Mum keeps coming along? She seems fine in most of our talks. She is. Slightly more melancholic, just like before any big change, but overall she's holding up. It just sucks to think about leaving. Understandable. It’s going to be different without you here. Hopefully it’ll be good for all of us, though. London’s where the jobs are in English teaching, and it’s just a dream city for travel and culture. And those big London salaries or so I'm told. Sure, they are plenty but it’s the cost of living in the city. You’re right about that, but the experience and benefits outweigh the expense for me. Well, at least you have some extra cash to cover the mortgage on the nice little flat you’ve found. Exactly. Thankfully, I got that sorted out. It’s in a good area, and the landlord seems cool. Just need to sort out the moving in stuff. Speaking of flat, and this might be a bit off-topic, but how’s your partner managing the news? He’s not from around here, right? No, he's from Glasgow. It’s another city to adapt to for him, but he's being great about it. There will be moments of frustration, but I think the cultural experiences will help. Glasgow – I spent a week there years ago. Lovely place. I’m sure he’ll love it, but it’s just different. Hopefully, he finds a good social scene to fit into. Again, agreed. He’s already searching for stuff online and he’s quite excited about the prospect of job opportunities and joining a local football team. That’s good. A good social connection can make all the difference. And company. I know that well, too. We better pull over to a services for a bit? I’m running low on coffee and I need to stretch my legs. We have about 15 minutes before the next service area. I can survive.

Right, so I think it's time we start making concrete plans for Mum's birthday meal. It'd be lovely to do something special for her. Absolutely. What are we thinking? Are we still on the idea of hosting it at your place and making the meal ourselves? Yeah, I was thinking that because it's her birthday and she's always been about making sure everyone's together. It makes sense to have it at home. Makes perfect sense. Okay, so let's discuss the menu. Are there any particular dishes she likes? Well, she's a sucker for fish. Always has been. But since she's been with this dementia, she's had a few issues with trying new things. So, perhaps we could keep it simple with something she knows and loves. Right. So a traditional English dinner perhaps? Fish and chips, a bit of roast beef or a nice stew? Exactly. But since it's her birthday and she likes fish, it might be a good idea to center the meal around that. Perhaps we could even do some variations of her favorite dishes. Sure, that makes sense. But how do we handle her preferences with the dementia? We should probably keep everything familiar. Absolutely. Sticking with known favorites and perhaps even serving the food in the same way she used to have it could help keep her comfortable and happy. A good point. Speaking of familiar, how about the table plan and seating arrangements? We should keep everything as normal as possible, don't we? Definitely. I was thinking we could arrange it exactly like it always is when we have dinner at my place. Just to make her feel like everything's on track and normal. Good idea. And should we have any extra help in case she needs it, perhaps someone to keep an eye on her? That's a good idea. Perhaps one of us can keep an extra watchful eye on her throughout the meal. We could also make sure everything's easy to reach and simple to use. Makes sense. And what about the decorations? Should we keep it simple like always or do something special for her birthday? I was thinking we could add a bit of a celebration touch. Maybe some extra candles and a cake. Just to make it feel like a special day. Nice. And since it's Saturday and we're having it at my place, I can take care of baking the cake if you'd like.

Yo, I've gotta go to the dentist to get me wisdom's taken out. Got a bit of a hole in one too n all. It's proper gnawing me out at the back of me mind. You had to deal with any of that? Oh, yes, I remember when I had mine done. It was just so uncomfortable! I had one hole in my tooth and another one in my gum because of the wisdom that was coming out. I'm right glad it's over with. Aye, I'm not looking forward to it. Think about it most days. You get any blunders, any tips on how to deal with the aftercare? Well, you have to be careful about what you eat, avoid sugary stuff, and make sure you keep the area clean. But honestly, following the dentist's instructions will do the trick. That makes sense. I want to avoid any infection or anything like that. Exactly. Also, when it comes to your parents, did you get any funny comments from them about it? Yeah, he was like, "Well, this is it. The end of your childhood dental experiences" and she was all "But they're called wisdom teeth, you assumed we'd grown wise beyond your years" so they were quite the jokesters about it. Haha, that's classic. Well, at least you've got a couple of laughs from it all. I must say, it feels good to finally tackle all these health things as an adult. Yeah, it feels good to finally deal with these things on your own. doesn't feel much like you're growing up until things like this start happening. Definitely. Speaking of growing up, planning to go back to uni this fall? Yeah, I just applied, thinking of doing a history degree. But it feels a bit odd, you know? Like, me and uni weren't that great of friends last time and now I'm planning to go back. Oh, change of heart then? Or maybe it's because you've got a bit more time to focus this time? A bit of both, I think. And also, I've realized I like uni life sorta. It's not the studying so much, it's the whole living away from home and managing stuff on your own. Clearly, I'm hearing a little maturity knocking at the door.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I made those lactose-free cakes and cookies for Alex's birthday party last year? They were a big hit even though the original recipe had cheese in it. No! That sounds fun! Can you make me some? Yeah, can you? And maybe use some of our big wooden chess and draughts pieces to act as coins? That would be cool for playing shop during Chinese New Year! I think that's a great idea actually. We could create our own little 'gold coins' with the chess and draughts pieces. And yes, of course, we can definitely make those cakes and cookies for the upcoming Chinese New Year celebrations. And can we dye your hair different colours while we make the cakes? It'll be like we're celebrating before the actual celebrations! That might be a bit too much for today. But we can definitely try out some fun hair ties or hair ornaments. What about some random acts of kindness? That would also go with the spirit of Chinese New Year, right? Absolutely, that's a brilliant idea! What if we made some homemade sweets or gifts for our neighbours? Or maybe cleaned up the park nearby? We could also use some of our old things and give them away as charity for the needy. Oh, that would be so fun! We could make little good luck bags with things like lactose-free cookies and tea, kind of like 'harmony parcels' for our neighbours. Yeah, and we could make little cards to go with them. We could write good luck wishes and our wishes for them for the new year! That's such a lovely idea! We can make a list of all the things we could do together. What if we teach Alex some new words in Chinese and make homemade decorations for our house too? That would be a great Chinese New Year project for all of us. We could even make some little lanterns out of those glass jars in the kitchen. And then we can light them up with fairy lights! That would look amazing. It would indeed. I love the enthusiasm you all have! So, when can we start? Alright, let's plan this out. Saturdays from now on, why don't we dedicate a couple of hours to these activities? We can make a schedule for our projects and act of kindness.

Mum, I've been meaning to talk to you about last year's car accident. Oh, sweetie, yes. I've been meaning to ask you how you're coping with everything that happened. Well, it's still a bit tough. I got a few scars, you know, just above my knee and a bit on my elbow. They're fading, but sometimes they still hurt. But mentally, how are you doing? You know, with all the doctors and things? Yeah, it was a bit overwhelming at first. But it's better now, okay. Like, I started reading more after the accident, just to take my mind off things. I've been reading Alice in Wonderland and it's actually really helped. That's good, I'm glad reading has helped you. What's been your favorite part so far? It's hard to pick just one, but I guess it's how Alice seems to just bounce back from all these weird and crazy things. It's like she's got this toughness or whatever. So, you see yourself in Alice? Maybe facing this accident has made you stronger, like Alice. I don't know, maybe. But it's weird, while I was in the hospital, they gave me this weird make-up thing to help hide the scars. And the nurse said I looked like a character from Alice in Wonderland, like the Queen of Hearts or something. Well, there you go. You're already channeling your inner Alice, and all those fantastic and scary characters. Okay, it wasn't exactly "channelling," more like looking like a mess, but yeah, I get what you mean. You know, I just got this beautiful costume for your music concert. I saw it matched with the Alice theme. What do you think? Oh, that's awesome! I love it, thanks so much! I knew you'd like it. Where did you find it? Online? Yeah, most of the time it's just easier. Plus, it allows so much variety. I found one for myself too actually. Really? That's cool. What about the internet in general? Sometimes it feels like it's just overuse and oversharing. But then I realised how much it helped me connect with other people who went through similar things. That's a great point. I agree. But it's also important to know when to disconnect, like read this really cool book instead...

Ah, I was pondering over the meeting we had last night. It felt like we were back in our teaching days, didn't it? This time though, our subject was local politics rather than English grammar. Indeed it did! I must say though, the fight this group is putting up against those wind turbines is quite admirable. It seems they've done their homework well and understand the local geography and wildlife quite well. Absolutely, it's very much about understanding local conditions and impacts. Our advice last night was mainly focused on how to respond to the planning appeals. It seems like these energy companies just don't seem to care about the local ecosystem. Exactly, and I believe that's where the government needs to step in with more support to research into better methods. Everyone seems to just pin their hopes on big solar panels or wind farms without considering how they might impact the local environment and wildlife. The government has its priorities wrong, as usual. They throw money at subsidies for these energy corporations, but seem reluctant to fund good scientific research on efficient and environmentally friendly solutions. Storage's the real key, I think. For sure. We mentioned to the group last night that they need to focus on convincing the planning committee of the need for more research into energy storage methods. It's a bit technical but it's the future. Absolutely right, the council and the planning committee have quite a lot of power but are under a lot of pressure from developers and energy companies. They need to be presented with a strong, well-researched case for why these wind turbines are not the answer. We discussed tactics and strategies and they will need to plan their approach carefully. And the 'politics' of it all, as you mentioned. It's like a whole different game. We've seen it during our teaching days, less so in the commerce world where I came from. True. The local council is a web of alliances and deals. They often get influenced by who's got the most lobbying power and influence. That’s what makes it a fight for the local community. And then you've got the energy companies, they often try to make sure the people most affected by these plans are just seen as 'NIMBYs' - not in my back yard. It's so much more than that though.

Right, now I think it's time we discuss who's going to teach you to drive. You know, I learned from my old mate at work, but he was more of a driving instructor than proper driving instructor. You should be doing this properly with a real instructor. Still, now, the cost, eh? Oh, absolutely. Going through an approved school or instructor is the way to go. Plus, it helps with insurance costs too. I've heard you can get discounts if you've learnt through an approved service. And it's not just money, it's about safety too. Learning from a proper instructor ensures we know you're going to be safe on the roads. Remember when I learned? It was quite different, we didn't have all these safety features in cars like you have now. True, true. And from what I've heard, insuring a learner's car is going to be quite pricey. Plus you need to look into the right cover. We've decided on a comprehensive policy, but we need to ensure you're fully covered, you know? Exactly. And it might be worth shopping around, speaking to insurers directly. Some offer discounts for new drivers if they've passed the test within a certain timeframe, for example. I can help with that if you want. You should. Good insurers are good to have at any time, not just when you're learning. They can be a bit pricey, but think of it like a necessary expense for ensuring you're protected. Right. Now, can we talk holidays? You've got that time off from work, so I was thinking maybe we could plan something? Just a small trip somewhere. doesn't have to be grand, just a bit of a change of scenery. Oh, that sounds wonderful! There are so many great places around the UK we haven't explored yet. I’ve always wanted to visit the Lake District. The Lake District is lovely. Or we could think about something closer to home, like going down to Cornwall. Last year we went to Devon, it was a great break. You could also help with the planning, might make it more enjoyable for you to learn. I hadn't thought of Cornwall or Devon, but both sound wonderful. And yes, helping with planning could be beneficial indeed for all of us. Speaking of planning, what are our plans for the coming week?

Oh, Dad, remember when you used to take me to those horse races when I was a teenager? It was always such an adventure! Ah, yes! You were quite the keen participant. Still have any interest in betting, though? A bit, just for fun. More likely to use the Facebook group than physical betting. Though, sometimes the notifications drive me mad. And the constant fracturing of attention, eh? All very distracting. True. Back in my day, if you wanted to know the weather, you had to look out the window. Or at least wait for the news. Not like the endless stream of digital predictions we have today. But seriously, have you seen the weather lately? They say it’s going to be a properly wet summer. Yes, looking like rain nearly every day. Reminds me of the summer when… well, never mind. Off track. Actually, that makes me think about Brighton. You and Mum used to tell stories about moving to Brighton after you met in the 50s. What made you decide on Brighton initially? Stunned at the question, chuckles. Well, we were young and wanted to get away from the city. Brighton offered promise and a bit of adventure, perhaps? Though, parking has never been easier. Exactly! We might have spoken about it before but can't park anywhere without spending hours nowadays… Well, Brighton was our own little piece of escape. And the fresh seafood! Never forget the days we’d have fish and chips right by the pier. Oh, I remember. You even made me eat fish and chips by the shore once. My first experience with proper seafood, but I was so intrigued by the whole environment. Indeed, that was before the time of global warming and plastic waste talk everywhere. It was simpler then, but still so much to learn from those days. Absolutely. It’s one of the reasons I try to focus on healthy eating now. Wonder what folks in the 50s thought about diet if they even considered it? Diet? We didn’t really think about it. We just ate what we had. Fresh produce was usually from the local market or your mum's... Dad, if only things were simpler now. I mean, I really try to eat healthily but it feels like every day is a battle with some fad diet or another. Don’t get on that bandwagon, kid.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that Shakespeare course last year's module? I found it super interesting, especially when we delved into the literary devices they used. Yeah, I remember. Shakespeare's been on my radar quite a bit lately. Still trying to get through his Collected Works though – massive undertaking, right? Absolutely! I mean, he's the master of complexity, but did you know that some of his most famous lines of sarcasm are still relevant today? “All the world’s a stage” – how true is that coming from someone who lived 500 years ago? Hahaha, totally – and the way he seemed to predict modern life's absurdities. "To thine own self be true" – applies even to relationships on Instagram! Exactly! What's new with you though? Anything interesting happening? Actually, I've been spending a lot of my free time learning how to play golf. Got my first set last week and crashed the first game entirely. But it's all about progress, right? Winning or not, that's so cool! Golf isn't exactly my thing, but learning new skills is always fascinating. Even the process of "winning" at something is interesting – the 'win' can be so subjective. For sure. I mean, you can't win at golf unless you're Tiger Woods, right? But hey, getting better is the 'win,' as long as you're having fun. Spot on! Speaking of competition, we’re probably in a similar boat as far as 'winning' goes when it comes to finding a job post-grad. Oh, that’s always a concern. I’m wondering, have you started applying anywhere yet or just planning? Just doing the planning phase for now. But I did apply to some internships and part-time jobs. We’re living in a time when job markets are tough, and personally, I feel like it's really about building experience, rather than winning a specific job right out the gates. Definitely. I'm in that same situation – more focused on getting experience and skill-building rather than securing a dream job right away. And speaking of names, what's up with British last names? So often show up in funny and unexpected places. Yeah, I laughed at the surname of this professor we had - Martin Black. I mean, sounds like he’s just predicting his future career as a professional. Totally random funny thinking! Haha, those seem to creep up everywhere.

Right, so I had this absolute nightmare of a day at work. We have this big conference coming up and I realized yesterday that we've only got a month to go and we're nowhere near ready. Oh no, that sounds stressful. How are you managing? Well, I've been working late days and nights, but honestly it feels like it's never ending. I totally get where you're coming from. I was fracturing out nails trying to deal with budget set for my production line yesterday. keeps changing right till the last moment. Yeah, that's been my life in labor jobs – always dealing with last moment changes and tight deadlines. Exactly! It just seems like there is never enough time. Yeah, but at the end of the day, well managed organization should prevent that right? It's supposed to be like that, but sometimes it feels like we're always firefighting. Did you grab a wine or not? Yeah, I grabbed a bottle. It's our favorite Merlot this time. That's always nice after a busy day. Speaking of drinks, have any of you made any good decisions about your daily drink choices lately? Well, I've been trying to cut down on my intake over the past couple of weeks. It's always a struggle, especially after a tough day like today! I've started drinking more water and less wine. And when I do drink wine, I make sure it doesn't come close to my 2 weekly units. I guess my daily drink of choice remains beer. But I am trying to be more mindful of how much and when I drink. I tried the whole drinking water routine for a while but it's just not as satisfying as wine or beer. But I know it's better for me, long term. True, but changing habits is tough. Anyone plan anything fun for this weekend? Well, for me it’s either a continuation of conference prep, or maybe a quick escape to the countryside for some peace and quiet. Speaking of country escapes, I was thinking about heading to Oxford for the weekend. Want to join? I would love to! But I’ve got to check if my conference prep can pause for a day. That sounds like a great idea. I've been feeling stressed lately and could use the break too.

Ah, marvellous weekend we've had haven't we? The eclipse was quite a sight. Indeed, it was a spectacle. Though I think it was a bit of a letdown. We were all excited and then it seemed to end just as quickly as it started! Oh, I just loved it! Seeing the moon slowly taking over and the darkening of everything, it was quite magical. Now, I was just thinking... I had a bit of a disagreement with the TV License people recently. They want me to still pay full price when I barely use my TV. That lazy lot! Can't they see that pensioners like us don't have much need for Television these days? Might just watch the news or a film. And the attitude of some of the younger staff. As if we are just old fogies who don't know what we're doing! Exactly! But speaking of creative things, have you watched the new painting programme? I saw a bit on it and thought it was quite enlightening for us non-artistic folk. Yes, that was actually a wonderful programme. One moment they were painting a flower and the next they were diving into the mysteries of the cosmos! The paint assumed mythical meanings of black holes and the beginnings of space. That is really something, isn't it? Who would've thought painting could cover such range? It also reminded me of how much time we spend arguing over political correctness. Seems as though no matter what you say, someone will find a fault in it. I know what you mean. It's like it's become a minefield. And then you have to be so careful with what you say or you're suddenly some kind of villain. More breathing room in conversations would be nice! True. Anyway, enough about that. How are those plants coming along? I was meaning to dive in to some gardening but it's been too cold lately. Oh, my garden is my sanctuary. I've been tending to my geraniums and they're doing fairly well. But I saw you put up a new owl box! How is that so far? Quite pleased with it! The owls are quite shy so we haven't seen them very often. But there are almost always signs that they've been around. Did you know, Costessey is a great place for owls.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new restaurant that's opened up in Newcastle? Yeah, I saw it on social media. I talked to someone who's tried it. They said it's really good. Really? What kind of food do they do? Apparently, it's a fusion of European and Asian cuisine. Sounds interesting, but I haven't had the chance to check it out yet. You know, I used to love trying out new restaurants when we were students. Remember how much time we spent driving around Sunderland and checking out all those new places? Even the ones that weren't all that great just because they were new! Haha, yes! I think my record for worst was that Thai place we went to in places of study. It was like they cooked the food with just soy sauce and nothing else. Oh, god, I completely forgot about that. It didn't even deserve to be called Thai food, let alone decent food! You know, it's funny how those kinds of experiences or even place names can trigger such vivid memories. I was just on a project in Winchester and it reminded me of that time we took the bus from Harpenden to Southampton. I had the 'divine' pleasure of sitting beside this person with the worst body odor I've ever encountered. Well, at least you're not equating nice place names with unpleasant experiences! Winchester's quite beautiful, especially the cathedral isn't it? Yeah, the cathedral in Winchester is stunning. And the houses around that area are quite old and charming doesn't they? But it's not just about the physical structures, it's the atmosphere and the history you feel when you're walking around those places. Absolutely, there's something special about old cathedrals isn't there? The way the light shines through those stained glass windows. It's almost... spiritual. Indeed. That and the silence within. While I was there, a group of children came in on a field trip. They were all whispering and trying to make the least amount of noise. It was adorable. Kids always manage to find the most unique ways to appreciate things, don't they? They definitely do. You know, kids and animals are almost universally welcomed anywhere, just for the effect of innocence they bring with them. Do you remember that time we went to St. Paul's in London?

Ah, marvellous weekend. I spent most of Saturday's afternoon in my garden. It's been quite therapeutic, watching the birds and tending to the flowers. Lovely! Mine's still a work in progress, isn't it? I must admit, this past week, I've been bombarded with questions from students about the difference between house sparrows and finches. Ah, absolutely. I'm quite fond of actually, identifying birdsong. There's something so peaceful and almost ancient about it. True. It's like they have their own language we're just slowly learning to understand. Idle, dear Idle, that's it! I had a rather interesting encounter with one bird recently, a robin that started visiting my garden. It started following me around, almost as if it was guided by an invisible thread. That's quite a unique experience. We've had robins in our garden too, but they've never been so forward. Well, it got so curious it would hop near me even while I was doing other tasks. Now that I think of it, it reminded me of feeding the birds when I was younger. You know, feeding birds can be quite a bonding experience. I remember in Chester, my parents had a bird table and we'd all gather around it in the mornings. Wonderful, isn't it? It's always surprising how much pleasure it can bring. Like a small, daily interaction with nature. I'm all for it. Though, sometimes I worry about the intrusive prowling of birds in my garden. Last week, the doves were so loud, my alarm clock had to compete to wake me up. Can you imagine, waking up to both a bird and an alarm? The avian alarm. If only we could program it to sound like birdsong instead of that irritatingly loud noise! Yes, perhaps we might wake up a bit more gently next time. Speaking of alarms, I just came from the dentist. I always take a bit of a nosebleed after a clean. Oh dear, I hope it wasn't too bad. Nosebleeds can be quite alarming, especially the first few times you experience them. No, not too bad. It just shows the importance of regular check-ups. Absolutely. And it's such a small price to pay for good oral health. Though, I do prefer feeding the birds over the dentist's chair any day! Agreed!

Ah, it's been ages hasn't it? How've things been with you since we last caught up? They've been good, thanks for asking. Had quite a few changes going on but I'm enjoying it all really. That’s great! I've had some questions on my mind regarding some conversations we've had in the past and I thought it might be a good idea to touch upon that now. Fire away. I'm all ears. I remember during one of our conversations, you mentioned something about IVF. You went through it, right? Did you have success with it in the end? I did have success, thankfully. It wasn't an easy journey but it was worth it. I ended up having two beautiful daughters from that process. Congratulations! That must have been a very emotional period for you, I can imagine. Yes, very emotional. But the end result? Absolutely worth it. I'm very grateful. Now, how about you? Have you ever considered any changes or new plans recently? I have actually. I've been mulling over a few ideas myself. I’ve been considering taking a break from teaching and maybe looking into another path that benefits from my educational background. Do tell, what's on your mind? Well, for a while now, I've been really interested in writing a book, maybe something related to my area of expertise, or even about my experiences as a teacher. But I also couldn't help but notice that you're a single parent now. How do you manage things with the girls and work? It's definitely challenging but rewarding at the same time. There are days when it feels overwhelming, of course. But I've learned to try and balance things as much as I can. The girls are good support too – they're growing up so quickly. It's impressive how you've been able to handle it all. I often think about the pressures and expectations single parents face and it really puts things into perspective. Absolutely. But in these busy times, I've found yoga to be quite a helpful tool. I mean, doesn't sound like it would help with the chaos of single parenthood and work, but it really does. Yeah, I've heard people rave about the benefits of yoga. Did you try it out randomly or came across it through work?

Ah, lovely to see you over for a cup of tea, Mr. Johnson. How are you finding retirement? Fine, fine. It's been a bit quiet, of course, but I'm not complaining. There's plenty of time to read and watch the telly. You know, things I never had time for when I was teaching. I'd expect as much. Being a teacher can be quite demanding, I'm sure. I'm right in the midst of it myself, trying to keep up with lesson plans and marking. It's a whole different ball game these days. When I started, there weren't as many exams and there wasn't as much paperwork. Technology, too - I used to write lesson plans in a notebook. Now, I hear you're doing most of it online. Ah, yes - the old notebook method! I still keep a paper planner. But everything is online now, so you're right - it's a different world. It also means we can reach out to students more easily, and that can be good. But it also means there's less of that personal touch, I think. That's a very valid point. I've seen that change over the years too. It's funny, I was thinking about this the other day. My older students used to argue with me about grammar, in good spirit of course. They'd say things like, "But Mrs. Johnson, it sounds better this way!" I get that, all the time. "But why can't we say it like this?" It's fantastic actually. It means they're thinking critically about the language and questioning established norms. Exactly, it proves they're learning the skills we're supposed to teach. Nowadays, though, I do worry sometimes if technology is getting in the way of actual learning. I mean, I grew up in Birmingham, just like you. Really? We're not far from each other. I come from Hitchin, but moved here to teach. Birmingham has a lot to offer, educationally and otherwise. You'd think so, wouldn't you? But over the years, there's been a decline in standard for local schools. Funding issues, you see. And crime - so much crime. Makes me worry for the future. Yes, the crime rate does concern me too. As a teacher, I've seen students affected by it in all sorts of ways. And the political rhetoric we hear sometimes, it's all about cuts and efficiency.

Yo, lads and lasses. What d'ye think about's this weekend? Got any plans for a decent film night? I've got a copy of 'The Guvnor' which I thought we could watch if anyone's interested. It's one of our classics up north, innit? That sounds grand! I'd like that. We could get some decent grub and make a whole thing out of it. Although, I'm not sure about this 'The Guvnor'... I've never heard of it before. Is it a movie about a fight promoter or what? Oh, sweetheart, 'The Guvnor' is about a boxer from Manchester, Gary Hall's day out. Classic British comedy. Though, let me tell ya, even up North, not all of us are boxing fans but it's a part of the culture we grew up with. And to be fair, it's a pretty lovable watch. Ron, you know how it is. English cinema, it's all about the charm. And it's funny because it's so far removed from our usual watch list but still, it's one of those films that can bring us all together and make us feel nostalgic, even if we're not from Manchester. Plus, who doesn't love a bit of 'Rae in the Hole'? Aye, 'Rae in the Hole' is bloody brilliant! It's all good though, no worries if it's not your cup of tea. But as for grub, what about some of these new, trendy takeaway places we've found? There's one that does proper, traditional Lancashire hotpot. Oh, that sounds ideal! I've been wanting to try some authentic Northern cuisine. We can just grab some curry from the Balti side of town, they do a decent job and won't break the bank either. I've been meaning to try it out for ages. Good shout. That and maybe some bonfire night treats, if we're lucky. It's nearing that time of year. Speaking of food, has anyone seen 'The Great British Baking Show'? The past season was brilliant. Reminded me of my gran's teachings. Again and again! That baking show never disappoints. Although, if we're being honest, I've had enough of fancy desserts. I'm craving something proper Northern. Like a good pie or some Stottie cake. Now that's a different story. Sure, let's ditch the fancy stuff.

Yo, anyone hear about that new gym opening in town? I’ve been looking for something new to shake things up. Yeah, I saw the ad. It’s supposed to be quite high tech. Better than my current one anyway. High tech is all well and good, but personally I just like a good piece of equipment and a buddy for motivation. Spot on. I've been using a new app to track my progress. It really helps keep me on track. Are you still using Gymshark? Yeah, been on it for a while. It’s quite good for routine and sticking to plans. I've just been to their shop in Cambridge, got some new gear. Their leggings are comfortable for yoga or even a run. Hence the importance of a good buddy system, so you're not just stuck on apps! True, but the tech these days can't be beaten. I mean, think about it, machines track everything for you, even your heart rate. Absolutely, it helps you see improvements and push yourself further. I just wish the prices weren't so steep. Yeah, but the quality and the results speak for themselves, right? Well, technology aside, travel is another thing. Anyone up for a trip? Possibly visiting all these new gyms?! Speaking of which, have you all seen the weather forecast for this weekend? Yeah, I saw that. It's supposed to be the perfect summer day. Ideal for a road trip or a hike. But the problem with great weather is the crowds, right? Every decent spot just gets packed. That's true, but it's a small price to pay for a sunny day. Plus, it's great for traveling and meeting new people. True. I mean, I've been listening to a podcast about visiting all of England's hidden gems. They're not always crowded. That sounds interesting! Can you suggest any? There's this one small village in Cumbria, it's called Bampton. Super off the beaten path, and almost breathtaking landscapes. I love those hidden spots. Always reveal something unique about a place. Totally makes sense thinking about it. So, anyone up for that trip to Cumbria this weekend? Definitely interested... but do any of our schedules allow for that? Well, yeah, we're all off work this weekend, right? Unless someone has a prior engagement? I don't, but youth camp starts Monday.

Oh, did you see that last move by Sterling? I swear today's match is more exciting than Jeopardy and Mastermind combined! You love your football, Alison! But I agree. It’s been quite the match, hasn't it? Now, questions for you - what’s the plan for Easter? Any traditions happening at your place this year? Oh absolutely! We usually end up with a lovely Easter brunch at home, and then later in the afternoon my family comes over for an egg hunt. It’s actually a pretty big deal for my siblings and their kids, keeps them all entertained. That sounds lovely! I used to love egg hunts as a kid. Do you remember that film we watched a while back, the one with the old man who finds that magic ticket? Hmm, I think you're referring to "Mr. Magorium's Wonder Emporium?" But if it's the one with the old man and the magical ticket, it might actually be "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory". No wait, he was more of a wealthy man given a magical ticket and it reminded me of both but it might be different film. Exactly! "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory"! You’re right though, that old man, Mr. Wonka, does come across as quite peculiar yet magical! Yeah, right, it’s that one. The chocolate in there looks so good but also makes me feel guilty for even thinking about all those calories. Well, it's Easter! A little indulgence can't hurt. Speaking of indulgence, did you hear about that new series on Netflix about the Manchester team? More football? Oh, I saw the preview for that. I'm actually quite excited. It’s another opportunity to learn more about the game and dive deep into the world of football and it’s rich history. Yeah, I'm diving into it after this match. I'm actually using some of that football history for my PhD, exploring how public perceptions of football clubs changed over the years. That’s fascinating! Your work must give you a unique perspective on the world of football, and even film. Some of these players are almost like mythic figures to us. Exactly! The players, the matches, everything - it's all part of a larger narrative. For example, I just watched something that compared the rivalry between Manchester and Liverpool to the rivalry between two characters in that old cliché film “When Harry Met Sally”.

Ah, look at these. These are from your trip to Glasgow, aren't they? You met up with the Joneses, right? That looks like the tea room down by the cathedral. Yeah, that's right. I was so impressed with the city. But my favorite part was going to the science center. It was so cool. But why are we going through old photos, eh? Well, it's to remember, darling. Even though you're always on your laptop or phone, these are memories you have made. And in your life, that just started. While your son, my grandson... Yes, memories are precious, aren't they? This one especially. This was taken on his first birthday, if I'm not wrong. You were so little then. Almost two years between these photos already! Time flies, doesn't it? We should make more of an effort to document these moments. Yeah, but it's hard when I'm trying to study or meet friends. Though, come to think of it, this London Marathon photo... Do you remember when we all went to watch it, all four of us? Oh yes, doesn't time fly? But it's moments like those we cherish. I hope he grows up seeing these and understands the importance of such events and the people who participated in his life. Glasgow, indeed. And think of all the years I spent teaching. I never thought I'd miss it as much as I do now, but changing the world one pupil at a time was very rewarding. Speaking of people making a difference, have you seen the news about the Iceland trip? I mean, those glaciers... if anyone wants to see a glacier up close and have a real adventure. We could all do with adventure, couldn't we? Although, maybe a cinema night with a fun film is more up my alley right now. Cinemas, fun fairs, that's what keeps the spirit young, however old one is. Remember the time we took the kids to the fun fair in Belfast? They had such a great time. Though, mostly youthful energy at that, eh? Indeed. The energy, the laughter. But why not combine fun fairs with something educational? We can all learn a thing or two. Yeah, like the Science Centre in Glasgow. Or even a rare film screening, a classic movie night. A film night? That's a great idea.

Ah, marvellous weekend. I'm so glad we decided to have Grace over today. The lentil stew is almost ready, and I've made a lemon and poppyseed cake for tea. Right, lovely to see you too, and the meal looks divine. I've been meaning to try a lentil stew for ages. "Lentil stew" makes me think of my childhood, actually. We used to make a similar thing back at home. Really? That's interesting. Did you eat it a lot when you were young, then? Oh, yes. My mum made it often. I used to love it. She had this old recipe book that was passed down from her mum. Oh, that's lovely. I suppose food can be tied to so many memories. Definitely. It's a shame that sometimes these recipes get lost over time. Absolutely. I've tried to write some of them down for the grandkids, but I'm sure I'm not doing them justice. They're missing out on the nuances that only come from being taught how to cook by watching the process. I think that's one of the things that sets traditional recipes apart - the way they're often taught orally, passed down by generations. Right. I remember when I first started cooking, my grandmother would always pull out her old book of recipes. She had notes scrawled in the margins all over the place. The old recipes weren’t written down too carefully either. There was always this 'A handful of flour' or 'Season to taste'. It was more an art of winging it based on what was in the cupboard. Speaking of which, do either of you still knit or crochet? It's one of those traditional skills that's making a bit of a comeback, but also seems to be slowly lost. I knit, though not as often as I used to. I've got a few projects on the go at home. I used to be quite into crochet when I was younger. Made a lot of blankets and scarves. I've just started to learn. I've got this crotcheted blanket for the little ones at home, and it's been a fun but slow process. You will get there. There's something so meditative about it. I know exactly what you mean. I used to sit for hours listening to the radio or watching the telly while I crocheted.

Right, so I was going over some of these old family photos the other day. Got me thinking; how did we turn out to be such good friends, when our routes in life could hardly have been more different? You, working all your life, and me... well, it just didn't work out like that, did it? You'd think it'd have been a recipe for disaster, wouldn't you? But we've always managed to find common ground. I think it's because we met in a time when life was simpler, and we didn't let the outside world define us. Simple, indeed. I remember when I was about 25, just had my first job, and thought this is it. This is the life I'll have. But then, things didn't quite pan out. And from there, it was a downhill spiral. I remember when I did my sixthform at Harrow, I was so determined to work and make a difference. But when it came to it, the work world just wasn't kind to me. I tried childminding, loved it, but it wasn't enough. So I ended up staying at home and raising children. I understand the sense of disappointment. Where did you get the strength from? Stamina and resilience are traits we learn to pick up, I suppose. And sometimes, you don't realize how strong you are till you have to be. Family keeps you grounded. Speaking of which, how have the family in Costessey been doing? Family's always been good. Smaller over the years, but good. Costessey's changed, it's not the village I grew up in anymore. But family ties, they're stronger than anything, aren't they? Definitely. I miss my days of childminding a bit, though. It wasn't just a job; it was a way to keep active, to feel useful. But I've enjoyed my retirement too, in its own way. We've both had a very changing journey, haven't we? Changing – and that’s what I suppose keeps things interesting. But sometimes I wonder if we're just lucky, or if there's something more to it. You want to know the secret to being lucky? Being content with what you have and managing to find joy in the everyday. Maybe our job wasn't defined by paychecks or societal expectations, but we found satisfaction in other things – friends like each other, family connections.

Oh, mates, it's been ages. How have you all been? I've just been super busy since the term started. I've got thirty bright little munchkins under my wing now, but I love every minute of it. Morning, Sarah! Really? Thirty? That's quite the hive of activity! I'm sure they keep you on your toes. I've been a bit swamped too - prepping for my new class, as I've graduated to older kids this term. They can be quite a handful! keeps me on my toes, but it's rewarding. Even with thirty, I'm sure it's nothing compared to what I used to have back in my early years of copywriting, dealing with even dozens of clients at the same time. But really, how do you find the new age group? Any particular challenges or fun moments you've had? Oh, there are loads of challenges, of course, but the fun moments are what make it all worth it. Just last week, we had a science lesson where we made a volcano. It was a total mess, but the kids were absolutely beside themselves with excitement. That sounds fun. I had a great time with my last class, they were good kids, but this new age group is quite interesting - they can't keep up with their hormones or their technology. It's like a whole different language I need to learn! I know exactly what you mean. Communication is key, no matter the age. We have similar challenges with 'digital language' in copywriting. Sometimes, it's like trying to decipher another language from the clients. Indeed! Speaking of challenges, I've just had to deal with a very sticky situation with the school's budget. They've been cutting costs, and we're really struggling for certain resources. It's making things a bit tricky. Oh, budget cuts are always a nightmare. I've heard of it happening in my area too. It's really tough on the kids. Education gets squeezed far too often for my liking. On a different note though, what do you all want for Christmas this year? Any wish list items yet? I've been thinking about getting some new books for my class. There's this brand new set of 'Stone Age to Iron Age' resources, and I've been meaning to show my kids everything from stone tools to pottery.

Ah, good day everyone. Lovely to see you all's here. I hope today's no too busy for us. I've got a thing about our neighbourhood, talked to a few folks, and well, there's been some changes. You know, new neighbors moving in and all.      Yeah, I've noticed that too. We've had a few new families arrive, and it's quite a mix. You'll get that in Liverpool, innit? But I have to say, I'm a bit worried about the new flat building opposite St. Michael's. Are you seeing it, too?      Yeah, I've seen it. I heard it's supposed to be some sort of affordable housing, but I'm not sure what that means for us, really.      Exactly, affordable for whom, though? Our council's been a bit quiet about this. And while it's important to provide housing solutions, sometimes I feel like they forget about the people already living here. You know, upgrading the area but barely considering the impact on the current residents.      Mr. ----, do you really think we'll get new neighbors? That would be so cool!      Yeah, it could be nice. But the thing is, we need to know if we're getting 'diverse' because they genuinely want to live and integrate with the community or if it's just bringing us new problems.      Ah, but diverse in what way? A mixed bag of, you know, different folk isn't in itself a bad thing. But you're right, we should also be concerned about if it'll increase rents and all that.      Right. It's about the balance between development and maintaining the community we already have here. I mean, we're one of the more culturally mixed areas in L8, and that's part of Liverpool’s charm!      I agree with that. But at the same time, we also need to deal with the housing shortage. Some of us are struggling to find affordable places here, and changing the character of the area too drastically might end up pricing people like us out of our own neighbourhood.      Yeah, like, I like it here just because it's home, you know? And I’ve always thought Liverpool was like a real community.      Absolutely right. Liverpool's about more than just housing; it’s the culture, the history... You all know that. But sometimes I worry that we're losing that.

Ah, marvellous weekend. I'm so excited about our upcoming trip to Nepal. It's been quite some time since I've ventured abroad. Do you remember your first trip, Beryl? Oh, yes indeed! I was 22 years old, and I spent three months backpacking through Europe. It was so eye-opening and life-changing, you know? I wish I could have done something of that sort when I was young. All I did was road trips with my friends up and down the country. But still, nothing beats the adventure and freedom of traveling, right? Exactly! Speaking of adventures, have you all had a chance to check out the new menu at our local village shop? I hear they even have dedicated gluten-free options now. Yes, I tried the new gluten-free sausage rolls last week. They were surprisingly good. It's great they're catering to more dietary requirements. Indeed. I've also noticed the farm shop around the corner is doing a good job of sourcing local produce. They even have a few exotic fruits now which are a bit of a treat. I'm so glad to hear that. As someone who's tried a few different diets throughout my life, it's lovely to see the range of choices. Speaking of food, do you all remember the rationing during the war? Of course, though I was very young at the time. I remember my grandmother always telling us how challenging it was to provide meals for the family with the limited ingredients they had. My mother-in-law survived on meager rations when she traveled from Siberia to Africa during the war. It's hard to imagine the hardships they faced. Indeed. I do recall my mother rationing everything during the war. I remember getting one of those little notebooks where we weren't supposed to eat more than a certain amount of butter or meat per week. It's quite fascinating how people managed to survive and even thrive with such restrictions. You know, it's interesting to see how our diets have evolved over the years. From rations to artisanal food in these new local shops. Indeed. And I must say, I've been experimenting with some of the recipes from that period. They're quite simple and still good. Yeah, I've tried them too. There's a certain charm in those old recipes, isn’t there?

Right, so I had this absolute nightmare of a day at work. We have this big conference coming up and I realized yesterday that we've only got a month to go and we're nowhere near ready. Oh no, that sounds terrible. How are you managing the stress, though? I've been working so much lately too and it's taking a lot out of me. I feel like my whole week has been just prepping for meetings right now. Oh absolutely, me too. But it's not even just the workload, it's all the little things that could go wrong and it's stressing me out. Like what if there's a power cut at the venue, or what if half the speakers cancel at the last minute? It just keeps me up at night. That’s really tough. I feel like that sometimes with production control. Things that might seem small can actually have a huge impact if they go wrong, right? Exactly! But sometimes we need to remind ourselves that we’re all in the same boat. I mean, we all have our own major projects and responsibilities. That's true. So I’m really hoping it all goes smoothly. I've been trying to stay positive and make lists and all that. But it doesn't help when the phone won’t stop ringing and my inbox is full of unanswered emails. Yeah, I know that feeling. Well, at least you're not alone in this. Like, my boss always seems to think we can add an extra project to the list at the last minute. One time they asked me to add a whole new production pipeline with like, three days' notice. But it proves that you're the one that can handle it, doesn’t it? You're reliable. Yeah, in some twisted way it does, I suppose. But it also just feels like they're setting me up for failure. If it helps, we can all vent about our work troubles next time we hangout and maybe offer advice or support each other. Definitely, that’s a plan. Speaking of next time – do we have any plans for the weekend? Actually, I was thinking we could do something chill. Maybe just a walk or a coffee someplace quiet? Sounds good. Maybe we can go to the Botanical Gardens or just walk along the river.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my day? I discovered today that the local council is planning to demolish and sell the old library building. It's just appalling, really. They say they're doing it to cut costs, but I can't believe they haven't considered the community's needs at all. No, you didn't. That's disappointing to hear. Libraries are so important, especially for those who can't afford to buy books or have internet at home. Exactly. And it's not just about the books. It's about community, you know? Like brain training exercises – without engaging activities, people just stay stagnant. It's similar to what's happening with their plans to cut down on local activities. They're ensuring our brains just turn to mush faster than need be. I see. Well, have you thought about doing something about it? A petition perhaps? Actually, I was thinking of that. But I barely have the time with my transcribing job and everything. It's not that I'm lazy, it's just that the volume of work keeps increasing while the time... doesn't. Ah, I know what you mean. My work as an administrator can be equally demanding. But in this case, I think a petition could make a real difference. What if we do it together? Two heads are usually better than one. Hmm, that's an idea. And in all fairness, I do get some time off from work. It couldn't hurt, and it’s definitely something needed. How do you think we could go about starting that? Well, first, we need to make sure we have a solid case, and understand what’s already being done or proposed. Once we have the facts, we can structure our petition to present the most compelling arguments. Great, we can use mnemonics to help us remember the key points too. Like PEAR . You always do that, don’t you? Creating these little memory aids? Yep, it helps, especially when so much of my job is about listening and memos. And brain training? Well, it’s useful, and it’s fun. I can tell. Anyway, about brain training. I started doing some myself recently. It feels good to challenge the grey matter. You will be just as surprised at how it helps your focus and problem-solving skills too. We could even share the best ones with the community as we campaign for the library.

Right, so I've been reading about educating children without school's influence. I discovered today that nearly every child of Jehovah's Witnesses is homeschooled. Quite fascinating, really. You're quite the scholar, are you now? I remember when you were a civil engineer, always questions and answers. It's fascinating though, and it makes me think about how my own children were raised. I always preferred minimal influence of outside factors as much as I could, even though they went to school. Exactly. Homeschooling would let you tailor the knowledge and values to what you think is best for your child. However, it does require a lot of time and dedication, doesn't it? Indeed. I had the luxury of being a childminder and could control the environment they were in. But it wasn't without challenges. It's a different conversation altogether, but I do wish our village could have better educational facilities. Ever noticed how good the schools are in Costessey compared to Mattishall? Yes, Costessey has a higher socio-economic status, on average, so I suppose it's expected. I often feel that our village could do with some more 'push' in education. It sets the tone for the community, you know? Well, politics and taxes – always a hot potato. I'd rather discuss more enjoyable topics, like food. Have you tried that new fish and chips place by the river? They say the batter is exquisite. I don't think so, but it's on my list now. I'm a bit of a traditionalist; I prefer my fish and chips on the beach if I'm eating out. More specifically, in Sheringham or Cromer, isn't it? Yes, yes. But now, with all these parking restrictions at the coast, it's getting a bit complicated to sit back and enjoy dinner without the worry of a parking fine. True – I remember when you had to pay in shillings and pence. Either way, it always felt worth it when you're having fresh fish and chips on the beach. And have you noticed how health conscious some restaurants are becoming? Over here, it's quite the culture shock going from traditional 'pies and mash' to healthier options. Yes, and I think it's good. But sometimes, you just want a good old-fashioned roast dinner. I must admit though, I've been trying to cut down...

Ah, marvellous to see you both again! It's been far too long. How was your trip to Tokyo? I've always wanted to go there, though talked about it rather than actually book a ticket. It was wonderful! The culture, the food, the sights. We were there for two weeks and barely scratched the surface. You really must go, Sarah. I'll keep it in mind. I'm actually struggling right now with a job that I'd rather not deal with. Transcribing logs. It's tedious, even for someone like me. Oh, I can imagine. I've had my fair share of dealing with piles of papers and notes. I used to find it quite calming, but that must depend on what is happening around. Exactly! Right now, it's the "who's on first" kind of thing with the neighbours. They seem to have taken a fancy to having log burners installed, despite the council disapproving of it in the area. That's a bit of a problem. Someone should probably talk to their next door neighbours or even reach out to the local council about it. Yes, but it might be better to start the conversation with the neighbours first. Sometimes these issues can be sorted out without involving the council. As a school master, I can tell you, sometimes people just don't consider how certain actions might impact others. Log burners might be noisy or affect property values. I've been trying really hard to keep everything quiet around the house, but all the drilling and hammering they've been doing makes it difficult. Well, maybe we can help out. As administrative roles, we could help draft a polite and non-confrontational note to them. More diplomacy, always better. I just tried to get the latest local news. Do you know that a new restaurant opened up just a couple of streets from us? It's quite fancy, but looks nice. I'll make sure to add it on my restaurant list. I do enjoy trying new places out. I'm intrigued. Fancy trying it out sometime? Could be a good evening out. And speaking of trying new things, have you tried the sweet shop that's opened up just next to it? They have the most delicious fudge... I've heard they also have quite a good deal on antiques there. Perhaps a visit to both the restaurant and the shop could be something fun.

Right, so I've been reading about this new policy on house buying. Apparently, they're proposing to lower the stamp duty. It could make a big difference to first-time buyers. That's right. There's quite a squeeze on young people trying to get into the housing market these days. As someone who's never had to work and isn't likely to be affected by property taxes, I suppose it's easy for me to say but I think it's a right move. Oh absolutely. All these new taxes and changes always seem to keeps coming backwards and forwards, don't they? Yes, indeed. But I've been thinking about our pensions lately. Do any of you know much about the new government reforms regarding that? I've heard bits and pieces. They're trying to boost the state pension. But the devil's always in the details, isn't it? It's not going to be a quick fix. True, true. I've often thought the government barely understands the struggles of the financially insecure. They claim this and that, but it's all talk. Absolutely. Now, talking about government this and that, have you all seen this new policy on recycling waste? I find the whole system is just a mess. Oh, recycling! It’s all very well and good to encourage us, but the logistics often become too much. Ah, the infamous brown bins saga! A friend of mine, who still works, tried to sort her recyclables really well. But then they refused them because, and I quote, "the wrong type of paper was mixed with the wrong type of glass." The bureaucracy! If they'd just make it simpler, more of us would be more compliant. It’s not just recycling, it’s just the way they always complicate matters. I used to regularly navigate Norfolk's roads when I was younger. But these days, with all these new Sat Navs and apps, it's like you need a degree in technology to just get from A to B. Oh, that's a tale I can attest to! Our grandkids try to show us these new gizmos, but I end up getting more lost than ever trying to follow the instructions! Technology could use a user manual for the elderly sometimes. But then again, the real job I used to have was civil engineering.

Ah, lads and lass, did I ever tell you about the problem I had with my laptop the other day? What happened, Dad? Is it fixed now? No need to worry, it's sorted. Still, though, the warranty, it’s kind of a bit questions. Which one? You got a warranty? Oh, yeah, I did. It's just, I didn't know if I had to send it back to the place where I bought it, or could I get it fixed locally here in town. You know, stuff like that, keeps me on my toes. [laughs] Well, depends on the policy. Sent it away to warranty or taken to a service centre. Yeah, but the thing is, we're planning this little road trip for the rugby. Wouldn't want to be without the laptop, you know? [toddler, playing with his food, speaks up] Did du grab it from Spain? Spain? [laughs] No, kid. But that’s actually a good question. You ever seen this jar of fajita sauce I brought back from Spain? I'm trying to decide if it's still good. Dad, Spanish food’s different. You know that. [laughs] Indeed, lad. But I'm curious to know if it's still good before I toss it. You could try it. You know, sometimes things from the store are good a lot longer than we expect. That’s true. But would anyone like it if I just popped the lid now? Everyone: [blank stares, then laughter] Maybe during the swimming trip? [chuckles] Oh, I love the enthusiasm, but I don’t think our swimsuits will appreciate it. [looking at the toddler and then speaking to Speaker_1] Perhaps changing the subject to something less... pungent might be a good idea. [laughs uneasily] Right, right. Let’s focus on the laptop. Did anyone else run into any tech issues recently? Not really, but have you heard about this new thing, you can turn your phone into a Wi-Fi extender for the laptop? I’ve heard something about that. Not sure how reliable it is though. [giggles] Wi-fi extender! [smiling] Yeah, like turning this [gestures to his phone] into a little booster for your computer. That could be handy for our road trip if the wireless signal isn’t very good in certain parts. Exactly. So, I was thinking maybe we should save that for another time if we need it.

Alright, kids, who first noticed that Dad brought home pizza today? Me! Me! I saw it when he walked in with that big box. And guess what? We're eating pizza while we talk about the Loch Ness monster! That's right, we're combining two of our favorite things right now. Now, who knows what we're trying to talk about for this part of the conversation? You said something about communication, right? Yes, we're going to talk about what's called 'non-verbal communication'. This is when we use things other than words to communicate. For example, when we're eating our pizza, we can't talk while we're chewing. So we use our eyes and hands to communicate instead. So sometimes we nod our heads or point to the pizza if we want someone to pass it? That's non-verbal communication? That's right! You guessed it. And there are other ways too. Like if I'm excited, I might wave my arms or jump up and down. But why do we need to talk about this? It's actually super important.
