It can help us understand each other better, especially if we're not speaking the same language. Can handstands be non-verbal communication? I mean, if I do a handstand, does it mean I'm happy or something? That might not always be the case, but handstands can express joy or confidence. And let me tell you, you're getting really good at those! I can do a handstand right now! Can I show you? Absolutely! But after you finish eating some pizza first. Yeah, and then maybe we can talk about fairy gardens? I want to make one for my birthday party. That sounds like so much fun! After the pizza, we'll definitely work on a fairy garden plan. And we almost forgot about Loch Ness! Is the Loch Ness monster real? Well, that's the fun part! We don't really know for sure. It's a mystery. A real monster! I hope it's real... because that would be so cool. It sure would! Now, let's finish our pizza and then get started on those handstands and fairy gardens. And after that, maybe we can even try to make our own Loch Ness monster stories! We would have to be very good authors for that! That's easy!

I've never eaten anything like this before. The seafood platter is amazing, isn't it? Oh, absolutely. Istrian cuisine is unreal. I wish we could replicate this at home. Yeah! But have you heard about the food tech course we had at school? It was something else, right? Food technology class, right? I was thinking... I wonder how they deal with food preservatives here. The seafood keeps coming right up alongside us. Well, there's always a balance between taste and preservation, isn't there? Absolutely, but have you noticed the diversity of animals around here? It’s a little odd, actually—so many different species in one area. It's because of the climate and geography here. It supports a wide range of flora and fauna. Yeah, and the climate here is quite warm compared to Bolton. Sure, but it's nothing compared to the different climates we want to visit. Where should we go next while the kids are still young? I was thinking somewhere we can enjoy the sun, like a Mediterranean beach. The kids would love that. But have you all seen the swimming pool area? It's right beside us. Oh, we've been over there already! It's awesome doesn't it? But it's a bit too busy for now. Too busy or just planning your next swimming trip? Both! Speaking of getting around, I hope we won't have any issues with immigration next time we travel globally. With everything happening nowadays... You mean like Ebola outbreaks and all? Exactly, that sort of thing. Makes global travel a bit more stressful. And then there’s the air travel itself—how it affects us physically. Did you hear about the new super-jets? They’re supposed to revolutionize air travel. Yeah, I've been following that. They're supposed to make travel less grueling. But, have you noticed how each company now has to contend with newer tech—like finding ways to make travel more eco-friendly... True. But while we're talking about technology, what about marijuana? I mean, it's legal here and in so many places abroad now. Though across the youth of England—like, where we’re from—the views on that are quite mixed. Some are quite open to it while others still have a more conservative view. I mean, I've heard it's like their regular morning coffee around here.

Right, so I had a bit of an issue with these debt collectors. Took me ages to figure out what was what. Oh, talked about that recently. Got some of those letters, right? Aye, I remember. You were a bit confused about what questions to ask, innit? Exactly! They kept on at me about sums I couldn't remember owing and dates... it was all a bit muddled. And how did you manage to sort it out, then? Oh, well, after a few calls and letters – and a few scares – I managed to confirm some of the debts were legitimate. Sent certified letters to those ones to make sure. But there was one company that kept sending demands for money I wasn't even sure we'd borrowed from them. Exactly, they're so convincing, you feel like you've got to pay out, right? That's right! And the letters they send are black on red, or whatever, looks official, doesn't it? Absolutely! I mean, they certainly make it sound like it's legal and everything. Well, we can't allow that. Good on you for sorting it out. Thanks, chap. It's a bit of a hassle, but once you know the right questions to ask... Aye, right, questions like 'Can you confirm the amount and the time of the loan', or 'Can you send verification of the company you're representing and their contact details' – that helps sort out the real from the scammers. That's useful to know. I've had some similar issues. Aye. Seems like the scammers try to make it complicated just to lure you into paying right away. If you're unsure, contact the financial ombudsman or get in touch with a local advice service. They can provide guidance. You'd think after all these years of dealing with these types, they'd refine their scams. But evidently, they still manage to catch people out. It's indeed a shame. Speaking of scammers, have you seen the adverts for PPI claims almost gone now? Used to be all over the telly. Ah, yes, that was a big deal for a while. I saw something about it in a current issue of The Observer. But now it seems there's less noise about it. Maybe because most of the big claims were already made. That could be, although a few still persist though, right?

Ah, after a day in court. I find it always so interesting. But also somewhat depressing. Oh, yes. It's not all champagne and roses, but I suppose that's the nature of our roles. Absolutely. As someone who teaches English, I've had the opportunity to explore the legal vocabulary and phrases, but seeing it in real life, it's quite different from reading about it in a book. Teaching? That must be a fulfilling job! I've always been impressed by how language can shape our societal norms and values. It is. I love it. But it's also had its challenges, you know. The language in our justice system, for instance, is often very formal and can be quite difficult for some students to understand. That's true. As a court usher, I've seen many people struggle with the language and procedures used in court. Exactly. And then there's the whole issue of social context. Words and phrases that might seem clear or straightforward can carry very different meanings within or outside the courtroom. Oh, absolutely. We see that all the time. For instance, what is "reasonable doubt" to one person might be very different to another. Indeed. And even within the realm of language, the level of education can play a significant role in how people understand and interpret the language used in court. That's a great point. And in my experience, it's not just about understanding the words themselves, but also about understanding the social and cultural context in which they're used. Agreed. It's the same with teaching, really. You have to consider the socio-economic and educational backgrounds of your students to effectively communicate the material. Yes, it's all so intertwined, isn't it? Education, employment, social norms... it's all interrelated. Yes, very much so. And speaking of which, have you noticed the weather lately? This rain never seems to stop. Oh, I know! It's been miserable. Although I suppose it's standard for this time of year. Still, when you're out and about as much as I am, you wish for a bit of sunshine. Agreed. However, this is quite the contrast to the sunshine we had when I was traveling to Spain a few years ago. The climate there was so different from here. Oh, I've always wanted to go to Spain.

You know what I've been thinking, we've all been so focused on what we don't have, that we've forgotten how lucky we are to have each other. Right! And we can play so many games, and rhymes! And isn't it lovely that we have a big, cozy room like this to play in? And the best part... we are all happy together! "Rain, rain, go away, come again another day!" Yes, isn't that just the best rhyme? But really, what's more important than that? I mean, even if we had lots of money, it wouldn't bring us real happiness if we didn't have each other, and this lovely space to enjoy together. But wouldn't it be nice if we also had... a big, big house with a playroom just for us? And we could go on adventures every day! That's true, a bigger house could be fun. But it's important to remember that having "stuff" doesn't always make us happy. Sometimes it's all the things we can't buy that matter most. Like what, Auntie? Well, for one, spending time together, having fun, being kind to one another, and being grateful for what we already have. If we have each other, and we’re healthy, and we have this lovely place and food and toys... isn’t that plenty? Yeah, kind of like how we were so excited to see Uncle John when he came over last week. And we also got presents from the local shop. That was fun! Exactly! It's all those little things that add up to make us happy. And it's great to have some extras, but they aren't the things that we really treasure. But what if we had lots of money like the people in those big houses? It's true some of those people are very happy, and maybe it's because the money gives them more choices and opportunities. But most importantly, they probably care for each other and have people to share things with, like us. Can we play a rhyming game? Sure, but I like this conversation. It's important... because lots of people think the more money you have, the happier you'll be. But really, many people with lots of money aren't happier. They become busier, maybe argue more, and are less happy than we are right now, together.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that Chinese tech company that's making waves these days? They've got this crazy AI that can predict and prevent natural disasters. Oh yeah, I've seen that! I think they're doing really well for themselves. But now, the thing that really interests me – do you have any idea how one would start an AI company or even make a patent for an invention of that scale? Honestly, I've actually been looking into that. I found this online course that says it all starts with an idea, and then you need a bit of coding experience. You'll need to protect your idea, so a patent application would be key. But it's such a complex process and I'm not sure if I could actually do it. That makes sense. I mean, there’s also a lot of investment involved, right? And the patent process isn't going to be cheap. But imagine if you were able to create something that could really make a difference. Exactly! But it's daunting. And what if we couldn't afford it? You know, between saving up for university and whatnot, I'm not really sure where I'd find the resources for something like that. True enough, but think about how much money you could save the world – and make. If what the Chinese company’s doing is any indication, it’s definitely plausible. Investment-wise, I’ve heard about some government initiatives to support tech startups, especially for kids who have innovative ideas. That'd be a game changer, wouldn’t it? If the government is actually supportive, and if there are legit ways for us to get funding... I'd be all for it. But it's tough to keep the focus when you're dealing with school and everything else. We should do some more digging on that. Maybe there's a way for us together to come up with an idea, apply for a project or something? We could pool our resources, skills. It’s worth a shot. Yeah, maybe. But you have to think about China and changing the world. It's scary but exhilarating. They’re doing some of the most forward-thinking stuff out there. For sure. I mean, just take a look at how China's developed over the past few decades – it's like 1985 to 2020, you know?

Oh, Lena, I haven't skied this much since our school trips. It's been ages. Yeah, I noticed you've practically landed a competition in freestyle skiing! If only – I'm just trying not to embarrass myself. You've been absolutely amazing though, and I'm jealous of your speed and poise. Well, I won't say no to a bit of friendly ribbing! But seriously, I'm just enjoying being out in nature, and it's great seeing you enjoy it too. Even if you have to pick your way down the hill like a cautious tortoise. Tortoise, huh? At least I'm consistent! Exactly. So have you thought about what we're doing this afternoon? The snow has held up beautifully, so if you're up for it, maybe we could head over to the off-piste area. It's not as crowded, and it should be fun. That sounds like a great idea! But don’t forget, we need to plan for a proper break at some point. We can’t ski through lunch, you know. Of course, of course. Do you want to meet for lunch at the mountain restaurant again today? Their lunch buffet is really nice. Yeah, let’s do that. How does 1:30 sound? Perfect. I'll ski down and meet you there. Just don't be too adventurous ahead of time. Don't worry, I won’t cause any ski patrol calls today. More importantly, do you want a few lessons, maybe? Our local instructor’s really good and since we’re here for another few days, it could make a huge difference. That’s very kind of you to think of. But I’m actually enjoying my own pace. Plus, if I mess up too much, I might not be able to keep up for lunch. Fair enough. I might consider lessons though – last time I checked my skiing skills were as outdated as my high school notes. Maybe we both could take lessons next ski holiday. I’ll look into it for us. Sounds like a plan. So, now that we’ve finalized the plan for the afternoon, any updates on that dinner party we’re supposed to attend this evening? Nothing specific yet, but I sent a few texts to some of the girls we've met here. They said it’s a casual thing at the hotel bar, so we should be good just showing up.

Ah, I see you've seen the bill for my last trip to the badminton shop. These strings breaking are really becoming costly. Yes, I've been thinking about the cost and the various methods we can use to overcome this issue. Have you ever tried using cable ties? They might not be the most conventional, but some folks swear by them for temporary fixes. Cable ties, really? Absolutely! It's not just about the cost, you see. The material, dimensions, how it's positioned — even how heavy it is can affect the longevity of the string. You'll need to think about all those factors. That's a good point. And I suppose we'd need to take into account the specifics of each case to decide on materials. Exactly! And then there's the whole "fleet" of racket strings. What do you mean by "fleet"? A group? Oh, it's just how some people in the sports world refer to a collection of items. But it seems like a weird use of the word "fleet", which I traditionally associate with ships. Now that I think of it, it might be quite confusing to some. I understand the confusion. "Fleet" often means a group of vehicles or ships. In the context of racket strings, people might be trying to convey owning or managing a variety of them. But it could indeed be misleading! I agree. A more accurate term, especially for non-experts, could be "collection" or "arsenal". For the primary school and secondary contexts, simpler terms and explanations would help a lot. Absolutely, it's about clarity and the ability to communicate effectively to your audience. Talking of communication... You know, I just had this mishap while doing my hair, thinking of the "fleet" business. I cut ear lobe and stripe in my hair by mistake instead. That’s quite a literal interpretation of changing the business plan! Yes, I suppose so! No real damage done, just a temporary new look. Anyway, if we're talking business, how do you think we should market this idea for sustainable string repair? That's a great question. Perhaps a blog or YouTube channel could work. Many people in the UK use these platforms to find solutions to everyday problems. Yeah, but we’d need to make it really relatable — funny and informative, so people see it's not just for experts.

"Excursion into the world of art, eh? Mind if I share a bit about my own little experiences? I may not be as learned as you two here but I've got a heart for it." "Please, John, share away. Art's for everyone. I've actually got some of my lectures notes about British art if you're interested." "And I can relate it to current trends if you'd like." "Aye, that'd be grand. I always wondered how the old masters like Constable or Turner made those landscapes appear so real, just like the Norfolk fields I grew up with." "I've always loved Constable - oh, the railways and that. He really captured the era." "Ah, yes - John Constable's influence was quite significant, especially with how he highlighted the English countryside. And he was actually born in Suffolk, just next door to Norfolk. His work's often seen as quintessentially English, much like the accent we use here." "Yep, that's what I mean. He captured the soul of the place, the way the light dances on the fields in the morning. It puts me in mind of my childhood - roaming the fields at sunrise, before school." "It's remarkable how Constable managed to capture atmosphere, John. There's a certain quality in his work, really grounding. John, you know, the way he rendered the clouds and the sky, that's something I've always been fascinated with myself in my own work. It plays with the viewer's perspective, doesn't it?" "Aye, the perspective, that's the true art, ain't it? Making people see the world through the eyes of another. I think that's what's so appealing about art, it connects us all despite our backgrounds." "Exactly. Art has this universal language. And Constable, he was really a pioneer in using nature as his subject. He wasn't just painting landscapes, he was exploring light and atmosphere in new ways." "That's so true, if you think about it. It's not just the objects in the painting. It's the relationships between them and the way he makes you feel." "There's a painting I remember seeing in Norwich once. A portrait by some local artist, can't recall the name now. But it was of a Norwich Market scene. It had this vitality to it, this life. That's what art should do, anyways - don't you think?"

Oh, did I ever tell you about that one stupid client who today insisted that every report needed to be in the past tense even though it was about future events? Had the audacity to call my project 'not professional'! Oh dear, isn't that one for the books? I had a patient today who was convinced that his 'difficulties' were caused by 'technical fractals' orbiting in the space between his ears. Fractals? I need that to explain why certain people 'melt my brain'! It's Friday night - bitch about your coworkers to their faces next week, but among family - we can relax. Was it as frustrating at work today as it sounds? Definitely. One of my biggest pet peeves is the misuse of language at work. Especially when it's from the top down. Make a typo in a report and you're lucky if people just ignore it. But if you correct someone's grammar or their misuse of 'effect' vs 'affect', watch out. Sure, I've come across that too. As a nurse, I often interact with people from different backgrounds, but the 'bare minimum' attitude to written communication really grinds my gears. Of course, technology has made it worse. Can't people even correct 'there their' in emails anymore? They're too busy worrying about the 'wrong' use of 'like' and 'basically' in their texts. Exactly. As if the 'rules' of language usage aren't subjective and dynamic enough without these people trying to prove how 'text-smart' they are! Speaking of dynamic, I wanted to discuss our cleaning schedule for next week. We've really been procrastinating on it. Oh, sure. I was gonna do some shopping after work today but I ended up just FaceTiming with sis all evening. And I thought I was the queen of procrastination! You got shopping done after all, didn't you? Or did you just go home and sit on the couch? Well, I did head out but came back with pizza and a bottle of wine. How can I be expected to clean with all that temptation just sitting in the fridge? I see. Well, we should definitely make any cleaning a team effort. We can get that done over the weekend. Perfect idea. And then maybe we can discuss our next Netflix series. Or not discuss it. Sometimes it's nice to just watch something and not over-analyze it.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my day? I discovered today that the intern is actually more efficient than me at some tasks. It's been a little humbling. That's hilarious. Especially now, as you're supposed to be the professional PA. But seriously, it got me thinking about "intelligence" versus "common sense" and how they can actually be quite mutually exclusive. Oh, I've got a story about that. Remember when I was working in IT, I had this colleague who, theoretically, was a genius. He could code like nobody's business. But, if I asked him where the kitchen in our office was, he'd be completely stumped. That's exactly what I mean. I suppose common sense doesn't always correlate with intelligence. Definitely. It's a different kind of knowledge, isn't it? But, then again, it often surprises me how these people are surprisingly useful in their own way. I guess so. But it's still a bit of a reality check for me, having to admit when someone is better at something I'm supposed to be good at. But isn't that what we're in this relationship for – to support and help each other, not be perfect? And besides, you have plenty of areas where you're amazing. Thanks, honey. That's sweet of you to say. I'm just speaking the truth. Anyway, you know what I've been noticing? I've found myself smoking more since we moved to Hungerford. Really? We should cut back. It's not healthy. I know. But it's a habit. We talked about quitting once, remember? Yes, and we really should. I mean, we both need to look after ourselves better. You're nearing 50 after all. I'm not that old yet. But I know what you mean. We need to set a better example for the children. Exactly. It's funny. Some of my best friends almost never smoke or drink. It's like... their priorities are different or they just don't have the same vices. That's a different culture, I suppose. But it's interesting how we sometimes get taken aback by others' habits. Definitely. I mean, in some cultures, if you don't drink alcohol, people might even question your masculinity. Really? Though, come to think of it, there are definitely social norms around drinking alcohol and smoking that seem absurd once you step back.

Oh, did I ever tell you about's day at the farm today? The children were absolutely fascinated. I've never seen such wide eyes! Oh, can you tell us about it? What did they do? Well, first, we arrived and got to meet the farm animals - lambs, pigs, even this little calf that was born just yesterday! And the children got to feed the sheep, right? That was Emma's favourite bit. Absolutely. She was absolutely fascinated by the baby sheep, and she even got to help feed them. And did they like the tractor ride? Yes, Emma and Jack absolutely loved the tractor ride. They were both gripping the seat so tightly! And what about your little ones? Didn't you enjoy it too, Emily and George? Oh, yes. Emily kept pointing out the different animals and asking me about them. And George couldn't stop giggling at the pigs rolling in the mud! That's sounds amazing! Maybe we should take a trip to the farm next weekend. I think the kids would love that. The farm is right near the village where we live. Speaking of which, I saw there's a new DVD at school. "The Little Mermaid". Do you think the kids would like that? Oh, they love Disney films. I'm sure they'd be thrilled to watch it. We should watch it together some evening. Maybe even make some popcorn and have a family movie night. That sounds perfect. Except, we've been having some issues with the children during snack time at school. Seems they just can't keep together during eating times. Yes, I noticed that too. George tried to share his sandwich with Emily but then he wanted it back. That’s typical child behaviour, but we'll need to address it. Perhaps sit them down after school and explain why it's important to share. That's a great idea. Teaching them about sharing, patience and so on. Hey, you two were great today. I heard you both shared your toys with the other children at the farm. That’s right, you shared during the picnic. You were such big girls and boys. That's exactly what I was talking about. We don’t want that good behaviour to just happen at the farm, we want it at school too. Do you remember how much fun it was to share today?

I've decided I need a new hobby. I have way too much time on my hands nowadays and knitting seems like such a calming one. I love that! I've always been fascinated by it and I think it’s a great hobby – you can even customize everything you make and it’s so rewarding when it turns out right. Exactly! I’ve been thinking about making some Easter-themed decorations. I bought a few packs of yarn in Easter colors. But I am a bit worried I might get too ambitious and end up with a bunch of weird, lumpy items. Well, if I can have any say in it, embrace your mistakes! Sometimes the most beautiful things come from unexpected outcomes. Yeah, but I’m not going to have any hope of being a knitting celebrity with the kind of mistakes I make! Hmm, maybe we should have an Easter knit night? We can both knit and share stories of our best and worst knitting mishaps. I’d love that! I've been meaning to learn more different stitches anyways. Plus, it'll be nice to focus on something other than work and the Olympics for once. Well, at least until the Olympics start again. Are you staying up late to watch them? Hmm, not really. I find it's easier to follow highlights the next day, honestly. But I have to admit, it's been amazing to see the diversity of talent from all over the world showing up. Very true! And it's also wonderful to see the different art and cultural influences coming through in the opening and closing ceremonies. I just wish more people could appreciate it without viewing it through a political lens. It's such a shame really. There's so much to celebrate when it comes to the Olympics. It's about unity and human achievement after all. Definitely. Speaking of which, have you seen any of the art exhibits currently in Cambridge? I heard there’s a new one at the Gallery on King’s Street featuring local artists. Yes, I have. It’s fantastic. I was particularly impressed by the blend of traditional technique and modern themes. I'd definitely like to check it out. It's really inspiring to see people thinking creatively outside the box. I've been wanting to get back into visiting museums and galleries too since this whole lockdown madness started...

Right, so I've been reading about this incredible museum in London's South Bank. They've got all these interactive exhibits and even some Imax and 3D cinema. It sounds like a fascinating afternoon out. What do you think? Aye, I think that sounds brilliant! But have you heard about the prices they charge now? It's a bit steep if you're on a tight budget, like me. Ah, right you are! I hadn't thought about that. But still, for a once-in-a-while treat, it's worth considering. Plus, public transport in London is quite pricey, but if you get the right ticket, you can save a bit. The trouble is, I've just lost my concession card so even that's not an option any more. And the places for public transport tickets can be a bit overwhelming if you're not used to them. Ah, I see your point. But looking on the London transport website can clarify things. And there are usually helpful staff around if you're unsure. Although, I'd never use those machines by myself. Aye, that's so true. But it's funny, when I used to commute to work, I found the dilly-dally prices on public transport absurd. Absolutely! The fare zones can be so confusing. It really depends on where you're going. But it's all very well laid out on the maps and diagrams, if you take the time to look. I suppose that's really for the benefit of us from the provinces, innit? Well, I would say that! Coming from up North myself, I remember how daunting it could be when you first arrive. But once you get the hang of things, it's less overwhelming. I just wish the prices were a bit more reasonable. On a fixed income, every penny counts. It's a fair point. But then again, it's all part of dealing with the modern world. As I'm always saying to my EFL students, it's a case of adapting and learning. I suppose that's true. But, as someone who never worked for most of their life, it does feel like a bit of a struggle sometimes. No apologies needed, my dear. We all have our battles. But let's not let that stop us from living life, shall we? Perhaps we could look into some sort of museum or Imax outing.

Right, so I'm going to suggest we host this year's Christmas dinner. I've got the perfect spot in mind, too. Oi, talked about that already. Got yourself down as organizer. Better get on with it then isn't it? Haha, exactly! So, how many folks do you think we'll be expecting? Besides us and the Baxters of course? I think it'll be around 8 or 9. I'd better start sending out invitations soon. Right, get on it. Also, shall we continue our usual tradition of seeing a movie on Christmas Eve? Saves the chaos for Christmas day, if you ask me. Yeah, that's a good idea. "It's a Wonderful Life" or "The Grinch"? "The Grinch" has to be it. Who could resist? On a serious note, I've also invited Alex and Emily. They're out here for the holiday, too. Lovely! That means it'll be a regular old fashioned Christmas with all the trimmings. For sure! We can keep it low key, no need for overly fancy décor. I'm all for that. Less stress, more time to enjoy ourselves. Absolutely. As for the dinner, we can't have the same old turkey and trimmings for a change, can we? Possibly, but it's familiar and easy. What do you propose? I'd suggest trying a roast beef. It's traditional but can also be quite versatile. How about incorporating some Asian flavors to give it a bit of a twist? That could work. We can design a menu that has English traditions mixed with some Chinese side dishes. I love that idea. And for dessert, I've been craving a traditional Christmas pudding. It will bring back memories. We can also consider a Chinese dessert as a nod to our changing holiday locations. Like a traditional mango pudding or something similar. That’s a brilliant idea! Either way, it looks like we've got a solid plan on our hands. It'll be fun to catch up with everyone and have a bit of a good time. Exactly! It'll be worth all the effort when we see everyone. I’ll start making the invitations now. And I'll start thinking about menus. Decided on Christmas Eve movie yet? Not yet, but this year, why don't we do something really different? Like maybe watch an interesting documentary? Something about the history of Christmas or the evolution of traditional meals?

Yo, anyone seen that stupid review on Twitter? Some bloke's annoyed because we're out of avocados. Yeah, I saw that. It's the internet for you. You can be anything, anywhere, at any time. Still, though, the customers, eh? Oh, absolutely. I had one yesterday. Woman came in and totally lost it because we ran out of her favorite cake. And the funny bit? I bet she's the same one who writes “this café is so cozy and homely, love it!” in another review. Hahaha, totally! Can't win with some people, can we? It's like they forget sometimes we're just a baker down the street, not Google. Yeah, but it's the bad reviews that stick, isn't it? Good customer service and everything else you do just gets glossed over. It's a shame really. True, but it's part of the job now. You just have to take it on the chin and try to not let it get you down. I don't know, it's frustrating though when you're busting your back to deliver and then someone just wants to paint you in the worst light because their expectations don't match reality. I hear you, Stella. Though, sometimes people just don't get how much work goes into serving them their daily dose of avocado toast. Exactly, or as I like to call it, "Artful Slice Warfare". Yeah, definitely a battle. Speaking of work, how's the new design for the bakery coming along, Jack? Oh, it's going surprisingly well, thank you for asking. I just added more of a rustic feel. I'm pretty confident people will love it. That's great to hear, mate. You know, it's funny when a business changing something so simple like décor can make such a big difference. True. I'm actually trying to work on the design for my café. I was thinking of something retro, but I'm not sure. Could use some input if anyone's free to brainstorm. Again and again with the design. I could help you out. What's the vibe you want to give? I want it to feel like a little slice of heaven for the customers. Comfortable, welcoming, but also with a touch of quirky fun to it. I know that sounds vague, but this place has character and... I don't know, it's hard to explain.

Oh, did I ever tell you about the time Oisin discovered he actually loves raspberries? No! Oh, please tell! I love raspberries, too! Well, it was the summer before he went to high school. We had a garden full of them, and he would always pick them and ruin them, never eating a single one. Poor Oisin, always picking them over-ripe, right? Yes! But suddenly, one day, he's eating this perfect raspberry in two seconds flat, just like that! That's impossible! He never liked them before! I know! It was like a miracle. We were all so surprised! Maybe it was because we had a lot of them growing. Sometimes when you have something around you all the time, you start to like it? Exactly! The exposure might have helped. And then there's the chocolate ice cream at the café up the hill. It's amazing, but I'm trying to have it less often. Remember, we all still have to eat our vegetables! I love carrots! Carrots are yummy, especially if you have them with a little bit of hummus! See, eating your vegetables doesn't have to be boring. And gardening can be so rewarding! You plant something, take care of it, and then—bam! You have something delicious to eat. Yeah! We could start a small garden at school if we asked our teacher. That's a fantastic idea! A class project could be such a fun way to learn about plants and where food comes from. What about biking? Oftentimes, after dinner, we like to go for a little bike ride. Biking is great! It's good exercise and such a lovely way to see the neighborhood. Plus, it’s a bit like playing outside, like when we were kids. Speaking of playing outside, I was thinking of getting some bird eggs for the gerbils. They seem so fascinated by them. Really? I'd never thought of that. Well, we should make sure they’re safe, of course. Some bird eggs could have harmful bacteria, I’d check that first. Yes, you’re right, I’ll check with the pet shop. Can we go for a walk afterwards, please? Absolutely! We can walk to the park after dinner and see if there are any birds we can spot. And maybe we can bring a book about birds. That sounds like a plan! Then we can even have a little competition to see who can identify the most different birds!

Oh, did I ever tell you about my eyebrow maintenance story? On the road to an important client meeting, I was clearly slumped out of sleep and talked to someone for the first time that day without masking. Oh, yes, please share! Go on, I love those kinds of stories. Well, picture this - I'm presenting to a potential new client, and I had overslept and hadn't plucked or shaped my brows properly that morning. As I was explaining our new service, I could see one of the clients slightly confused and not really looking at my face. Oh dear, what happened? So, I noticed that one of my eyebrows had a little rogue hair that was practically making a 'V' shape. Hence, she was kind of staring at my brow instead of listening to what I was saying. That must have been quite an awkward moment. Definitely! Eventually, I realised what was distracting her and had to rummage through my pocket for a mirror and tweezers, which resulted in laughter all around. We ended up having a positive meeting though! It sounds like the make or break moment wasn’t the product you were selling but your brows! Exactly. The moral is perhaps that attention to detail, no matter how small, is always in play. It’s all about timing and presentation, isn’t it? But it proves that no matter the occupation, we all have our 'behind the scenes' stories. Speaking of presentation, who's up for the weekly food shop this week? I can do it, but I noticed we're running low on milk and bread. Right, and maybe some eggs? While you’re at it, can you also pick up some new cleaning gloves? Old ones are starting to wear out. Sure thing. Wonderful, thanks! And, by the way, I thought we might want to arrange a family lunch out next week. Just to have a bit of a break. That sounds lovely. We could all do with a complete break from work and chores. Yes, and it’ll be good to catch up properly. Since you’re retired, do you have any preferences for where to go? We could try that new Italian place downtown. That sounds nice. I’d love that. Shall we message the others and confirm a day and time? Yes, and maybe while we're at it, can someone help me with the Gro's cleaning?

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time during Grace’s sign language class? Not yet, but you must have, you usually don't let anything slip through. No, this was a first! You know how she questions everything? She's got the curiosity of a cat! Well, the sign language teacher was explaining how to sign "hungry", and Grace got up and pointed right at her stomach. Oh, you must have been so proud! I was beyond proud! The teacher had a field day. It just shows how much even tiny children can absorb when you immerse them in language from such an early age. Absolutely. Hence your enthusiasm about weaning? She's going to be learning language even more quickly with different tastes and textures, right? That's right. I want to start weaning her next week. You know, between us, I'm really nervous though. For? You're doing everything right. It's normal to be apprehensive, but remember, you’ve handled every other parenting milestone just fine! Thanks. I don't know, I just feel like this is a big step, you know? Leaving formula behind. She's been so good with just breastmilk or formula up till now. Of course! But think of it as a positive step towards her growing independence, and all the exciting new foods and textures she can try! Yeah, that's a better way to frame it. And weaning also makes it easier to share meals together as a family. true, true. How are your plans for the week looking? On Tuesday evening, I've got another session of couple's sign language class with Gary. We're just really enjoying it. That's so great! It’s really cool to see couples committing to learning together. What’s your next sign you're working on? We're working on "I love you" at the moment. It’s actually quite intricate! You have to make the shape of the letter 'I', then the shape of the letter 'L', then 'Y', and finally a 'U' with your fingers. I’ll show you when you come. Oh, I’d love that. And do you have any plans for the baby this week? No set plans but any suggestions? Except for the weaning, that is. Not if that's out of the question now! Yes, let’s postpone the babies' social calendar for now, shall we?

Oh, isn't this wonderful? I feel like I've been away from nature for too long. Definitely. There's something about the peace and quiet that just can't be found in the city. We're lucky to have access to places like this so close to where we live. Absolutely. I've always loved the way Norwich, where I'm from, is surrounded by so much countryside. But this is even better, it feels untouched, unspoiled. You can tell it's been conserved really well. True. I have similar feelings from my London upbringing, I think there is a craving for the raw, unbuilt aspect of nature that our urban environment can't quite provide. Look, there's a village on top of that hill. It's just... picturesque. Let me take a closer look. Yes, it's lovely. The thatched roofs, the old church on the village green... The villagers have done a great job of retaining traditional features too. I love the way everything here seems to blend in with the landscape. Norwich used to have quite a few thatched cottages, but sadly most were replaced over the decades. This place still has an old-world charm in spades. I'm not sure London ever had that many thatched cottages. But it's the same principle, isn't it? The influence of the local heritage, the understanding that certain things should be preserved. Precisely. Our research tends to focus on the impact of urbanization on communities and landscapes. It's interesting to think about preservation versus development, particularly in rural areas. True, but changing the natural environment also affects the local culture, doesn’t it? The countryside is not only a physical place but also a cultural landscape. Absolutely. The structure of society, local customs, all of these things are shaped by where we live and work. Our research often touches on how education and socio-economic factors influence this. We could probably do with looking at some of that in our upcoming projects. Our students always seem to be enthusiastic about those topics, especially our countryside focused ones. That could work really well. And given that both of our backgrounds are in education—especially in topics that tie together culture, history, and environment—I think we’d make a great team on that project. Definitely! Though we must keep in mind that our, shall we say, "academic privilege" allows us to approach the subject differently than the local living here.

Yo, mate, did you seen any of the latest Marvel movies? I was thinking of going to see it this weekend, but I haven't yet. Thoughts? Yeah, I've seen Endgame. It was epic! One day we're looking for one specific text, another day we're organising the digital versions of each paper.

Ah, isn't it wonderful to unwind like this, just walking through the countryside? Nothing beats the peace and quiet away from the hustle and bustle of the city, wouldn't you say? Definitely, Alison. The air’s nice and fresh and the grass underfoot is a welcome change from the concrete back in London. It’s also really refreshing to be out and about without the backdrop of a city skyline. Absolutely, right? Although I do occasionally miss the urban gardens. Our very own Norwich has some lovely green spaces, even if it's not quite as expansive as this. Yes, Norwich does have some hidden gems. I've been there a few times, despite being a Londoner. But then again, I think there is something truly unique about the countryside here in Norfolk. The way nature stretches out before us, making you feel as though you’re venturing into the unknown every time you step outside. True! And the flowers! I love how we have such a variety here, don't you? And right now, it seems like every possible type of wildflower is in bloom. I never tire of walking through the fields and spotting a new species I hadn't noticed before. I find the diversity pretty impressive myself. The rural economy, while certainly different from the urban one, relies heavily on the diversity and health of these natural resources, right? It's like the diversity of flowers mirrors the diverse sources of income here in the countryside – from tourism to farming to cash crops, all interconnected but different. Indeed, and each has its own challenges and trends, much like the flowers. For example, over the past years, the rise in cash crops has meant that some fields that used to be lush with different wildflowers and local species are now dedicated to one single crop or just left fallow. That’s true, and it’s a trade-off, isn’t it? On one hand, it’s economically advantageous to allocate space for high value crops or environmentally friendly but profitable crops like hemp or sunflowers. On the other hand, the changing landscape has an impact on biodiversity and potentially on tourism, as people often come to see a variety of landscapes and natural beauty, not just endless fields of one type of plant. Exactly! And it's not just about the immediate economic benefits; it has an ecological impact too.

Yo, mate, did you manage to sort out the tickets for the match on Saturday? Yeah, I managed to snag a couple. It's going to be a blast! Cheers for that. Still trying to sort the parking, though. Ah, lovely to see you over for a cup of coffee, Susan. I was just reading about that celebrity trial in the paper today. Fascinating isn't it, the way these high-profile cases are always so dramatic? Ah, I can't believe how much of a difference it's made working part-time since having the baby. It's been such a relief not having to shuttle back and forth from Milton Keynes every day. So, I've been thinking a lot about the future lately. We've all had our fair share of stress and uncertainty, especially since graduating and trying to find our place in the world. Definitely. Exactly! I've been thinking about possibly getting another postgrad certificate in something related to my current job as a production controller. For me, it's about making sure I have as many tools as possible in my belt. Not to mention, it could be fun to specialize in something. That makes sense. But the more I learned, the more I realized it's not just about what I want to do, but what the industry is looking for and what the real-world opportunities are. What do you say we make some plans for the summer? Like just something casual. A picnic or a weekend away. Could be fun and give us a break from thinking about 5-year plans. That sounds perfect. Oh, did I ever tell you about's this stupid story? On Friday night, I was at Alex's celebration and clearly slumped out after two pints of cider. Got chatting to this guy, right? Or maybe we're all just successful in living out our covert intimacy issues through envy of strangers’ boyfriends or accents. Oh, absolutely. Alright, I'm so glad we've all managed to make today's dinner. It's been one of those days where the hours just tick by, hasn't it? Yeah, mum. It feels like I've been waiting all day for dinner! Well, let's hope it's good enough for all the hard work you put in today, and for you, [Speaker_4], getting back from school too. Absolutely. If I'm not getting battered or bruised this time around, maybe! Well, no guarantees there, but we sure can try to watch. Sure, but I need someone to play goalie. Oh, Lena, I'm so glad we've got these beautiful Redwoods to look at while we're driving. It feels so different to what we're used to back home doesn't it? These trees are absolutely massive! But seriously, places like this remind me of the importance of preserving natural beauty. Definitely. We're so lucky to have places like these in our world. It also makes me wish we could have something like this closer to home. But I guess we couldn’t transplant a whole forest, could we? No, definitely not! But that doesn’t mean we can’t support and protect what we have wherever we are. I completely agree. Where did you get the idea for this trip, actually? It was actually a mixture of work, really. So, are you enjoying the downtime away from working? Actually it's been fantastic. I needed a break from the routine anyway and this is just perfect. Nature, nice weather... just what I needed. It’s good for the soul, I’m sure. You always were a bit of a nature girl since we were at uni, weren’t you? Yeah, I guess you could say that. I’ve always been drawn to it. Alright lads, who was surprised by the Irish accent when today's delivery arrived? I was actually thinking chicken kievs sound suspiciously Russian. Granny used to say, "Life's too short for boring food." I think she'd approve of experimental chicken kievs. Especially if they still taste like home. Exactly. I've decided I need more vintage stuff in my life. Got a bit carried away on eBay last weekend. Anything interesting? Found this beautiful set of vintage cups and saucers. I was thinking maybe just a bottle of good wine and some baking from the market, but if there's anything else you want to do... No, no, just keep the focus on good food and company. What about the market you mentioned? Got any plans this weekend? Yeah, I was thinking of going. I heard they're going to have some new vendors this week. That sounds fun. And maybe some new crafty things for the home? Exactly. Here comes your kitchen full of vintage and crafty pieces. Yes, well, you know I love my eclectic mix. I love it too. Dinner should be ready in about ten minutes if you want to plate it?

Yo, how's business going? I've been seeing all these news about banking and money laundering; it sounds pretty involved. Oh, it's always a headache, really. Most of my clients are small to medium-sized businesses, so we've got to make sure everything is above-board – no funny questions from the authorities. But even with all the checks, it's not a guarantee, is it? I mean, you can never be too sure with some people, can you? That's very true. You've got to trust your instinct, knowledge of your clients, and, of course, the law. And these days, with more and more businesses conducting international transactions, the risks are higher. Yeah, and the fines for money laundering can be huge even if you didn't intend to break the law. Absolutely. That's why I decided to go for a post-grad in finance, specifically in compliance. It's been invaluable in understanding all these nuances. And businesses, even legitimate ones, still struggle to understand the legal aspects of this. I mean, it's not just about being honest; it's about keeping the right records, knowing who your partners are, the whole nine yards. It's a real balancing act. On one hand, you've got to ensure your business runs smoothly and you're making a profit. On the other, you can't be complacent about your legal obligations or you could end up facing really serious penalties. Did you see that news about some big-name business getting fined for unknowingly laundering money? Yeah, it was huge. The company's reputation took a hit, and if it was smaller, it could've easily gone under. I just don't understand how people keep getting caught up in it, though. It's usually due to naivety, or in some cases, greed. People see a chance for a quick profit and don't consider the risks. Or sometimes it's because they're dealing with phantom clients or associates who turn out to be fronts. Reminds me of that documentary we watched last year about international money laundering through casinos and real estate. Yes, it's quite sophisticated in some cases. But what's equally interesting are the efforts governments are making to close these loopholes. And sometimes it seems like they're working against each other. One country tightens up regulations and businesses just move to another.

Oh, did I ever tell you about the weather we had last week? The sun was shinning so brightly, and yet it was so chilly, so strange! Yes, isn't the weather just so unpredictable? But I guess that's part of the fun! Besides, there's nothing better than a good cup of coffee to warm up the bones, isn't there? Definitely! Nothing really globally notable but you might want to check out the changing of the seasons in Birmingham. There is an annual event around this time of year. Ah, the Light Festival. I suppose we could go one weekend and... Or, if anyone is free, we could go as a small group? It might be nice to mix things up from the usual family gatherings. What a great idea! And speaking of gatherings, have we made any decisions about the summer holiday?

Oh, did I just type that or say it? I'm getting so used to speaking South Eastern English that I forget how it sounds when written. I love that about regional dialects. They're so unique and tell us so much about a person's background. Exactly! I sometimes get caught out with my own Southeast accent. When I'm back in Malaysia, they always tease me about it. Oh, I've got that too coming from Sweden and Chile. It's like my brain has multiple language settings. Even though I've always spoken English at home, there's definitely been a shift in the way I use words since moving to London. You know, city slang and all that. Oh totally. And the London accent is so distinct. Even though it's just a short train ride from here. Yeah, sometimes I get creative with how I use English when I'm around my family and friends in Malaysia. It's like a whole different tongue for them. So, have you guys noticed that? How our language choices can be so much about our identity. I find the English language is really fun to play with, but sometimes it feels like a label. Like if you use a certain word, people can guess where you're from or what kind of background you have. That's so true. I remember during university, one of my flatmates from Glasgow would always use words that were really unusual to me, but meant the exact same thing. Like when I asked for a 'rubber' in Malaysia and the teacher just stared at me. Turns out, in Malaysia, that means eraser. Right. And in the UK, rubber can mean both a pencil eraser and a contraceptive. I once used that in a meeting at a newspaper job and couple people chuckled but were too polite to confront me. That's a great example. Language can be so nuanced and contextual. It does make me think about the role of language in our jobs though. As a publishing assistant, I always have to be conscious of using 'standard' English, but also understanding the regional contexts. Again, agreed. As an assistant editor, I almost unintentionally adapt to the local dialect of the book we're working on. That must be challenging, adjusting your language for different audiences or contexts. I've been in similar situations.

We should also check if we need any particular permissions or insurance for the rally. Right, so add that to the to-do list. And while we're at it, let's sort out the planning for the rally itself. Yeah, got a rough outline in mind but we need to fine-tune.

Oh, did I ever tell you about last night? I ended up in the hospital because of my arm. I was clearly overdoing it, talked about enjoying chicken nuggets down by the canal. Chickened it and ended up in hospital? That's a new phrasebook entry! Was there an accident? Or was it just a precaution? Kind of a bit of both. I'd been walking around too much and it just acted up during the night. Ended up with a few X-rays and some pain killers but I'm fine now. Well, you have to say staying in wasn't your specialty just like the nuggets were. I guess you can say that. Anyway, I should probably rest properly from now on. Definitely do. We've all been having a tough week. Between illness, exhaustion, and barely keeping up with assignments, it feels like it's all coming to a head. So true. I was really sick a couple of days ago, too. Just felt so tired and unwell. I know what you mean. I assumed I was just exhausted after the uni week so far, but the hospital visit was a definite wake-up call. Yeah, it's like our bodies are catching up with us after the first term. Exactly. And we’re probably also not getting enough downtime. I mean, I know I don't. Always something happening or something else to do. And then on top of everything, we have to deal with boys or general stress about the future, right? As if a broken arm, blurred vision, and pounding headache aren’t enough drama already. Oh, for sure. Last night was a bonfire of emotional overload for sure. It's like our bodies are telling us that university life isn’t just about studying and having fun, it's also about taking care of ourselves. And maybe not letting ourselves get swept up in the social whirlwind so much. We all almost lost this week because of overdoing it in one way or another. Do you think it’s the university environment or just our personal habits? Maybe a mix of both? Probably both. We're independent now and that can often mean we neglect our own health while we try to navigate all these new responsibilities. Plus, we're probably a bit like old mice on a wheel, perpetually tired but can't stop, right?

Ah, I can't believe how much of a blast it was at Dad's 80th. It was lovely seeing everyone together again wasn't it? Yeah, unreal! Made me feel like we were all siblings really. Specially the games and the food! Especially the food! I've had Yorkshire puddings and roast beef for the past week. I know! Grandma's cooking never goes out of style. But even better than that, I loved hearing about everyone's adventures. You know, before we all moved around. That's true, isn't it? I used to love listening to Auntie Sally talk about her travels. And even though she was always a bit of a tease, her stories were always so vivid. Yeah, and Grandad's sea exploration stories! He did mention exploring Yorkshire during his younger years as well, didn't he? That's right! Did he tell you about his adventures on the Humber or the Ouse? Yeah, that was so cool! He said he spent quite some time studying the river's wildlife. He was always very interested in the natural world, wasn't he? It's part of what brought him and your grandma together really, their shared love for nature. Ah, I didn't know that! Aww, that's sweet. It's really good to keep those things in mind. It reminds us all where we come from and what our families value. But it wasn't just about the past though, was it? Uncle Tom's new business venture sounds quite exciting if I understood it right? More exciting than his diving escapades! Yes, I noticed a lot of interest. It seems he's got quite the following on social media already. That’s amazing! I hope he's successful. Definitely. It's always good to see family make their own way. I'm sure his experience with numbers from his exam marking will help! That’s true! And maybe one day I’ll end up taking a Maths class under his watchful eye. As if! But you never know, you might be a bright spark in the subject. Always a possibility! So, what about all these family gatherings and parties? Want to organize another soon? We could, but it's nice to not overdo it, isn't it? Sometimes it's good to leave time for quieter moments too, less overwhelming for everyone. Though, come to think of it, next time maybe there could be more outdoor activities if at all possible.

Dad, did you remember to pack our water bottles? I don't want to have to buy more water when we're out and about. Oh yeah, love. We've got plenty of refillable ones. And I even packed some tea and coffee – do you want some before we hit the road? Yeah, that would be great. Have you thought where we're going to stop for lunch? I'd love to get some roadside fish and chips. Ah, well, I was thinking we could try and find a quaint little village – they usually have some lovely little cafes and pubs that serve proper British food. Though, let's not go too far off track. That sounds like a plan. Is the journey going to be long? Well, we're driving from Manchester to Cornwall, so it's going to be a few hours. But we can play some games or listen to music if it gets boring. You know, for the next few days, we'll be staying in a lovely manor house? I've booked it, just thought you might like it. A manor house? That sounds amazing! I can already imagine the big rooms and maybe even a secret passage... Well, let's hope for the secret passages – though I'm not sure you'd fit through most of them, you're getting quite tall! Alright, alright. But really, what’s the best place to park when we get there? I've read that it's a bit tight for parking in Cornwall sometimes. You're right on that, so I did book a parking place in the village where the manor house is. It’s usually a bit easier, less of a headache. But it should be fine. That’s good. What about our trip's itinerary, have you and mum thought about what we're doing each day? Well, we thought we’d spend a day at the beach, go and see some of the famous landmarks, maybe visit a local market. We might also pop into a local bookstore – they said they have a great selection of kids’ books. And if you're feeling up to it, we could maybe go see a film or two when we're there. Do you like Jurassic Park? Oh, I love it! I've watched all the films at least a dozen times. But I suppose we could check if they've got any good DVDs there to borrow.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I was transcribing the audio of an important meeting and I missed a key point because of the deep, soothing Scottish accent of one of the speakers? I had to re-listen to that part so many times, the poor man's accent was starting to sound like a lullaby to me! That sounds like a right job hazard doesn't it? Missing critical information because of the speaker's accent! Ah, accents, how they can add so much character to language but complicate our lives as well! As a headmistress, I've had to deal with kids with all sorts of accents in our classrooms. It just shows how diverse even our small corner of the country is. Absolutely. And each region, even within the same nation, has its own history and cultural influences that shape the language. It's a wonderful tapestry, isn't it? Right. And these regional variations can sometimes lead to misunderstandings or simply quirks in communication. I once had a coworker from Wales who would say this odd phrase that I only learned later meant "that's not right" or "that's silly." It took me ages to figure out the context beyond the literal meaning of the words. Well, at least you weren't trying to keep up with one of my apprentices who speaks Welsh as his first language. Now, that's an accent that can be tough even for a Welsh-born man to fully understand sometimes! Despite the challenges, it doesn't change the fact that it's a remarkable testament to how rich and diverse our culture is. And it teaches us understanding and patience, if nothing else. Exactly! I think those are two of the most important skills anyone can have. I've learned that since transcribing all sorts of accents and dialects. It's really broadened my perspective on language and people. True, but changing the subject slightly, how are things going with your production carpentry work? Oh, it's been a busy few months. Just finishing up on a set for a production company. And I finally found the right team to help me with the project proposals. Things are looking good, and I’ve even had a few more inquiries than I had hoped for. That's great to hear! Always good to have a steady stream of work.

Alright, girls! Let's move on from Mother's Day today. We have quite a few plans already, but how about we talk about what we're going to do for Forest School on Tuesday? Forest School is so much fun! Can we go again soon? We love playing there! Yeah and learning about nature and stuff. Like the time we learnt about the different types of trees and then we made tree faces. That was awesome, wasn't it? And remember how we planted those wildflower seeds? Think about all the blooms we'll see this summer! I can't wait to see all the flowers. Maybe we can have a picnic there in Easter break? That’s a fantastic idea! We’ll have to discuss it with Mum and Dad to make sure it works out. Can you explain what a 'picnic' means again? Of course, my dear. A picnic is when we eat outside. We often take food with us and lay out a blanket and sit on the grass. It's really nice, especially in this lovely weather we have in Spring. I understand now. That sounds magical! It can be. Now, let’s talk about something interesting. Did you know the expression 'raining cats and dogs' isn’t quite literal? What, it’s not? But isn't it just a way of saying it's raining really hard? No, I don’t know. Is it something else? Exactly. It's an idiom. An idiom is a phrase or saying that’s understood to have a different or less literal meaning from what's actually being said. So, when we say 'it's raining cats and dogs', we mean it's raining very heavily. But originally, back in 17th century England, it was thought that if you saw cats and dogs fighting in the street, there was going to be a heavy storm. That's wild. So, it's just because of animals, isn't it? But why would animals fighting mean rain? That's almost right. The idea was if the animals were fighting, heavy rain was expected soon. Now, it's just a funny way to talk about a heavy rain. So, we can say it just means 'rain'? Pretty much. It's just a fun, old expression to say when it's pouring outside. I like that. I think using English like this makes it more interesting.

Hi Sarah, I hope you're doing okay today. I know we've been chatting less often lately; how are you and John managing with everything that's been going on? Ah, well, thanks for asking. To be quite frank, it's been quite a rollercoaster, but we're trying to face it head-on. John’s had his share of health scares and, as you might remember, his sister passed away quite suddenly from cancer last year. It's actually influenced our perspective a lot, especially on how we value time and health. But even with all that, we're slowly rebuilding our lives. Oh, sweetheart, I'm so sorry to hear about your sister. I remember how close she and I used to be back in Sutton. Sent my condolences at the time, but I didn’t really get a chance to talk about it in depth. It's not easy, you know. Her sudden loss really shocked us all, but it has made us more mindful and appreciative of each day. It's also been a catalyst for us to rethink health priorities and try to live life more fully. We've started those yoga classes I told you about; it's helping us cope with this new reality. That sounds like a great idea. I've been thinking about doing something similar, but never got around to it. Seeing the impact on you and John has really made me think, you know? It's surprising sometimes how we can spend years ignoring certain signs until a wake-up call comes along. It's funny how we do that, isn't it? We're both from working backgrounds, always juggling deadlines and responsibilities. Health often ends up at the bottom of the list. But after facing that, we've learned to prioritize self-care more. Just last weekend, we took the kids on a family trip to the countryside. It was really needed. Oh, that sounds lovely! I always loved those trips. Do the kids seem to be handling things okay? They're resilient, but they do have their moments. Our daughter has started asking a lot of 'big questions' about life and death, which can be tough to navigate. Our son is more of a 'deal with it now, worry later' type, but we're making sure they both feel safe and heard. It’s all about balance, right?

Alright, I'm pretty sure our's is one of those today. The sun is shinning through the windows and clearly the noise from the street is already at a high level. Yes, the day just can't get any better! But let's face it, we both have to start our day soon. What's on your mind? Well actually, I've been thinking a lot about my classes and how to make them more engaging. As you know, I'm teaching a range of languages at my school here but I've noticed that the interest in S Korean is growing significantly. Oh yes, I've noticed that too. You know, I was privileged to attend a Korean language session during my study abroad in Seoul - oh, the food, the culture, the way of living... everything is so different and so fascinating. Absolutely! While food, of course, speaks for itself , it's actually the language itself that I'm interested in - the grammatical structure or lack thereof. It's so different from English or any Latin-based language, right? Oh totally! Even the writing system is so foreign to us. And while the 'eos', 'as', and 'sim' particles can be so confusing at the start, the more you learn, the more it starts making sense. Yeah, right, it's almost like they build sentences in a completely different way. But that's what I find so intriguing. We have so much to learn about language through diversity! Well, I guess the same can be said about the food. Don't you find that certain food combinations work or just 'click' the way they do in their cultural context, but don't feel right to us, for instance? Ah, exactly! Like kimchi with rice? It's just so natural to them and yet, for us, it takes some changing of habits to appreciate it. Or maybe it's because of our cultural exposure. I mean, in South Korea, food is such a huge part of their culture, right? And like, the way they treat animals or animals are perceived in food preparation... That's such a sensitive topic, isn't it? I've had a few students who were vegetarian or vegan and they came with certain challenges in adapting to the local food. Especially with meat-centric dishes, it can be quite tough. True... that reminds me, I've been experimenting with some... uh, um... vegetarian stir fry?

Oh, did I mention my first year's flat was flooded? On the third floor of course, water pipes burst and everything. I was so deep into reading Cloud Atlas at the time, thought I was right in the middle of one of its stories or something. That's quite the situation. I had a flood in my room once too, but it was just a washing machine issue, not that exciting. Speaking of exciting, this pizza is amazing. Who made this? That would be me! I just added all my favorite ingredients. There's even extra chilli flakes for those who like spicy food. It’s like you read my mind. I adore spicy food. Was it from that recent camping trip where you cooked everything on the campfire? Actually, no. It was inspired by our recent traveling in Africa. Everything seems to have a bit of heat over there. Speaking of traveling, have you heard any updates or plans on the gang's upcoming trip to Manchester this summer? Nothing specific yet, but we’re definitely planning something. Maybe another camping trip. After seeing the flooding in Lancaster, I thought maybe somewhere safer for us, you know? Yeah, Lancaster really took a hit from that flood. I’m glad we all made it safe here in Lancaster in time. Did you guys all move here because of the uni? I know I moved from Stockport, but it was mainly for the courses and the place itself seemed so different from Manchester or Birmingham. I come from Birmingham, so it’s been quite the change, but in a good way! The university's always buzzing with something. Speaking of which, did you all catch the University Challenge last week? It was epic. Oh, yes! I DVR’d it. We could sit together and watch it recreationally sometime, though. Fun idea! I just bought Hungry Hippos because I saw them online and they look like such a laugh. Oh, good one. That’ll go well with our post-quiz sessions in the common room. You know how competitive those can get. Competitive? How can something as funny and silly as Hungry Hippos be competitive? Oh, believe me, anything with a score or any sort of edge can get pretty competitive among friends. I bet Articulate would get very serious if we played it too. Speaking of games, we should play Heads Up at our next house dinner.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new development project in Sunderland? It's supposed to be huge and bring in loads of new jobs and stuff. Thought it'd be talked about at work more, but no one's batted an eye yet. Aye, yeah, I saw a bit about that in the news. Must be quite exciting for folk back home, eh? Absolutely! It's a bit big of a deal, right? Might be able to bring some economic growth back to the north. Definitely. Though, as an engineer, I'll tell you, seeing large-scale projects like that creates opportunities for thousands of jobs across all levels. From design and planning to actual construction work. That's right, yeah. So what's the project all about? Was it from big government initiative or private investors making moves? As far as I understand, it's a mix of both. The government has a £500 million pledge for the project, which is expected to create over 5,000 jobs in engineering and construction. The project's aim is to create a hub or a business cluster that could catalyze further development in the region. It's certainly ambitious, but if it works out, it could significantly boost the local economy. Blimey, that's a lot of jobs! It must be a welcome relief to the local community, especially after the decline of the shipbuilding industry. It is indeed. Though as an outsider looking in, one can't help but think about the potential challenges too, considering the region's history and all. What do you think about that? Hmm, good point. But it's not just about the jobs, you know? It's about hope, kind of. Giving people back in Sunderland something to look forward to, making them feel the region's worth it again. I just wish more people were talking about it. Seems like it's just me getting all worked up about it. It's natural to be excited and it's great that you are. Perhaps changing the conversation where you are can help spread the word. Plus, if it does all go well, that could be a huge case study for similar projects in other parts of the country. Sunderland, as you know, has historically been quite an industrial area. True that. You know, it's funny, when I used to spend my summer holidays in Sunderland as a kid, there were all these shipyards and factories and factories.

Right, well I'm not sure about you lot, but I've had a right old time this morning. My back's been playing up and the rain out there is just talked about old England. Can't be any worse than this though, right? Oh, yes, I entirely agree with you on that. It's just so dismal out there. I've got a terrible headache this morning, part of my usual post-rain patter, I'm afraid. Erm, yeah, it's not ideal weather out there, is it? But it's not all bad. You'll always find someone who's got it worse than you. I heard about a tractor stuck in the mud in the village, that's a sight worth grumbling over, just like the weather. [chuckles] Yeah, but even that tells you we're still well-off. As for your back, Uncle Tom, have you tried the new spine exercises on the health app on your phone? I know how you're a bit technophobic, but it could help. And it's free. [skeptical] Health app? What is that? I’m more of a stick and tree branch type person when it comes to health issues. [laughs] I know, I know. But in all seriousness, Uncle Tom, it's the modern age, we've all got to embrace it somewhat. [grumbling] Aye, right, all these new techs and gadgets. I remember when all we had was a transistor radio. Actually, that reminds me, I came across a nice portable radio that's also a Bluetooth speaker and the sound quality is superb. Very useful for our family gatherings and such. Oh, really? That sounds interesting. More convenient than those old fashioned TVs, isn't it? [grumbling yet intrigued] Aye, perhaps. But I still miss the days of proper TV sets and listening to the radio on a sunny day. These modern gadgets are all complicated. Well, they are easier for us to navigate these days. I often have my grandchildren over when their working parents can't manage them. It’s all about making things easier for them and for us. True. [pauses, then almost as an afterthought] Wonder what the weather will be like next weekend when Norwich is playing. [excitedly] Oh, aren't they playing against Cardiff? I've heard their defense is rather weak this season. [adding with a huff] I wouldn't bet on it if I were you.

Girls, I can't believe we're all gathered here without our bf's. Makes me miss mine too. Honestly, I talked to Joe last week, and he still hasn't proposed. Still? You must be waiting for a sign from the universe or something. LOL, something like that. But seriously, I feel like my family is always subtly hinting at it too. My Sam seems very set for it. But even so, marriage is a big commitment. True, but isn't it also a beautiful promise of forever with the person you love? Absolutely. I just hope that when I find my forever, he'll be as keen on having kids as I am. What's wrong with being a career woman and not wanting kids? Nothing at all, but sometimes it feels society expects you to want a family after marriage. Exactly. It's like it should be the natural next step. But honestly, I'm not sure if I'm ready yet. Yeah, it's pressure. I mean, I'm barely twenty-five and everyone keeps asking when I'm getting married. And the wedding planning hasn't even started, can't even think about kids. Maybe we need to set boundaries about that sort of thing, no? For sure. And if they can't respect that, maybe they're not really good friends and family. Agreed. But it's tough because marriage and kids are so idealized. Honestly, I just want a simple, intimate wedding. No fuss. I like the idea of a small, family dinner. Just as long as we can have a proper wedding cake! LOL! Can't forget the cake. Speaking of which, my mum asked if I'd like her to help out with the wedding planning. Be careful what you wish for. She's always willing to help though. But she's definitely got her own vision. Mine too. She wants the whole nine yards. As long as you enjoy it, that's all that matters. For sure. I just wish all these conversations could wait for another two years or so. I know right. Just focus on your work, love your life, and everything else will follow naturally. Absolutely, but it's hard when everyone is always asking. At least we're all in this together. Totally. Let's get one thing straight for the next party or family event: No wedding or kids talk allowed unless I bring it up.

Right, so I was on the computer yesterday afternoon, trying to send an email to our granddaughter. Now, I was using that windows thing, and I don't know much about it, but suddenly all of these boxes and lines came up. I was like, "What on earth have I done, now?" Oh, dear! You've probably clicked on something you weren't supposed to. It happens to me all the time. Yes, fractals or whatever they're called. I had to explain that to my oldest keeps coming across them on his phone. He thinks they're game levels or something. Exactly! Like that. But I've just had enough today. I really don't get this stuff. Well, you're not alone, there. I've tried following a few tutorials online, but they all seem to assume you know more than you do. It's like they're speaking a language from Mars or something. You two might want to check out the library's technology course. They offer free sessions for beginners. A course, you say? That might be a bit much for this old head. Well, if not a course, they often have volunteers who'll sit with you while you learn. Quite useful. You know, it's the money, really. It's always the money. If technology was free, I'd spend all day trying to figure it out. Oh, isn't it just the way of the world? The things we'd do, couldn't afford. And yet, they expect you to have email and all that nowadays. True, but the internet has so many free resources. If you know where to look. But the problem is, finding them takes time, and that's what I don't have. Okay, okay, let's ease off on money for a bit. What about horses? I've heard you've been looking into some horse riding classes here in Costessey. Ah, horses! Now that's something I can understand. I've had a few lessons, and it's been quite a challenge, but it's enjoyable. Gives me exercise, too. And a chance to get out of this house, I suppose? Yes, that too. It's like a job, getting the horse ready and out for a ride. Felt a bit like work, actually. That's excellent! So, what's been the biggest challenge for you? Balance, handling the reins?
