Ah, lovely to see you over for a cup of tea, Uncle John. How are you finding these quiet moments after working so hard at your business for so many years? You know, it's been a bit of an adjustment, to be honest. People keep telling me, 'You're retired now, enjoy it!' But it’s funny isn't it? You spend most of your life looking forward to this moment and when it arrives, you suddenly realize you don't actually have as much to do. It can be that way, can't it? I guess it's like when you get used to being busy, and then suddenly you've got all this free time. What have you been filling your days with? Well, let me tell you, even retired, I can't help but look back fondly on my career. I've been making time each week to help out at the local community centre here in Birmingham, which is keeping me connected and giving back a bit. Otherwise, it's been a bit of a struggle finding a routine, shall we say. It's wonderful that you're giving back to the community though! And I'm sure it makes a big difference to the youth there. It does, thank you for saying so. You know, I sometimes think I should have done something like that while I was still working. But its hard to balance work, family, and community when you're managing a business. Absolutely. I imagine it's tough to juggle, especially when your job is so demanding in itself. Speaking of demanding jobs, I've been really enjoying my postgrad course on linguistics and working as a language teacher. But weren’t you always passionate about languages? I remember you holding 'language sessions' for us as kids, didn’t you? Oh, absolutely! It’s something I’ve always loved. I tried to get the rest of you hooked on learning languages since a young age. And now as a teacher, I really see the impact it can have on people and their understanding of the world. It's great to see you following your passion. I wish I could've done more with that when I was younger. Our generation didn't have as many opportunities in education. I know, education has really changed over the years. It's wonderful that the younger generations have so many possibilities.

Oh, did you both celebrate Valentine's Day or have anything fun planned? I just spent the whole day watching movies and eating pizza at home alone. It wouldn't have been so bad if I hadn't been constantly Snapchatting at least 5 friends that they should have booked a table at that new Italian place yesterday because it was just so overbooked and now I'm stuck with leftovers for the weekend. I'm right there with you, mate. I thought I was gonna treat myself to a fancy movie date with my current flame but guess what? He bailed on me last minute blaming some family Thanksgiving celebration. Like, lazy excuse much? Oh, absolutely. But let’s not dwell on the negative. I bet the cinema food was good, right? I've heard the new cinema we tried out last week has amazing popcorn and even a chocolate fountain you can dip your popcorn in - sounds like a fun idea if you didn't mind paying an arm and a leg for it. Oh, yeah, sure, next time I'll just remember to tie myself to a chair and eat popcorn for dinner instead of trying for something a bit more exciting. Exactly. Speaking of food, I was at this new café today trying to pick up some coffee and apparently the queue was so long, it was spiraling out of control. Someone even started selling their own coffee in there, it was hilarious. Tell, I'm all ears. So, this woman, real casual, she walks in with her own coffee cups and starts selling coffee to others in the queue, saying it’s all part of her “emergency caffeine plan”. Everyone’s just staring, but nobody stops her, so I guess, she gets a free coffee for the day? That's classic. So, what movie did you end up watching then? Oh, just some rom-com. It was okay, but nothing spectacular. I was just more into the idea of treating myself than the movie itself. I did find out it's actually available in our university library, so at least I can watch it again if I want to. Again, me with the lack of plans. Got almost nothing lined up for the weekend. Maybe I should just put up with those leftovers I mentioned earlier and have my own little pizza and movie night.

Oh, so many topics we've got to cover. Politics first? It's been quite a week. Yeah, talked about little else. What are your thoughts on the latest? Well, now that the dust has settled a bit – do you find it odd that racism is so rife and yet we make gestures and say, "We've come so far"? Of course I do. It's frustrating and it feels like we're stuck in an endless cycle. As a journalist, I've seen it in the most unlikely of places, from the city to the suburbs – it's rooted in all corners. It's like in our work too, just trying to make even a small change can be so infuriating sometimes. Yeah, work politics. They can be so draining. I just landed this great story on the housing crisis and it's opened my eyes. It's not just a lack of affordable housing, it's the whole system that doesn't care. That's insane. As an architect, I've seen it too. So many of us are passionate about making changes, designing sustainable and affordable spaces but the planning system is so...restrictive. The capitalism bit comes in – it's about profit, not people. Exactly! And the council seems more interested in green spaces for luxury developments over community facilities. I know right, it feels like the whole system is in service of the few. But you know what, we should also be talking about what we're going to order! These noodles look amazing doesn't they? Oh, food and politics, the perfect combo. I’m getting the vegan chili noodles, you want to share? Actually, I was tempted by the Panang curry since we've been talking about international politics. Thai or Indian, but whichever way you cut it, it's all about capitalism ruining a great kitchen. Right, it's a bit more spicy for the situation. Let's share. Perfect, alright. So, if we're talking about making plans to change things, have you thought about what you could do in your journalism? Actually, I've been getting into more investigative work. I believe telling stories that challenge the status quo is a good start. But I can't do it alone – we need more voices, more diverse voices in our media. Totally agree. And...we need to support our local media when it's left-leaning, if it's challenging the system, we gotta back it up.

Right, so I'm going to have to start thinking about going back to work soon. I mean, it's been what? Almost six months since the baby started nursery. It's just... the thought of leaving her behind, you know? It's really hard for me. I know mum, but have you thought about just going part-time or a flexible work schedule? There's got to be a way you can balance work and the baby without having to leave her at the nursery full-time. Oh, I've thought about it, but it's not as simple as that. You'll have no idea how much pressure there is at work. They expect you to be at your best, all the time, despite... you know, your life just being turned upside down. Yeah, but there's maternity leave laws now, right? They have to be flexible. And what about your own career development? It's not going to be there waiting for you forever if you take a break too long. That's true. But it feels so... selfish. As if all my previous life expectations are now being thrown out or delayed. What was I thinking? I mean this is it. This is life now, and it's not just about me. And it shouldn’t be just about you, now. But it doesn't mean you have to give up your ambitions or the career you've built. It's about finding a balance. I know. I know. But it's different when it's actually happening. You're always thinking life is going to go back to 'normal' after maternity leave, but it's like... doesn't. True. But the baby weeing off the breast is also happening, right? That must be tough too. Oh, don't get me started on that. It's a whole other level of emotional rollercoaster. But look at it this way, you've been doing it all for so long now, and changing the feeding routine will help her develop her own independence too. Yeah, I know. I know. It’s just... when do I get back to being 'me'? This isn't just about me going back to work; it's about reclaiming my own identity. There's no set timeline for that. But you have to take things one step at a time. Start with the work thing, talk to HR.

Right, so I had a bit of an incident at work today. We have these new camera systems installed and one of them caught someone shoplifting. I had to give a statement to the police, and let me tell you, it was quite the experience. Oh, dear! That must have been stressful. Did they catch the thief? No, they didn't. It was a young kid, probably around 20. He took a few items, and I had to describe him to the police. It was quite... weird, to be honest. You don't usually get to do that kind of thing in your day job. Did they ask any questions that had nothing to do with the incident? Quite a few. They wanted to know what I was doing at the precise time, my relationship with the camera system, even my personal life. They were quite thorough, but I understand why they need to ask all those questions. Yeah, it can be very intrusive, but I guess it's all part of the process. Did it take a long time? A couple of hours, but it was more the waiting time than anything else. One moment they had me, then they left for 45 minutes because they had to go attend to something else. It was quite inconvenient. Speaking of inconvenience, I saw my EE phone bill last week and... well, it's rather high. I'm not sure why I'm paying that much as I don't use it that much. Did you go through your usage? It happens all the time. Sometimes you're overcharged for data or unused services. Or maybe there's a premium service you unwittingly signed up for. You should check on all those if you haven't already. That happened to me once with the Tesco mobile service. I was being billed for a service I never asked for. If you think they made a mistake, definitely contact them. EE should be able to sort it out for you. Yeah, I think that's what I'll do. Thanks for the advice. Sure thing. Now, what about you two? Anything new on the job front? I've been organizing the staff for the week. We've got a new product line coming in and I have to make sure everyone knows how to handle it. It's going well so far, but it can be stressful.

Yo, mate, welcome back to Bedford! How was the move's been treating you? Yeah, it's been quite an adventure, mate. Everything's settling down, and I've even managed to plant a decent herb garden in our backyard. That's great! Herbs are always a good addition to any meal. By the way, have you seen the latest episode of "Spartacus: Blood and Sand"? I just can't get enough of that show! Nah, actually I've been busy sorting out the garden and haven't had time. But I do know that those early deaths really grip the audience, don't they? It's like, by the time you get used to a character, they're just like - poof! Gone. Exactly! Though I feel like the writers do a good job of making sure each character still has an impact. It's amazing how much they can convey even in a short amount of time on screen. Absolutely, mate. And you ever grab a cup of black tea with lemon for me next time you're at home or whenever you come over? For me, a good cuppa is always a good touch for any conversation, even if it's just the two of us. You bet! I'll make sure to bring over a couple of bags of Earl Grey, my go-to. Though I must say, I've been using my new mortar and pestle for crushing herbs and spices more than for making tea. There's something satisfying about the process, don't you think? Definitely, mate. Smashing that stuff up makes you feel like a proper apothecary! I've always wondered how people used to do it without fancy technology. Except, I guess, all they had was just these two things. True enough, and it’s also a great workout, isn't it? Who needs the gym when you’ve got a pestle? Ha, spot on! Speaking of which, have you ever considered changing the theme of our next get-together? Last time we met up, it was a bit on the Roman history side, and while that’s interesting, I was thinking we could mix it up. That’s a great idea! Maybe we could do food? We could show off our culinary skills with some recipes. I could do British fare and you could do something Cypriot. We could also do a swap and learn something new.

Yo, how was your English test yesterday? Did you finish it all? I was so worried about the essay part. Well, it went alright. I thought the essay was a bit challenging but I finished it. How about you? Oh, I barely managed to get through the questions. I kind of got stuck on the comprehension part. But then, I thought of the way Mr. Hargrove explained it in class and I managed to answer the rest. That's good! I always remember how Mr. Hargrove explains. He makes everything so simple. Yeah, he's awesome! Did you see how he conducted the orchestra today? It was really impressive. Oh, yes! He's got such a knack for getting everyone in sync. I feel like I could do a bit better with that. Exactly! Maybe he could give us some tips. Let's ask him sometime. What about art and French? How are your lessons going in those? Art's okay, I love the new teacher. She's so cute and encouraging. But I'm struggling with French. It's just so confusing. Same here. I keep mixing the verb conjugations. But don't worry, I hear that our French teacher, Madame Dupont, is bringing us a fun project soon. Oh, nice! I'd love that. Anything to take our minds off the silly verbs. Exactly! Hey, did you hear about Sarah and Tom? Apparently they're having a bit of a feud in English class because they both want the lead in the play. No way! Why, what happened? I don’t know the full story but I heard it's because they both want a higher mark, and they think being in the play will impress our English teacher, Mrs. Richardson. Oh, that's so immature. But I get it, we all want a good grade. It’s just so silly to argue over something like that, especially when we are supposed to be supportive of each other. Right. But I guess it's just one of those things we see happening a lot at school. True. Speaking of school, what do you think of the new student in our class? Haven't really got to know her yet. She seems nice though. Yeah, she joined the school just last week. Someone told me she moved here from London. That’s cool. Hopefully, she'll be part of the wind-band, if she's a musician.

Hello again, dear! How are you? It's been ages since we last met. How's life treating you? Hello! I've just finished my exams, so I'm feeling pretty good. But now, the waiting game begins! Ah, the suspense of waiting for results. It's a bit like watching a sports match right? Exciting, nerve-wracking, but worth it in the end. Definitely. You know, it's funny, during soccer practice the other day, our coach asked about our favorite teams and I discovered I'm the only one from Yorkshire. Everyone else is from Newcastle or Darlington. Ah, a Yorkie at heart even in the midst of Newcastle and Darlington fans. That's understandable though, Newcastle has an excellent football team. Yeah, it's been a struggle, admit it! But I love it. It's got a different rhythm and the fans are really passionate. So, have you followed any sports? Maybe a football team from Darlington? Well, yes and no. I'm not a big follower of team sports, but I have been interested in some of the politics surrounding the different leagues. For instance, there's been a lot of discussion about money in the game lately. Oh right, I've heard about that. It's all about the big clubs buying up top players, isn't it? Shows the inequality in the sport. Exactly. It's not the players that I'm against, but the behind-the-scenes deals that make it harder for smaller clubs to compete. Reminds me of the ongoing debate about wealth distribution in our country too, isn't it? Yeah, it does. It's just that sports are supposed to be equal, you know? Not discriminating based on the team's size or wealth. An interesting point, son. Education for me was always about equality of opportunity, and it seems it's a similar issue in so many areas of life. Speaking of which, I found it quite frustrating when I was teaching. There was so much focus on the results and the funding went to where the 'top' students were, not necessarily where they were needed the most. Exactly. The concentration of resources keeps perpetuating the cycle where the rich schools often get more, and those that need it the most suffer. So, what would be a good way to change that? That's a tough question, but some experts suggest across-the-board funding, instead of just focusing on schools based on their past results.

Speaker_1 :   I've been thinking about obesity lately after teaching about it in my class. It's so sad to think that some of our family members might need to fight this battle later in life. Especially now, with the rising stats and all. We need to keep an eye on what we eat and make sure we stay active, don't we?   Speaker_2 :   Obesity? It's not just about keeps changing diet, dearie. It's in the genes too. I swear, when you look at the way our family's always struggled with weight, it's like it's written into our DNA.  Speaker_3 :  Well, I don't think it's all about genetics. I've seen many people change their lifestyle and lose weight. It's about the choices you make, not just family history. But I do see what you mean about family tendencies.      I'm sure both genetics and lifestyle play a part. But what if we started reinforcing this from a young age? Our children are growing up in an era different from when we were young. Their habits may set them up for obesity if we're not careful. Have you noticed the rise in obesity even within our own family over the years? It's concerning.   Speaker_4 :   As a lecturer in health studies, I have to agree with you, Speak 1. But it's not just about family habits. Driving less and walking more can make a difference. I've noticed since the introduction of cycling lanes in London, there's been a significant increase in people walking and cycling. Maybe we could encourage more of that here?      Well, I drive for a living. I'd be out of a job if people stopped driving. But I’ve had my fair share of walking too, after all those hours in workshops. While I agree on changing habits, we also need to consider the impact on industries.      You know what I find interesting in these discussions of health is the role of religion. Some belief systems truly guide people to make better choices for their bodies. Maybe we should consider that aspect too?      Interesting point, but it's quite complex. While there might be health benefits associated with certain religious practices or diets, it's not a universally applicable solution. What about generational differences and access to health information?      That brings me to another topic that interests me - surgery.

I've been meaning to ask you, have you had a chance to learn how to use Moodle properly yet? Oh, the infamous Moodle. You know I've tried to navigate it, but I must admit it can be quite frustrating at times. I know exactly what you mean. I've been teaching a part-time course and it's been difficult to wrap my head around all the features. Well, that's because it's really a very powerful tool when you know how to use it properly. What do you mean by that? Well, it's not just about uploading your lecture slides and assigning some homework. Moodle can actually help us track student progress, engage them in discussion forums, even use it as a platform for quizzes and exams. It's a very versatile platform if you grasp how to use it. Really? I had no idea. Sure. For instance, this semester I'm using it to connect all my resources, links, and media in one place. Students can access everything they need right from the course page. Do you think you could walk me through some of these features? Absolutely! I'd love to, especially if it'll make your life easier. Let's really dig into it then. That would be fantastic! So, if you just log in to the Moodle site and go to your course page... I see what you mean now! This is actually quite advanced. Exactly. And I know it seems overwhelming when you first take a look at it, but once you get comfortable with the basics, it's an enormous time-saver. I think this is going to make all the difference in my course next semester. That's the plan! You know, this makes me wish we could use something similar for our university work too. Well, the issue might be that Moodle was originally developed for educational purposes, so it's a bit like using a specific tool for a very specific task. But, it's a great example of using tech right to support teaching and learning, and maybe there are similar platforms for professional development at our university. That's a good point. There must be some platform that can help us streamline our department's workflow. Absolutely. We can definitely look into that. I have some contacts who have been experimenting with similar tools. So, essentially, under the guise of learning Moodle for my course, you've given me food for thought about our own professional development.

Ah, I can't believe we're finally getting tickets to that play. I've been hearing so much about it. I've been meaning to see it for ages, and now that we've got the chance to go together, I'm really excited. Did you get a look at the tickets? Yeah, I booked us for Friday evening, thought that might be a good night. It's a bit out of our way, of course, but the play's worth it. Definitely! I've heard it's a fantastic production. Speaking of which, have you started seeing any signs of jetlag from our trip last week? I've been sleeping a bit later than usual, that's for sure. But otherwise, I think I'm adjusting just fine. How about you? I'm feeling pretty normal, apart from a slightly earlier bedtime which is probably just a leftover from our trip. It didn't affect me as much, I think, because I slept on the plane. You didn't get any rest at all, did you? No, not really. For me, sleeping on a plane is always quite challenging. But I guess it's all part of traveling, right? Exactly. And now that we're back, let’s make sure our routine is back to normal. Have you noticed any other changes since we got back? Other changes? In what sense? Well, since we've been talking about babies for a while now, I was wondering, have you noticed if anything feels different? Oh, doesn't everything feel different after a couple of weeks away? But now you mention it, yeah, our conversation has been quite different lately. We've been planning more things for future, less about daily routine, more about togetherness and a family. That's a good point. I've definitely noticed that too. It's like we're already mentally preparing for this new chapter. Exactly. It's really scary but exciting at the same time. We've been talking a bit more about what we want our future to look like. I know, right? I mean, having children is going to change our lives, obviously, but it's such a great change. Absolutely. And speaking of which, have you noticed if there are any more baby-sized things we need to start thinking about? We've been pretty diligent about our prep so far, but I just realized we need to start decorating the nursery.

Ah, speaking of other countries, did you hear anything about your friend in Libya recently? I read that there are ongoing issues around the oil and Wahhabi influence there. Yes, I've kept in touch. Things are complicated, really. Many are worried because of the political unrest, but also because of the spread of Wahabbism. It's troubling and often overshadows the struggle for stability and democracy. I can only imagine. But I have another question. I know you're NRPSI certified for Arabic. Have you ever worked professionally in Germany alongside English? That seems like an interesting mix. Oh, absolutely! It's a very engaging combination. I've had opportunities to work with both languages professionally in various settings. Though, to be honest, English is more demanded due to its global status in business and academia. That's interesting, and probably very useful given your dual background. I sometimes find it challenging to balance language duties at work with family engagements. You seem to manage very well though. It's a matter of routine and understanding the context, I suppose. And I have to say, speaking languages has given me a unique view of this world. One moment you see the commonality in all cultures, and the next the deep political structures that divide us. Very true. Speaking of divide, how’s your family handling the ongoing visa issues? I heard the UK has made it harder to get a visa recently for families like yours, or for people who might be looking to settle here. It's been a nuisance for sure. The process is lengthy and often unpredictable. But my family is hoping to visit soon. I've been helping them with the applications, but it's tough. Makes the progress we make as a society seem quite behind when it comes to global connectivity and understanding. Absolutely. Seems like the young people are those most affected by these changes, aren't they? It’s so important that our policies reflect the reality of interconnected lives, rather than just acting on suspicion or security alone. Indeed. While I agree on changing the policies to be more inclusive and reasonable, it’s also about education and dialogue. We need more integration programs for young people, in schools for example. I've seen in my own work, how much impact understanding different cultures can have on breaking down walls. So true.

I've decided I need a new TV. The one we have today is nearly 10 years old and it's clearly showing its age. I talked to a friend the other day and she said they just replaced their TV with one of those nice smart ones and it's been a game changer. A new TV, eh? I was thinking the same thing, but did you consider that they're hardly cost-effective considering how often new models come out? Oh, I know that! But it's not just about the tech, it's about the size too. I want one of those big screen ones for the roast lamb we've just had. It's just more relaxing to watch a good film or a football match on a proper screen. Ah, yes - the old roast lamb. And to think you used to complain about the table being too small, now you want a bigger TV... It's all about scale, isn't it? Anyway, about the TV, I agree with you - it's worth the investment. But maybe instead of a new one this year, we could look at next year when there's likely to be a better deal with the new models coming out? Good idea! I hadn't thought about waiting. Although, let's also not forget the Scottish tablet I wanted. Oh, right, the tablet. You silly goose, you still want a tablet to keep your life in order? I don't think it's ridiculous! It's a hell of a lot more efficient than my current phone. Plus, think of all the times I've needed to make notes in a hurry and my phone just isn't the best for that. She's got a point. Writing notes on paper or even on your phone is nowhere near as straightforward for us older folks and it's always easier to use a dedicated device. Good for her, though, she’s been trying to be more organized. But for me, I've had just as much trouble with my notes so I'm definitely nodding to that. Besides, it’ll be something for me to be interested in. I've almost gone through my list of new TV shows worth watching. Perhaps a tablet could even help you keep track of those dog walks too? You two know nothing about dogs, but I hear a tablet might be... Don't worry, I know better than to try and use that as an excuse.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new vegan bakery place that just opened up in town? Yeah, I've heard about it. It's the one just down by the bus station. Aye, I tried their vegan chocolate cake – it's actually quite good! I went last week and got this amazing fruit scone. It was healthy and tasted great, you know, actually very good for a vegan bakery. That's true! keeps coming up in conversations with people in town. Yeah, it's a great alternative for us who are trying to be more conscious about what we eat. Absolutely, speaking of which, have you noticed the bill for food in the flat is always a bit high? Agreed, it's partly because of the preferences of the flatmates, but also because of the sometimes unnecessary purchases. I think we should start doing a weekly shop together. It'd stop all the individual buying and help us watch the expenditure. For sure! We could make a shopping list, see what everyone wants and balance it out. Plus, it would be more sociable too! Great idea. We could even figure out the most cost-effective way to do it, right? Like using coins at certain shops or making the most of buying in bulk. Totally! We could also look for discounts or coupons. I've been doing really well with that at home. That's a good point about shopping wisely. I could likely share some tips from my mum – she's always finding the best deals. That'd be awesome, thanks! I just hate seeing things go to waste. Seems like the flat's fridge always ends up a bit chaotic, doesn't it? Yes, and another thing – we should come up with some rules for keeping it organized. Someone should take responsibility for tidying the fridge and changing the bins every week. Good call! We can also make a bit more effort when we cook to not make more than we need. If we just make what we need, we'd probably waste less too. Definitely! It's all about the little things, like using the leftovers. I used to almost never eat leftovers at home, but living in this flat has taught me to appreciate them. That's a mindset shift we've all had to make living here, I guess. Yeah, for sure. Cooking often too feels like a group effort here...

Alright, girls! Let's move on from games for a bit. I have an important announcement. Tomorrow, I'll be taking a baking lesson into my class! Oooh, baking! Can we help? Yeah! Can we make cupcakes? Ah, that sounds like a great idea! But, of course, as much as I'd love to have your help in the actual lesson, that might be a bit tricky. Think about it this way. You'll tell your friends about the lesson after. But I want to help! You'll help me bake for the lesson here at home, but for the lesson itself, let's say you'll be little sous pastry chefs and help me measure out ingredients, watch closely, and learn tricks and tips! Cool! So we get to make our own cupcakes today and tomorrow we'll do it in the class? Precisely! Yay! Can we still make the 'Tomodachi Life' cake for mum’s half birthday though? Absolutely, my little bakers! But first, for today, perhaps we could go through what we'd typically do in a lesson in class: the why, the what, and the how. Why do we need to learn baking? Well, first off, it's fun! But also, understanding measurements, temperatures, and mixing ingredients can help you in other areas too – like math, science, and even a bit of language. Ooh, can we use maths to know how much flour or sugar to use? That's a great idea! As we bake today, we can actually do a mini lesson on that – make it fun! What if we make something go wrong? It happens to the best of us! That's part of the fun. We learn from our mistakes. Remember the book we found in Morrisons? Maybe there are similar mistakes in that too. Yeah! The one about baking disasters. Exactly. We can even use that as a way to inspire this lesson. How about...we do a few different recipes, one that's sure to be a disaster, just for fun? A baking disaster party! Can we make it look intentional, like we did it on purpose? Oh, that would be genius! So, for the lesson tomorrow, we have our objective set: to engage, inspire, and enjoy the process, even with baking fails. That brings me to another task for you two. What's that? We need to find a specific book for our classroom library.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my online conquests? On Facebook. Facebook, the land of endless adventures, isn't it? Are you still involved in the 'Captain Specs' persona now? Oh yes! I just can't seem to let it go. It's such a fun way to interact with my students. I get to share interesting articles and reminders, all the while I'm trying to keep up this secondary life as this flamboyant character who is far removed from the real me. You really love to create this alternate identity for yourself, don't you? It's quite amusing. But did your students ever figure out that it's you? No, not yet! I've been making sure the clues are subtle enough. It's all about balance - you can't let the mask slip too far or it ceases to be fun. And you're quite good at it. You should consider writing a guide on online personas. I'm sure it would be a hit with the psychology crowd. Now that's an idea! I think most of us have some level of duality in our online presence. It's a way of exploring different facets of our personality, isn't it? Perhaps, but sometimes I worry about people who take it too far. Look at all the fake news spreading through Facebook and other platforms. That's a different issue altogether. Despite its downsides, doesn't Facebook open up a global community for discussion and the sharing of ideas? I agree, if one is discerning enough. The problem is, not everyone has the skills or the time to be discerning. Which is why we as educators have a role to play. Teach our students how to critically assess information, how to engage in constructive dialogue online. Absolutely. On a different note, I've been thinking of buying a new car and I just can't decide what to get. I mean, there are so many options now... Oh, and what's the dilemma? Is it something specific, like fuel economy or space? Well, I've always been a petrolhead. But with more and more manufacturers turning electric, I'm not sure. I mean, I love the thrill of driving a fast car, but I also want to do my bit for the environment. That's a really tough choice. On one hand, electric cars are becoming more efficient and have a lower environmental impact.

Yo, mate, did you seen any of the sales targets move today? Our manager was getting tight; he's been on at us all about meeting the month's quota. Oh yeah, I did. There was quite a squeeze for the new tech gadget deal. But honestly, I think part of the problem is the sales strategy. Do you think it would make a difference if we moved some stuff around in the store to catch eyes more? Or maybe... right now, as I look at this film, isn't it funny how much marketing tactics even kid's films use? Cloudy with a chance of meatballs uses this whole idea that, okay, you can create anything – literally – with food, just like these fancy products are supposed to make your life easier. Ah, that’s a good point. But even that film’s making me think of all this stuff doesn’t help my appetite. Been nothing but coffee and the occasional sandwich today. Sorry to hear that. You're not doing too well are you? Let me stop this film for a sec. Nah, this is actually interesting. Just see if you can pause it for a sec. You know, actually, the TV remote’s gotten a lot more complicated over the years, right? What if I tell you there's a hidden meaning in it – like a metaphor for current jobs or perhaps gender roles? Instead of manually controlling something , think of it like having control over your life, and all these buttons and features are like the choices you have. Huh, I kind of see what you’re saying, but I think all these design flaws just make people feel the opposite – less in control of their lives. Like, why must TVs, and life, be so complicated? Exactly! Now, that's something we really should talk about sometime – feminism, consumerism, changing the world. But sure, on to another complicated thing: how's your feminism vibe? I know you're thinking about studying it more seriously. Yeah, it's on my mind a lot actually. And it's got me thinking about so many things – even how the adverts for this film almost unintentionally reinforce certain gender norms or class divisions. Boys playing with these big machines and girls with cooking? It’s just like these stereotypes we’re always fighting. You're really getting into all that stuff aren’t you?

Ah, Phil, great to see you again! How was your day? I've been hearing so much about the Premier League lately. Did you catch the latest Liverpool match? Ah, well, yeah, I did, mate! Wasn't exactly the best match, if you ask me. But hey, what can you do, innit? You've got to support the Reds, eh? Absolutely! I wish I could have made it to Anfield again, though I had a lecture series going on. Anyway, I've been following how Liverpool is doing alongside the whole political scene in Britain. I mean, we've had our fair share of change, haven't we? I heard that. New Labour did some good stuff, just like the Sports Council, but sometimes I wish they did more for the places like Liverpool. We still have our share of problems, mate. Exactly, Phil! It's a bit complex, isn’t it? New Labour, under Tony Blair, got a lot of things done, but like you said, it seems like the benefits didn't reach all the places they should have. True that. I don’t usually get into politics much, but you’re right. Tony Blair was good with his words but sometimes seemed too focused on the bigger picture and forgot about the little people like us. It's a common critique. As a lecturer, I spend a lot of time discussing this with my students. Interestingly, many of them feel the same way. Blair was a master in political communication, really good at explaining his vision, but sometimes, I think, he overlooked the 'stakeholders' on the ground - doesn't matter if that's a small town in the north of England or elsewhere. You're spot on, mate! I just drive people around the city and hear all their stories, you know? Every day I meet someone, they always talk about how things haven't changed much since Blair's time. Yes, that's a great perspective, and it really makes me think about how policy implementation varies so much depending on where you are. It’s a good thing we have people out on the ground, like you, who can give us a glimpse of what's really happening. I thought I was just a taxi driver, mate! Haha! No, seriously, it’s good to be able to share insights like this once in a while. It’s like...

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I was doing some BNC recordings in South London? It was fascinating! The varieties of English, the pronunciations... the whole experience was quite enriching. Oh, yes, I remember hearing about that on Linked In! I must have missed the post though. What was it like? It was a bit overwhelming at first, you know? So many different ways of speaking English in such a small geographical space. And then there's how it differs from our local dialects here in Aylesbury. Oh, you English always talk about your dialects and accents, don't you? It must be quite a bit to take in for someone visiting from abroad. Yeah, even as a Welsh person moving around England, I've found it interesting! Though, I have to say, I've met many Londoners who can't understand Wales accent at all. Well, English English and Welsh English or even Cornish English are different enough that sometimes it's like we're speaking different languages! That's fun though, no? I wish we had such distinctions. Mostly, where I'm from, everyone speaks more or less the same, or at least, people from different regions can easily understand each other. Speaking of accents, have you tried using different accents on social media? I recently saw a post from @LondonLife and they have this feature that changes your voice with a click. Seriously? There's an app that can change your accent like that? That's wild! I wonder how people would react if I suddenly started speaking in Received Pronunciation on Twitter. Oh, it's mainly for entertainment purposes, but it can be fun! I've tried it a couple of times, but honestly, I prefer my own accent. Accents are part of our identity, after all. Definitely. Though some people I know in Wales say they sometimes put on a more American or Australian accent when they're on holiday abroad. Might be for safety or just so people understand them better. I've heard that too. Even I've done it before. There's a little bit of fear involved when you travel abroad and you're not sure if you'll be understood. Oh, I can relate. I'm quite scared of flying actually. I know it's irrational but...I mean, what if the plane goes down? That's completely normal, and there are loads of people who feel the same.

Yo, mate, did you finish reading that novel you've been banging on about? Yeah, I managed to squeeze it in during my train ride this morning. Got some down time to myself. Cool. Any thoughts? Really liked it. The way the author uses metaphors to bring London to life reminded me of the city itself. It's like a living, breathing character in the book. I see that. You're always so good at breaking it down. Speaking of living and breathing, how are your interns going? Oh, those kids. They're good, but they're all so eager. I have to remind them that even if they're early in their careers, their work is valuable. Agree on that. I've seen it a lot with students. What's new with the house project? Ah, project. Still finding out if we can splurge on that fancy kitchen. Your idea of a fancy kitchen and my would probably be very different. I’m a simple guy. A Foreman grill and a bottle of red and I’m good. I'm more of a comfort zone person, while you? You’re about new experiences in food. Absolutely. Have you seen those Japanese ramen places popping up? Their eggs are to die for. Aye, I've had one or two ramen meals. The cheese corn ramen really caught my eye, but I'd probably go for a classic tonkotsu. Mmm… that sounds like it. So, is the plan still to do Christmas this year at our place? I thought so. As long as you're not against it, we can make it a family affair, as always. No, love it. Just got couple of small things left to buy. That’s good. Because I’ve been meaning to ask, are you ready to start seriously looking at your post-uni career plans? Yeah, I know. I've been thinking it. I've got a few potential internships coming up, might be a good way to get my foot in the door. That sounds like a good plan. I've got some contacts in the field. We could set up a meet and talk if you want. That’d be great. I really appreciate your connections. No problem at all. You've been helpful to me often too, so this is just giving back. That's so kind. By the way, what's new with work?

Ah, I can't believe how much of a difference it's made to have Grace take up that Pilates class. She's so much less stressed and I've noticed she's been sleeping better too. Yes, I've heard that. Exercise classes are so beneficial for both physical and mental health. Speaking of which, I just started a yoga class and it's been a game-changer for my flexibility and my mood. That's great to hear, I've always wanted to try yoga but never seem to fit it into my schedule. How is it going alongside work and everything else? It's been manageable. I've been setting aside one evening a week for just that, and I've been really enjoying the calmness of it. It's surprisingly difficult, but in a good way. Ah, yes - "in a good way" is definitely the way to describe exercise. It's amazing how quickly you can feel your body change with regular exercise. I also love how you can tailor it to what you like and what your body needs. Absolutely, and that's one thing I love about yoga. It's so adaptable. I have a friend who started doing it for back pain and now she's training to become an instructor. That's inspiring. I've always thought about taking up a new sport, perhaps tennis or even cycling, but never seem to find the time or the motivation. Perhaps I should try to make more of an effort. Definitely. Finding a sport or class that you really enjoy makes it much easier to stick with, and it doesn't even feel like "exercise" if you like it doesn't it? But it's also about finding the right time. For me, it works better in the evening because I don't have to rush in the morning. true, I try to go for a jog in the morning but often it feels like it's getting in the way of everything else. It does feel nice though, getting out in the fresh air. Yes, and changing the scenery can also help. I was on a reporting trip last year and I ended up jogging along the beach every morning. It was amazing. Beautiful, isn't it? And it's surprising how much we see things when we're not rushing. Speaking of places, have either of you been abroad recently?

I've decided I need a teaching break. I have these students today that nearly drove me mad. You know, the ones who think they're right about everything even when the evidence is glaringly against them? Oh yes, I know the type. That questions the status of 'lecturer' as a profession for the mentally and emotionally stable. Now, don't start! Teaching isn't that bad. It can be rewarding when you see that light bulb moment. But let me tell you, today it felt more like a reality TV show. Well, you have to say that's one of the benefits of online teaching - you can mute them. But seriously, I feel you. Sometimes I think about how many fingers I could be threading while teaching and just staring at the watch hoping the hour moves faster. Exactly! But seriously, it's those same students who end up being so surprised when they realize they actually don't know their stuff at all. For me, it's usually a specific moment when they connect the dots and suddenly their understanding of a concept significantly improves. That's what makes it all worth while. For sure. Speaking of which, I met one of our former students at a conference last week. He's gone on to do his PhD and is now working at a major media company. It's always a proud moment when someone tells you how your teaching has influenced their path. And that’s what keeps me going – when I hear how my classes helped someone else understand the subject better and the impact that has on their lives or work. Except, unfortunately, I don’t hear about it often enough. More reason for those post-graduation surveys, isn’t it? We probably just need to remind students to fill them out. Oh, but we should! We could benefit from feedback and also help ourselves see the impact we’re actually having. Yes! But for now, I have a different kind of impact in my life... This Chinese weather has been a disaster for my nails. Your nails almost gone yet again? How do you manage to keep doing that? I just don’t seem skilled at nail care. Especially in this heat and humidity, it’s a real struggle. You're right, it’s not just the nails... I’ve had any sort of personal hygiene routine that requires keeping something dry, ruined here.

Ah, lovely to see you, Tom. How have you been? I have to say, the gym's quite busy today. Yeah, it's always chaos around this time of day. Are you still enjoying your new role as a language teacher? Really love it, Tom. It's such a breath of fresh air after years of working in the corporate world. I feel like my life has a bit more meaning now. That's fantastic, Sarah. I'm very happy for you. It must be rewarding teaching people new skills, something else altogether than being a company director. Exactly! Although, I'm always nostalgic about the company I used to work for in London. We had a fantastic team there. Did you ever watch that new documentary series on the BBC about big brands? Ah, no, I haven't had a chance to watch it yet, but I do remember some of the big topics it covered. What did you think of the section about Oxbridge admissions? Oh, it was quite enlightening. I didn't realize the extent of the implicit bias that still exists in this sector. One of my students was applying to Oxford, so that was a timely conversation with her. Yeah, it's a fascinating subject. I think the more we can bring these things to the forefront, the more we can work towards changing them. Speaking of university, are you planning to do any further study? Actually, I was in two minds about it for a bit, but I'd love to get a PhD in Linguistics one day. But I don't think I'll realistically start that until my daughter is a bit older. That's understandable. I don't envy you trying to do studies with a career and raising a family, but it's definitely achievable. I took my graduate studies part time when I was younger and managed just fine. Thanks for the encouragement, Tom. It means a lot coming from someone like you who's so achieved. Achieved? I wouldn't go that far. But it's always better to listen to success stories from someone who's done something similar, isn't it? Definitely. So, what about you? How's the company doing? We're managing, business is as usual in the manufacturing sector. I swear though, I'm starting to believe in some of these crazy conspiracy theories.

Dad, did you ever read Jamaica Inn by Daphne du Maurier? It's set in Cornwall and I thought it would be such a good book to read before our holiday. Ah, isn't it great now, the road, all those colours – acres of green, some kind of ginger fields near the sea? I remember my childhood holidays, the car journeys were my favourite part, the anticipation of seeing the sea, actually, seeing the sea never gets old. Yeah, nothing beats seeing the sea for the first time, seeing the Cornish houses and the lazy beach – I'm really looking forward to it. And I've been listening to the Wizard of Oz audiobook just cos it's set somewhere 'far away', you know? Ah, yes, oh we've driven past that place before. And speaking of journeys, you remember reading Sherlock Holmes? Oh, definitely, dad! My favourite is the Hound of the Baskervilles. I love it when Sherlock solves the mysteries so smoothly and the English landscape is always so intricately described. Yeah, and it's funny how both Sherlock and Lewis Carroll have this same "English-ness" about them, no? A bit of eccentricity, lots of landscape detail. What do you mean by "English-ness"? I think it's all about this love for the landscape, and the way English folks describe things, you know, the flowers and the birds, and the houses too – there's always a description of how they look in the stories. And the language is so lush, so full of detailed observations. Yeah, the way they describe things – the descriptions in fairy tales too. I was thinking, we could keep track of the different flowers and birds we see on our trip. That's a great idea! There must be lots of different species in Cornwall. We'll need a guidebook for that. Oh, and I was wondering, if we need to send any texts or emails when we're there. We always take our phones with us. We can show you how we used to communicate before those. Morse code and telegrams. Even telex in my day. No way! Morse code? Yes, we used to send messages using dots and dashes. It was the only way often, especially when dealing with foreigners across... over the ocean. That's so... ancient! Not to mention, a bit like braille, right? Yes! That's true! It's all about encoding and decoding messages.

Right, so I had this absolute nightmare of a day at work. We have these new fellows coming in and they seem to be struggling with the corpus system we've got. It's supposed to make their jobs easier but they're just getting tangled up in it. Morning, dear! That does sound like a right old mix-up. I remember when I used to work with BT and we had systems that took days to understand. It makes me think of how quickly things can change. Do you remember those days, Sam? Yeah, well, let me tell you, technologies change but some things stay the same. Even back in Manchester, our computer training seemed like a chore but I guess that's just the nature of work. It just needs patience to learn. Exactly! But it can be frustrating when you're trying to make things smoother and they're still getting stuck. I can imagine. We've had similar issues with software updates at work. But, you know, it's all about teaching them the ropes and giving them the time. Sometimes it's the older folks who struggle but also sometimes it's the younger ones who just can't keep it on track. Well, that's a fair point. I never really got on well with technology while I was working. I always felt it was more of a complication than a help. But, you know, it's different for people like you, technology is probably second nature. It is, but even then, it can still be a challenge in itself sometimes, like trying to keep everything organized and running smoothly, and all the while dealing with the "oldies" who don't quite get it. True, but the progress that technology has brought us is remarkable. Just like we've made all these advancements from your generation working the phones at BT to artificial intelligence handling most of those roles nowadays. Speaking of which, do you remember when we used to have to personally meet people to set up phones or ins and outs? And nowadays it's all online. You'd think after all these years of it, people would've adapted but some are still not comfortable with new technologies. I suppose it just takes time for everyone. It's indeed a generational thing. And it's not just about technology, look at how education has changed.

Mum, I can't believe I'm finally back home! It's been ages since we've caught up like this. How's everything been at home? Everything's fine, dear. Just the usual, I suppose. Right now we're in the middle of preparing for the move, so the house is a bit chaotic. Oh, I see. Moving day isn't too far off then? Not as far off as I'd like, to be honest! But we're making good progress. And how was your flight coming back? You look a bit jet-lagged. Jet-lagged? No, not really. I think I just need a good cup of tea and a decent night's sleep. It just felt really strange to leave Miami. You're probably just tired from the travel. Now, let's get that sorted. How about we have a quiet cup of tea and a bit of sandwiches? We've decided on a lot of creative breakfast sandwiches in the new place, so I thought it would be good if you could approve them. That sounds perfect. I hope you remember to include some Forager cakes. I don't know what it is about them, but they always make me feel better after a long flight. Forager cakes? Of course. We'll make sure they make the cut. Thanks, Mum. You're always so considerate about these things. It's always a pleasure, especially for you. By the way, how are the plans for your new apartment? Did you manage to get all the necessities sorted and transferred over? Yeah, things are slowly falling into place. I've got a few friends coming to help me move the heavy stuff. I do hope we can make it in without too much hassle. Good luck with that. I remember when you used to move so easily as a teenager. Nowadays, I see all the heavy things you've accumulated over the years. Yeah, I guess years of collecting books and teaching materials can do that to you. But honestly, I think some of that stuff should probably go. Wise decision, dear. I mean, you've got zero weaver fish yet, right? Ah, no weaver fish yet. But maybe in the new place... Well, I'm not sure that's a priority . Speaking of plans, have you thought about who to invite to the housewarming party? We were thinking just immediate family and closest friends for the practical one.

I've decided I need more plants in my flat. I've been meaning to do this for ages. It's about time I stop living like a single student and actually make my space a bit more homey. Just don’t fill the whole place up, or we'll start calling it the Amazon and not Cambridge. Oh, I might just give you that nickname, seeing as you never seem to leave the library. Hey, at least I'm keeping busy, unlike some people I know. Fair enough. So what did your week look like? I know you're doing research. It was good, I've been reading up on a few case studies. And I started compiling my data for the dissertation. But between you and me, I've also been looking for a new hairstyle. My hair's been the same length and style for ages. Oh, really? I love the change-up, I think you'd look brilliant with a new style. We could even do it together, see if we both like it. That would be fun! The last time we altered our hairstyles together was for the uni ball, and we ended up looking like we belonged in a different decade. Definitely, I'd take that risk again. Speaking of things that change, isn't it bizarre how the NHS is always in the news? One day, they're running fantastic and the next they're in a crisis. It is, it's like they keep the public on their toes. But it's not just the NHS, I've been hearing about petrol shortages everywhere. More logistics issues in the supply chain? I was thinking of grabbing a car for the next year since public transport is unreliable. Yes, that's a great idea but then there's the whole petrol issue. I've also been thinking about my younger cousins and the changes in A-Level reforms. I know, it's not fair on them either. It’s like the education system is so unstable, it's hard to keep up. Exactly, and what's even more worrying is the impact on mental health. These kinds of uncertainties aren't good for young people. Absolutely. We need to make sure our young people feel stable and supported, especially through their late teenage years. You know, we're lucky our higher socio-economic status means we're less affected by these things.

Right, so I'm going to stop smoking for real this time. I have enough of this. The cost is crazy and honestly, it's causing me anxiety when I can't have a cigarette. Good for you! That's a great decision. I'm not a smoker but I've seen how it affects people. I've got a lecture on the black plague at uni next week. Have you guys learned anything about it yet? Erm, yeah. It was massive. Killed nearly a third of Europe's population. Crazy when you think about it. Deadly. I heard about the social impacts too - like, jobs were short because everyone was dying. Yeah, and then there's the whole finance part. Wasn't there a lot of economic change even after the plague had passed? Yeah, lots of workers died, supply and demand went all out of whack. Labor conditions changed, wages rose because there were less people to do the work. And don't forget about the power struggle or lack thereof. Monarchs and nobles were facing this crisis, too. That's true. Thinking about it, has any of you applied for university while the 'Rona is still affecting the world? I applied during lockdown, but apparently the university process is quite different now. More online stuff, less face-to-face interviews perhaps? Yeah, Cambridge does seem to be more online for interviews now, but we’re used to learning all about it. I applied during the break myself and found that it wasn't as bad as expected. There were more virtual open days and sessions, but I could still meet with advisors and stuff. That’s good to know. Our sixth form didn't really prepare us for all of it. We’re just winging it, to be honest. Oh, really? There must be some areas where you feel unprepared. Finance stuff, mostly. Like, budgeting for uni, loans, fees... I don't know how to apply for student finance or anything. I thought I was going to have a real job to handle that. Now it looks like I'll have to be even more frugal than I thought. You all should look into websites and resources, or talk to advisors. Our school had a few webinars. Yeah, I'll definitely do that. Also, feminism has been a big topic in our politics class. How do you all see the movement nowadays?

I've been thinking a lot about friendships lately. I've realized that sometimes, you just outgrow people and you know they don't contribute much to your life anymore, but it's hard to just cut ties. How about you, have you ever found yourself in this situation? Oh, definitely! I've had friends who I used to see all the time, but over time, our lives and interests have just gone in different directions and it feels unnatural to keep forcing those connections. But still, it can be hard to actually cut them out of your life, right? Absolutely, it's like you want to be kind and not hurt their feelings, but deep down, you know you'd be better off without them. Yeah. One of my friends, from uni, we were inseparable. But after graduating and moving to different parts of the country, we realized we just weren't on the same page anymore. That seems common. I've had friends like that too, from various stages of life. It's like, for whatever reason, their presence in your life doesn't serve you any more? Maybe it's because it feels more obligatory than meaningful. Exactly. I think most of us have that one or two friends we feel guilty about seeing, but if we're honest with ourselves, we'd rather spend time with people who actually share our current interests or values. Definitely. Like, my friend Sarah, for example, she's always been a bit in-your-face, really needy. Now that we’re both in our thirties, I find it exhausting trying to meet her needs all the time. It's like it's sucking the energy out of me. That sounds familiar. I had a friend who was always falling apart, and while it was true that I wanted to help her, I also felt drained of my own energy. She'd always complain about everything, even when we were having fun or discussing something positive. Exactly, and changing the subject never seemed to work. You end up stuck in a cycle of negativity because you don't know how to make them see things differently. True, but it's hard to know how to end things nicely. Right. It's definitely easier said than done. I think there are almost two phases: realizing you don't want to see them as much anymore, and then actually actively reducing your contact without feeling guilty or mean.

Ah, Mum, it's so great to have you here. We've been swamped with deadlines and exams lately, but I've managed to catch up on a bit of reading. Had the chance to read some Shakespeare recently. Oh, that's lovely! I haven’t seen many of your generation enjoy his plays. Shakespeare’s work isn’t always easy for them to understand. Well, that may be, but I'm of the generation that still reads. Tablets and Kindles are secondary for us. The joy of holding a physical book and slowly turning the pages is immense, I tell you! I couldn't agree more. Remember when we used to read together? I used to love picking out books for both of us to discuss. You even started reading some of the classics before most of your peers did. True, I suppose. Though I have to admit, while Shakespeare's words are timeless, its language can be a tad tricky sometimes. But, you know, that's part of the fun, right? Deciphering those deep meanings and hidden nuances. Absolutely! And remember, not only was reading so important to us, but so was art. Remember when you were little, and I used to take you to art exhibitions? I do. I loved those days. It was always so exciting to see the different types of art and learn about their stories. And then later, when I started creating my own art, you were always so supportive, even if it wasn't always the most skillful... Well, art is subjective anyway, isn't it? But I was proud of you for trying and for the creativity and the progress that you made. You were incredibly supportive, Mum. I was planning to visit the new exhibition in town soon. More contemporary art this time, a bit different from what we used to visit. Do you think you might want to come along? Of course! I'd love to. That sounds like a great opportunity to see a new changing of the guard in art. And perhaps we might find something that connects both of our worlds – yours of university art history and my own more experience-based appreciation of it. That truly would be fantastic. It’s always interesting to see how art changes over time. Besides, it’ll be nice to have you there. You often see things in art that I miss.

I've decided I need to eat before I head to the gym today. I've heard it's better to fuel up before intense exercise, haven't you? You're quite right about that. A balanced meal can give you the energy you need for a good workout. It kind of makes me wonder about the times I went to the gym straight after school, with my stomach growling the whole time . I know! I used to do it for so long without even thinking twice about it. Now, at my age, I realize my body needs to be treated with more kindness . Exactly. As I've been training to be a teacher of English as a foreign language, I’ve also been learning about health and wellness in other places. The concept varies quite a bit depending on the culture. Like? Well, for instance, in many Asian cultures, breakfast is considered the most important meal of the day, similar to what we’re told in Britain. But in some parts of the US, it seems like the opposite – they often skip breakfast and just head to the gym on an empty stomach. That is quite interesting. I guess everyone has their own way of doing things. For sure. Speaking of which, I also learned that the concept of time is very different across cultures. Yeah, right, like in some places they're very punctual, but here in Poland, time seems to be quite... flexible . Exactly! I was talking to a Polish friend and she mentioned that "Polish time" exists because of the flexible attitude towards appointment times. I thought that was pretty funny . More like "relaxed timing" . I've had it hit me quite a few times while traveling here. Like when we were trying to find that one restaurant in Białka and it took us hours to find it because changing plans on the go is just part of the day’s plan. Definitely. It’s been quite an adventure this campervan journey so far, hasn’t it? Absolutely! And speaking of adventures, do you want to grab a quick bite before we head to the gym? I could do with some fueling up before we head there. Good idea. I was thinking about that too. We could try some traditional Polish food before. Perfect. I heard about this one place in Tarnow where they serve excellent pierogi.

Ah, marvellous weekend we've had haven't we? The weather was just right for the garden, isn't that right Auntie Ethel? Indeed, yes! Made for a right nice day to be out and about. Still, now, the showers we've had lately do bring questions if this will be one of those years where we see less of summer than we'd like. I've heard there might be a fair bit more rain on the way according to the forecast. Which means I'll have to keeps an eye on the plants. You know how quickly those spider veins can form on the tomatoes if they don't get enough sunlight. Well, Jane, your garden certainly keeps you on your toes. I remember when I was teaching, there was always a little spider or two in the classrooms making the children squeal. Exactly! My students did exactly the same during our recent garden project. One of them was very interested in the kinds of spiders we have around here. Off we went to the top of Pastures for a bit of spotting. For spotting spiders, it's always best to go out when it's not too hot or busy isn't it? You prefer the mornings, while the dew is still fresh. Morning is certainly best. It's nice and cool and the spiders have barely begun their web-spinning for the day. The kids were fascinated by their intricate webs, especially after we learned about different species in class. Now, spiders are one thing, but what's been going on over at Noone's lately? How's things with that power cut the other week? Oh, it was quite an ordeal, I must say. Took us a good few hours to get everything sorted again, but we managed. More a concern was the frozen milk, really. I'd almost forgotten what a fridge looked like without power for so long. Freezing milk and all! Silly me thinking it's changing the world to just add a bit of extra water after it's thawed out. You'd make a fine old-time homemaker in these situations. Well, it's surprising how much we rely on these little appliances isn't it? But it's situations like that remind me of Granny's stories about during the war, just being grateful for what you had and making do.

Mum, Dad, and Auntie Mary, I'm so excited about our family holiday this year. Where are we going and when do we leave? Ah, little one, we are off to Cornwall, just like every year! We leave in about two weeks now, the 1st of July. We love Cornwall because it's just so beautiful isn't it? You guys are going to have the time of your life! Yeah, the beaches, the hikes, and the local ice cream. It's always a treat keeps coming back. Plus, there's this town called St Ives that we've always wanted to visit again. It's full of artists and musicians, just like dear old Pete used to be. Cornwall! I love it! So, what about the caravan? And can we do some surfing this year? And bring Lulu, our dog? Sure, we'll bring Lulu! And as for surfing, we'll have to see the conditions when we get there. But we'll definitely try if it's possible. As for the caravan, yes, we'll be renting one again. It's a wonderful way to experience the countryside! Ah, I'm sure we'll have a great time with the kids trying their hand at surfing. St Ives has its own beach for surfers - we can't miss that. Yay! I'll look into surfing lessons online! And is it okay if I bring my friends Emma and James? We've been planning a sleepover all year and this would be perfect timing? Hmm, that's a great idea, but we'll need to check the caravan to make sure it can accommodate them. And also, let the boys bring their parents into the conversation, we don't want any unexpected surprises, do we? Speaking of friends, is anyone else coming this year? Last year, we had that lovely Mrs. Jenkins from next door, but I think she might be changing plans. No one else is planning to join us that we've heard from. But I'm sure you three will keep each other entertained, right? And take advantage of the scenic walks, the food, and the local attractions! This is going to be the best holiday ever! I'll make sure to plan some fun activities. We could also do a treasure hunt. I saw a really cool idea online. Oh, treasure hunts are always fun. I remember when we used to do those on holidays.

Yo, I can't believe what we just watched! 10 things I hate about you is like, sooo much better than what we normally watch. Do you think they actually meant it when they said all those mean things about each other at the beginning? Oh, definitely, I think they were being serious at first. But it’s so hilarious and awkward at the same time. Like when Julia starts offering them cash to take her to the prom and things... But actually, I felt a bit bad for Cameron though. He was genuinely trying to help out and keeps getting rebuffed by people because they think he’s odd. Oh, totally! It’s kinda cruel, isn’t it? But, you know, that’s just high school. Everyone’s a bit messed up in their own way. Exactly! Speaking of messed up, have you even started on that English project? It’s due soon and I still haven’t even begun the research part. Oh no, I know! School’s been so crazy, it’s like they’re trying to stress us out on purpose. Anyway, I'm still trying to watch all these film analyses on YouTube to get a better understanding of the themes. It’s actually pretty interesting. Video analyses? That doesn’t sound fun at all! I'm just trying to cram as much in as possible the day before its due, let's be real. What about you, have you gotten any SATs prep done? Like, not really. I feel like we still have time before the exam in June, but I do need to start soon. Maybe we should study together? That could help and make it less boring. Yeah, that could work. We could also watch some analysis videos together? Just to make it a bit more fun. And maybe if one of us knows things the other doesn't, it could help us both revise. Brilliant idea! I was actually thinking we could also plan a trip to London this summer. My cousin who lives there said she’d show us around. She’s always got so many great tips for the best places to go. Oh, that would be amazing! I’ve never been but I want to see all of the famous spots like Buckingham Palace. Plus, my sister said there are some super cool museums for anyone interested in art and history.

Right, so I was on Facebook yesterday and I came across an old school friend who'd lost their job due to health issues. It's tough, innit? Times are tough for everyone, particularly if you've got health problems. Indeed, it's a real challenge, isn't it? I heard about a family member who got chicken pox and ended up having to stay home for weeks. It's not just the discomfort but the financial strain as well, right? Absolutely, and it can also bring up issues of OCD for some people, like a fear of contaminating others or losing control over their environment. It's not just physical health that gets affected but mental health too. As lecturers, we do get a glimpse of that through student experiences. That's a good point, Speaker_3. I've noticed even among colleagues, that kind of anxiety can manifest in all sorts of ways, including mild OCD. And it's important we address it because it can really impact productivity and overall wellbeing. That's true. But you know, it also made me think about faith and what comfort it provides. Some people turn to religion in times of crisis. I mean, I've always liked the idea that there's some bigger picture, some greater plan, you know? It's comforting, particularly when life's tough. I'm more agnostic, but I can see where people find solace in faith. It's a different world for people who have that sort of structure, isn't it? But isn't it also sometimes... conflicting? Like, when things go wrong, some people might question their faith. That's a very real issue, Speaker_2. Faith is inconsistent for many, which can lead to more stress, like a double-edged sword if you're in crisis and the faith isn't providing the comfort you need. It's complex. True. I think it comes down to personal perspective and individual experience. Some people find great strength in faith, while others find solace in other things, like family or community. You know, I've always thought that it's a bit more straightforward when you're from a traditional background where faith was just part of life, but for us, it's different. I never really got taught about it growing up, except for what I picked up at school, and even that could be inconsistent.

Oh, did I ever tell you lot about my family's disastrous holiday to Germany? Oh, Germany? Again? Yo, mate! It's been ages. How have you been? Hey! It's been ages too! I've been well, just been busy with work and all the usual stuff. Made some life-changing changes actually - wife's pregnant. I was thinking of Avril's situation while I was out today. I just can't imagine how she's carrying on, knowing what she does. It's truly admirable. It's amazing how we procrastinate with something until someone we know goes through something like this. But it's essential to stay on top of it.

So, I hear you're planning a trip to Lancaster soon? We've been meaning to visit the coast too, have you decided what specific places you're going to? Yeah, I've thought about it. Yo, mate, did you hear about that new band that's been making waves these days? They're called The Archers. I've been listening to their stuff non-stop since I heard 'em on BBC Introducing. Oh, did I just kill Sydney or what? I was so worried that I'd mess up and lose the entire team. You did indeed, but remember, this is just a game. And you've now given the med team a bit of a challenge to overcome. Speaking of challenges, I've just realized my character has a brilliant idea to block the spread of the disease by implementing a country-wide stay-in-setting strategy. Which, ironically, is how we're all still surviving at the moment in real life. That’s a clever approach, Player 3. I used that strategy last time in London. Though let’s hope it works better here. Tracking the disease's dynamics and managing the research and supply chains—it's as if we're handling a very large, international public health crisis. That's very true. I find the resource management most difficult. The limited supply of the cure means that we need to make tough decisions about who to prioritize and who to sacrifice, not something anyone enjoys. Absolutely, and while the game simplifies things, real-world disease management has all these facets. I remember a colleague suggesting that we really need more coordination between local health authorities and international cooperation to combat pandemics effectively. That’s a very real issue. But it proves the point of the game—that global health is a global responsibility. Except, unfortunately, global politics doesn’t always reflect that ideal. More reason for those of us who can, to get involved in local charities and initiatives that support global health efforts. Game or real life, small actions can collectively make a big difference. True. While we’re dealing with the “disease,” I find my nerves are getting a good workout. Let's not forget the fun and relaxation we're also having, though. It's such a different atmosphere playing this here in the cottage, away from city life. Agreed. The peace and quiet almost makes this threat feel less real. But maybe that's also what makes these discussions and game-play so valuable—it’s reminding us of things we don’t want to forget or take for granted.

Oh, did you both see last year's CBeebies pantomime? It was super fun! I remember how much Lucy loved it. It's always a highlight of our Christmas shows. Yeah! I loved it too! Right, so I'm considering moving. I'm pretty sure I've had enough of this city. The pollution is getting ridiculous and the council never seems to do anything about it. So, I was browsing through one of my old family photo albums over the weekend and discovered pictures of my childhood toys. Did either of you have a favorite toy when you were growing up? But I do remember questions were asked if Sindy was "suitable" for me as a child, considering she was "girl"-oriented. And I was completely obsessed with my Etch A Sketch. I used to create these complex drawings and then get frustrated when they would get randomly mixed up. Hahaha, I can imagine! I think such toys had a lot of influence on our creativity and fine motor skills. It just shows how different even our toys could be depending on where we grew up, doesn't it? Exactly. Hence the importance of regional dialects and cultures, which often heavily influence these kinds of things. True. But have you ever noticed how these things can also be linked to socio-economic status? Some toys were far more common or accessible depending on what family you came from.
