For instance, in my family, as we grew up, things like the video games and computer become more prominent. But it wasn't so for families like mine, or for some less well off families in our region. And in Peterborough, I remember more outdoor games being popular growing up, much less focus on indoor activities and "toys". Peterborough had its own socio-economic dynamics that influenced it. As accountant, it's clear to me that these differences reflect the broader economic conditions people face. It definitely does. Coming back to a slightly happier note, anyone remember a favorite family meal from childhood? For me, it was definitely Sunday roast. Nothing compared to that. From Yorkshire pudding to roasted chicken, it was always a treat on Sundays. Oh, yes! Noonie’s buttered vegetables were a highlight of Sunday lunches in my family. I thought I was the only one who loved the sweetness of carrots and peas in buttery sauce! It's just a classic. And the way these meals are made, they really embody the essence of regional cooking, don't you think? Absolutely! I remember when I moved to Essex as a young adult and had difficulty finding certain ingredients I was used to.

"I've been meaning to ask you two, what's the best new show on BBC?" "You mean on TV or on iPlayer? I really enjoyed 'Loki' and I think it’s a standout show at the moment." "Me too! Although, I wish they'd make more episodes of 'Normal People'. That show had such an impact on me. But speaking of TV... how is it that engineers still get away with not being hot in TV shows?" "Ah, the eternal stereotype. But, honestly, I’m glad. It's almost refreshing. It just says 'we're here to get the job done, not be the life of the party'. "Right? Though I guess that means we're also not being depicted as the tragic love interests." "That might be a blessing in disguise. But, seriously, it's funny because engineering is so far removed from that stereotype. I mean, I used to work with a guy who could fix a circuit and cook a three-course meal at the same time. Not to mention, write a dissertation on quantum mechanics over the weekend." "Exactly! The diversity in our field is overlooked. It's not all about pipes and wrenches." "Or, to use an even more inaccurate stereotype, trains all day. It's a lot more varied than people think. Communication is a key skill for engineering, and a lot of it is about working with people to design and implement solutions." "Well, I kind of see parallels in our jobs, in that way. As a language teacher, I have to consider how my students learn and communicate, and in journalism, I’m always thinking about the reader and how I can make complex topics understandable. "Same for me. I've had to write reports, explain complex mechanical concepts to clients who aren't engineers... You'd be surprised how often you use analogies that are more about everyday life than about machines." "I just hope that stereotypes in our field don't influence young people’s choices for careers. It might be a small part of the show, but it’s still a form of representation. And if almost all of the young boys in TV shows care most about getting the girls or beating out the bully, that doesn’t exactly show a diverse range of interests or values." "Absolutely. For example, in 'Normal People', the lead characters are often shown studying, exploring their interests and hobbies, and relating to each other on that level.

Speaking of which, I've been thinking a lot about pollution and how it affects our health. Do you both feel the same concern? Mm, yeah, that's a topic I’ve been following recently. Air pollution, especially in this context, is a concern. I've come across some interesting research linking gardening and green spaces to positive mental health outcomes. It’s another reason why I need to make time for more gardening myself. That’s fascinating. And yet, it's also a bit ironic, isn’t it? I mean, we're surrounded by nature here, and in many ways, it's a shield from urban pollution. Definitely. I've been looking at incorporating more air-purifying plants into my garden at home. Not just for aesthetics, but for the perceived health benefits, too. That's smart. Plants like the peace lily or the spider plant are renowned for their air-purifying qualities. Oh, I didn't know that about spider plants. That's something I can easily include in a small apartment. You know, it's things like this that often get overlooked in our hectic lives. And yet, these small changes in our daily lives, they truly add up. I’ve found that for myself, mindfulness has been a game changer. Simply taking a few minutes each day to be present in nature, like this, has improved my mental health considerably. Mm, absolutely. Even the act of gardening itself can be meditative. The physicality, the focus on nurturing something that grows and prospers... You know, we often talk about the practical aspects of health—diet, exercise, etc. But I think we forget about the importance of the environment too, not just for our physical health but for our mental wellbeing.

I've been thinking a lot about our accents lately. I mean, we all have quite distinctive ones. I've noticed how even though we grew up in pretty close proximity, there are still some pretty marked differences. That's very true! I've always heard questions about my Harlow accent. You know, it's not as strong as the ones you get in London or rural East Anglia but it's definitely there. But actually, I've always found it really friendly-sounding. Yeah, well, let me speak for my crowd here, I've got a pretty classic East End accent – and not just any old accent, mind you, a very specific Bethnal Green London accent. It just says 'home' to me. That's lovely! I'm making sure to preserve mine. As a student of linguistics, I find it fascinating how the smallest details of speech can be so regionally specific. Yeah, but I've always thought it was weird how accents can sometimes shift over time, even within the same place. Like, my parents were both from Kent, but they sounded pretty different from each other, even if they both said "Kent" Exactly. My wife used to say my accent was a mix of cockney, Whitechapel and a bit of Bethnal Green street slang. She’d correct me all the time. That’s really interesting. I never thought of the generational shift in accents. And with the rise of mobile devices, I wonder how our unique voices would be recognized by voice assistants. I mean, mine probably sounds very 'standard South-East English' to them, but if one of us had a stronger regional accent, would it be accurately recognized? I haven’t noticed much with Alexa at home, but I’ve had trouble with autocorrect on my phone sometimes. It always wants to change 'seaside' to 'sides'. That's exactly it! Devices sometimes make us sound more 'posh' than we actually are. But it’s funny when it gets it right too. I remember once, Siri was trying to understand my brother who's got a very strong Chatham accent. Speaking of technology and voice recognition, have you all seen those bicycles that can be controlled using voice commands? No, actually! I just watched something on YouTube about smart bikes and that was the first I’d heard of that. How’s that for the future? Yeah, it feels like we're moving into sci-fi territory here.

Alright, boys, who's ready for some supper? Me! I've been starving all day! Good, good. Today we're having baked Alaska. It's a bit of a fun one – do you both know how it's made? Is it one of those complicated fancy desserts you always make, Aunt Sarah? Close, very close. It's essentially ice cream, baked for a very short time in an extremely hot oven. Like, the ice cream doesn't melt? That's the fun part. The sponge cake wrapped around the ice cream protects it from the heat. Try it, you'll see. I will! Can I help with anything? Actually, yes. Can you help me grate the cheese? Sure. I can do that! Great! We're going to stick with cheddar for this dish, but if you're interested in making it more exciting next time, we can try adding some parmesan. Okay, why can't we do that now? Honestly, because I want you to enjoy the baked Alaska first in all its glory. You can experiment with your own version later, and we can have a cooking 'lab' where you learn how to make it properly. Yeah, like a science experiment! Exactly! And let the boys know that done properly, baking can be a science experiment. So, Aunt Sarah, when did you start cooking these fancy things? Well, honestly, it's been a bit of a journey. I started really getting into baking when I was around your age. Really? Yeah. I always liked helping my mum in the kitchen, but it was when I started making sweet treats for my friends at school that I realized how good it made everyone feel. You used to bake for your friends? Yep. It was something fun we could all share. That must have taken a lot of time and effort... It did, but the reactions from my friends made it totally worth it. By the way, how's your job going? Are you mostly busy with recruiting at the moment? It's been going well, thank you for asking. Recruiting is always a challenge but I enjoy it. It feels very different from teaching, which I did a lot of in my early career. I've never really understood what recruitment is about. Isn't it kind of like when you have to pick a team for a game? It can be a bit like that.

Ah, marvellous weekend so far, haven't we? The breakfast you've prepared is nearly too good to eat. I've never seen such an array of pastries before. I know, isn't it just? I thought you'd like a traditional Welsh breakfast while you're here. Absolutely, and the eggs are perfect, by the way. Speaking of food, I'm still dreaming of that breakfast I had in New York last year. All that American-style pancakes and maple syrup... Oh, we could try those pancakes sometime. They're not unlike our Welsh crempog, really. I used to have them from a little café just near where I live in Swansea. Swansea, isn't it? That's where we first met, during those conference days. I've never forgotten how wonderful the seafood was there. Yes, it was. And you were quite the adventurer, even taking up those flying lessons while you were here. Well, I'm not sure if I'd call it 'adventurous' so much as a 'tick off the bucket list' activity. But it was exhilarating, I must admit. Quite a thrill to be up in the air seeing Swansea from a different perspective. Oh, you're always one for experiences. I'd love to try flying one day, but for now, I can only admire from the ground. Maybe we'll have to arrange a lesson together when you come to us in Shipley. Deal! Speaking of plans, what’s your schedule for the day? Shall we just take it easy together, or do you have any... events planned? Ah, nothing too much. I was thinking we might meet up with a few of my other friends for a coffee later. But first, changing the subject, have you seen on social media how often people are complaining about refuse collection these days? Yes, just the other day, my neighbour was lamenting about the new collection times. It does seem to cause such an uproar. Yes... but it's quite the culture shock here sometimes compared to Japan, where I used to live. They have such strict rules but the system works so elegantly. That’s something I will say about Japan — their systems seem to run like clockwork. I suppose it’s a cultural thing, hailing from an engineering background myself, I can appreciate that sort of efficiency. Exactly! In terms of living, though, I found Japan amazing.

I've got an incredible story about running late. I was supposed to meet you guys at 10 am for scrabble, but I overslept and only got here at 10:45. Right when I arrived, I spilled coffee all over the floor, adding drama to the chaos. Wow, I knew you were a bit of a slow starter but that's quite a story. I'm glad you made it, though. And here we are, playing scrabble with people who most probably won't get there on time next time, right? True, true. But hey, I got here, despite the odds. So, what word was it that made you spill the coffee? It was 'defenestration'. I was trying to add a vowel, and oh, I didn't. 'Defenestration'? That's a pretty good word for a scrabble game. Someone should make a joke about it now. Sure, sure. We could say it was the only time I've literally thrown words out the window. That's pretty good. So what's the origin of that word? It's from Latin, 'fenestra', for 'window'. Defenestration is the act of throwing someone out a window. It was a popular form of execution or punishment for treason back in the day. I didn't know that. I thought it meant a type of redesigning the window layout. No, it’s much more... dramatic. I won't say anything about defenestration in future meetings with you, Alex. Appreciated, thanks. While we're on changing the topics, how are your graduate courses going? They are challenging, but interesting. I'm studying English Literature, exploring how children's books can influence social norms. It’s fascinating, really. That's something I've always been interested in. I remember almost all of my A Level texts were classics or socially relevant literature. I still love children's books. I liked reading “In the Night Kitchen” to my niece. But now she's grown a bit and prefers Harry Potter. I know that story... about you not being the most literature-enthusiastic person when it comes to children's books though. Very true. But let's not worry about that now. You, Alex, did an A level in English Literature? Yep. Had to go through all the Brontë sisters, Austen, and that dreaded section on perspectives of war poetry. Yeah, war poetry is one of those things you're either passionate about or just find it a bit grim.

Ah, martha, it's so lovely to have you round. We don't get many visitors these days, you know. Oh, thank you old chap. It's always a pleasure to be here, you know that. Just, you know, sitting here on the sofa, it's so quiet isn't it? I find myself reminiscing more often these days. You and I have had some good times, havent we? Indeed we have. Norwich, Costessey, keeps coming back to me, how would I forget? You know, it's funny, those memories. It's nostalgic, isn't it? The simplicity of things. Though, let me tell you, even then, there were issues. The whole unemployment issue, for instance. It never let up even when we were younger. Exactly, Richard. It was a struggle. We both decided not to work out of... frustration maybe. Frustration, I suppose. But also a lack of opportunities. I mean, I left school quite young, didn't have any qualifications, so jobs were hard to come by. Oh, I understand. I managed to go a bit further than you with the 'A' levels. Still, employment was scarce. And we can't blame the system entirely. Well, perhaps we could, but that wouldn't solve anything, would it? We made do, however we could. You're right, life is what we make of it. Even in our 'retirement'. Despite the lack of formal work, we've found ways to keep ourselves busy and the years fruitful. Indeed we have. I started doing some voluntary work at the local library, that helped me keep my mind sharp. And you weren't too bad with the children either. I've seen some of the kids you looked after. It's one of the joys of life, you know. Seeing a young mind grow. It's rewarding even without a paycheck. Definitely. Though some times I do wish... well, I often think about what it would be like to truly be back in the employment pool. To be needed, so to speak. I know how you feel. But Richard, almost 70, you have to admit, job hunting would be quite... challenging. I mean, ageism is a thing. Totally. Still, I keep my CV up to date, just in case there's something out there for someone like me. I know you do, and that's good. It keeps your skills fresh and it's good for the mind.

Right, so I've been reading about this new app that's been making waves. It's basically like a digital notebook for your recipes. Seems like it could be handy, especially considering our chicken supper tonight and the various ingredients we're using here. A recipe app, you say? That’s quite interesting! I have a digital kindle and I could definitely see myself using something like that. As a teacher, I'm often on the lookout for ways to make things more organized and streamlined. Sounds very useful for us. I remember how keeps coming up with new recipes. It seems like she uses a notebook most of the time, but an app could be quicker and more engaging for her, don’t you think? Absolutely. Plus, with features like meal planning and grocery lists, it could simplify life in the kitchen. I've heard it also connects directly to certain supermarkets to help you build your shopping list. That's quite impressive. I've tried apps like that before but they always seem a bit rigid. Like, you can't improvise if you're out of an ingredient or if you want to make a substitution. So, does it have any flexibility? So, I've come across reviews that mention different levels of flexibility. Some users say it's quite adaptable while others argue it's a bit limiting in terms of the pre-built recipes and suggested ingredients. It really depends on your style of cooking. Ah, I see. Like most things, I suppose. Speaking of things that are tricky to substitute in recipes: potatoes. They're key in a lot of British dishes and they have so many different varieties. Yes, definitely! Which is why I've always used the 'Maris Piper' variety; it seems to be the most versatile, doesn’t it? Right. Seems to be the most common in UK recipes. I tried the 'King Edward' ones for a traditional Sunday roast. They were good, but a bit softer and perhaps less suited for certain dishes. True. While 'King Edwards' are great for roasting, especially if you want a softer inside and crispy outside, sometimes you do need something for mash or in stews. For example, if we decided to make beef stew after tonight's chicken. Right, so the 'Maris Pipers' are great for dishes where you want a firmer, more almost waxy texture.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new restaurant that just opened up on Grace Street? They've got an all-day breakfast menu that sounds superb. Thought maybe we should check it out next weekend, what do you reckon? Yeah, that sounds good! Just after we watch the Premier League on Sunday. Who's playing this week? Manchester United and Tottenham. Should be a real cracker. Have you watched any good films recently? I managed to catch 'Tenet' last week. It was weird, but I get why it got so many awards. You game enough to try and follow it? Oh, for sure! I just need to set aside some time. Between essays and seminars, it's like my to-do list never ends. Yeah, same here. By the way, did you see this news article about parliament? It's crazy talk about Brexit, again. No, I didn't. But honestly, I barely have time to check the news. It's like this black hole of politics between assignments and course mates asking for help or running late to lectures. Ha, totally get it. I've been meaning to read The Lie by Helen Dunmore, though. Heard it's good. Haven't heard of that one. But I know we were discussing the Shakespeare series on TV in the last seminar. Yeah, that was interesting. Professor Ainsworth made some great points about how they're modernizing the context but keeping the dialogue intact. I'm glad they're doing it that way. I think it helps us connect with Shakespeare in a more relatable way. Makes the characters seem less like fairy tale figures and more like people you could actually meet. That's true. Now, let's get back to the fun stuff! Stag weekend anyone? We talked about it at the last football game but haven't had time to plan anything concrete. How about Reading? They've got some great places to drink and the football stadium's not too far off. I'm up for that, especially if we can fit in a game for good luck. But before we start planning, what do you think about trying out those new gaming consoles? Ooh, have you heard about the reviews for the new Playstation? I've been looking forward to it. Maybe we could get a little more free time and game together. Sounds good to me.

Ah, it's been ages! I've been so busy with coordinating this new project but today's the first day of my holiday weekend. I was thinking we could grab brunch here at Greens. What are you up to these days? Still up and running the show, though I kind of regret agreeing to work weekends for this new Pearson campaign. It's been non-stop and I'm looking forward to taking a break, just like you. Now that you mention it, your job seems very demanding. The marketing field is so fast-paced, right? Oh, it's all about surviving the pressure. But I have to say, it's stimulating, too. I just have to make sure I balance work and life, like you said you were trying. Exactly! Speaking of balance, I've been making time for yoga and trying to cook healthier meals. It's actually quite rewarding when it works out. That's great! I've been meaning to start a little healthier routine myself, but I always get distracted by the never-ending list of what's new in the digital or print sphere. Oh, totally get it! I've been trying these new recipes from a blogger I follow. You should check it out, the Vegan plant-based ones are so simple and yummy. Maybe we can swap tips after brunch. Well, actually, my work already gave me a break from all my COHAs right now, so this is my chance to actually catch up, really catch up. We have so much to catch up on! So, how's your family been? They're doing well. Mum's still proud and always asking when I'll start raking in the money in marketing. Hehe, same here. At family gatherings, they always question my choice of job. "Are you sure you didn't miss out on being a lawyer?" Exactly! I always laugh it off but deep down, it can be a bit frustrating. Absolutely. On a different note, I'm sure you're not surprised I've moved on from my last relationship, but I've heard he's finally found someone else. It's so bizarre to hear that after all the drama we went through. Really? Yeah, I laughed at the thought of him settling down with someone. Did you hear if it's serious or just rebound stuff? Apparently, it's serious and she's actually really nice.

I've decided I need more plants in my flat. I've got so much space now that it's just ridiculous not to use it for greenery. Ah, you've really caught onto the plant trend now, haven't you? I remember when you were just putting up with tiny succulents because they were low maintenance and didn't need much light. Yeah, I was quite the minimalist when it comes to plants before. But my mum always had so many and now I'm slowly catching onto it. Your mum's garden is always a sight to behold, isn't it? She's been teaching you all about different types of plants, varieties, and whatnot. Oh, she's been an incredible teacher. She started teaching me how to look after a bit of a garden when I was about 15. But now she's also been guiding me on the types of plants that are good for indoors. She swears by peace lilies and spider plants - they're really low maintenance. For me, it's all about cooking and eating what I grow. When I was living with my parents in Birmingham, we had a small garden and we'd grow our own vegetables. It's amazing how different the produce tastes when it's freshly picked, right out of your own garden. Absolutely! But while I'd love to grow my own herbs and such, I still can't seem to keep them alive long enough. They're always dying on me. That's because you're overwatering them. Most likely doesn't come from the Sunderland upbringing . Greenery thrives best when you leave them alone for a bit. Well, I try to give them a schedule, but maybe that's my problem. I should probably learn to be a bit more spontaneous with plant care. Well, you've got the science background for the research part of it. You're probably doing everything by the book. Yeah, well, sometimes I think my scientific approach can be a bit too much for them. So, what have you decided to start with? Are you going for something almost impossible to kill or just edible? I started with a peace lily. It's doing well so far. And then I think I'll get something a bit more challenging. But now that you mention food plants... that's definitely something I'd like to explore.

Ah, good morning, Peter. How was your weekend? Mine's been quite eventful. My grandkids visited and we had a wonderful football match out in the park. They're getting quite good at it. You know how it is with kids at that age. Still improving and yet the competition spirit is already there – quite amusing really! Ah, lovely! I'd have loved to have seen that, but my weekend was somewhat quieter. Spent most of it dealing with marking and I couldn't help but wonder if it's all worth it sometimes. As much as I enjoy it, it seems like an endless game of snooker, ping-ponging between lazy students and overly strict markers at the university. I completely understand that feeling, Peter. But then you get the occasional gem amongst the sea of less motivated ones. Like that essay from last year on the importance of community policing – stellar. It made me appreciate the whole marking process again. That sometimes makes it all worthwhile, doesn't it? But have you seen that recent news story about snooker players and their young families? I find that their off-table lives are as interesting as their games. For instance, this young player from the north – I've forgotten his name – has young children running around with his wife. Reminds you that we're all 'ordinary' folk with the same sorts of troubles and joys. Ah, yes! It does humanize them, doesn't it? Makes them more relatable even as they're racking up points on the green baize. I've been trying my hand at gardening myself, actually. It’s a therapeutic activity. But it's been quite a challenge. Just like marking, I find that you've got to have patience for progress to show. Absolutely! I couldn’t agree more. A career in academia or the garden, you’ve got to keep at it, and often the smallest progress is the most gratifying. Speaking of careers, I was having a conversation with one of my students about joining the police force and the armed forces. While I provided some guidance, I couldn’t help but think about the drastic lifestyle changes they'd face. Yes, indeed. It’s a significant decision and certainly not one to be taken lightly. As a professor, I've seen students go down both of those paths and it's quite the rollercoaster journey.

Alright, I don't think we've ever had such a packed summer. Oooo, so many fun things to do! Indeed. We've got the Christening coming up, and then your birthday two weekends later. Yeah, quite a lot going on. I hope we can manage it all without too much stress. And will there be cake and presents at the Christening too? Well, probably there will be a few treats for the guests, but I wouldn't count on a present for you just yet, you're not the one being christened after all! Right. Well, we'll see what we can arrange. Mummy, can we talk about what we might get Granny and Granddad for their present? That's a good idea. What do you think? Maybe something nice for their garden, or something they've wanted but not got around to buying themselves? Hmm. Maybe they could use a new garden shed? A garden shed sounds like a practical gift for them, but let's see what ideas you both come up with, we still have time before the event. Okay, good idea. What do you like about that? Because, it's big and tall, and we could put lots of things in it! Sounds like a plan. Now let's talk about your birthday plans, weren't we thinking of having a small party for you? Yeah, I think that's a great idea. Just a small family and a couple of close friends. And party games, and a big cake! Alright, we'll see what we can do about the party games. We can all help with the party. I could even bake a cake if you want. You're very sweet. I might just let you help with the decorations. A skilled decorator is always appreciated. Yes, decorations! I can help! I know what to use too! That's nice of you both to want to help. Let's start making a list of what we need though, and then we can start dividing tasks up. I'd like to come up with a guest list and send out invites soon. What's an invite? It's a note that lets our friends know about your party so they can come join in the fun. But I want to make one! You can help! We can write it together, and then you can decorate it.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time we went to New York for your sister's wedding? It was absolute chaos, but so much fun. Not really. I was only 14 at the time, wasn’t I? What was the highlight? Did anything go wrong? Oh absolutely. I think I had too many Manhattan cocktails for my own good during that trip. Oh no, I can picture that. And I suppose that's why the wedding wasn't just any typical, down to earth affair? Perhaps a bit more than "typical"! Anyway, moving on from my boozy exploits, you guys want to discuss plans for your own holidays? We were thinking of going to visit your sister in Scotland this summer. But we've also talked about maybe saving up for next year and doing a city break. New York? Maybe Paris this time? Oh, New York is lovely! But Paris is fun too. Paris? Really? Yeah, we've discussed it. I love Paris, it's so lovely. But New York, that's really for the food lovers . I mean, you can't beat a New York bagel or pizza slice. True, that's kind of a food heaven. Except, we've been meaning to lose some weight . More a food hell, then? Hell yes, when it comes to trying all those amazing foods while trying to stick to a healthy diet! Definitely. Anyway, if we do end up going to Paris, it'll just be a weekend, unlike New York which might need at least five days if we want to see everything properly. That's a good point. New York is a huge city with so much to see. Yeah. And planning our weekends – we were thinking of just driving to Lichfield and spending some time outdoors this weekend, maybe go to the nature reserve... Oh, that sounds lovely! Absolutely. The weather prediction says it might be a bit on the cooler side, but perfect for a hike. It would be good to check, don't want to catch a cold. We can always take an umbrella. That's a plan! Who said we can't prepare for summer in the spring? True. What about next weekend? Do you want to plan something with us? Oh, next weekend... We've been meaning to catch up with an old friend who's moving abroad soon. Ah, that's a close friend, right?

Yo, mate, got a sec? I need some advice on this dissertation. I'm really stuck; every time I try to organize my thoughts, it just seems to get worse. For sure. Want to grab a chair and we can sit down and have a look, maybe share some strategies? Yeah, cheers. I've got a bunch of articles, a few lecture notes, and a bunch of questions and prompts from my supervisor, but I don't know how to tie everything together. Right, get out all your stuff then. We can start by brainstorming, see if we can identify key themes or areas you need to explore more. Okay, sure. First of all, let's take a breather. Maybe looking at all this at once is overwhelming. Make a cup of tea? Nah, I'd rather get on with it if that's alright. I've got a deadline coming up that I'm a bit anxious about. Alright, alright. No pressure. Where do we start? What's the focus of your dissertation? It’s about the influence of public policy on the socio-economic development of certain post-industrial towns in the North. Like, perhaps look at areas where there have been significant policy changes or new initiatives over the past few decades. Yeah, that's exactly what I'm trying to get my head around. How do I structure that into a coherent narrative? Have you thought about starting with a statement on the current state or understanding in your area of study? Something like "Despite ongoing policy initiatives in post-industrial areas, the socio-economic gaps are still significant." Mmm, okay. Then I could move on to explore the potential reasons why policy hasn't led to the expected outcomes. Exactly. You could also use a historical approach—look at previous policy interventions that were supposed to make a difference but didn't. That makes sense. Then maybe I can identify patterns or flaws that could give some insight into what future policy should look like. Excellent. That could lead nicely into a critical analysis of current or proposed policies. Yeah, and I could use some of these examples from the North to discuss broader implications. So, just to recap, you're looking at the impact of public policy on socio-economic development, using case studies from the North of England, aiming to critique current or proposed policies, and then drawing out some broader implications or suggestions.

Alright mates, so who first wants to share their dreams? Well, I'll kick us off, shall I? As a teacher, I dream of one day starting my own school or education project, something that empowers kids to learn in an environment that truly nurtures their passions and creativity. And me! I wish I could have a big, fluffy dog! I'd name him Sam! Sam indeed! That's a great name. You'll need to convince Mom, though. Well, starting a school won't be just like owning a puppy, sweetie. True. But both are well within reach if you have the right strategy and a bit of luck. But what if we win the lottery? Wouldn’t that make big things like starting a school or buying a dog super possible? So, you're betting on the lottery to turn this around, are you? Yeah! If I win, I'll definitely buy Sam, the biggest dog ever! Do we also get a staff of dog walkers and a personal chef then? A chef for Sam, yes! Cooking silly treats and stuff! An entire dog bakery, perhaps? Wait, a bakery for dogs? No, silly, I meant we’d make treats for Sam. More sensibly, winning the lottery could be a good springboard for our dreams. If we pooled our money and channeled it towards something meaningful, like my educational project or a dog-friendly home, it could be a great dream shared by all. True. It’s not just about personal fantasies, though. Our dreams and dreams of those we care about, like our kids, should be intertwined for sustainable happiness. BUT still, could have Sam. That's almost as important as a school for me right now! Sam plus school! Okay, so here's a compromise. Let's say if we were to win big, like speak this year's Powerball... We could fund our dreams, be it Sam or the school, but also think of giving back, right? Yeah, that's how it should be. Use it as a means to better ourselves and, in turn, help others. Maybe even build a trust for local educational initiatives or a dog sanctuary. Yay! A dog sanctuary! I’d take care of Sam and other dogs there, too. I'd come every weekend! See, it starts with something small and personal but can grow into something bigger and more impactful.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that A&E scandal from Sunderland? It was all over the news these past couple of days. Yeah, I talked to someone who works there and well, let's just say, it's really worrying isn't it? People should be able to trust those kind of institutions. Exactly! I mean, I've got a friend who went in after his accident and, well, they didn't treat him with the care and respect he deserved. Oh, that's terrible! As a consultant engineer, I guess I've had my share of minor injuries but seeing someone you care about being mistreated like that would be really tough to take. It's disgusting. This is the kind of thing that makes you wonder what's going wrong in our healthcare system. Yeah, and it's not just about healthcare, it's about treating people with human dignity, no matter what service they're looking for. It's fundamental. Absolutely. And you know, these people trusted those hospitals. They went there expecting to be helped, not left feeling like they're on some kind of assembly line. We really need to raise our voices about this, don't we? I couldn't agree more. I assumed we had the best system in the world, but if this is happening regularly... Regularly? It seems like it. And it's not just about calling out individual A&E departments either, it's about the whole system, the management, the oversight. True, it's the larger problem of underfunding and overworked staff that's leading to these kinds of failures. I think so too. As someone who works in administrative roles, I've seen the burden of understaffing and insufficient resources firsthand. It's just not right. And, as a consultant, I've noticed a lot of stress and burnout among professionals. It's not just about staffing numbers, it's about the framework and support you have to work with. Yeah, I've heard some really disheartening stories. What if we start putting more pressure on our local and national representatives? Let's make sure they know we care about this issue deeply and we won't let it slide. I was thinking about starting a petition, something almost like this. There's already been a bit of a local stir about these incidents. If we can gather more voices...

Ah, George, welcome back from your travels to the United States. I have to say, the current state of international affairs is quite concerning. This new trade tariffs and the ongoing tensions with the Koreas. Have you managed to catch up on the news while you were there? Thanks, old chap! One of the business owners I spoke to in the States was lamenting that it's difficult for his business to connect with potential clients from abroad. This platform could potentially solve that. You know how these large corporations can swoop in and do things on a much larger scale, especially when it comes to online platforms. Absolutely. That's why our local focus could be our strength.

Ah, marvellous to see you again! How's life treating you these days? You know, aside from work and all that. Everything's well, thanks for asking. You look as though you've been really busy too. Keeping you busy? As per usual! You know how it is when you’ve got growing children. The joys of university apps and the stress of wanting to make sure they're all set up for their future.

Aye, I'm thinkin' of buyin' a new camera. I've been takin' more interest in photography since my last trip to Spain. That sounds like a great idea. Yeah, most pros have started movin’ to mirrorless over the last few years. They’re still stellar in terms of quality, but they’re more user-friendly and easier to carry around. Make sense. What about brands? I've heard good things about Canon and Nikon. Both are excellent brands. Canon especially has a wide range of beginner-friendly options. I'm more partial to Nikon though, but it really comes down to personal preference. I might just have to give them both a go and see which feels right. Any other things to consider when you're usin’ a camera, especially for travel? Absolutely. Comfort is key, right, especially if you’re gonna be haulin’ it around all day. One thing to consider is the weight and size. Another is battery life. You don't want to be stuck in a beautiful location with no power. That would be a nightmare. And one more thing - weather conditions. You should look into cameras with good weather sealing. If you’re planin’ on takin’ photos on a rainy day or near the sea, you’ll want somethin’ that can handle it. That's a great point. We’ve had some really miserable weather lately, and I’ve often thought of it. I know! The weather here’s been so unpredictable. I’ve actually been takin’ advantage of it to capture some dramatic stormy photos. That sounds cool! Is it difficult to take those kinds of photos? It can be challenging. The light changes so quickly and it can be tricky to balance the settings to get a good shot. But with practice, you get the hang of it. You’ve taken some great ones, that’s for sure. I've always admired the way the Scottish weather creates such vivid, interesting light.

Right, so I've been thinking. I need to finalize plans for the week. On Monday, I've got that meeting at council and then the rehearsal for the local pantomime. Got all that on my spreadsheet. Right, so I had this absolute nightmare of a day at work. We have this big conference coming up and I realized yesterday that we've only got a month to go and we're nowhere near ready. But the catering is the major headache. Have you tried looking for other options in Cambridge or even nearby towns? I have, but everything is either booked out or just not suitable. So, how’s everything else going? The life side of things, I mean. Life is good, thanks for asking. I've been trying to reorganize my wardrobe because I'm kind of stuck in a rut with my clothes. Been buying the same or similar stuff for ages. That’s a universal problem, isn’t it? I feel the same about mine. Do you ever go to thrift shops or charity shops? Anyway, I've also started trying out new skincare routines. You know, being kinder to my skin. It's been surprisingly... upsetting at times. It’s like realising I’ve been treating myself harshly for years. Do you guys have any tips? I've been into organic skincare. It really makes a difference. You could try a bit of that? Definitely try it. We could even share some tips when you've got some time.

Right, now I'm going to make us a proper pot of tea. Toothin' hot; just like we like. Whole milk and no sweetener for me, thank you. Are you still making tea the way your mum taught you? No, wait—you never really worked, did you? You've always just been at home? Well, er, that's part of my story. I wish I could have made better of things, but... [softly] And here we are, making tea, still with whole milk and no sugar... I used to do this for my students. [lightly teasing] And here I used to run a nursery in Harrow. Might have been the only proper job I ever had before... well, we all know about that now. [from another room] Ah, tea time! I'll be right there. [to Speaker_4] Ah, Mrs. Jenkins, lovely to have you join us! We're just reminiscing about old times. Past and present all mixed up together, isn't it? [sitting down] I'm sorry to see you've both retired from... well, everything. Still, good tea can lift anyone's spirits, can't it? Indeed. Speaking of spirits, do we have any biscuits? A bit of a crunch would go well with this tea, if you ask me. Oh, we certainly do. I baked these shortbreads last week. They're still quite fresh, I think. [smiling] I'd say that's a wise choice, Harold. Shortbread is the perfect tea companion. [serving the tea and biscuits] There you go, everyone. Take the time, enjoy it. We weren't always so... limited in our choice of employment or worldly experiences. [teasingly] Harold's right, though. There's a comfort in routine, a familiarity in the simple things like tea and biscuits. True. I spent most of my time teaching in Manchester. The kids always loved a cup of tea and a biscuit after a busy lunch break. [chuckling] And here we are. Tea and biscuits, no students to fuss over. Just us. I used to think if I had more money or a proper job things would be better. But now, sitting here, I realize it's not just about that. It's about what we have—each other, this quiet moment, and a good cup of tea. [nodding] I know exactly what you mean. I used to think the solution to my problems was just around the corner, as long as I worked harder or had more of this or that.

I've decided I need to take an art class. I discovered today that I have zero creativity and that realization was quite shocking. Oh, that's great! You've always been good with words so it could be a fun challenge. What made you decide that? You'd definitely be the best at explaining "What my pencil means"! Absolutely, we'll need to hire you for all our family gatherings to keeps things interesting. Oh, yes. I was at the pub last night and took an extremely verbal approach to explaining my pint selection. The barman wasn't sure if to laugh or to call for back-up. Tell us more! What happened? Well, you see, I thought I'd do something sophisticated and decided on a craft beer. So, I started explaining the different malts and hops and the various tasting notes. It got quite elaborate. Sounds like a stereotypical moment from a sitcom. I can just imagine. "This pint has a hint of citrus zest, a touch of spice in the finish, and substantial bitterness that's, you know, quite refreshing after a long day." Ah, nearly. The barman just stared at me for a moment and then said, "So in simpler terms, it's bitter?" Oh dear, you need that art class to balance things out! Maybe you should focus on performance art, dear. I bet you could make a great interpretative dancer of pub drinking. I think that's a career I'd consider if I were losing my mind. Speaking of careers, have you heard about the changes in CRB checks? I read somewhere online that they're changing to DBS checks now. Oh yes, they've replaced the old CRB checks because of issues with the structure and accessibility. I mean, having to pay for a check every time you switched jobs or volunteered was ridiculous. Absolutely, and the new system allows for the checks to be shared between employers. It's a much better system. What does DBS stand for anyway? It's for the Disclosure and Barring Service. Makes sense that they'd update the name given the changes. Anyway, I managed a pub quiz recently and it was a nightmare organizing the teams. They argue about everything, even about whose turn it is to choose the answer. I had one customer the other day, thought that living in a hotel was like living at home.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my flatmate Grace? On the day before we went away, she was frantic about forgetting to book the tickets for her chicken supper tea-fest. You should've seen her! Running around like a headless chicken and then realizes she booked the wrong kind – she wanted questions and answers kind of game but instead she booked a complete make-your-own-takeaway buffet! Grace, always the life of the party, even in the dullest moments. And get this, guess who actually enjoyed it? Me! I swear, that Thanksgiving-style feast was one of the best meals of the month! It's always the unexpected things. Though, let me tell you, even with all the work-life balance we're supposed to have, I feel like I'm running around just like Grace that day. Hence, my biggest thanks is actually getting some time off, even if it's just a relaxing retreat in our own room. Is everything okay? You seemed a bit more stressed than usual this week. No, really, it's fine, just a lot of patients on the ward right now, and a few of them have been keeping me up at night. Where did you get that tea? It smells amazing. Ah, the secret family recipe. It's a bit of a tradition at our place – always serve the best tea when we're catching up. You know what? Just being here, talking and enjoying some downtime is exactly what I needed. How was your holiday? It was great, Thanks for asking. We went to Brighton for a weekend and it was lovely. We went to the Pavilion, the arcade, and did a bit of shopping. The food there was just amazing, especially the seafood. I really should have made a better effort to remember some names so I could recommend them back here. Sounds lovely! And I should probably make more of an effort to try some new things off the meal plan at home… maybe it's time to make that chicken supper for us? Actually, yes, let's do that! I can show you Grace's meme of the week: Please. I could almost use this right now. You know what else I realised? I really need to get my house in order. The place was a bit of a mess after our trip. Maybe we can figure out a system or something?

I was thinking of calling Laura today. We have to check on her; it's been ages. Of course, we need to. How's she been managing the treatment and all? It's tough to hear her voice sometimes, but she's definitely strong. She hasn't given up yet, even though the prognosis isn't great... But I have been thinking... I wonder how her place is coming along. Are you talking about the cottage they're renovating? Yes, exactly. I heard they're deciding whether to move there permanently after treatment, or maybe just use it as a retreat away from London. That could be a good change for her. I suppose it depends on how she feels about being out of the city. It also depends on how much work the place needs. Knowing Laura, she's been doing most of it herself. That's one of the reasons I love this village. You get quite involved with people's lives here. Indeed. Speaking of the village, did you check the online listings? Ah, yes, actually. There's one cottage for sale just up the road that I think might interest us. You're thinking about moving from London here, permanently? Potentially, yes. The commute to the university isn't too bad, and it would be good for our lifestyle, especially with kids in the future... or sooner, depending on when we decide to start the family. It's a big change. But if you're comfortable with it, I'm all for it. It would be lovely to have Laura closer by and spend more time here. It might also be good for her to have a bit more company when she's ready. Our children could grow up playing together, just like when we were young. That thought brings tears to my eyes. Again, health permitting. You're right, of course. I was getting ahead of myself. Nothing wrong with dreaming though. True. So, shall I call Laura first? Definitely. And then perhaps we can schedule a visit to the cottage for next week. Yes, that sounds like a good plan. So, what time shall I ring her? How about around six? She usually finishes her treatment by then and might be more relaxed. Six it is. Thanks, It'll help to know how she's feeling today. No problem at all. And if we do decide to move here, just think of all the times we could have with her.

Yo, mate, gotta say, I've got a few things that really get on my nerves. Like, what's with folk nipping about without putting their shoes on, fookin' dirty the whole carpet? Oh, sorry to interrupt, but now that you've brought it up, I do have questions. What kind of shoes are you referring to? I mean, people sometimes wear boots while out, but I don't see the big deal about minimalist shoes or slippers at home. Oh, I get that, keeps coming backwards and forwards with people working from home. You get used to being comfy, but fuck it creates extra work for us. Plus, some just step in and out with dirty shoes. Smell of rain, mud, and whatever else is on the streets. Yeah, I see your point. And the dust, it does get all over the place. Though, you can't control the weather, can you? Exactly! But, you know, it's just good manners, people. Wear slippers at home. Keep the outside stuff out. Plus, what's even worse is when people leave a mess in the common kitchen. Like, who leaves a pasta dish with sauce all over the stoves? Right, the kitchen is one of my pet peeves too. It's like people think it's the cleaners' job. I mean, we're all adults here, we should be able to clean up after ourselves. And don't even get me started on noise. Like, I've got no problem with a bit of banter or music, but there's always someone playing it full blast at 11pm. Gives me the lurgi. Noise pollution is definitely a challenge here. Some people have the habit of being too loud in communal spaces without realizing it might be disturbing others, especially during the early hours. And another thing - couple of chaps have been leaving their bikes outside, blocking the way. I mean, it's a pain changing the alarm routine just because someone forgets where they parked. True. I've had some issues with that too. Imagine having to set up a new path when you're already juggling with your tasks. And topping it all off - littering. It's right next to the bin, yet they'll throw their rubbish wherever. Littering, yeah. It's a mystery to me why people don't see the point of putting their trash in the right place.

I keep bumping into so many English people while traveling. Makes me feel like every resort is just one big council estate! . You're right though, you see more of our neighbors on the beaches in the med than you do in St. Mary's back home. It's funny though, people say the same about package tours. You're just a bunch of Brits in a strange country, all doing the same thing, talking the same way. Right, it's like a mini Britain abroad! True, but at least with package tours you don’t have to worry about getting lost. Though, have you ever taken a tour around Brussels? Those Christmas markets are something else! Yeah! I went to Antwerp last year and it was wonderful. The ice skating rink in the town square, all the beautifully wrapped packages and toys, the smell of mulled wine... But the traffic was a bit of a nightmare! Mm, yeah, English folks and traffic never mix well, do they? For me, it's the amount of traffic in Harlow though. True. Where did you all study while the 'Rae was growing up in Harlow? Ah, UEA Norwich for me. Well, actually, for uni I did, but for most of my A-levels I was at school in Gillingham. Harlow Sixth Form for me, couldn’t have been more different from UEA! . How about you, Mr. Well, I'd like to say I studied, but... . No, less fortunate side of education, I'm afraid. I just tried to learn as much as I could on my own since retirement. It's never too late to learn and explore, you know? You've certainly got a wealth of life experience. I'm glad I could return to some part-time studies later in life. Makes everyday tasks feel more meaningful and all. It does. It does give you a different perspective. Speaking of studying, I always found languages the most interesting. Wish I had gone on to learn more in my youth. I love learning languages, too! I've got a bit of a grasp on French and Spanish, learned during our family trips. Really? You're finding that helpful in your job as a care assistant? Oh, absolutely. We get a lot of patients from various backgrounds, especially in the care home where I work. Being able to communicate a little in their language, even if it's just basics, can make a difference, you know?

Yo, Mum, did you hear about that equality vote last year? Yeah, I did. It's all about ensuring that the laws don't discriminate against anyone because of their gender, race, religion, sexual orientation, you name it. Was quite the debate though, wasn't it? Yeah, some folks just don't get it. It's like, what's the problem with making sure everyone's equal? I'm right there with you, Son. But, you know, it's complicated for some people. We've been discussing it in school. It seems like many people get it mixed up with, like, 'political correctness gone mad' or something. I know! They say 'it wasn't that bad before, why change now?' But what about the people who were actually suffering before? The same people saying 'it wasn't that bad' might be the ones who have had everything handed to them on a silver platter due to their privilege, right? Exactly. It's about recognizing and respecting the struggles people face because of these things. And it's not just about those big landmark changes or laws, it's about the everyday attitudes and behaviors. Totally. So, do you think Ireland is good with this kind of stuff? I assumed we'd be more progressive here. We are, to an extent, but we're far from perfect. There's still a lot of work to be done, especially in ensuring that all identities are represented equally, especially in politics. But there has been progress, slowly but surely. I read about that Senator who changed their gender and everyone was like 'sure, why would that affect anything?' It just shows the progress we're making. Indeed. Progress on all fronts is what we need. But the fact that such announcements are making headlines shows that there's a ways to go. Okay, but what about Ireland's politics in general? Is it all about equality and stuff or are they just as insincere as British politicians? You can never really know for sure, but there seems to be a genuine effort here. For example, some parties have explicitly stated their commitment to equality, and there's more representation of minority groups in the legislature than there used to be. Still, it's funny when you look at it. Politicians go on about 'what the people want' or 'representing the real Ireland' but sometimes it seems like they're just trying to get votes.

Right, so I was going over some of Grandpa's old tools the other day. You know, he left me his old lathe and a bunch of bits and pieces. I think I found something really interesting. You two remember when I got the video from our neighbors the other day? Ah, yes! The one with the tiny hamster stuck in a microwave? You'd think they'd have some better ideas for a prank! Oh, I couldn't believe it! That was priceless! Speaking of keepsakes, I still have my grandmother's old recipe book. Wonder if we could try cooking something from it. It's full of traditional English dishes from my hometown. That sounds wonderful. What's the dish that you have your eye on? Well, let me see. There's this lovely recipe for a slow-cooked Gloucester beef casserole. It's a bit time-consuming, but oh so worth it! Ooh, that sounds delicious! And considering we've got the whole day free, why not give it a try? Yes, it's been ages since I've done some proper cooking. Now, I'll need the recipe, though. Where did you put that book? I think it's over there, on that shelf, right behind the knick-knacks. Aha! Found it. You know, considering we’re talking about cooking, I never did understand why they used to put hamsters in microwaves… I suppose it proves how technology can be both intriguing and terrifying, doesn’t it? Oh, look, here it is. I'll read it out while we prep. Excellent idea! "To make the Gloucester beef casserole, we first need two pounds of beef, cut into chunks…" Let's see if we have all the ingredients. And by the way, what was that about using the lathe? Oh right. So, while I was going through Grandpa's toolbox, I found this very peculiar little device. Looks like a little punch or something, but it's got carved initials on it. Was he into woodworking too? He had a small workshop at the back of the house when I was growing up. Used to make little things for us kids—a wooden boat once, a birdhouse, that kind of thing.

I've been educating myself on mirror-writing during my lunch today. Did you know Leonardo da Vinci did it and many believe it was to avoid theft of his ideas? Fascinating. I've just heard the bank interest rates have gone up again. I'm not sure I understand why they keep making it harder for us to save. Yes, and of course, as soon as there's an increase, they slap it onto us. It's another reason we need to manage our debt better. Speaking of which, did either of you see those new figures on house prices? Houses in London are just ridiculous, just like the cat who recently broke into the post office in Britain. Wasn't that a crazy story? They even had a photo of it sitting on the counter. It reminded me of the cryptic crossword we did last week. One of the clues was "Animal that likes sending letters", and it was the cat, of course. Speaking of puzzles, I spent quite some time on my crossword today. I did find the American political news difficult to follow though. It seems the system over there can be so... transactional. And now they're even charging for plastic bags over there too! Can't the governments agree on some sort of consistent, reasonable approach to environmental issues? I read an article about charging fees for plastic bags and apparently it’s having positive effects in certain areas. But it's tough to keep the progress when there’s so much political gridlock everywhere. But the point is less about who's doing what and more about making a real change, isn't it? Speaking of change, I've also been thinking of our kids' generation. While they're dealing with the world today, are they ready to handle these kinds of issues appropriately? Yes, certainly. But also, it's just as important for us to show them how to use technology effectively while also being aware of its limitations and potential pitfalls. That's very true. Our youngsters are all about instant gratification and information but they need to learn about information literacy and critical thinking. It's a new kind of literacy really. Yes, all these conversations seem to be about the impact of the modern world. And while that's... ...um, fascinating, yeah? Exactly! What can I say, a dinner conversation with family and friends never lacks diversity.

I've never seen you three so engrossed in these electronic toys. I thought we were having a quiet evening and you'd be reading or playing with Lego rather than these screens. Hi mum!
