Accommodation aside, do you remember our first outings together after we all settled in? Our colleges for our post-graduate courses must have been quite memorable. Oh, indeed! And have you ever told the story of your infamous trip for your post-graduate course in dentistry? That must have gone somewhat ...unexpectedly. Ah, yes! I had the joys of flying to Athens for my postgrad.

Ah, marvellous to finally meet you in person, Marion. I've heard so much about your work as a language therapist. I must say, it's a truly fascinating field. You're very kind, dear! Yes, it was deeply rewarding and challenging all at once. I spent years helping people find their voice, literally and figuratively. It's a profession close to my heart. Absolutely, I can imagine. I'm right there with you, with my years as an artist and antique dealer. It was always about bringing character and history to life, don't you think? Indeed, yes. There's such a timeless beauty to both art and verbal communication, isn't there? Absolutely, just like the antiques you would deal with - each piece has a story to tell. Exactly. And what a career you have had. I can imagine the myriad of interesting items you've encountered over the years. Did anything stand out in particular, a most memorable piece? Oh, well there have been so many, but one that really comes to mind was a rare portrait by a lesser-known English painter. I managed to identify it after a lot of research and brought it back to the gallery. It turned out to be quite valuable. That's remarkable. Stumbling upon undiscovered treasures is truly the golden age of an antique dealer, isn't it? Absolutely. But it also takes dedication and patience, which can be akin to therapy in itself, as I imagine your work is. Very true. And that’s what I needed when I retired from my full-time practice - a change of pace and something new to focus on. As much as I loved my work, it could be emotionally draining at times. I can imagine. The commerce side of being an art dealer wasn't always easy either, particularly when I had to explain the value of a piece to skeptical buyers. It could feel like therapy itself, trying to convince people of an item's worth! Yes, that does sound like a sort of therapy of its own – convincing people of art's value. But you've had success, and that must feel wonderful. Oh, yes, indeed it does. It feels like a small triumph every time a piece finds its rightful home. And now, you have the freedom to enjoy retirement and do things at your own pace, no? Yes, although I do miss the constant buzz of running the gallery, it’s nice to not be tied to it 24/7.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new tattoo parlor's opening? I'm seriously considering getting a new one before Christmas. Omg, talked about that recently. Got some of their designs printed. Want to check out their work first? Totally. I kind of want something festive this time. Maybe a candy cane or a little Christmas pudding. Haha, brilliant idea! Or you could go for something more subtle... I'd love to get a small star for my wrist. Yeah, a small star would look great. I just need to find the right parlor and artist. [gets distracted by the food] Ah, mate, almost forgot. We have to cut up those veggies for the dinner we're making tonight. Yeah, [chuckles] definitely on that.   [Pause while cutting up veggies and occasionally conversing with each other. Ron, a mutual very close friend, enters the kitchen.]   Ron, great timing! Just talking about tattoos and Christmas puddings. For a moment there I thought it was unusual, but then I saw Riordan. [entering the kitchen with a tray of freshly baked goods] Ah, don't worry, I've got all the Christmasy things covered, right [looks at the conversation and chuckles]? Ah, Ron, you always know how to bring things together. Between the talk of tattoos and puddings, you could've shown up talking about Christmas trees or lights and we'd still be in sync! Or baking! But it's good to keep the conversation [winks] edible and festive, right? I've actually been thinking of planning a small Christmas dinner or dessert party soon. More food festivities! That sounds amazing, Ron. Do you have any ideas already? Not really, but I was thinking about making some traditional British Christmas desserts and some modern twists. Maybe a gingerbread house or some candy cane fudge? Ooh, Ron, if you need any help for that or just want a taste tester [laughs], I'm your guy. Thanks! It would be awesome to have both of you. You could even bring some ideas from your baker friends or just general desserts ideas. You know how to make those. [smirks] And don't forget those Christmas candies. Always a hit. Definitely. I might also consider finding some new decorative ideas. Maybe some... I don't know, handmade decorations or unique ornaments. That’s a great angle. There are some amazing local artisans these days who sell amazing handmade decorations.

Mum, I can't believe we're leaving Cambridge already. It's been such an amazing time. The uni is truly incredible. Oh, yes. It has been, hasn't it? Cambridge University is one of the best in the world. But now, the real world beckons – London is calling again! Yeah, and I've got a lot to think about. Next year, I'll be starting my Masters and I'm right at the beginning of writing my thesis. And how is that progressing? Are you still interested in medieval history? Yeah, I am. Even though there have been moments where I wondered if I was going down a niche path. But then I think of the thrill of discovery, and I'm back in. Ah, the thrill of discovery. I remember when you started your undergrad and everything seemed so overwhelming. But you're doing fine. I know, it's just there's so much to juggle – the thesis, potential job applications, possible uni lecturer positions, and then there's the living arrangements problem. Ah, yes. Living arrangements. Have you thought about moving back into the old family house with me? You know, you could save while you're job hunting. Honestly, I hadn't really considered that. It's a bit of a peculiar feeling, moving back in with you. But I'd be glad to have a roof over my head. Don't be silly, it would be no problem at all. You're always welcome here. Plus, it gives you the opportunity to learn a bit more about the publishing industry too, which might come in handy if you decide to apply to be an editor one day. That's very thoughtful of you, Mum, but do you think I'd ever be as good as you? You've been doing this for decades. Oh, darling, that's not the point. There's room for everyone in the industry. But also, never underestimate yourself. You've got a keen mind and a good style, which I've seen in your essays. Cheers, that means a lot coming from you. I do need to consider all my options realistically though. Absolutely right. Just remember, there's no rush. Enjoy this time in your life. Whether you choose to go into academia or something else, it will be a journey of discovery. Yeah, but still thinking about Oxford. I wonder what their medieval history programme is like.

Ah, what a lovely day at the Cambridge Law Faculty. I attended today's Alumni Day 2. It's always such a delight to meet people from so many different walks of life. Hi there! Yes, absolutely. I thoroughly enjoyed the lectures today too. We do get questions on some varied subjects, don’t we? Absolutely! I was just discussing with Speaker_3 about the session on language research. Have you listened to that one? Not yet, but I would love to. You know, I’m actually an administrator in the language research department. Oh, that's fascinating! I work as a co-ordinator in the same field. Ah, language research! Absolutely fascinating! What are your thoughts on the current trends? Well, from what I understand, looking at how languages are evolving and how historical linguistics might provide insights into the past is pretty exciting. And it seems like there's growing interest in languages less traditionally studied, like Chinese or even languages used in ancient trading routes like Sanskrit or Arabic. Oh, absolutely. We're focusing a lot on those too. I've been working on some projects looking at the transactional codes used in ancient documents found in Arab, Persian, and Greek coins. It's incredible how much history is embedded in those linguistic patterns. That sounds right up my alley. I've actually been in several excavations, really trying to understand the life of the people, and a big part of that is through language and linguistics. But it's not just about the written word, is it? Archeology plays a massive role. I find it so thrilling to think about excavating entire villages and the insights you can gain from that. Exactly! The amount of knowledge hidden in the ground can be astounding. I recall one excavation in an ancient village in Greece where we found language changing according to where in the village things were found. Like, certain dialect structures only appeared in the more affluent parts. That's fascinating! I've heard such stories but always find them so captivating. The social hierarchy demonstrated through language. Yes, and it's not just in the past. We can also see those dynamics in modern contexts, particularly around socioeconomic status. Our research department has found similar patterns in contemporary urban areas. Absolutely. And when it comes to university lectures, I sometimes find I have to adapt my approach to address students from different linguistic backgrounds.

Right, so I'm going to apply for a few teaching assistant's roles during my placement. It'd be quite cool to get some teaching experience before I finish my degree. Oh, that's great! You'll be ideal for that. A bit of classroom experience will definitely help with your CV. And isn't it lovely that something as important as teaching still doesn't require a degree? It says something about where our priorities should lie actually. Definitely. Our education system can sometimes feel so out of touch with what really matters, don't you think? You get people with all sorts of degrees but struggling to get jobs in their field. I know what you mean. I had a friend who just graduated with a business degree but was stuck working in a part-time role at a big company. Exactly. Hence why I'm glad I'm doing something practical like baking. It requires skill and creativity, but it's also creative and very hands-on. And running a café isn't all about just serving coffee. You've got to handle finances, deals, human resources... it's a real business. And it's all about making different parts of society connect, isn’t it? I sometimes think the arts – film, music, food even – they all do that. They're things that bring us together, beyond class or whatever. Ah, speaking of bringing people together... have you seen that viral video where the kids decided to do their class project as a group to help out at a homeless shelter? I found it really uplifting and thought-provoking. Yeah, that's a fantastic story. Makes the heart swell, doesn't it? It's a great example of young people stepping up and seeing beyond their own issues. It's also interesting that these kinds of project often come from kids who aren't necessarily confident in traditional academic settings. Yes, that's a great point Julie. Kids with dyslexia, or even just those who learn differently, often find themselves marginalized in our current education system. I've seen that first-hand. I've worked with kids at a dyslexia support group and they're often so creative and innovative. It's just a shame that our education system isn't set up to embrace those kinds of skills more. Absolutely. I've got a few friends who are brilliant and dyslexic, but struggled with certain aspects of school because the curriculum didn't cater to their strengths.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that online workshop I attended today? The guest lecturer was talking about the latest research on mental health in the academic sector. It was particularly disheartening. You know how long hours and ridiculous expectations can leave us drained. Yes, I agree. We're often expected to perform and work far beyond our actual "normal" hours. It makes me wonder, how can we actually change that without... I don't know, presenting ourselves as somehow less dedicated? Exactly. It's this weird catch-22. Express concerns and be seen as less committed, or just keep riding the burnout train to professionalism. So what's the solution? Engage in a little 'civil disobedience'? Exactly, or find ways to gently push back without drawing too much attention. But, you know, in the long run, it should be about the quality of work and not the hours you spend on it. We also talked about politics. Did you watch that debate this week? Not enough time with the kids. Where did you get the time? Honestly, it's the one hour I allow myself at the end of the day before bed for a little adult conversation. Considering the silly things they waste time on, really? But anyway, what did you make of it all? Well, I thought it was a bit... predictable? The usual claims and counter-claims. But what really struck me was how much the discussion veered into side issues instead of sticking to the main points. Exactly. It's another classic case of 'playing to their base' rather than confronting real problems. You know, that's what gets me. Our politicians seem to forget that the issues we're dealing with, healthcare, economy, are real people's lives we're talking about. True. Though, let's not turn this into a full-blown political argument... We're out for a drink, and I believe my pint is starting to get warm. Forgive me, I get carried away sometimes. You're right, let's focus on more pleasant things. How's... um, your DIY project coming along? Honestly, still on the waiting list for the suppliers to deliver that new boiler. It's like, another week and at this point I might as well build it myself. Well, as someone who recently had a similar ordeal with her boiler, I can sympathize. It's so frustrating, especially when it's something you can't delay.

Ah, marvellous weekend. I managed to finish that book about wildlife conservation. Fascinating stuff really. Did you hear about the new initiative they've got up their sleeve? Yes! It's about the resurgence of certain species that were thought to be extinct. I read about it on the publisher's website just yesterday. You know, it's amazing how technology and the Internet have changed how we access and share information. True. I was browsing through some science blogs and came across articles about how drones are being used to monitor wildlife now. Quite impressive. Back when I was teaching, this stuff was just beginning, but now it's become quite commonplace. And it's not just technology. The government is also putting a lot of effort into conservation, which is great. Yes, but I wonder if we're doing enough. And what about the climate? That's a worry, isn't it? Absolutely, the effects of climate change on wildlife are distressing. But it's good to see people taking this seriously now. Perhaps we should plan a family holiday that involves a bit of this sort of ecological activity? Like a volunteer trip or something. That's a wonderful idea. I assumed we'd just have a quiet holiday at the in-laws this year, but that sounds interesting. It could be quite educational too. Perhaps we could look into some local conservation groups while we're at it, see if we can contribute in some small way. I can help with the research. We might even be able to inspire some of these ideas into the publication work I do. That's kind of you to offer. You could write a piece about it, and maybe one day it could become the next big thing in our field. I just wish more people were as engaged as we are. We need more awareness and action. Yes, that's true. But every little helps, right? While I was dealing with the articles about that new science fiction film series they mentioned at the office today, I was surprised by the response. People are eager for these sorts of discussions, and if we can channel it into something truly impactful, it could make a difference. You're absolutely right. And while we're on the topic of films, I heard they're remaking a classic we all grew up with.

Ah, so James, you've been bingeing on those new video games these past few weeks. What's caught your eye this time? Yeah, I've been playing a lot of "Triple Danger" lately. It's just so addictive, Dad! The challenges, the questions, the kind of strategy you need... and it's not even a brain-tickler or anything like that, it's just so normal and relatable, you know? Well, it sounds fun even if it is "just normal." Right, let me speak from my end too, seeing as how I'm a bit lazy in the gaming world. What's so addictive about it, really? Honestly, it's the mix. It's not all puzzles or wars or magic - which we all get bored of at some point - it's kind of a game about everyday life, but with challenges and stuff. Like, sometimes you need creative thinking, sometimes you need to react fast, and sometimes it's just common sense. And it's got a multiplayer option too, so playing with friends or even online makes it more fun. Makes sense. It sounds like different levels of difficulty with unexpected quirks. The unpredictability can hook you in, I suppose. Exactly! And it also has a lot of variables. It can change quite a lot depending on your choices, so every playthrough is different. I love that, it feels fresh every time. Mama, I'm building a castle with these blocks! Ah, the architect is busy too, we can't ignore that talent. And let the future career begin. Can the young man try his hand at a few real-life challenges for a minute? For example, how about a castle made of newspaper? No, Mama, blocks! Right, sure. Speaking of challenges though, does it have levels or quests or something like that? Yeah. The structure is kind of like a series of questions or challenges, like mini-games within the game. You win points for each and it unlocks more stuff. And if you're online, you can play them against real people. Ah, sounds like a mix of "Who Wants to be a Millionaire" and "Candy Crush," but with more depth. Exactly! And it's not just winning or losing; you can also share the best/funniest/funniest losses with friends online. That might be a real draw for you, sharing that kind of gameplay. I did it!

Right, now I'm going to make sure to remember to pick up groceries before today's road trip. Can't have us running out of food halfway to our destination, can we? Oh absolutely, dear! And perhaps we should also bring some extra snacks for the children, they get quite hungry after a few hours in the car. Speaking of the ride, have you all seen the news about that ghost train service? I'm just thinking, perhaps our journey will be less eventful than that. Right, let's hope so. By the way, have you been to the Christmas shop in Norwich lately? They have such fun stuff, and I just have to get a few more gifts for the family and my boyfriend. Ah, the boyfriend of course. Speaking of which, did you hear the news about the car service that went wrong? Apparently, it's a common issue with that model. We should make sure our vehicle is in good shape before our journey. As a teacher, I always tell my students to check things thoroughly, especially on long trips. Funny you should say that. We were actually discussing at school how cars have developed over the years. It's incredible to think about all the technology that goes into them. Yes, and just as art has evolved, so has technology. But I also love old things, like antiques and vintage. It's amazing how elegantly they were designed, especially our family's old carriage that my granddad keeps in the barn.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my day at work? We had the most hilarious situation. A patient thought he was a Renaissance painter and talked about creating his "masterpiece" on the wall. Did the meds go awry? We've had some odd cases before but that one takes the cake. But seriously, how are the others at work treating you? Ah, I'd say they're still very supportive. It's important, especially if you're creative like you are. I love it! Being a copywriter is so varied. One day I'm writing about exotic destinations and the next, I'm tasked with coming up with a catchphrase for a cleaning product. It's both a challenge and exciting. That sounds quite neat, while I'm stuck in meetings and paperwork in my department. It must be nice to have such a diverse workload. Indeed, but it's not all fun and games. I had a patient this morning who wanted me to paint his toenails for him because he believed he'd been inspired by a divine vision. I would say that it proves the saying "we're all artists in our own way"! Except, I guess, in his case... literally. Well, as long as everyone's healthy and having a good time. Speaking of fun, are we getting anywhere on choosing a birthday gift for Sarah? Not really, and it's been on my mind a lot lately. You know how she's been feeling stressed lately? I thought maybe something relaxing or a bit decadent? A spa voucher sounds just right. She always talks about needing a break. Or perhaps a zero gravity chair? Or have we considered something health-related? Maybe a mindfulness book or an upscale yoga class package deal? Good ideas. I was thinking towards something indulgent but healthy. A gourmet food basket perhaps or a funny and witty book to take her mind off things? You're right, healthy indulgences work best... I'll look into some combinations of those.

Right, so I was going over some of these old family photos the other day. Got me thinking; these are moments we'll never get back. Made me realize how much life has changed, particularly since all of this lockdown business. Indeed. Especially now, without power, it’s kind of like going back in time. Absolutely, and it makes me think about how life would have been before socialism and all modern conveniences of course. Now, with no power, we're truly facing how life used to be... Right, it's kind of like Big Brother but without the electricity. It really makes you see things differently. I used to love going out in London with my mates just like you'd see on those old films - we'd party in the docks and then go home to warm homes. Now, it's like a scene from Little Britain without the laugh. Yes, and with all these changes, it makes me wish we could have a society that understands these struggles better. Maybe even grab a few politicians and let them see for themselves what it's really like without the comforts we often take for granted. We could call it 'Life without Power: The Virtual Tour' for Parliament. Indeed, and all these while the 'higher professional' sectors in politics think they make all the decisions that affect us, really don't consider the impact on people like us. Absolutely, but perhaps that's why programs like Big Brother resonate with so many in Britain: it really is a microcosm of society. It captures all the complexities and social dynamics that we can't quite articulate in everyday conversation. On another note, has anyone seen the new 'shopping deals'? I went to the market yesterday and it was like the days of my childhood again - commerce was personal and the prices weren't outrageous. Shopping? Speaking of which, I met Lady Richardson in town last week and she was talking about these new dog boutiques and how you can browse without the entire experience changing online. That’s quite interesting… Physical shopping has a charm to it. Although I suppose online shopping is for those who like it quiet or those who don’t have much choice with their busy schedules. Back to the original topic though, the church has been great. They even have meetings without power which almost feels like a new communal experience.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that film we watched last week? The one that was set in Yorkshire, and clearly the writers had no clue about Yorkshire dialect! No, which one was it? Was it the one about the band? No, this was a drama. I think it was called "The Troublesome Yorkshire Gathering" or something like that. I think I might know it. And how was it wrong about Yorkshire dialect? Well, first, they pronounced certain words all wrong. Like, they said 'y'all' instead of 'thou' or 'thee'. I can see how that would be a bit of a mix-up! And secondly, they said 'lass' instead of 'lassie'. That seems minor, doesn’t it? Well, to those of us from Yorkshire, these are not minor details! They're part of our identity and culture. I see. You’re right, though, while the 'y'all' thing is genuinely North American English. Exactly! It's like they mixed accents for no reason at all. Speaking of accents, your mother always talks about her time in Lewisham. Did you grow up speaking the 'standard' London accent? I certainly have a hint of it, but it's not as strong as some people from Lewisham or Croydon, say. I don't really notice it unless people point it out or ask me to repeat something. I find the blurred boundaries between local dialects are really fascinating. You know, in Lewisham, we have a mix of Cockney, Estuary, and other influences. That's interesting. It’s like a linguistic party in our mouths, isn't it? Absolutely. But, do you think local dialects should be represented more accurately in films or TV shows? Definitely. I think it can help with acceptance and understanding of cultural differences. It’s like... if I went to see a film set in, say, Glasgow, and the actors all sounded like they were from Cambridge, I'd feel a bit cheated. You'd feel the film was disrespecting the place, right? Or over-romanticizing it? Exactly! It’s better when they get it right. Like that brilliant film about Manchester, "24 Hour Party People". They got the Mancunian dialect spot on, and that added so much to the film. True successful films about places often pay attention to those details. It makes the story feel more authentic. And it's not just films. Sometimes TV shows do it too.

Right, so I've been reading about this Scottish Independence referendum and I must say, it's really got me thinking. Yeah, it sounds big. But what does it all mean? You're not really into politics, are you? Well, I am when it catches my eye and today it definitely has. You see, what's got me is that part about the history. Have you ever learned about this at school? Not really, but we talked about it a bit in history lessons. You know, like when people wanted to become independent from England and stuff like that, long ago. Yes, exactly! It goes way back but I think this time it's a bit different. It’s like Scotland is asking to leave the UK again. Is that like Brexit but just Scotland? Yes, a bit like that. But there's more to it. Scotland was part of the UK for a very long time, since the year 1707. And it's only been in the last few decades that there's really been a serious push for independence. Now, with this referendum this year, Scots are voting whether they want to stay in the UK or become an independent country. Wow! So it's about becoming completely separate? Yes, that's right. They would have their own government, their own laws, their own finances, everything. Like, if you could imagine us, sitting here in Malton, but in an independent Yorkshire, maybe with its own laws, its own regional parliament... That's quite hard to imagine doesn't it? But it makes sense if they think it's better for them. Exactly. And there are many reasons why people in Scotland might want independence. One of them is oil in the North Sea. Scotland, as a part of the UK, gets a share of the revenues from oil. If they become independent, they would keep all of it. Also, and this is important, cultural identity. Many people in Scotland feel that Scotland should be making its own decisions, not just follow what happens in Westminster. Westminster? Is that like the British Parliament? That’s the main one. Parliament in London, where most of our laws are made. So, the argument for independence is that Scots could have more control over their own affairs. But what if they become independent? Won't things change a lot? Yes, everything from economy to society to international trade.

Listening to Jeremy Kyle, it's almost as though he purposefully pronounces every word to its fullest extent. It feels so different to how we actually talk, don't you think? You wouldn't hear many people say 'therapist' like he does. Oh, absolutely. It's like the accent stays in the books and never makes it out onto his tongue. It's a bit funny, actually. 'Therapyst!' It's weird how even though he's a North Country lad like us, his accent disappears completely when he's on TV. And have you noticed, despite being northerners, our accents are so different, yet so similar? It's like the differences are just in the places of certain vowels or the way we say words like 'bus' or 'bath'. Exactly! It's all about the elision and pronunciation, isn't it? Like, in my neck of the woods , we'd say 'bath' like 'barth', but here in Chester, or even Doncaster, it's more like 'bath'. And on Jeremy Kyle, it's like he says 'bath' as if the 'th' is a separate word all on its own. And the way we drop certain sounds or blend them together. Like, instead of saying 'going to university', we might say 'gonna uni'. A bit like how Jeremy Kyle still says 'going to therapy' when we all really just say 'going to therapy'. That's a great example of elision! I mean, doesn't it feel like Jeremy speaks in full sentences and we use contractions? It's like he wants to make sure we understand every word precisely. Seems like he's more worried about being misunderstood than just relating to his audience. I mean, it's fun to listen to, but it does seem a bit forced at times. And what's with all the guests?! They all sound so dramatic. It's like they forget to use contractions or anything unless they're yelling. Don't you find it a bit comical? Oh, it's so funny. Reminds me of when we were watching last week and one of the guests said, 'I am going to the doctor'. It was like they were reading from a script in the Queen's English. Yeah, and have you noticed how Jeremy always says everything so slowly and carefully too? It's almost like he's teaching us how to talk. 'I, uh, am going... to see the... uh, doctor.'

Oh, did you see that last move by Sterling? I swear today's match is more exciting than Jeopardy and Mastermind combined! You love your football, Alison! But I agree. It’s been quite the match, hasn't it? Now, questions for you - what’s the plan for baby names if it’s a boy? Ah, well, I'm right at the start of this I know, but Sam and I discussed it last weekend. We're keeps coming backwards and forwards between Jasper and Finn. Jasper's a great name! But I'm also fond of Finn. Yeah, we like it too. But then there's the whole question of whether the baby will 'look like a Finn' when it grows up. You know how it is. Oh absolutely, the naming process is a wild ride. But, Alison, when you decide, make sure you pick a good nickname. You never know, it's the nicknames that stick in the end. I'm fully prepared for that, believe me. Now, back to the game. Where is the fun in talking about names while the action's still on? True that. But really, can't help but think about the future when they grow up – like whether they'd play football or perhaps be more into knitting like you. Ah, knitting, yes. It’s a hobby that's surprisingly therapeutic. Have you taken up any new hobbies during this PhD marathon you're on? Well, I do try to keep knitting as a stress reliever, but between lectures and papers, it's hard to keep up. But I do find it really helps me concentrate sometimes. Exactly! Now, while they're figuring out whether football or knitting is their thing, what about the Olympics? You sure you won't end up stuck in a knitting event? Ha! Well, I suppose if there was a 'thesis knitting' event, I’d be a shoo-in for the gold. Excellent. That's almost as competitive as this game being played here. Speaking of competitive, looks like we're up to something big. Yeah, I know. You can almost see the tension in the room. And I thought I was tense about baby names. So, speaking of the Olympics, which event are you most excited to watch this year? To be honest, I'm really looking forward to watching the Athletics. That’s when you see the real grit of sport.

I've just watched The Bee Movie with the kids. I never realized how much it talks about royalty. It's funny how they portrayed it, though, isn't it? Yes! Barry the bee and Vanessa the florist. I kind of want to have a Royal fruit party now. Do you think they have Royal fruits, you know, special ones? Well, of course, as a British person, we can't resist bringing it back to royalty! There's an interesting history behind Royal fruits. Back in the Middle Ages, certain foods were considered 'royal' because they were rare and expensive. Think of things like pomegranates, oranges, and pineapples. Really? So, do we actually pay to get into the Royal palaces now? I mean, aren't they public? Well, not all of them are free. Buckingham Palace, for instance, you can visit certain parts of it for a fee. But it’s worth it. So, can anyone pay to go and live in Buckingham Palace or Windsor Castle if they want? I wish! We have a very fascinating system in the UK. We're a constitutional monarchy, which means we have a Queen or King, but we’re also governed by laws made by Parliament, not the monarch alone. A bit like in The Bee Movie, where they argue about the inherent rights of bees. But in our case, we're also a democracy. So no, you can't just move into a Royal palace, but… I want to be a politician then, so I can change laws if I want to! That’s ambitious! We also have a fascinating tradition of 'public access' to our palaces at certain times of the year. But, personally, if I could choose, I'd rather be a teacher than a monarch or a politician. Hmmm, I was thinking more along the lines of wanting to be like King Arthur or someone important like that. And I thought being a zero was kinda cool last year! Being a zero... That's a new kind of royal power I hadn't considered! Do you think if we got vitamins, we could be royalty? Well, vitamins can help your body grow healthy and strong, but I’m not sure they'd award you a kingdom! But if we're really strong and healthy, maybe we could climb up these really high mountains from the Bee Movie and be like heroes?

Oh, I'm so glad we stopped here. I needed a break. It's been quite an eventful day. I know. You were right though, Alison, we should have gone to that new disposal site instead of the old one – way more questions there! Was there a lot of rubbish today? Yes, quite a bit. But we did find some very nice old furniture. I wish I had more time to restore it. You know, speak of the devil, we could try those new 'upcycling' apps to check the value! You two are just looking for excuses to stop drinking coffee and get stuck into another project, aren't you? Maybe. And maybe I’ll even use those interior design apps to help with the project. While you're at it, Alison, you could also start planning our potential move. You've been on about it for ages now! I know, I do. It's just everything seems to be getting so cluttered here. Cluttered? What do you mean? Well, things just seem to be piling up. It's not like when we were younger – we could keep everything under control then. True, Alison. As we get older, it can be overwhelming. It’s all part of this 'clearing out' process we've been talking about. But it's hard to decide what to keep and what to let go of. So you're just planning to throw everything out? No, no, nothing so drastic. But... We found a lovely antique table at the tip, and we were thinking of restoring it. Maybe we could turn it into a coffee table or something. That’s a great idea! I could help out – I’ve got some experience with woodwork after all. And speaking of 'clearing out', have you seen the latest episode of that TV show about organizing and decluttering? Some of the ideas they have are genius. Yes, I love that show. They always have such innovative ideas. Ooh, will you let me watch it with you next time? I love TV. Of course, we can watch it together. On that note, did you hear about Lucy’s wedding plans? It’s going to be a stag party to remember! Yes! She’s going to Thirsk for it, isn't she? That’s right! You know, I once visited Thirsk years ago. It’s a lovely town, but I hope the party won’t be too wild!

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new museum that's opening up in the city? They've got an exhibit on northern industry, and from what I've heard, it sounds pretty fascinating. Yeah, I've seen the ads. It's just what the area needs. We're flooded with tourists and students, so it’s about time we had some attractions that truly represent the city. Absolutely. I'm actually considering suggesting it to my language students. Maybe we can plan a class trip for next term. That’s a great idea. You'll need to book ahead, though. Parking in the city can be a nightmare at the best of times and I can imagine it'll get worse once it opens. True. Speaking of parking, did you actually manage to get your car fixed? I saw you were having issues last week. Ah, yeah, the mechanic had it sorted out eventually. Just a little thing, but it kept happening. Glad it's over now. Good to hear. I swear, these cars always seem to break or get issues at the most inconvenient time. Tell me about it! Anyway, how was your day at the school? It was good, thanks. The students are learning quickly, but we're running out of textbooks, so we're having to do more digital lessons. Ah, that can be a real challenge, right? I've had issues with that at the practice too, really trying to keep everything up to date. Exactly. Plus, I've been thinking about doing a master's, but the cost is quite the deterrent. You should definitely do it, if it’s something you’re passionate about. But yeah, the cost can be a challenge. Perhaps we could create a budget plan? That's a good idea. I was thinking about discussing it with my boss too, maybe there's some kind of sponsorship or part-time work available. It might be worth a shot. I know a few people that were able to work part-time while doing their post-grad. Either way, it's something worth exploring. Yeah, definitely. Speaking of plans, did you hear the Johnson's are moving house? Oh yeah, I saw them posting about it on Facebook. Clearly, they're pretty excited, but I can imagine it must be a lot of hassle. It’s a big decision, isn’t it?

Yo, how was your weekend? Watch any good shows on Netflix? Yeah, watched quite a few. I've been bingeing on 'Peaky Blinders'. It's unreal! Have you seen it? Still have to get into it, but I’ve heard fantastic things. I’ve been obsessed with 'Stranger Things'. I mean, totally vibing with the whole '90s nostalgia thing. Oh man, I love that show too! I find myself comparing it to my own childhood even though it’s totally unrealistic, haha. Exactly, but isn't that the best kind of show? Makes you feel like a part of something despite being so far removed. Definitely. Speaking of childhood, did you see the trailer for 'Toy Story 4'? I'm beyond excited. Yeah, I want to cry already. I used to love looking for my toys in the closet and thinking they could come to life. That’s so adorable. It brings back so many memories. And those early Disney movies or even 'The Simpsons'? I’m this close to just rewatching all of it. I’ve been rewatching 'The Lion King' and still can’t believe it. Goodness, the music! Absolutely! And can't forget the cartoons. I spend way too much time streaming 'Bluey'. It's so wholesome. Oh my god, I love that show! They're just so relatable and the animation is great. What do you do to relax? Hmm, I'm really into tattoos lately. I'm thinking of getting my own but can't decide on the design yet. That sounds cool! I love the idea of personal expression through art. I just tried to relax over the weekend by watching football. We won our match, so it was a good time. Nice! That's always a good stress reliever. I’ve also been trying to explore new cafes around here. Anyone good by any chance? Oh for sure! There's this one place just near campus called 'The Bubble' - so cute, super cozy, and the coffee is amazing! They also do a great brunch. Sounds perfect. I should check it out. I just read an awesome review on Instagram about it actually. Do you follow a certain page or just scroll through random recommendations? Both, actually. I have a few favorite food bloggers but I also love stumbling onto new places when I’m just scrolling. That's interesting. I just use it for keeping up with my friends and random thoughts really.

Yo, I was browsing on the internet yesterday and came across an idea online. What if we skyped and played some Pokémon together? Maybe compete in a battle or two. It sounds fun, don't you think? I love that idea, but considering Oisin is napping at the moment, we might just have to plan this for later. Besides, Pokémon has taken the world by storm again! Da-da! Wait, did Oisin just say "da-da" or "Pikachu"? Haha! I think we have a Pokémon expert in training here, just like you, even if he can't quite say it yet. Speaking of expertise, did either of you try making those DIY Pokémon costumes? They look pretty cool online. Actually, yeah! I thought about making one. It didn't turn out exactly as planned, but it was fun. Next time, I'll probably try harder. You know, for the next battle. Maybe Oisin can team up and we can play some Pokémon together, even if he can't battle with his pacifiers yet. That would be awesome! Anyway, about skyping, have you thought about what time works best for you both? Considering our schedules... Yeah, I can probably be available in the evening after my homework. How about you? Well, the evenings are usually when Oisin goes to bed, but we could do earlier if you're not busy during the day. He seems to know more about Pokémon than us! Perhaps he'll be the champion one day. You know, after he learns to use a controller... For sure! Speaking of food, have you ever tried Ramen? We could arrange a Ramen night. You could even wear your best skinny jeans and make it a theme night! I LOVE Ramen! That’s a brilliant idea! And yes, I’ll definitely wear skinny jeans. You know, we could even make it a Pokémon Ramen night? Customize our DIY Pokémon costumes for the event? Yeah, that would be perfect! Okay, so to recap, we are planning a skype session, maybe with a Pokémon battle, followed by Ramen night, with Pokémon themed selfies perhaps? And probably, a toddler expert who doesn’t speak but knows everything about Pokémon. It's settled then. A plan is born. Just need to figure out the exact time and maybe sneak in some guitar lessons before we start. Speaking of which, have either of you ever tried to play Pokémon on the guitar?

Ah, I can't believe how much of our childhood we can remember from just these old toys. Look at this gardening set! Do you remember how we used to spend hours pretending to plant flowers and harvest vegetables? It's absurd now, but at the time, it was the most important job in the world! Oh, absolutely! I had completely forgotten about that. But do you remember the Bako set? Of course! It was my favorite actually. We used to build incredible creations with those blocks. I think I spent even more time playing with that than with the gardening set. You'd always be the one who knew exactly what we were building — a house, a bridge, a castle. It's amazing how much creativity we had as children. Yes, and what about the excitement of getting a new set of blocks or discovering a new way we could use them? And the disappointment when we'd lose a certain piece, which would sometimes mean the destruction of our entire building project! Oh, the frustration! But it was always worth it in the end. And it's interesting how those early experiences might have influenced our adult lives in some way. We both ended up working in quite creative fields, or at least, ones that involved some form of building or creation. That's true. I ended up in teaching; it's all about building people's knowledge, really. And you in university management... well, you were always good at organizing things, weren't you? Hmm, maybe. But it wasn't really about organizing things back then, was it? It was about creating something entirely from our imagination with very limited resources. Indeed. And how we persevered even when things didn't turn out as planned. That's definitely one skill that has helped me in career and life. Definitely a good skill to have. But look at this mess we're making just talking about old toys. It proves the old adage that nostalgia can be quite chaotic! Perhaps changing the subject to something less nostalgically messy might be a good idea. Absolutely! How about this weather we're having? It seems to be quite wetter than usual this summer. It does seem to be raining a lot. And yet, it still feels quite warm. Unsettling almost. Though, I suppose it's better than having no rain at all.

Oh, did you see that?? I almost got hit by a mosquito. I swear, they're getting more aggressive each year! You're right though, Alison! They seem to thrive on the muggy weather we've been having. It's not even summer yet! I've been taking them out on short strolls to get them some fresh air, but honestly... I'd almost rather deal with roadworks. Are you serious?! Well, I guess we've all got our pet peeves. I can't stand tractor drivers passing slow vehicles on single file roads. Yes, and city traffic... that's a whole different beast! And the railways, don't get started on that. I've heard of people going nuts because there's yet another 'engineering works' on their line... And these people travel on trains every day. You'd think by now they'd have figured out how to do repairs without causing chaos? Maybe it's just optimism at this point. Speaking of chaos, did you know that we might actually have that indie gig we wanted in August? What? Which one? The one I told you about earlier this year, you know, the one with that one band that... really understands chaos in music? Oh, that 'chaotic indie' band I'd been wanting us to check out? The 'Aural Disarray'. I saw that they're playing just outside town next month. I just looked, they are! That would be so much fun! Of course, that's if we can manage and find a babysitter. True. Well, we'll see. I'm sure we can figure something out. If not just for us, for little Olivia too. Maybe it'll be one of her first gigs! She could even wear ear defenders if it gets too loud. Alison, you always think ahead. Can't help it. So, what about company at the gig? Any other book club friends interested? I'll ask. We've been meaning to stir up the old literature crew again anyway. Perfect. It'd be great to see everyone. Definitely. Speaking of reviving group activities, did you attend that opera performance in town last weekend? Unfortunately no. But I've heard it was excellent. We should catch up soon, though I've got that new project on global literature I'm planning to introduce this semester. That sounds ambitious. I think a lot of students need to mix up their reading list.

Yo, mate, had a good day yesterday? Honestly, not much to mention really. Got interviewed for a graduate job again yesterday, but I really don't think I've got the experience they need. Ah, that's a shame buddy, but don't get down, you'll find something that's right for you. Yeah, keeps coming up. Anyway, how was your day? You game for a bit of an exercise routine to get us both in shape? Might just sneak in a bit of golf, mate. My game's been off lately, need to get back on track. Speaking of golf, I saw your mum sent a package for you today. What was it? Ah, just some uni books for the next few months, and what looked like a new set of clubs? Maybe a birthday present from home. Nice, I hope they help. You've been in good form the past couple of weeks, hasn’t you? Can't complain, been focused on getting my game back, but it's tricky isn't it? Especially when you're trying to balance life around the golf circuit. Definitely, but you've always been good about the balance between sport and personal life. You were serious about your studies before all this golf fever hit, weren’t you? Yeah, I had to put uni on hold to focus on the sport, but I’m hoping to maybe do some part-time study in future. Good plan, education is important. You know, I’ve been thinking about writing more these days. Just trying to find my voice. That’s great! You’ll find it mate, just pick up a good book, maybe some poetry and start from there. There’s something about the rhythm of words that can really capture your thoughts. That’s a good idea, I just need to find the time and discipline. Watching too much TV or scrolling on the phone can really drain the motivation. Got to limit that a bit, really though. I did try turning my phone off from 7 pm onwards; it helps massively. I'll give that a shot. Maybe we can turn our phones off simultaneously from now on? We can catch up over a good meal instead. Sorted, I’m in for anything that means less screen time. Want to do it tonight? I could cook something. That sounds lovely. Something simple.

Ah, did you hear that, Alan's singing voice is actually getting better. Yeah, his rendition of "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star" was quite impressive for a four-year-old though, wasn't it? Between you and me, I think he's going to have quite a passion for the arts. Maybe he'll even make a career of it one day, who knows? That'd be fantastic. As a matter of fact, we were discussing this before dinner, planning on enrolling him in some drama or music classes once he's a bit older and ready to start. Dada, doodle, docka... He's already trying to join the conversation, isn't he? He's always so eager to join the adult conversations, bless him. Off we go now, shall we? Someone should probably help mam here get dinner served or we'll be here all evening. I can help, Grandma. I can fetch plates and cutlery. Ah, that’s a kind boy, thank you. Alan really looks up to you, by the way. He loves playing video games with you, doesn’t he? Yeah, we play a lot of Fortnite together. But we always have to be careful not to get too "clouded" up in the game doesn’t we, Granddaddy? "Clouded" is a new word, isn’t it? We'll have to remind you to get your head back out of the cloud, literally. Sure thing, Granddaddy. But can we play another match next week? We'll see. We're changing the arrangement to not have screen time on weekdays after all. Can't we make an exception? I think we need to stick to the plan if we want him to do well in school. Ok, no screen, no screen. I love hearing him agree, even if he doesn't understand. Speaking of films, did any of us catch anything worth mentioning this week? I watched "Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker" over the weekend. It was epic! I heard good things about that one though it was a bit of a controversial ending from what I've read. You tech heads and your sci-fi. I'm more about older films myself but the graphics are impressive don't get me wrong. Yeah, the CGI was absolutely amazing. Doodle, do do do! It seems our dinner guest here, our very own Alan, needs our attention before he causes a huge mess.

I've got something to share that's almost as hilarious as today's ANON sleeping in his pants incident. Go on, tell us. So yesterday, ANON was nodding off and suddenly, he awoke with a start, his face kind of red. You know what he was doing? He was sleeping in his pants, completely! And? Did he... I don't know... fall off the couch or something? No, worse... or better, depending on your point of view. He was in the middle of deciding whether to call the builder today about those house extension plans. So he was dreaming about carpentry? Exactly! He said we need an extra bedroom and a separate study and then all of a sudden he's saying, "Wait, but where's the extension?!" And then... boom. He's scratching his head and we see that his pants are on his knees. Sounds like he was firmly in his bedroom... or his pants. He's always been a bit of a daydreamer.
