Oh, so many Christmases from so many different places. I still can't quite wrap my head around the idea of Christmas in warm weather. It sounds surreal! Exactly! I remember when I was little, Christmas was always snowing in Manila, because we kind of adopted the Western tradition and moved it to December, even though it’s hot as blazes there at that time. But actually, as I grew up, we started celebrating local traditions too. It was always about family, food, and togetherness. That's fascinating, isn't it? Even though our ways of celebrating Christmas can be so different, the heart of it – spending time with your loved ones – is universal. Speaking of traditions, what about the foods we eat on Christmas? Yeah! For us, it's all about the traditional Christmas dinner: turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and a variety of vegetables. But I know in some parts of the world, it's all about seafood or other entirely different dishes. In Manila, we traditionally have 'Noche Buena'. It's this big feast on Christmas Eve, filled with ham, cheese, sweets, and lots of fruit. And because of the heat, we often have it at around 7 in the evening, as opposed to the midnight feast here, right? Well, actually, for families like mine, it's not as focused on a big feast, especially after we got old. We'd usually have a really early Christmas dinner, around 11, and focus more on presents and carols. Plus, I've traveled quite a bit myself, so I've seen different kinds of feasts. Oh, speaking of traveling, what if one day we could visit the different places we talk about? More specifically, those that we weren't born in. That would be wonderful! I've always wanted to visit Bath again. There's something about its history and architecture that draws me in. And of course, a chance to taste the traditional Christmas fare there. I've always been fascinated by the concept of diasporas and how traditions can evolve. For example, in the Philippines, we adopt Western traditions so fully, yet at the same time, we're so rich in our own indigenous holiday practices. Speaking of diasporas, it's interesting how our job histories and life experiences can sometimes outshine our birthplaces. I spent a good part of my career working in various parts of the UK and abroad, so I feel just as much at home in different regions as I do in Bognor Regis.

Ah, marvellous weekend. I managed to finish an entire online workshop on transcribing Victorian era documents. Such an intriguing period, and such a challenging task! That sounds fascinating! Are you still enjoying working from home as a transcriber? Really? It's given me some kind of freedom I never thought possible. I mean, I can work at my own pace and my schedule is pretty flexible. The only disadvantage is, I have to be strict with myself not to get too distracted by the TV. But even that keeps changing now due to this whole detective series binge... Which one? I've started watching True Detective too. These crime dramas really keep you on your toes, don't they? Yes, exactly! I started with Line of Duty but now I'm hooked on the new season of Liar. And to be honest, it's partly because of my work. It's made me more aware of different speech patterns and such. That's interesting! So, you're learning from your job and it's influencing your TV shows. Definitely! For instance, listening to accents from different parts of the country, it's amazing how many different ways people pronounce certain words. And it's all in the transcriptions, so I've got to be on the ball. Absolutely! And do you find your work interesting? Oh, yes! A lot of the documents I transcribe are old newspapers or journals, sometimes even diaries. One time, I transcribed a diary from a soldier during World War I. It was incredibly moving. But it must be quite taxing too, focusing so much on detailed work. Yes, it can be. That's why I love to wind down with a Kindle and a good novel, preferably a detective novel. I've been meaning to get to the latest Agatha Christie. Agatha Christie! I've been meaning to get to The Mysterious Affair at Styles. It's one of my favourites. Definitely do. The foreshadowing is brilliant. But I have a Kindle challenge for us. I suggest we each read at least one book from a different genre. Kind of broaden our horizons. That sounds like fun. I almost always read non-fiction but maybe it's time for a change. Yeah, I've been meaning to read more fiction too. This could be a great opportunity. And why not set a target for the book club discussion?

Right, so I was going over some of these old beans from's passport. Lookin' back; it's been quite an education, innit? Certainly is, isn't it? Especially here in the UK, isn't it? All the ways things have changed, yet they remain the same. Absolutely, and sometimes it feels like we're stuck in a time warp. I've seen this with my own business as well. I mean, technology has transformed so much for us. But even with all these changes, the core values - support, community, knowledge - remain essential, don't they? True, true. These days, it's all about that technology, isn't it? Me, I like things a bit simpler. I never was one for gadgets, but my grandkids... they're another story altogether, aren't they? Exactly! But it's also about making sure we're adapting, not just resisting change. We need to stay relevant if we're going to help the younger generation. They don't always ask for advice but when they do, it's good to be able to give them something practical, don't you think? I agree. Speaking of practical, how about we talk about something that's really practical for us? Like, we should probably get a move on and organise these "old beans" I was talking about doesn't it? Sort out the house a bit. Oh, definitely! And maybe while we're at it, we can do something for the community. You know, sort of give back? Like, help a few families, maybe? That's a wonderful idea! If we pooled our resources and expertise, we could do something quite substantial, don't you think? And it would also keep us active, engaged. It's good for the soul, after all. I suppose you're right. It's not just about just keepin' busy, it's about meanin' somethin', ain't it? Absolutely! And it might be a way of passing on our... skills and wisdom, to the younger generation. Whether they ask for it or not. I believe that's inherently valuable. Thank you both for being open to that idea. I've been kicking around a few notions on that front, too.

Oh, I'm so glad we've wrapped up "The Last Twenty Minutes of Horace" before clocking off. It was a bit of a drag this time around.      Yes, I've found that the poetry, though interesting, can be quite dense at times.      But it definitely exercises the mind. Yeah, and it's always interesting to see the new titles. Plus, I've heard there might be some useful ELT materials among those.      Sounds like a plan. Great, glad to have you all. Now, about the party – are we serving food or is it just a casual gathering around the new books?      I was thinking food wouldn't go amiss, but a buffet style so it's easy and casual.      Agreed. Just keep the cups of coffee coming and we're all good! Speaking of which, just before we met, I saw a beetle outside the window. It was trying to get in!      Oh no, are you sure it’s safe?      I've no idea, but I think we should help it out. Perhaps it just got lost.      Why not? It’s not every day we have a company insect.      Company insect... I like that. So, we scoop it up and release it outside safely, yeah?      Absolutely. I wonder if it’s a type from the local ecosystem.      That would be fascinating. We could ask Dr. Thompson if she knows anything about local insects.

Mum, I can't believe we're finally out for dinner together. It feels like ages. How has your week been? You seemed really busy when I called you earlier. Anything exciting at work? Ah, lovely to see you, Sarah. How have you been? [The cleaner arrives, and upon seeing Speaker_1, they warmly smile] Oh, thank you for asking! I've been alright. Just got out of work for the day. [Chuckles] I wish I could remember it as well as you do. Anyway, there's another thing that's worrying me. Yo, how's uni going for you? Thought you'd be banging on about your lectures by now, lol. Honestly, I miss uni even less than I thought I would. It's all a bit overwhelming at times, especially the coursework, but I am enjoying the freedom – and the student discounts! Aye, I knew uni would hit you like that. So, people back home probably reckon I'm wasting my postgrad for jobs like this. Hey, don't knock it! You're doing really well. And besides, we’re always juggling a few balls. But the perks – getting to meet people, try new drinks, a few nasty, blurred drinking nights... it’s not all bad. I know what you mean. It’s funny, one of my lecturers said something really similar about uni life – dealing with the ups and downs, keeping on top of things. I guess we both juggle a bit more than we bargained for. Yep, that's life isn't it? And it's surprising how much bartending has helped me handle that. You learn so much about human nature, about how to listen, about managing ups and downs, just in different form. I bet. I wish my coursework came with such bonuses.

Alright mates, so who's got any plans for the holidays? I've been thinking of heading back to Manchester and spend some time with the family, but I'm not sure yet. Well, it sounds like some of us are off to make some new experiences, and maybe some new friends. That sounds like fun. Enjoy your holidays, everyone. Same to you.

Oh, did you see that last move by Sterling? I swear today's match is more exciting than Jeopardy and Mastermind combined! You love your football, Alison! But I agree. Ah, so I heard you've been binge-watching those old black and white films again, grandma. Ah yes, dearie, I've been indulging. There's something quite captivating about the way they tell stories, don’t ya think? Now, questions are this kind of storytelling missing in the films today? Or are people just settling for convenient plot twists and fancy effects? Oh, I think there's room for both. Plenty of modern films tell captivating stories alongside impressive visuals. But I do get what you mean, there is something elegant about those old timers. Exactly. It’s like the difference between a digital clock and an old grandfather clock. The grandfather clock may need winding but the tick-tock is comforting and has character. Exactly! Now, tell me, what was the last film you saw that made you sit back and say, "Now that was good storytelling". Well, for me, it was "The Thin Red Line". Ah, yeah, Netflix or something like that. I used to rent DVDs though. Remember those? Oh, good times! I can only recall the films I saw at the cinema when I was younger, and they didn’t need fancy effects to mesmerize us. Just the prowess of the actors. The influence of technology is a topic for another day, isn’t it? You know, I’ve been seeing your bike tucked away, project manager. How goes that new motorbike? It’s been a bit of a rollercoaster, to be honest. The maintenance’s been more than I bargained for. But it sure is a joy to ride on a good day. A motorbike? I thought you just bought that flashy car. I remember driving all across Cheshire and Lancashire on my old bike. The freedom it gave me...I miss that kind of freedom sometimes. Ah, yes, the freedom of simpler times... I’d love to see you on that bike now, dearie. You’d make it a handsome sight.

Alright, kids! As you know, today is Pancake Day. Why don't we try making pancakes together after dinner? It'll be fun and you can learn how to cook. You know, maybe there’s a short story or movie about children going on fun adventures in Paris, don't you?

I've decided I need more friends who's as obsessed with Chinese food as I am. Who knew that ordering takeout was such an adventure? Ah, I was just going over some of Grandpa's old stories. He had so many great experiences during his time as an accountant at such reputable companies. Ah, the views! But these days, it seems like air travel is getting riskier and riskier. I never thought I'd see the day when air safety was this concerning. That's true, especially with all the news about cutbacks and budget restrictions. I'm sure it must be a worry for the pilots and the crew. Well, let's change the subject to something a bit more light-hearted. Speaking of old times, I was thinking of making some rice krispy cakes for the family get-together later. Oh, those are a real treat! But it's a bit of a bother now, isn't it, all this 'Scan As You Go' business at supermarkets? I liked it better when you just had to hand your list to the checkout clerk. Much less of a fuss. I know what you mean but it's quite convenient, really. Especially when you're in a rush or dealing with a big shop. True, true. I do find it gets a bit confusing when you're buying certain items like insurance, though. All these new terms and conditions. Ah, insurance! You were telling me about the premium you had to pay for your new house, weren't you? Yes! It was quite a chunk of change, plus now with these new build houses, they all seem to require additional insurance plans. I know what you mean. I hear a lot about that with new builds but any recommendations on a good broker to go to?

Alright, kids! As you know, this week is Chinese New Year. It's a super cool festival that happens in China and around the world, where people celebrate the beginning of a new year according to the Chinese lunar calendar. Ooh, ooh! Can we do drawings of dragons today? Yeah, and can we talk about planets too? I saw this cool video about the solar system and I want to learn more! That's a great idea, kids. First, let's draw dragons. They're fun to draw, and they're a big deal in Chinese culture. Remember, dragons are considered to be good luck in China. They're not like scary monsters in fairy tales. I know! That's what made me want to draw one. I'll do black and red, like fire! And I'll make mine in various colors. I saw a video where they said dragons can be all sorts of colors. For sure! We can make it interesting and fun. Anyone want to draw planets as well? Or maybe the Chinese New Year's traditional zodiac, the Year of the Ox. Wait, what's a zodiac? It's like a symbol or animal for each year in their calendar. This year is the Year of the Ox in China. We can combine them! I'll draw the planets and then put the ox next to it. Brilliant idea! That sounds really cool. I'll do the sun first. How do we draw fire again, mum? If you think of fire as lots of wiggly lines that are red, orange, and yellow, you can make it look fiery. And for the planets, do they have to be round? Yes, planets and suns are usually represented as circles because that's how they look in space. And don't worry if your dragon or ox isn't perfect. This is about having fun and learning. I'm having fun! Me too! This is a great example of blended learning - we're doing art, culture, and a bit of science here. Is this... is this the planet Mercury? That's really good, Kiddo! I think so, yes. How about trying to include some stars around it? Brilliant! Now, let's talk about what we might eat for Chinese New Year dinner! Usually, families have certain foods that are considered lucky, like noodles, dumplings, and fish, because their names or appearance symbolize things like long life or prosperity.

Yo, mate, Rome is absolute fire. Thought it was just gonna be pasta and gods today but no, it's more. Whole city's pumping. Thought you'd enjoy the weather; it's proper unreal down here. Yeah, it’s nice isn't it, the sunshine, but I kind of miss the rain back home. I knew you’d say that. You and your British socialism. And have you guys checked out our Airbnb? It’s a quaint little place near the Trevi Fountain, nothing too fancy but it’s got everything we need. Actually, I have. Looks decent. Idk, I’ve been used to hostels and stuff. This is a bit cosier. Yeah, we thought we’d sample some real Roman cuisine tonight - pasta maybe, or pizza. And maybe a gelato. Ooh, that sounds like a plan. But Ron, you know how family can get when you’re out and travelling? Are you good with your folks back home? Ah, right. I hope so. My parents are cool with me being this independent, but maybe they worry a bit. My folks are always pretty chill. Where are you all planning to travel to after here? We were thinking to head to the Amalfi Coast next. It looks stunning from the photos. Ooh, that's a good call. Beautiful beaches. But isn't the language barrier a bit of a challenge? Bit, but we've got that covered. I've been doing some Italian classes online, and it's actually pretty easy to pick up. You should see me now, mate. I can order things and ask for directions no worries. More or less. Australian accents aren’t that tough to navigate in English, but Italian does throw me a bit. It's quite musical, really. While you’re dealing with the Italian Accent, I deal with the confusion of people who think I’m from Dublin because I talk like some Aussie. Ah, always take pride in where you're from, indeed. Though, honestly, the Australian accent is pretty funny to me still. Yea, but it’s quite unique in its own way. You all do say ‘G'day mate’ all the time? Occasionally, mate. But not constantly. You know, it’s interesting, hearing all this. I never noticed... I kind of have a bit of an Aussie twang? Maybe from listening to too many podcasts? Yeah, I get that.

Oh, so many topics! Hen do's or baking first? Or perhaps we should just talk about everything since none of us know what to expect. I'm here for the hen do’s. A friend just got married and it was a blast – we painted questions on her clothes with marker pens! I’ve been thinking about doing that. Do you think it would ruin her dress? Erm, maybe not the best idea. But we used washable markers. She just washed it when she got home. Oh, that’s hilarious. But dear, I’ve been wanting to get into baking. Could any of you please teach me? I’d love to! I even bring a few recipes. Hmm, I have one too. Maybe we could have a baking session together once in a while? That sounds great! And this coffee shop has free Wi-Fi, right? We could look up recipes online. Interesting idea! Wouldn’t that be a fun way to hang out and learn something new? Definitely. And speaking of which, I also really want to try my hand at making custom sugar cookies. Oh, I saw those online! They’re so cute. Yeah, and they’re not that difficult once you get the hang of it. So the plan is, we all get together and do a baking and craft session, and if one of us has a hen do or party coming up, we can try those fun games. Sounds like a plan to me. We should also consider planning some craft items for the hen do’s. You know, like customized party favors or decorations. I’ve been wanting to try my hand at macrame – it looks so cool but I don’t know where to start! Maybe we can pick up some good tutorials online. And while we're at it, let's also plan a meetup just to catch up with friends. I haven’t seen everyone in a while. That’s a great idea. How about we set up a group for craft and baking sessions, and also plan a girls' night... or afternoon, any time when we’re all free. Perfect! I’ll make the group and invite everyone. Maybe next week? I'd say next week is fine, but maybe let's decide on a few fun activities for that get-together. I was thinking, what about a game night?

Yo, mate, gotta say, cooking with you is always an experience. But I'm really not feeling too good today, caught something off my mate at uni. Sorry to hear that, but I'm glad you're managing to cook. Still, now, let's not involve me in your sickly questions if you're feeling rough. You do know that I make my living talking, right? Yeah, I know, and I'm sorry for the constant tangents. Just trying to distract myself. Fine, fine. Tangents away. So, how's your appetite? Barely there, to be honest. These little chicken livers I'm cooking smell nice though. Chicken livers? That's ambitious. You're actually going to eat that, aren't you? Yeah, and hope to God it's cooked properly so the taste doesn't remind me too much of my sickness. Well, let me just assure you, I've been in this kitchen long enough to know the recipe. That's more comforting than I can describe. I'm just worried about giving it to you, you know? Not sure the taste will cut through your discerning instructor palate. Don't worry about that, at all. I'm more interested in your well-being. Though, come on, it's cooked with love – your love, to be specific – so I'd be an idiot not to try it. [laughs] Okay, okay, I'll get you some. And maybe you can help me get up the energy to finish cooking properly. Just keep the livers away from my student food and we're good. [laughs] Right. Now, let's get serious: have you been to any nice hotels recently? Speaking of food, yes. Just returned from couple of weeks in Wales for a conference. The hotel was top-notch, but honestly, the best food I had was from a small village on my free day. Real homemade stuff, though. I'm sure. But for me, I've had just one hotel experience, and it was dire. Oh? What happened? The breakfast was the most mediocre, overpriced muffin I've ever had and the wi-fi cost extra. Not surprised. Hotels are usually a hit or miss. Especially if you're not thinking to book outside the well-known chains. Exactly. I should've done more research. Maybe I'll look into some travel guides next time. That's a good idea.

Ah, I was browsing birthday cards yesterday and I couldn't help but notice how hard it is to find cards that truly capture how old we're getting. I mean, thirty years ago, 'Happy birthday and many more to come' still felt fitting, but nowadays, I feel it just doesn't quite cut it, does it? Oh, definitely. It's kind of embarrassing sometimes, looking at the ages on the cards. I remember when I was teaching, it actually influenced how I'd frame those birthday cards for my class. Right, exactly. You'd always try to make it sound like it was a milestone, but really, birthdays started to feel like just another passing year, especially after I hit 50. Indeed. I had the same problem. And sometimes, when I’d write them for my kids, I’d choose ones that were more about hope and new beginnings rather than just another year. That was wise. But, do you remember in primary school, when we used to make our own birthday cards? There was a lot of love and effort in those cards, even though the art was sometimes... questionable. Oh, certainly. And it wasn’t just the card; it's the thought. You know, I sometimes still marvel at the art projects we did. Like, think of all the time and energy that went into making those handmade cards. It was such a different time. It really was. I remember one year, one of the kids made a card and stuck all these hand-drawn calendar fobs on it, and it was fantastic. I recall that doesn’t come close to the crafting skills some of the parents had. Some would make such elaborate cards, including hand-puppet shows if you opened it at the right angle or such. Ah, yes! The ones that had little flaps that folded out to reveal another message or drawing. It was really quite impressive. From crafting to teaching, I always found it interesting that despite advancements in educational tools, there's a certain satisfaction in using simpler, hands-on art for learning. Our kids used to love art and craft in school. Absolutely, and for sports like hockey – boots! You would not believe the condition those hockey boots were in. Some kids never took them off during the hockey season. Clearly demonstrating their complete and utter dedication to the sport! Although, occasionally, the smell wasn't something I liked being reminded of.

Right, so I've been keeping an eye on the local news. We have these two fellows across the road who have been working on their front garden. I don't know much about them, but seems like they're doing a right job of it. That's lovely to hear, Dad! You've always been keen on gardening. Maybe they could give you some tips when you're getting your new garden sorted? I was thinking the same, Sarah. Might be worth a chat. You know, local DIY can be quite valuable. Speaking of gardens, let me tell you about this bloke I met at the walking group. Says his garden is quite the talk of the village. I might have to ask him for some advice too. That would be great, Margaret. But back to the topic, did either of you hear about the railways causing disruptions again? Yeah, I caught a snippet on the news. They're looking for ways to improve the service, but in the meantime, it's causing a bit of a headache for those heading into town. And here I thought we were done with that. Now that ANON is taking up a new job, this could be quite a problem. I'm sure it will be sorted soon, but for now, we need to make the most of the trips when the trains are running normally, right, ANON? Indeed. And speaking of your new job, ANON, how's it going so far? It's been a bit of an adjustment, but overall, quite enjoyable. I'm getting used to the commute and the team is very friendly. But it's not just about the job now, is it? How's the house, dear? I've heard you've done a lot of the work yourself. Yes, that's right! I've been putting in a lot of hours. It's been fun getting everything sorted. Just waiting for me to finish up the last few projects. That's great! I remember changing a place can be stressful, especially when you do most of the work yourself. I'm sure it's not easy, but it's paid off. The house looks lovely so far. Reminds me of my own DIY years. And have you found any good pubs nearby? You know how much ANON loves a pint over the weekend. Yes, there's a really nice one just a short walk from the house.

Yo, mate, did you seen any of that latest Cyber Monday's online shopping deals? I'm thinking of getting myself some new headphones and a gaming mouse. Oh yeah, I saw some decent deals. There was a discount on the new gaming chair that just came out too, but I didn’t do much shopping because I kind of feel guilty spending money when I’m not even working. Man, that makes sense, but you can't actually spend money without... I dunno, working? Unless it’s for necessities... Right, exactly. But it's just hard to see all those cool gadgets and not feel a bit... envious, I suppose. Plus I’ve been relying on the government allowance so far, just trying to make ends meet. Definitely tough, but hey, at least you're making the effort, that's what matters. You're not just slacking off or anything, are you? Noh, I’m not. I’m barely out of school and juggling various applications and studies. It’s tough, but I'm trying to stay positive and focused on my future. For me, it's hard to stick to a study routine though when there's always the temptation to scroll through social media or online fun stuff. Yeah, I can see that. Sticking to a routine is hard when there's not much stimulation otherwise. I used to have some routine when I had a part-time job or something, but since I lost my job, it feels like every day is a waste of time... Alright, don't say that. You're working hard through all this, applying for jobs and things. It's not easy and it's not your fault. You're right. Thanks for saying that. Maybe I need to consider some more serious side hustles or try to learn new skills to put on my CV. The digital world is booming now, right? If I could just pick up some coding skills or something useful... That's exactly what I’ve been trying to do. I’ve joined some online courses on code and programming, and I’m also reading a lot about technology. I’ve even been dabbling with some online tutorials. It’s tough but it’s worth it, I think. Yeah, definitely worth it. But have you found any good resources for those kinds of things? I've had a look around but all the real job platforms seem to require experience and stuff I don't have yet.

Right, so I've been looking at heating options for the new house. I was thinking about getting insulation and perhaps installing some underfloor heating. It sounds costly, but I think it could save money in the long run. Hi there, isn't the weather just lovely today? You know, I've always heard questions about this kind of thing at school. The students often ask about energy efficiency. But, I've never encountered underfloor heating. What makes you think it's a good investment? Oh, I've got some experience with that. I've actually installed it in my own home several years ago and, yes, it was initially expensive, but it's made all the difference, especially on cold Devon mornings. Right, and it's even more important when you consider our current energy bills. But, I'm not sure if it's the best option for this particular house. It's quite old. The age of the house shouldn’t be much of a problem. In fact, it might even work better in an older house because the floor structure will absorb and retain heat more effectively. That's a good point. Now that you mention it, I do remember that from one of the construction courses I took at university. It's all about thermal mass and heat retention. However, the upfront cost still has me in doubt. You know, the local council can often give grants for home improvements like insulation and heating system upgrades. It's worth looking into as it could help offset the cost. True, and I guess I should also consider the life of the house, and all the future energy savings it could bring. But I don't want to break the bank either. Well, you're retired now, you should be able to enjoy the benefits without worrying too much about future career milestones or the like. Yes, exactly. I've been enjoying my retirement far too much to think about money all the time. While you're planning the heating, what about the lunch today? Are we all making something or ordering in? Well, I thought we could make something. Maybe some of that delicious scones we always make for our coastal walks. And perhaps some lunch-bread for the dogs too. That sounds perfect! And after lunch, could we plan our coastal walk? I was thinking of the route along the beach at Ilfracombe.

Right, so I had a fascinating day today at work. We've been looking at this new data set and it's really suggesting that there's a strong link between sleep deprivation and mental health issues. That's really interesting, isn't it? Especially now, with so many people working from home and blurring the lines between personal and work time. Exactly. It's like the whole world has been sleep-deprived and stressed for the past year. I mean, I've seen it in my own work too - so many patients struggling with anxiety and depression right now. Definitely, and it's not just mental health – it's physical health too. I was reading recently about how sleep deprivation can increase your risk of cardiac problems and even diabetes. Yes, absolutely. And it's crazy that we still don't prioritise sleep as much as we should. I mean, you can't function well if you're not sleeping well, right? Totally. I've noticed it even in our kids. They're on their devices till late at night and then can't settle, and we end up arguing because they're grumpy in the morning. I've seen that too. The other day Lucas came to me complaining about his exam prep and I realised he'd been going to bed so late. Stunned at the apparent oblivion he was in regarding the link between sleep and performance. Ah, the world would be less stressful if people understood that, wouldn't it? But isn't it also a bit about social attitudes? Everyone seems to be trying to get a 'life hack' and working more and more hours, leading to less and less sleep. Absolutely. There's kind of this 'heroic' work ethic that's celebrated if you're working late and sacrificing sleep. But who's truly benefiting in the long term? No one. We need a societal shift. And perhaps companies will start to see the productivity benefits of encouraging healthy sleep habits in employees. From personal experience, when I make sure to get 7-8 hours sleep, I can take on a lot more next day – more focused, better decision making. Yep, when you think about it, sleep is one of the most zero-cost interventions we could potentially do for improving mental and physical health. And it's right there, available for everyone if they just prioritise it.

Oh, did I ever tell you about my Dad? He was a bit eccentric, he was superstitious about left-handed people. Always telling me 'left-handed people make better artists' as if that somehow mattered to a nurse. You know, I've always heard rumors about left-handed people being more creative or artistic. I've got a left-handed friend who's an amazing painter. And my sister, she's a leftie too. She says she finds it difficult sometimes with things like right-handed scissors. Crazy how our world is primarily designed for right-handed people, isn't it? Yeah, I used to have trouble fitting in as a decorator, just cos I'm left-handed. But I've learned to adapt. Made a good living out of it though! And what about you, Sarah? Did you find being left-handed a challenge as a nurse? Actually, no. I think it's made me more careful and aware of what I'm doing. I have to focus more on what I'm doing with this hand, you know? Well, that makes sense. Attention to detail is key in our jobs, right? Indeed. Speaking of which, I saw a left-handed coffee cup the other day. First time I've seen one like that, nice design though. Oh, I'd love that as a gift. One thing though, we should chat about all the fantastic local food and restaurants over there. I saw a new one pop up in Ashford where Lena works which looks stunning. Oh yeah, it's Italian and they have great pizza. The owner's really passionate about his food and the place. That sounds lovely. Speaking of food, did anyone see that animal welfare programme on last night's TV? Some really disheartening stuff but also some inspirational people changing the world. Yeah, it's heart-wrenching but also gets us motivated to do our bit. I've been thinking of getting a puppy from a rescue centre soon. You’ll be overwhelmed! But good on you. Just think of all the care job opportunities that come with looking after animals. Speaking of jobs and care. How are finances? Seems like we're all managing just about okay but could always be better, right? We're surviving, to be honest. But like Lena was just saying, with a new pup, that’d add another expense though.

Right, so I'm going to make homemade pasta for dinner. I have these beautiful fresh ingredients; these are all from local sources. I want to make sure it's authentic. You're quite the cook, aren't you now? Is it just me or isn't making pasta from scratch a lot of work? It's not so bad once you get into the rhythm, and I love how it tastes so much better than store-bought. You know, I used to make pasta from scratch when I was younger. After the war, pasta was expensive, and I used to make it from whatever I could buy cheaply like flour and eggs. That's actually really nice of you to share that, thanks. Really? So it was more out of necessity back then? More necessity than anything else. But it made it special in its own way. And speaking of homemade, I've this fantastic recipe for a Tuscan Chicken Risotto that I want to try as well. I'm thinking of pairing it with this local white wine. That sounds incredible! Do you also plan to travel? I mean, you have quite the knack for regional dishes. Actually, I love traveling, especially to Italy. I've been in Tuscany a few times and the food is just unbelievable. I've never been myself, but I've heard tales from your travels. Yes, one of my favorite things about going abroad is getting to try all the local cuisine. Have you eaten in any Michelin-starred restaurants while you were there? Just one, but it was amazing. It's called La Leggenda dei Frati and it's in a very small village. I've never had that privilege. I suppose retirement didn't afford me the same opportunities as today, when people travel more and so much more easily. We're very fortunate for what we have today. Yeah, definitely. It's like... compared to older times, I mean. I was reading about traditional British dishes. It seems things used to be much simpler, more focused on local ingredients, which I really love about all these regional foods. I suppose it makes sense given that transportation was a challenge and any type of foreign ingredient would've been considered exotic. That's right. I remember these long car trips from Timperley to Manchester, and it wasn't just about going into the city for shopping or work, but because that's where you found different food.

Oh, Justin, I'm so glad we've got some time today to finalize our class together. I've been thinking about it all week and I have a few ideas that I'd love to run by you first. That sounds great, Rachel. Let's get questions off the table before we start planning the class structure. Besides, I've got some of my own ideas that might help us get the best balance between language learning and culture appreciation. Right, so here's my starting point. I think it might be most productive if we start with a wider topic, like 'A Day in the Life of Modern Britain'. What do you think? It's a very relatable topic for our students here in China and it covers a broad range. Ah, yes, that's a good starting point. It's broad and gives a lot of room for discussion. But I'd also suggest breaking it down further. For instance, we could have different subsections like work-life balance, food habits, popular culture, and general lifestyle norms. That's a great way to diversify content. One thing we should keep in mind is balance between the different aspects of daily life. We don't want to overemphasize 'office life', given the current employment trends towards more flexible working and remote work. Absolutely, technology is changing workplaces rapidly, so current trends would be important to include. Speaking of which, how about a sub-section on the role of technology in daily life? For instance, mobile usage, apps, and social media? Oh, yes, that would be topical. But we might need to be careful not to get too caught up in technology if it’s not directly relevant to the rest of the class. More broadly, do you think a focus on British meals and food culture would be appreciated? We could discuss different traditional dishes, perhaps even couple it with a cooking class if that's feasible. I think that'll work. Food is always a great conversation starter. Plus, if we tie it to a practical activity, it can make the class more engaging. For example, a meal planning session where they have to choose dishes for different occasions. That sounds fantastic! And for the theoretical aspect, could we maybe include insights from British pop culture, like TV shows and films? We could use those to illustrate certain points or to practice comprehension and discussion.

Ah, I can't believe we're having to move again. We've lived here for nearly ten years and now we have to pack everything up. It's not all bad, isn't it? We can finally have that bigger house we've always wanted, and this place is supposed to have a fantastic coffee machine! Indeed, the coffee machine is a major selling point, isn't it? All very well for us, but even that keeps breaking down. Oh, yes. It's not just the machine, though. What's with the removal and storage costs these days? It's almost cheaper just to buy new things. And the best part is, we can finally get rid of all this clutter. Though I have to say, I'm a bit fearful of the cost. It's the equivalent of an additional mortgage payment, isn't it? And it feels like it's every service's price that's risen. I still find it odd that the removal company is charging this much. Absolutely. It's like anything to do with moving is now the most expensive job. I don't even want to imagine what storage will cost. What about politics now? Have you both been following the Labour leadership race? Hmm, it's all silly isn't it? Seems more about who can be the most idealistic without offering much in terms of practicality. I know what you mean. It's like it's back to the days of old, idealism without a plan. Except, nowadays, it all feels so... unrealistic. It's strange, isn't it? We thought, as a society, we'd become more pragmatic since the days of old. But now it seems we're reverting to idealism for the sake of it. As someone who was always pragmatic in their profession, I struggle to see how any of those ideas for the oil industry can be put into practice without a proper, solid business structure. Exactly! It's like we're just seeking to feel better about the situation rather than actually doing something about it. There's also the matter of job creation and the political rhetoric we keep hearing, isn’t there? “Get the unemployed back to work” they say, but with no clear plans, it’s just talk. Sure, they often promise grand schemes but seem to leave out the most important part – the practicality.

Yo, anyone fancy a pint or some of that fancy beans from's passport? I discovered today that nearly every major city has waterways like rivers and canals. Do you know much about these? I love that! I've spent time rowing up and down the Thames, but I never knew London has over 200 miles of canals. It's insane! That's a great point, but I've also heard some of these canals are still used for trade, right? Like bringing goods into the heart of the city keeps it green somehow? I've seen canal boats, dude. Like in Australia, they call 'em barges. But, what's with this pub you're in London? Is it just cos it's fancy or is there something specific to look out for? Oh, oh! Just found this little detail. London’s Hammersmith Bridge is the exact spot where the boundary moves from one side of the Thames to the other. So you could technically have one foot in London and the other in… well, Outer London or whatever it's called. So, like, if you were standing on the bridge, it would be quite the geographical anomaly. I’ve heard about these quirky river names though, while the 'River Thames' is well known, St. John’s River and other minor streams also flow through the city. Absolutely, like the River Lea for example, it's pretty big in East London where we are now isn't it? Speaking of rivers, have you all tried Omega 3 from "proper fish" like mackerel and things? But it's tough to keep the lads interested when it comes to finding good places to eat seafood in the city. We should grab some soon then, there’s a good place near Greenwich with amazingly fresh fish right by the water. If we're going to talk about food, did you know about this place in North London that does kosher-style sandwiches but changing the ingredients to not be kosher is like they’re breaking a law of bread? Haha, sure! But for me, I’m a huge fan of real, proper condiments. And by proper, I mean not that overpriced sweet chili sauce everyone seems to drown everything in right now. I know just what you mean. We had a heated argument in the break room about whether hot sauce or aioli should be the default condiment.

Right, so I had this absolute nightmare of a date last night. I was swiping through Tinder and he was super cute in his pictures. But let me tell you, in real life, he was a total letdown. He spent the entire date talking about himself and his favourite football team. Oh bless! Sounds just like the hell of a night I went on recently. A guy showed up at my place and just decided to sit on my sofa and ruin my favourite show without even asking if I minded! Oh that's terrible! Are you still on Tinder then? Yeah, I am. Even though there have been a few weirdos along the way, I've been lucky enough to meet some really nice people too. Like my housemate Emma, she met someone through there and they're actually really cool. Yeah, Tinder can be pretty hit-or-miss. On the one hand, there's more variety and you get to check out people beforehand. But then you have the risk of meeting someone who's not what they claim to be or just gross. I completely agree! I recently had a guy who just started this argument about politics and it was so weird. I’ve had some pretty quirky experiences too. I had this date where the guy kept asking me if I was a 'good girl' or if I could be 'bad' at certain things. That's quite intimate for a first date though, right? Absolutely! You should never really have to question your morals or values on a first date. And certainly not about that stuff. First dates should be about getting to know each other and having a bit of fun. True! It's like we've been all warned about creeps online but sometimes the creepiest stuff happens in real life. I know, right? The worst part for me was that I felt like I had to think of a solid excuse to get out of there because he just wouldn’t take the hint to end it. Accidents happen, especially when nerves are involved. I was on a date once where I fumbled some spoons and ended up yelling 'I'M NOT A NINJA!' mid-conversation. Haha! That's so ridiculous! But still, could have been pretty awkward if he didn’t find it funny too. I guess you’ve got to have a sense of humor on these things.

Right, so I was watching the news yesterday and they were discussing job benefits. I found it really interesting how politicians talk about getting people back to work, but don't seem to have a clue about the realities of finding a job. Especially for us, really. Indeed, I couldn't agree more. Both of us haven't worked for years because of one problem or another and now, they're making it harder and harder to even get the benefits we're entitled to. Exactly! I used to work as a childminder and it was physically demanding. Now, my body can't handle it anymore, but they don't seem to care. They just seem to think that because someone is not working, that they're not contributing. And then there was the discussion about universal credit. Wasn't that supposed to make everything simpler? Instead, it's just created more confusion and delays. The government has no idea what it's like on the ground. Their policies seem to be designed by people who have never actually been in our shoes. I remember when I worked, I took on extra jobs just to get by. But now, if I tried to do that, they'd count that as working and then they'd cut my benefits. Makes no sense. Exactly! It’s as if they're forgetting that people who are long-term unemployed often have health issues, or family commitments, or vocational barriers that prevent them from working full-time. Or maybe they just don't care! They expect us to somehow get jobs that don’t even exist, and all the while, we're struggling to make ends meet. But it's not just about the money. It’s about the dignity and the self-worth. When all they seem to do is punish you for not being able to work, it's soul-destroying. True. I used to be a civil engineer. I was proud of my work and felt like I was contributing to society. But now it feels like we're invisible, just changing the numbers from dependency to unemployment on some government spreadsheet. It’s that invisibility that’s the hardest part for me. I used to feel useful. Now, it feels like I'm just a statistic. And it's not just us. I used to have so many mothers who were searching for jobs almost as soon as their children started school.

Oh, did I tell you about my day? It was chaotic. The traffic was terrible on my way to meet with a potential donor for our charity event. You're quite the indispensable ally for the cause now, aren't you? How did it go? Took me an hour longer than I expected but the meeting itself went well. I think we might just get the funding we need. That's great to hear. You're putting in a lot of time and effort. Evenings like these remind me to appreciate the little things. You're very understanding, by the way, even when I get stuck in traffic. Well, you do well to keep going. What's for dinner? It smells amazing! It's a traditional English dish, a beef stew. My mum used to make it for us on Sundays. It brings back so many memories. So, business has been keeping you away from the kitchen a lot lately, huh? Truth be told, yes. I assumed we'd order in tonight. Good thing I changed my mind. It really does feel like a different time when we manage to have a home-cooked meal together. A bit like those dinners we used to have before the kids moved out, really. That's true. And now with all the events leading up to their weddings next year it's back to busy for us. Well, busy or not, it's the memories we make together that count, right? Very true. Speaking of which, did you see Game of Thrones last night? It was quite the episode! Sorry, honey. Busy day on my end too. I did manage to catch up a bit on the news before dinner. Figures, you're so much into your work, even your leisure time is work-related! Well, you know how it goes. Every donor counts in the charity world. I know, I know. But now that we're having dinner, could you please change the TV to a different channel? I want to watch that episode before dessert. Of course, no problem. That's really all the television I'll ever ask for, promise. At your service, always. Thank you. You know, what we might need next is a bit more intimacy in our evening routines. Maybe some alone time, just the two of us. Yeah, that won't be a bad thing either. Maybe we could plan a weekend away sometime soon.

Oh, I don't know, I've been feeling so under the weather these past few days. It's not just the cold here, I think. It must be all the garlic they use here. You can almost smell it now, can't you? You do have a sense of humour, don't you? I've been fine, just a bit tired from our class schedules right now. We've got exams coming up and the kids are getting a bit stressed. I remember those days. Wondering if I'll ever feel 'at home' in a job again. I've been doing these part-time TEFL gigs from time to time, but to be honest, even that seems daunting when you've been out of the employment market for so long. It must be tough. I sometimes feel guilty when I see your posts on Facebook - looking for work, or just expressing how you're feeling. But, it's like you're in a different world now. It's not so easy to find something that feels like 'you', especially at this stage in life. Yeah... it's funny, I find myself looking at all these fun posts on Instagram, while I'm stuck here. People on holiday, enjoying the sun, and I'm trying to figure out why the weather in Poland is so gloomy all year round! I know right, it feels like the sky is always in mourning here, doesn't it? But honestly, we should focus on the positives. And we're here, aren't we? Just been talking about moving somewhere sunnier for a bit. You're right. I am grateful for this little flat in the corner of Tarnow. It's strange - in England, I lived in Cambridge, always felt a strong sense of belonging there since my family's been there for generations. Here, it's different. It's new, but also... it's home now too, in a way. You know? I do. I think when you've been feeling so displaced for so long, everywhere becomes just 'home' for a bit. And maybe that's not such a bad thing? Again, agreed. Talking about almost going 'home' just for the sake of a funeral. As if I needed one more reminder why I feel displaced. No, of course not. But I hope you do manage to go if you feel it's important.

Oh, so many options here! Usually I stick to a good old English breakfast tea, but what's yours, Sarah? I've taken to Earl Grey. There's something about the citrus notes that perks me up for a busy day of lectures and surveys questions. I see, and surveys, how’s that part-time job coming along? Any big projects brewing? Actually, yeah. Currently working with a data collection agency, it's really interesting, actually. Lots of insights emerging from the data, fascinating stuff. But sometimes I wish there were more hours in the day just to catch up on some more reading. Really? So what about the work-life balance? Was it always your plan to juggle studying and working? Kind of, I suppose. The pay helps and it's looking good on my resume, too. Plus, it gives me a little bit of independence, financially speaking. But it can be tricky. Sometimes I feel like I'm playing catch up or running on fumes. Sure, I've been there, even if not as busy as you. Balancing work and life is a challenge for sure. Especially in London, the cost of living is quite steep, so it's good you're bringing in some income. Exactly. And I'd rather be making some money, even if it is part-time, in my field, really learning by doing, you know? That's a great approach, learning while earning. Plus, doesn't your agency offer you a free tea round too? You'd think so, but no... just the usual pay. How disappointing. At my job, they always make sure we are well caffeinated whenever we're working on a tight deadline. But enough about work, are you seeing any of your friends soon? Definitely. We're planning a weekend trip to Brighton next month, all my uni friends. It’s going to be fun, though. Fun but expensive, just like everything else in Brighton. Always is. And you’d want to grab some of those juicy Brighton pasties while you're there? You know it! Well, I can't let our discussion get too food-focused, but I do need to grab a pasty before we leave. Care to join? You're not just a copywriter, you're a foodie copywriter. Sure thing! A trusty British pasty for both of us, please. Barman: Here you go, lovely! Mmm, smells good.

Oh, did I oversleep?? Morning's already here, hasn't it? Oooo, yes! Wake up, sleepyhead! Are we still going to the circus training class today? Circus training ?? Oh right! But how did you know? I heard your plan the other night with Mum. You said we could learn how to juggle! Yes, juggling! And we could try balancing on a tightrope. I'd love to do that. Is balancing easy to learn? Not exactly. It takes practice, but it's a lot of fun. And the instructors are very patient. Did I hear you say circus before? Ah, you did! Did I grab it from somewhere? I learned it from Grandpa! For a time, this skill was on his list of things to learn but he never got around to it because he thought it was fun but too hard. It is hard, but it's also really rewarding when you get the hang of it. And remember how Grandpa always said, "Hard yakka means money makka"? What does that mean? It's an Australian phrase Grandpa loved. It basically means that hard work brings in good pay. Is that like 'no pain, no gain'? More or less. But it was just one of his funny sayings. Grandpa used to say a lot of things he learned or made up. That’s funny! Speaking of fun things to learn, after our circus class, I was thinking we could head back for a late lunch, then enjoy some snacks and watch the sunset. And maybe we could practice Australian phrases together! Like 'How's it going mate?' Or 'G'day!' We could. But first, we need to get ready for the circus. And before all that, we still need to get something to eat. I saw that the Neon Moon is happening this weekend. I know it’s not today, but... What’s a Neon Moon? It’s this really cool event where they have a lot of activities, performances, and of course, lots of very brightly colored neon lights. It's all about creativity and having fun. Is it going to be as fun as the circus training? I think so! And it’s somewhere near Cambridge. Maybe we could go after the circus class? If we have time. That does sound like a good plan. We'll see how the day goes. And what about lunch and snacks? Are we going to eat when we get back?

Did you hear that's what they were just discussing on the Today programme? They said the Conservatives' decision to cut public funding for arts and education programmes is likely to have a devastating impact on communities all over England and Wales. It's just so short-sighted, isn't it? Especially when we're just now starting to recover from COVID. I heard it, of course. Now, don't get me started. As someone who spends most of his time in an academic setting, I can tell you this kind of thing has always irked me, but it's particularly frustrating now. We're supposed to be building back stronger, but I worry we're just cutting our own legs out from under us. Is it really that bad? I mean, isn't this all just part of saving money? Well, it's not as simple as that, dear. While saving money might be a goal, cutting programmes that enrich people's lives and promote culture doesn't actually save us money in the long term. It's like they're only thinking about the short-term budget, not about the value these programmes provide in terms of community cohesion, talent development, and even economic vitality. Exactly. And it's not just about the money, it's about the ripple effect. For example, think about community arts programmes - they're not just about culture, they're also about health benefits, social skills, and even reducing crime rates. And educational programmes? They’re about equipping the next generation with the skills they need to succeed in a rapidly changing world. But if they're not 'essential', then maybe we should cut them? Perhaps you won't mind when the local library closes and there's no more adult literacy classes, or when the only thing on at the theatre is a commercial pop concert instead of a local production of Twelfth Night. Look, this isn't just some abstract argument. There are studies. For example, a study from 2015 by the Arts Council found that for every £1 invested in the arts, an additional £4 was generated elsewhere in the economy. Really? Not just that. The arts also boost tourism, they improve mental health, they raise a community's profile. For example, in Wales, there's been this initiative to use cultural events to bring people together across... ...the language barriers and build a stronger sense of Welsh identity.

Alright, kids, who first wants to tell their story? We're all sitting here, and I thought it would be fun to create our own stories. Remember, the stories can be as wild and wacky as you like. Me! Me! I've been thinking about it since yesterday and I know what my story's going to be about! It's about a magical tree that gives you whatever you wish for, as long as you pick an apple from it and eat it. That sounds wonderful, Emily. You can tell it to us, and then we'll brainstorm some fun ideas for your magical tree. Can I tell a story too? Please, please? Of course, Jack. Try to remember your whole story. We'll help if you get stuck. It's about a little rabbit who decided to go on a journey around the world. He wanted to meet all the different animals and learn their languages. But at the end, he realized his home village was the best place. That's so sweet, Jack. You have quite the imagination, both of you. Yeah, and we can include both of our ideas. Maybe in Emily’s story, the magical tree lives in the rabbit's home village? And the tree can help the rabbit talk to animals from around the world? Yeah! Or, maybe the rabbit is silly and wishes for all the animals to speak English, but then he realizes he likes learning all the different languages. I love that idea, Jack. It teaches a great lesson about appreciating the diversity of languages and cultures. Yes! And maybe in my story the tree gives the rabbit a special apple that lets him understand all the languages! That's brilliant! And perhaps in my story, the magical tree only gives one wish each year, and the rabbit’s village decides to use their wish for something to help all the animals in the world? That's a great way to make the story teach a valuable lesson. Suddenly, there is a silence, as they all stop to think. So, what do we do next? We could perhaps flesh out more details or even draw some of the scenes. Maybe use this as a warm-up activity for when we go to the Linton Book Festival next month. Ooh, that idea just made everything better! Maybe there's even a special Helen Moss story we could create while we're there.

I've decided I'm going to become a vegetarian. I just can't justify it any more, watching all those documentaries on animal cruelty... That's a brave choice! I've been thinking about it too and I agree, it's a compelling moral argument. Especially when you consider all the alternatives we now have - I mean, have you heard of synthetic meat? Yeah, I've heard about that. 'Cultured meat', 'shmeat', or whatever... I think it could be a game-changer for our food industry. Exactly! It's produced from animal cells, but grown in a lab. No need for animal slaughter, just like no soy is involved. I think that's fantastic, especially if it can taste similar to traditional meat. That sounds amazing. But what about the rest of us, who aren't ready to give up on burgers or chicken yet? Do you think there's a middle ground? There should be - that's the beauty of varying preferences. But even if you aren't ready to go full on vegetarian or embrace synthetic meat, there's always the option to eat less meat, cut down on factory-farmed meat, or explore plant-based alternatives. And even within that, the food choices can be mind-boggling. I mean, have you guys tried those 'Beyond Meat' burgers? Almost exactly like beef... I'm definitely going to give it a try! But I've also been considering if I should start taking vitamin tablets... I keep reading how we often lack certain vitamins due to our diets, especially as vegetarians. That's a good point. Vitamin deficiency can be a real issue, especially for those on more restrictive diets. But at the same time, it's all about balance and making sure you're getting enough of everything. From leafy greens to beans - the natural sources are usually the best way to go. Definitely. But some supplements can be helpful, for sure. I know a lot of people take B12 supplements as vegetarians, since it's found mostly in animal products. B12 right. Okay, thanks guys. I'll definitely look into all of this. As long as you're informed and taking things at your own pace. And remember, our food choices are so much more than just about us. They have a ripple effect that can influence industries, economies... even politics and... Don't get into a full essay, Jamie!

Right, so I'm going to make homemade pasta for dinner. I have all the ingredients. I hope it turns out okay since it will be the first time I'm using this new pasta machine. You're quite brave to try that on your own, aren't you? I remember when you first moved back to Kent from London. You were always complaining about the pasta and the bread. Yes! I've heard you say it's harder to get decent pastries out there. But coming from a creative writing background, I'd say that can be a whole different kind of challenge... Oh, absolutely! It's not about the ingredients at all; it's about having a good pasta machine and then actually kneading the dough by hand to give it the right texture. I've watched Anthony Bourdain making pasta on his travels. He said that even the locals made certain pasta differently depending on the town. True, and yet we both agree, there's something special about traditional Italian food. I've been following this Italian chef on YouTube and she makes it look so easy. For me, it's the stories that come with food that are just as important as the taste. Like the time I visited Italy and they took me through the whole process of making fresh pasta from scratch. It was a real cultural experience. Exactly. I used to have this washing machine that had a really annoying timer. It was like it had a mind of its own. Finally got rid of it in the spring clear-out. But you never fully appreciate the importance of a good washing machine until you've got a bad one! Or a good slow cooker! I swear the best meal I've ever had was from one of those. Made me reconsider my skepticism towards it. Speaking of appliances, do any of you remember the time... Oh, yes. The time Uncle Joe tried to use the slow cooker as a slow cooker but then it became a slow heater! We all had a good laugh about it. Or when Dad tried out this new internet provider for the house. He kept saying it was like trying to communicate with someone who spoke a different language. And then finally, one day, it just worked! Oh, and have you all seen the new series on Channel 4 about the 'Tidy Up' technique?

Alright, boys, who first noticed that Dad uses these whimsical butterfly-shaped forks at dinner? I think I saw it the first time we had that fish. It was so ridiculous and funny! Yeah, and then he explained something about his mom always buying them at the market and it became a family tradition. Tradition indeed. I'm just glad we're keeping with it. Two minutes silence now before we start supper. It's nice keepsake for birthdays, don't you think? I guess, but why two minutes? Maybe it's because birthdays have 12 months in a year, just like the two minutes. Quite creative, both of you. And yes, well-done. Two minutes of silence is a nice way to reflect on the day and being grateful for yet another year. Now, let's talk about Russia. We recently watched a fascinating documentary on the Russian people and it struck both of you. What did you find most interesting, speaking of or as much as an 11-year-old can absorb it? Yeah, it was the different landscapes. One minute it was endless forests, and then we saw the cities and how different it is in the St. Petersburg area. And the food! They have such unique dishes. I know right, all those comforting stews and soups. It's really telling about their history and culture. But it's also quite a big country, isn't it? One of the largest, geographically speaking. It extends from Eastern Europe across Northern Asia, which is one reason it has such varied landscapes and cultures. Have you ever thought of taking a trip there? I'd love that! It's definitely on my bucket list but as of now, it's just a dream. However, it's a great idea for a future shared adventure. Or maybe we could learn some Russian? What do you think? I think that's an excellent idea, my dear. Learning a new language always opens up new doors and understanding of a culture. Just then the doorbell rings and it's the delivery of their supper dishes almost ready. Clearly, timing is everything tonight, isn’t it? Let’s give these a few minutes then we’ll dive in. In the mean time, let's just enjoy company and conversation while supper is being prepared. We can even share the Russian recipes you've collected?

Oh, did I ever tell you about our holidays in Cornwall? We took the children to Adventure Island last year and they just loved it! You mean that big theme park with all the water rides? Yes, exactly! They had so much fun. We had planned the visit around the V&A exhibition in London but the kids just wanted to keep playing games and rides instead. They're so much fun even if keeps changing plans. Definitely, and it's a great alternative for a family holiday. What about Cornwall, dear? I've been wanting to check out some of their restaurants with gluten-free options. Emma seems to be having some food intolerance issues lately. Yes, she's started rejecting some of her favorite foods lately, which is stressful. I know, it's been a little challenging. We're going to spend some time this semester figuring out what she's reacting to. Hopefully, we'll find something that works. Have you considered allergy testing? It might give you some good answers. We actually have an appointment with the pediatrician next week to discuss it further. Maybe we can also plan the holiday around some local gluten-free restaurants for her. That sounds like a good plan. Maybe we can even try some of those for us too? Absolutely! No one should miss out on good food because of dietary restrictions. Actually, that reminds me of the V&A exhibition I was planning to visit the next time. They always have great food options in the cafe. Speaking of food, I've been thinking about this pasta recipe with gluten-free pasta that one of my students taught me. She’s from Italy so I assumed it'll be authentic. You mean you're going to try it out in the new term? Exactly. I thought it might be useful to share with the students who have dietary restrictions. And it’ll be a good chance for me to practice before trying it out at home. That's a great idea. Do you need a helping hand with the ingredients or anything before you start? That'd be lovely. I could use a partner in crime to figure this out. And... Speaking of practical matters, I need to get started on the exam marking soon. I managed to leave it all until the last moment, as usual. Don't worry, we're here for you.

Yo, mate, did you finish that history coursework last night? Nah, not quite. I was watching that new Star Wars movie after dinner and then got side-tracked with some gaming. You managed to finish yours? Still working on it, to be honest. But I do love questions on the Tudor times and the Industrial Revolution. It's easier to focus than the more modern stuff, you know? Same here actually. I've always found those older periods easier to grasp. Anyway, did you hear that keeps changing the due date again? Crazy stuff. Yeah, that's been a theme with our history teacher. Always shifting deadlines. But hey, I guess that's just another part of life. Might just sneak down to the High Street, get a walk in, clear my head. Sure, sounds good. Plus, we might see some of the other mates. Have they decided the theme for the upcoming party yet? Haven't heard, but I'm hoping it's not going to be a boring one. Let's hope it's something cool, like 80s or a movie theme. For me, a Harry Potter theme would be epic! Yeah, or a Game of Thrones. That would be sick! Speaking of which, did you notice how they changed the school’s rules about biking to school? Yeah, they basically banned it unless you keep it in the bike shed. I'm not sure I agree with that, especially during good weather. It's one of the best ways for us to get some exercise. Agreed, totally overkill. I don't think anyone would ever misuse that, it's not like we can't handle our bikes. You're right. And what if one’s family can’t afford a shed or something? It’s just another rule that doesn’t make sense, if you ask me. True. Anyway, another thing - did you hear about those who were picked to be prefects? Not really, but who'll it be? I'm hoping my friend Emma gets it, she's always so helpful. I don't know for sure but I heard it might be Tom from our class. He's always well-organized and responsible. It'll be good to have him as a prefect. Agreed. Hopefully they’ll make it a fair choice. Wonder what the job will entail though. Not sure about the details but I think it's mostly organizing events or helping our teachers.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new bike shop opening up near the university? Yeah, I saw it the other day. I talked to someone who works there and they've got some pretty sweet deals. Really? That's great! I've been thinking of getting a new bike. The roads near here are getting pretty busy and a bike ride would be a good change of pace. True. Although be careful with that route, there's been a lot of road work lately and some of it is really rough on bikes. Oh, that's okay. I've been there before. But yeah, maybe I need to check out some off-road trails in our area. Might avoid those bumpy roads. You're in luck then. The recent initiative to expand the old rail trail near us has been a success and it's now a great place for cycling, especially with your mountain bike. That sounds brilliant! Do you fancy going there over the weekend? Absolutely. As for the weekend, I heard there's a big cricket match on at Headingley. We could go there on Saturday, see the match and then hit the trails on Sunday. Brilliant plan! I love cricket, it's such a British classic. But the main priority for me is trying to stay active, given my desk job. Totally understand, nice to mix things up. Though, I'm a bit worried about the crowds at Headingley, but I've got some contacts who might be able to get us some decent seats. That would be amazing! And then, it's back to your place for a Sunday brunch, or we could even cook up some grub, depending on how tired we are after the bike ride. Sounds like a plan. I've always wanted to try a Sunday roast since you've been talking about it. Your mum's recipe is legendary, right? Yes, my mum does make an amazing roast. You'd love it. I'm sure I would. So, what say we make this official? Bike ride on Sunday, followed by a Sunday roast at your place? Sounds like a plan to me! I'll start prepping the roast and you can book the tickets to Headingley. Good. I’ll text you the details about the tickets as soon as I've finalized everything. Thanks, mate. Looking forward to it. Same here.

Guys, I'm starving. I don't think I've eaten since lunchtime. Why don't we try that new Chinese place that opened up around the corner? I heard it's got really good food. I'm all for that. Especially now, after this whole day cooped up at home. A stir-fry would hit the spot. But I've never been there, have you? Yes, I've been there once, actually. The food was okay, but service was a bit slow. But I've got a keepsake that might make it better - they've got a game where you win a free meal if you guess how many chilli peppers are in the spiciest dish. That actually sounds fun, just like the games we used to play as kids. But can we really trust our taste buds to guess the number of chilli peppers? It's worth a try, I suppose. It might make ordering more interesting. But let's not rely solely on the game, let's also call ahead and see if it's busy. Last thing we need is to wait around for an hour or more. Great idea. Here, let me make the call. Hi, I'm calling to make a reservation for two. How long is the wait time at the moment? Uh-huh... Okay, so it's about 15-20 minutes? That sounds manageable. Exactly, they say about 15-20 minutes. So I'm making a reservation for you two and me. Just to make sure, they also mentioned that their spiciest dish is the 'Dragon's Breath'. Just noting it down, in case you're interested in trying it. More like 'Dragon's Sneeze', isn't it? Could be. But either way, we can try guessing the number of chilli peppers and maybe win a free meal. Right, so we've got 15-20 minutes to wait. What do we do in the meantime? I was thinking we could watch something, take a break. And maybe we can all make a list of our favorite Chinese food dishes. Who knows, we might find something new to try. Yeah, or just scroll through social media or YouTube for a bit. That sounds like a plan. We've got plenty of time until our reservation. I just realized, I could also check if they have any... I don't know, special menus or anything.

Ah, Phil, been meaning to catch up for ages! How's things been treating you? You know, aside from the usual chaos that comes with practising nursing? Cheers, mate! You know how it is. It's been a bit of a whirlwind this year. The NHS – always something new. Hospital stays for me last summer gave me a bit of an insight into that world, I must say. There's a lot to be proud of there, despite all the criticisms and setbacks. Absolutely. Nurses and doctors are the backbone of it all. But, you know, the pressure they deal with – it's quite something else. Can't imagine. Though, let me tell you, even as an academic, the pressures we face in our places of work aren’t that dissimilar. True that. Management and all the red tape they love to inject. Still, it's rewarding when it all comes together. Absolutely. When teaching goes well, it's like a whole different world. I had a student gain a PhD this year. It was a proud moment. That's brilliant, congratulations! Now that's what I call a good day at work. Quite. Speaking of the good and the bad, how's your neighbour situation? I heard there was a bit of an uproar about the noise? Oh, yeah. That guy in the flat above has got no idea about shared living or the concept of peace and quiet. Young chap, probably couldn't care less. I know the feeling. I've had my fair share with students and the lounge next to my flat. At least you've got some less noisy side of town, Anfield being quieter than the city. Liverpool as a whole is pretty unique. Different city, but same type of characters, I reckon. Indeed! But, I've also been thinking about escaping Liverpool for a bit. Been meaning to travel to Finland next year – heard the scenery is stunning and they've got some of the best healthcare in the world. Finland's always on my travel list too. They've done an impressive job with their healthcare system and education. Their healthcare is quite the model. Maybe I could learn a thing or two from them and bring it back here. Could learn from anyone, really. Each country has its own strengths. I've been to Finland a couple of times for conferences, great place.

Ah, good to see you, ANON. How've things been? All right, thanks for asking. It's been a bit of a struggle at times. Got my pension sorted out but I still can't quite make ends meet. Still, life goes on, you know? I understand that situation all too well. The government's welfare policies, eh? Sometimes they seem more focused on spinning the truth rather than addressing the real problems of people like you and me out here. Oh, I agree completely! They talk about cuts and austerity, but where does it really cut? The people, that's where. They say they want to encourage people to work, but jobs are scarce and training programs are a joke. Indeed. I teach English to international students in the city, and a lot of them tell me about how they came here to work and build a better life. But with rising costs, it's getting harder for them too. That's the immigrant story over and over. And now people are blaming them for everything. Someone should tell these politicians their own people need help as much as the immigrants. It's certainly problematic how immigration gets blamed for all issues. We're a long way from the kind of society we had after the war. Back then, immigrants helped rebuild the country. Absolutely! And now, people forget or don't want to remember that history. But the jobs aren't there for the native born, neither. It's a false narrative, playing on peoples' fears rather than addressing real issues. You're right again. I saw on the news the other day that police action in the city is inconsistent. There were riots because of perceived mistreatment of black youths by police, and now...the narrative shifts to the protesters being violent. More sensationalism, less sense. The police are acting more like soldiers than protectors. And when they do act, it's often disproportionate to the situation. True. And changing the subject to immigrants sure helps shift public opinion. You can say that again. I've lived in this city all my life and never seen it like this. I couldn't agree more. But let me tell you a funny anecdote: This week, I had a student from India who almost got into trouble because he was eating a sandwich in the street during lunchtime. I had to explain that he’s allowed to eat on the street in Liverpool.

Alright, I'm pretty sure no one here uses these types today. I mean, when was the last time you heard someone saying "reet" in this city? Oh, come on, it's still used! You might not hear it in Cambridge, but in the north and northeast, it's still pretty common. I wish I could get away with using "reet" at work. But, I think my colleagues would think it was a typo if I wrote it in an email. Interestingly, 'reet' is quite similar to 'right' in some northern dialects. I used to have trouble understanding my London colleagues when they said 'alreet' or 'y'know what I mean? Was a bit tricky at first. Definitely. I've heard of people saying 'awreet' even in some parts of Leeds sometimes. But, we're in Cambridge, so maybe it's safer to stick with standard English here.
