So, what brings you to Cambridge today or are you just checking in on us before a meeting? Yeah, just thought I'd come and grab some lunch with you all. I've got a meeting later but wanted to catch up. It's been ages since we all met up, hasn't it? Definitely! Plus, I'd love to hear more about your work as a corpus administrator. I've been working on a project with dialects and it would be great to get a different perspective. I'd be interested too! Corpus administrator, it's not exactly the most common job, so it would be nice to hear more about it. Yeah, really. So, what does a typical day look like for you? And do you ever deal with regional dialects in your work? That's something I've found very fascinating in my publishing work. Oh, absolutely. I deal with all sorts of linguistic data, not just dialects but also different accents, terminology...things like that. And it's always interesting trying to pinpoint where some of these phrases are from. Did you have to adjust your own dialect when you moved down to London for the job? I swear, after living down here for a few years, my Northern accent got a bit...mixed. Yeah, I went through that too. At first, it was finding that balance between maintaining your roots and...adapting. But the more I work with language data, the more I realized it's not about losing a dialect, but using it as a tool.

Ah, mate, did you catch any of that latest series on BBC Four? I found it really thought-provoking, exploring the impacts of the internet on our culture. It’s always fascinating how these technologies shape various aspects of our lives, you know? Actually, I did, but I kind of switched off after the first half hour. It was a bit too theoretical for my taste. I prefer something a bit more concrete, like that brilliant series on modern China they had on the other night. I couldn’t believe how much they discussed about their language policies and how it affected minority groups. Fascinating stuff. Oh, that one was incredible! I mean, have you noticed how much the emphasis on language learning has shifted over the years? When I was at school, French and German were the only options. Nowadays, there’s so much more variety, even in the South West. What’s been your experience with teaching and language learning? It’s been quite positive, to be honest. I’ve had classes where students were eager to learn, but often found themselves juggling various priorities. Technology can be both a blessing and a curse in those cases. I’ve even used some online platforms that allow real-time language exchange, which is quite innovative. I’ve heard about those. It’s kind of neat, the way it connects people from all over the world. Though at the same time, it’s interesting how we can often become too reliant on technology, isn’t it? Sometimes I worry that we’re losing some of that depth in our interactions. True, there’s definitely a trade-off. But it also opens up so much more access, especially for people who wouldn’t have had the opportunity otherwise. True enough. Speaking of that, how about this new app for vocabulary learning? I’ve seen some of my students use it and the feedback is great. You just get these little daily reminders and quizzes. I should look into that. I’m always on the lookout for tools that can help my students. Though I’ve found that some technical issues can be a pain - the last time we tried to set up an online class, the platform just wouldn’t work properly. Ah, yes, that’s always such a headache, isn't it? Still, I guess it's better than zero access.

Ah, marvellous to see you both again! You've had a safe journey today? The traffic sounds like it's been a bit of a nightmare from what I've been told. Yes, quite a squeeze on the A1 now and then! But we made it – no major questions on the exam just now. Aye, well, that's grand to hear. I've been wondering, how's the new job going? The maths exams, innit? Oh, it's still a bit of a task. You'll always find one or two surprises. But the students seemed quite keen today. Reminds me of the time I was taken to task for not knowing the correct side of the slide rule when I was at school. They even had an invitation to see the headmaster about it! Oh, Mr... was it Ron? Yes, we both remember that! Quite so. Now, how about you both help with the tea while I set this place up a bit? We need a nice quiet spot for our visitors. Sure thing, Grandma! The kettle, the biscuits, the tea pot... I think I'm all over it. Ah, careful now, lad! You wouldn't want to spill any tea on Aunty's favourite tea set. Remember, Yorkshire tea in the mug, English breakfast on the side. Oh, hush, now. We don't want him thinking that's a maths problem too complicated for him. Everyone laughs. Alright, if you're all set then, let's get this side of the room tidied up and a few treats on the table. The afternoon’s looking grand – warm sunlight and all. What do you think we should do later today? Well, I was hoping we could watch a film or something. Maybe something from the '60s? I heard you both have a lot of stories from that time. Oh, that's a good idea! I've got some old vinyls if anyone wants to listen to music as well. Ah, there's almost nothing like sitting down to listen to the real thing. The quality's so much better than anything digital. That sounds fine. Let's decide on something after tea. How about something that won't keep your grandfather up too late, though? He's not as young as he was when any of the movies from that era first came out. Aye, and I'll make sure to keep from over-sharing any old stories about the crumpet youth of Yorkshire at that time.

Oh, did you take a look at those photos we took during our summer road trip? I was just going through them and thinking about how much I miss those little adventures. Oh, absolutely. I've just been through them too. There's one of us at Stonehenge looking like complete tourists. "Complete tourists" is a bit generous, don't you think? We were at least trying to look nonchalant while posing for that picture! True. It's kind of funny looking back at ourselves, isn't it? Like time has stopped and we're just stuck in that moment. It really is. Makes me wish we could just bottle that feeling of freedom and spontaneity. We never really do those kinds of impulsive trips anymore. We're a bit too settled now, aren't we? But it's okay. I think we've managed to find a good balance. And these trips we're taking now are more... planned for sure, but they're still filled with new experiences. Like our last trip to Shanghai this summer. Absolutely. We should try to make time for those trips, while the kids are still young and they can enjoy them too. And while they still think it's fun to travel with us! Can't wait for them to be teenagers and decide we're "uncool" for dragging them around the world. That's a whole different kind of adventure! Speaking of the kids, have you noticed how much they've changed? They're acting all grown up lately. Yes, it's both a joy and a little bit heartbreaking. I keep catching myself thinking they're getting too big too fast. Exactly. I was just thinking the other day - the past few years have just zoomed by. They do. I remember when people used to say "time flies when you're having children"... I never fully appreciated it until now! It's wild, isn’t it? But it's also a privilege. We're lucky to have them, to have them here with us. Absolutely. Have you spoken to our friend Emily lately? Sure did. I actually met her up while running some errands the other day. She's still in that interesting phase of life, isn't she? Oh yeah, she's still figuring things out. I love catching up with her though, she's always got such a fresh perspective.

Yo, I can't believe what happened last night! Oh what happened? This guy I've been talking to online for a while, he invited me out but ended up ditching me at the last minute. That's so lame! Why did he do that? Honestly, I have no idea. And to make it worse, he didn't even bother to text or call. I had to call him up and he didn't even pick up! That's such a dick move! Exactly! Like, what is even the point of chatting and making plans if he just forgets about me? So what happened when you saw him in the canteen today? I tried to ignore him but he came over and started this whole charade about needing to do some work with his mates and couldn't cancel... Like, that's just so infuriating. How did you handle it? I was so polite, like "Oh that's so cool, don't worry about it." But inside I was like "What a dick!" You handled it way better than I would've. I'd probably have told him where to go. I wanted to, honestly, but there's just something about being nice and not causing a scene especially in a place like this. Yeah, but sometimes you gotta let people know their actions are not okay. I know, but doesn't come naturally to me. I've always been the one that tries to avoid conflict... I get that, but it’s also important to stand up for yourself. You deserve better, you know? I do. I really do. It just gets to me when I see so many people around us who just don't have any respect for others. It does suck. But it's also making us stronger, facing these things. True. I guess in a way, it’s preparing us for the real world, isn't it? Definitely. It reminds me of that lecture we had the other day about social media and the image you present online. Oh yeah! We had that discussion about how we want to be perceived and all that. Exactly. And sometimes our online image can be completely different from who we are in real life. Totally. I've had a few instances where people thought I was one thing purely based on my Instagram account, but really I'm just a regular girl trying to make it through uni.

Ah, marvellous weekend so far, haven't we? The peas and chips today were nearly too good to resist. Oh, absolutely. It's the small things like this that make family time so special. Agreed, though I must say, the questions grandma asked just now had me thinking. What about? She asked about this Fifa football game that our nephew's been talking about. All he says is “this team is better than that team”. She wanted to know how he could make such claims without being a professional, you know? Hilarious isn't she? I used to have similar conversations in my math class, just trying to explain why certain relationships among numbers made sense. But in the end, I guess it's all about making the case, isn't it? Exactly, and it's not just about math or football, is it? It's about how we present our arguments, whether it's over peas and chips or about potential careers. It got me thinking about the world our nephew is growing up in, where he's exposed to so much information and argumentation on the internet. Absolutely. It's pretty impressive how much he's assumed moral responsibility for 'his' team. Kids in this digital age are learning about culpability in such interesting ways, aren't they? Fascinating, really. I used to wonder if my students could see past mere opinion to understand why one argument was stronger than the other. They'd often claim things based on "it’s popular" or "everyone says so”. But now I wonder: doesn’t real moral responsibility begin when you start seeing things for how they actually are? I think that’s right. It’s about understanding the underlying rules or principles that govern why something may be better or truer. Much like the rules of Fifa football or the way a country's economy works. It’s about understanding those before we dive deep into making claims or choosing sides. But also, where does culpability come into this? Like when your nephew says, “This team’s losing because they didn’t play well.” Does he also talk about his own responsibility when his team isn't so brilliant? That’s the sweet spot, isn’t it? Teaching children and even ourselves about those internal rules, about personal and collective responsibility. It's not just about pointing fingers but also about looking inward.

Right, so I'm going to bin strike to my first point. Did you manage to catch the news about the bin strikes around here? They're talking about it being sorted out by next week, but I've still got a heap of rubbish at home that I need to sort out. Yeah, heard about it. I just hope they sort it out soon. But speaking of sorting, have you heard about the new recycling scheme they're starting? Apparently, they're actually looking into fracturing out different types of plastics now and how it affects our drinking water. That's a good point. You know, I was reading an article about different types of drinking water – tap, bottled, filtered, etc. I used to only drink bottled water, but after reading that, I'm considering making the switch to filtered tap water. Was less of a carbon footprint and all that. That's great! One less thing to worry about when it comes to living more sustainably. I never thought much about drinking water until last year. I had this blackout at home for a couple of days and I was left with only stored water. For a retired man like me, it was quite an adventure, let me tell you. I can imagine! But speaking of adventures, the weather forecast says it should be nice today. How about we go for a walk along the beach in Brighton? It's been ages since we've all gone out as a group. That sounds lovely! And we could even pack a picnic. One thing though, we should probably get all the rubbish from the strike sorted out first. But it's not just about the rubbish, it's about finding our glasses, remembering where we put our lunch or just generally navigating around the flat. Ah, the joys of flat-sharing. Speaking of navigating, have you checked out this new app for storing contacts? It's voice recognition software, no need for you to even type! That's interesting. Can it set up a BlackBerry phone though? Grandpa here had some trouble with his the other day. BlackBerry? I thought they stopped making phones like that years ago! Well, let's see... BlackBerry is quite old-fashioned technology now. But I could give it a try. I might need some guidance though. We've got all the time until our family visiting this weekend.

Oh, I'm so glad we decided to have a cuppa here. It's been ages since I've had a proper English breakfast, and this coffee is actually not bad at all. You know how homesick you can get when you're far from home? Oh, absolutely. I had the worst time staying in Spain last summer. But this place, Tarnow, has its charm. I've been settled here for a while now, teaching English. How's it going with you? Still doing some teaching on the side? Yeah, but mostly part-time. I've been lazy, to be honest. I've been semi-retired for a while now. But sometimes I do some private TEFL sessions to keep myself occupied. That sounds nice. I feel the same - sometimes we need a break. And being a full-time teacher can be tiring, especially with the pressure to prepare students for exams. Absolutely, that's a big responsibility. I remember when I used to do it full-time. I had a student once, really keen but struggling with reading comprehension. I spent extra hours with him, provided some extra resources, even got him a pair of English readers. You know, it's amazing how much of an impact you can have in a student’s life. Yes, it's incredibly rewarding when students make progress, isn't it? Although, sometimes it feels like you carry their success as your own in your mind, like if they fail, it's somehow your failure too. That's true. But it's part of the job, and the feelings that come with it are what make it so worthwhile. I do miss the challenge though. Maybe I should start taking on more students side of things. Definitely do. You'd be great at it. Speaking of students, did you hear about last night’s football match? No, not yet. What happened? We haven't caught up on anything. Oh, Manchester United won! And I heard it was a nail-biter, 2-1. I thought I might get a message from my football buddy, Josh, but he was too busy celebrating. Ah, yes, Manchester United. I do love those Saturday afternoon results, even if I don’t watch the matches as much as I used to. Reminds me of back home, though. Exactly. Sometimes I feel a pang of homesickness over here but any mention of football or British media... or um, a decent cup of tea... brings me right back.

Right, so I had this absolute nightmare of a day at work. We have this big conference coming up and I realized yesterday that we've only got a month to go and we're nowhere near ready. Oh no, that sounds stressful. What’s causing the hold-up, though? Aha! I've had similar situations before. What kind of conference is it? Is it academic or corporate? It's actually a tech conference. I had thought we were going to set up a registration system early on, but that’s still not ready. And then there’s the speakers, we’ve invited, but we haven’t had responses yet. Does anyone else have any say in getting these things done? Not like you have to deal with everything by yourself. Ah, yes - there’s my boss, but he’s on holiday right now and he left me in charge. It’s a bit too much responsibility, especially considering I’ve only been in this role a few months. You’re doing well to admit it, though. It takes a lot to admit you’re in over your head. So who can you call in on maybe? Well, there’s a colleague who’s been doing this for years and is very experienced. I was hoping he would offer to help out, but he’s been so busy with other projects. Well, technology-wise, maybe you could look to outsourcing or perhaps look into some ready-made conference management platforms? Yeah, that’s a good point actually. I don’t have to do everything from scratch. Plus, I don’t have to break myself in trying. And how are you managing the stress? You’re a graduate and you're in a fairly demanding job already. Honestly? I’m trying a few things, like drinking herbal tea and yoga. But sometimes I just want to shout at my computer! We've all been there, love. While you’re dealing with all this, how are you finding time for dating? Not so much. Let’s say work’s been quite a defender of my single life. That’s understandable, though. Maybe when the conference is over, focus on that for a bit. You could even look into apps like Bumble or Hinge. Yeah, I’ve heard good things about those. Perhaps I need to allocate some time for that. Speaking of allocating time, I just realized I need to apply for a new labourer role I saw advertised this morning.

Ah, I've been meaning to catch up on my teaching duties. We have these Chinese fellows coming over and I wanted to brush up on my knowledge of their language and culture. That's great. Want to discuss the layout of our park here? I noticed the lime trees look particularly stunning this season. Oh yes, the lime trees are beautiful. Speaking of trees, have you noticed how often pandas are used in Chinese representation? There must be a reason for that. That's an interesting point. I remember when I was researching for a project about wildlife in China. There's this interesting contrast between the landscape and the wildlife there. Exactly, and I also came across this story in one of my Chinese friends’ posts about a boy catching a pigeon. It was in the context of village life in Tibet or somewhere similar. What's that all about? It's probably just a simple anecdote about village life, but as a researcher, I can tell you that in many parts of rural China, similar stories are common. It's often about life's simple joys and village dynamics. That's fascinating. So different from this park, for example. Have you ever driven through these rural areas? I find the layout pretty challenging. How do you handle driving there? Oh, absolutely. The main thing is to slow down and anticipate turns or animals on the road. You have to be careful with livestock – cows, pigs or whatever – roaming freely. Yes, I've had close calls with some really huge cows in Devon when we’re driving round there. But what's been your experience? Getting to the Isle of White doesn’t seem that complicated. It's straightforward, but the roads can be quite narrow, especially in the summer. We went there once during the peak season and it was surprisingly busy. I just tried this salted caramel cake. Do you think our colleague would like it? Perhaps, but she's quite health-conscious. You should know, but we should also keep an eye out for any coworkers who are on a diet. True. I'm also curious if our Chinese colleagues like any of these trinkets we bought. We always take something so we don’t leave empty-handed, but I’m not sure if they’ll appreciate them. You could use WeChat, they almost all have that.

Yo, mate, did you manage to sort out the last bits of the family get-together? Need to confirm the venue and the guest list. Yeah, the venue is down as Surrey but I need to finalize it later today. Still waiting on a few guests, though. But yeah, on questions you need answered: what's the rough time frame for the event and the budget for food and drinks? I think we settled on evening time, around 5 or 6, so people can set off from work and avoid peak traffic. And I reckon we should aim for about £500 to £700 for the food and drinks – that should cover everything from finger foods to a barbecue. Perfect, that sounds like a good starting point. I'll confirm the venue but from what I've researched, the old manor house in Surrey has plenty of space and it's quiet enough that we won't be bothered. Ron, the old manor house in Surrey? That spot? That's ace! Did you grab a look at their beer garden, too? Perfect for those summer vibes. For sure! We can have it on the lawns if it's good enough for everyone. I’ve also looked at a few catering options and we can either have everything handled by them or go for more of a DIY approach to keep costs down. DIY sounds manageable, but for a group this size maybe having some help wouldn’t be a bad idea. Also, is there a rough plan for the guest list? We need to make sure we’ve got enough of everything if everyone comes and some don’t. The guest list is the toughest part. There are about 30 or so confirmed attendees, but I’ve got a few more who are ‘probably’ going to join. I’ll try to get those final confirmations later today, too. Good job. If we think 35 or so, £500 should cover it but if it goes up to 40 or 45, we might need to sit on that budget a bit tighter. Absolutely, we can adjust as we get closer and final confirmations. Also, have you thought about activities or entertainment? It might be nice to have some structure to the evening. True, could be. Not sure yet... Maybe we could set up a few lawn games or even a little quiz.

Oh, mates, I haven't seen any of you for ages. It's been quite the turn around since uni and work started taking over our social lives. You're telling me! I feel like it's only the weekend, but the week feels like an eternity. Totally, but we've all been through that right? I mean, we've all got jobs, social lives... I'd almost forgotten what a 'relaxed' conversation even looks like. Oh, we've all got our fair share of lazy weekends – mine usually involve sleeping till noon and sticking to the closest pub. Sounds like heaven. Though I read that in the long term, oversleeping can actually lead to an invitation to more illness. Really? That's new to me. But speaking of illness... how's Sarah doing? I barely see her around Cambridge lately. Sarah's not doing too well, unfortunately. She's been battling a bit of an illness for a couple of months now. It started as a common cold but it turned into something more complicated. She's been to the doc a few times but the meds seem to be doing the trick. That's really not good. I remember she was saying something about feeling exhausted ALL the time. Can't imagine what that's like. Exactly. It's really hard to keep up when your body's just not cooperating. And on top of that, she's been doing her dissertation and things are getting quite hectic. Poor Sarah. If she needs anything, let me know. We can always come over together and help or just keep her company. That would be so lovely of you. I'll definitely let her know. It means a lot that you all are so supportive. You okay with it all? You seem really busy these days… To be honest, it’s been quite a rough couple of months, but I manage. Work's been demanding, and then helping Sarah out here and there. Ah, I know the feeling. When work and friend problems combine... Friend problems? What are you on about? Just small stuff. Someone at work not pulling their weight, finding it hard to balance work with social... Don't worry, it's nothing big. I'm just like anyone else, juggling life as best as I can. At least you're not juggling work and uni like poor Sarah at the moment.

Oh, did I tell you about our new team member Grace? On her first day of work, she accidentally sent a confidential email out to the entire office. Everyone was laughing, but of course, we had to remind her about email privacy rules. Still, she's really nice, though! Oh no, that must have been a bit embarrassing. But good thing it was a relatively harmless mistake, I suppose? Or did Grace ruin something important? Actually, no, it was just a mundane document about changing our filing system, nothing major. We all had a good laugh about it, and she's been adjusting well. She’s actually quite good at her role, and I’ve been training her. Well, as long as she wasn’t trying to send a scandalous email to the whole office. Anyway, I had a bit of an interesting case at work today. We had a patient who had just gone through a very messy breakup, and she was in quite a state. It was my job to help her through it and try to get her to see that sometimes these things happen and it’s okay to feel upset but also that there is a future. That's such a tough job, especially when it's with young people. How did you handle it? Well, in my experience, often the hardest part is trying to make them see the bigger picture while still acknowledging their current pain. It's like giving them permission to feel hurt while also reminding them that there will be good days again. Yeah, I can imagine. I also deal with some pretty tough stuff in my job sometimes. Just the other day, we had a project that had to be restructured due to budget cuts. The team was worried about job security and everyone was on edge. That must have been stressful. How’d you handle it as the co-ordinator? I had to be very transparent. I scheduled a team meeting, laid out all the facts as I knew them, and told them honestly that while we couldn’t control the changing circumstances, we could control how we responded to them. I emphasized the skills of every team member and that there’s always opportunity in change, even if it’s hard. It was tough seeing them take it so personally, but at the end of the day, they appreciated the honest approach.

Alright, kids, who first wants to tell us a legend today? We've got books and folk tales all about good versus evil from our deep, rich history. I do! I do! I love the one about the Dragon of Brinsop – do you remember that, Emma? Yeah! A knight fought a dragon and saved the village! Now, that's a good tale. Our very own ancient history. But remember, keeps it simple for the others. Sylvana, Malachi, tell me, what do you think 'good' and 'evil' mean? Good is like being kind. And evil is like being ... ... mean. Or like making people do things that they don’t want to. Like the dragon making people fearful. That’s a good start. But in many stories, it’s not always about good people versus entirely evil ones. Sometimes it’s between kindness and something else, like greed or fear. Is that like the story of Robin Hood? Exactly! The sheriff wasn’t evil in the way a dragon is in most tales, but rather he embodied greed and unfairness. And Robin Hood fought against that. He stole from the rich to help the poor, but he was considered 'good' because of his kindness. So, it means you can be good even if you have to do something 'bad'? Not quite. It means sometimes the lines between good and evil aren't always black and white. Let’s look at another one. The story of the Miser’s Hen – the miser was very stingy and a bit nasty, but the Hen turned out to be more kind and helpful. So, being good doesn’t always mean you’re always doing the 'right' thing according to rules? No, it's about being kind-hearted, thinking about others. The most important lesson is that being kind, respectful, and truly caring about others is what truly matters, regardless of the situation. So even if the person you're helping has done something 'bad', you can still be kind to them? That's a great example. Even if someone isn't being kind or fair, thinking about them with kindness and understanding can be 'good'. Are there any modern stories... or do people any more write about good vs. evil? Oh, absolutely. Modern stories explore these themes in different ways. Books, movies; they make us think about the complexities of goodness and the many shades of wrongdoing.

So, I hear that your weekend was quite eventful, running's still on your mind today. How's that leg feeling? Thanks for asking. It's still a bit sore but I managed to get through the school video project without too much trouble. Did the kids have a fun time? Oh yes! We had a blast! We got to ride the bus out into the countryside and film scenes for the school film. But it was very tiring and I had to sit down a lot. That must have been a lot of standing and walking for you. I suppose seeing all those new places was exciting despite the discomfort. Yeah, I really enjoyed it! We had to climb a big hill to get to this amazing view for the film. But after that, my legs were really tired - oh, and did I mention I wanted a doughnut? We've decided that if you're going to aspire to be film stars, you should at least have the perks of the job. Maybe we can bake some next weekend? That sounds amazing! I can bring some of my favorite recipes from school, or we can even make different toppings for the doughnuts! Actually, about that... in my effort to make sure the running machines at the gym weren't packed last night after work... Hmm, what's the big deal? Well, considering we’re talking about doughnuts and film stars and working out... I saw a new treadmill they've installed that's quite unique. It's the one that feels kind of like running outside. Except, it's on a screen and... you know, it's fancy. Oh, I'd like to see that. Does it really feel different from the traditional ones? Apparently, it's designed to simulate real terrain so it's changing the incline and even the texture supposedly. It’s supposed to be better for joints too – which might be something for your sore leg to experience. I want to run on that! Can we go see it today after school? Yeah, and maybe we can make a film about our experience of running on a mountain or through a forest or something! I like where this is going. But remember, we need to prioritize that doughnut baking for next weekend. I wouldn't dare suggest otherwise. But first things first, if anyone's up for it, we could try that treadmill thing after school today.

Ah, George, it's good to see you! How's life treating you these days? You know, aside from the usual niggles that come with our age, of course. Right, well, isn't that the life, eh? You know, I've been keeping busy with the business. It's been a bit of a rollercoaster lately, but we're managing. And aside from that, I've been trying to stay healthy, as much as I can, considering the pandemic and all. Absolutely, it's been quite the challenge for all of us, hasn't it? I've been trying to stay active as well, but with the knee and back, it gets a bit tricky. Though, the Gym says it's improving, so hopefully, that's a good sign. That's good to hear. And what about your political views? Still thinking of throwing your hat into the ring for the local Greens? Ah, well, it's tempting. You know, this town needs more green thinking, if you ask me. But joining a party at my age? I'm not sure. I'm more likely to end up as a delegate for them rather than running for office myself. I can see that. You know, politics isn't as simple as it used to be, right? What about the job market here in Brighton? You keep teaching, I'm assuming? Yeah, teaching, it's a steady job isn't it? But as you know, it's not without its challenges, and the pay never quite matches the effort. Still, I enjoy it. It keeps me connected with the younger generation and helps keep the grey matter active. Right, I've seen you around at some of those boot sales, haven't I? You must be good at finding bargains! Ah, well, it's a game, George. You have to spot what's good, but also know when to walk away. You never know what you might find, do you? I know what you mean. I've picked up a few useful items over the years. Though, my wife would probably say I have too many things now! Oh, I know the feeling. My wife used to almost faint when I came home with all the books I found. But relationships are good. How's life with Margaret? Still keeping you on your toes? Ah, she does. But all in good fun.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that plant workshop I attended? It was practically an all-day lecture on the finer points of indoor gardening. No, you didn't mention it. I'm all about trying to bring a bit of greenery into my student digs, but I don't think I could commit to a whole day. It was... intense. They covered everything from terrariums to hydroponics. But it was actually really interesting. I'd be interested to hear, actually. Tell me, anything stand out as particularly useful? Well, they did a whole segment on low-maintenance plants. You know, for when you're really busy and still want a little bit of nature around. They even discussed how well different types thrive in modern homes. That's exactly what I need! I was thinking of buying some succulents, but then my partner said something about them not needing much water and I thought, "Well, if I can't ever remember to water them, maybe they're not the best idea..." Succulents are great! They're perfect if you're a bit forgetful. And the 'bare minimum' label they gave them was 'looks interesting and lives'. That's exactly my kind of plant! But seriously, any specific tips? Oh, definitely! They mentioned that really good drainage is key for succulents, and they might not love direct sunlight all day. So if you have a spot with good indirect sunlight, it's perfect. Very useful! Thanks, that's really helpful. No worries. More importantly, do you think I can convince my partner that a small succulent garden in our living room is a good idea? You should try. If it's anything like convincing me to try pasties, it'll be a fun argument to watch. Oh, I hadn't thought of that. I introduced my partner to pasties when we first started dating, and at first, he was like, "Why would I want to eat a pie in a pastry case?" Did you use the 'it's just like a hand pie, but better' argument? Exactly. And then, of course, there's the 'it's a traditional British treat that you have to try' argument. Worked like a charm. I think arguments about food usually work. At least that's my experience. Definitely. Though sometimes, the arguments get more about the politics and social implications of certain foods. Like what, successful cuisines being influenced by colonial histories?

I've been meaning to ask you, have you ever had your students surprise you with an unusual topic? Oh, absolutely. It's the best part of being a lecturer. Last year, I had a group of students researching and presenting on the cultural impact of TV violence. It was quite fascinating, really. We had some really deep discussions about how narrative and physical violence intertwine, and the effects it has on society. Fascinating, I'd love to hear more. I've also had some... interesting keepsakes given to me by students. Remember my blue Peter badge collection? Of course! How can I forget? I used that as an example in one of my lectures just last week to illustrate how children are indoctrinated into systems of recognition from a young age. Yes, and funnily enough, I just found this old one from the 80s where they decided to collect badges from different years. It's quite a peculiar little testament to child culture. It's also interesting to ponder what that might say about what or who we value. Now that I think of it, it might be quite telling that we're having this discussion in Norfolk as well - I often feel that traditional English values and culture are more 'felt' in rural areas in a way they aren't in cities. I think that's a bit of a stereotype, but there might be some truth to it. Living in Norwich as I do, it's certainly more... traditional in many ways than London. But that also means we’re quite culturally and socially dormant compared to the capital. Hmm, I would say that it's not dormant, but perhaps more preserved. The influence of technology and globalization has certainly been slower to reach here than in London. But the flip side is that there's definitely more community togetherness and a stronger sense of tradition. On that note, did you see the article about those young squatters who were featured in The Guardian? That's quite a generation gap, isn't it? You mean the one about how a lot of young people are choosing to squat for political reasons or just for housing? I did see that. It's quite a stark contrast to how most people in our age group see property and ownership. It's a subject that touches on class and socioeconomic issues.

Ah, lovely weather today, isn't it? I was just out in the garden, and it's so warm and sunny. Reminds me of the days when I was younger and had more energy to be out here all the time. You always were an energetic one, John. Still are, if I'm honest. Yes, I suppose so. Now, I just potter about. But, talking about energy and hard work, I was just thinking about how backwards our country seems. All these young people... I mean, we had to work from a young age. I remember my parents, they worked so hard, and I used to help out in their shop. My parents did the same. They started their own business, running a small shop in Harrow. It was hard work but rewarding. I sometimes think we relied heavily on those shop owners back then, for livelihood and community. And these days, it seems like the younger generation doesn't understand what that kind of work entails or even wants to. Nowadays, so many of them want to be teachers or engineers, or whatever is "in" at the moment. Quite. I remember in my school days, we had a mixture of ambitious youngsters, like us apparently now, and some who didn't exactly know what they wanted to be but were willing to learn and work hard, no matter what. Well, we did have a good science teacher who encouraged me to pursue biology. I don't think I would have thought of that on my own. Just goes to show, the education system and the teachers can make a huge difference. More now than ever, it seems. And, speaking of work ethic, it brings me to a different topic altogether. I was looking through some old photos last week, from when I was in and around Costessey. Do any of you remember the old abattoir on the outskirts? Oh yes, sure. It used to stink and all but it was a working class area so we were used to it. My father used to work there sometimes, as a casual labourer. Yes, and yet, most of us wouldn't care to reminisce about those times. I recall my parents were quite proud of the work ethic associated with it. But it's interesting how food has changed. Now, everyone seems so particular about where their food comes from but back then, we ate what was available and affordable.

Ah, James, I'm curious. I remember you first started working here as an Associate Lecturer. What did you do before that? Thanks for asking, Sarah! I actually used to work in recruitment. It was quite a change from academia. I spent about five years in this industry, mostly for a company called Morgan Talent Development. It was an interesting time, but I'd definitely say it honed my analytical skills and taught me a lot about human dynamics. Fascinating! I can see how that would be beneficial. But what made you want to move into academic work? Initially, it was the long working hours and stress. I have to say, I've been enjoying the benefits of a more balanced work-life in academia. But the real draw was my interest in research and teaching. I always felt there was a lot I could contribute to the field even outside of recruitment. And being here at ANON has been a great place to start, I must say. Absolutely, your expertise seems to have been a great asset to our team. Did your experiences in recruitment influence your approach to teaching or the way you evaluate students? Definitely. For instance, I often apply what I learned from assessing candidates' skills and abilities to different learning outcomes in my courses. It helps me to evaluate students' academic literacy beyond their technical skills. It's more about identifying their ability to communicate effectively, critically analyze, and apply knowledge in a practical context. Ah, I see. I'd love to explore that further, especially in the context of academic writing in our courses. I've noticed that sometimes students struggle with the level of writing expected in postgrad and PhD-level work. Do you think there might be a gap in where we're introducing and reinforcing these skills? Absolutely, Sarah. I've observed that when students come from varied educational backgrounds or less research-focused contexts, there may be a steep learning curve in terms of academic writing and literacy. I've noticed that sometimes we tend to assume students already have this skill set, but that's not always the case. Exactly, and changing the assumption can help us tailor our support more effectively. I've also seen that advanced reading skills, especially when it comes to navigating complex academic texts, are often where students struggle first. Have you found anything similar?

Alright mates, let's get this social gathering started. So who here is from Manchester then? I'm from Bolton actually, you? Oh, Bolton, great! Born and bred in Bradford myself. Ahem, I'm from a little village in the North of England, near Manchester actually. Oh, I'm from an even smaller village, it's called something like Malhotra Village in India, but now I'm a student here in Manchester. India?! That's so cool, we don't have too many international students from India in our circle. Welcome! Thank you! It's nice to meet all of you. So, everyone here is studying in the University of Salford, right? Yep. I'm doing my graduate degree in History here. For me, it's Business studies. It's been pretty interesting. I'm in Politics and International Relations. The subjects all around the world interest me. Politics is quite interesting right now, isn't it? Especially with Brexit and everything. Yeah, definitely, it affects us all here in different ways. For example, for some of us it meant we could afford to stay in the UK for our education because of a sudden change in the exchange rate. True, and the uncertainty has given us all a lot to think about, especially for those of us planning to work in Britain after the graduation. I just tried to get a part time job. The flood of Europeans trying to get settled before Brexit hit the market quite hard for entry level jobs. That’s quite tough! I actually interned for a historical research project on Yorkshire’s relation to pre-Brexit policy. Fascinating stuff but also showed me how intricate these political currents are. That’s so cool, I’ve always been fascinated by historical policy influences. Speaking of historical influences, ever heard of this joke? "Why did the Yorkshire man go to university?" Nope! "Because he needed a higher education." That's brilliant! We could really use a laugh here in the library. So, who’s the best at using the resources here? I feel like I could use some tips. I love the University Library here. The 24-hour opening on weekends is what you get used to living away from home, I suppose. There’s also some insanely helpful resources I've stumbled upon. Really? Like what? Oh, for example, there's a rare book room, a skills and information team who lead workshops and support on things like reference, citation, academic writing - really underrated resources.

Right, so I've been reading this great article in last month's "QWERTY" magazine about the history of communication technology. Fascinating stuff! Did you know that even back in World War I, they were already using radio telegraphy? No, I wasn’t aware! That’s quite something. I've been interested in the military because my granddad was in the army. But I've always been more into technology rather than the history aspect. Ah, I see! I find the history of how we communicate so interesting. It’s like, alongside all the major battles and strategies, there was this parallel revolution in how people communicated over vast distances. Definitely makes sense, considering how vital communication is in wartime. It must have made a huge difference to what happened during each battle, even if we can't measure it statistically or whatever. Exactly! It’s almost like history's often forgotten sidekick. True, and yet how it’s changed the world dramatically over the past century or so. I couldn’t imagine not being able to send a message to someone instantly now, or even just talk to them in real time. Precisely! I mean, even if we're busy or far apart, we’re always just a message or phone call away. It’s interesting to think about what the future holds, though. I mean, with all the technology we have now, who knows what the next decade might look like? Oh absolutely! I mean, we’re already seeing so much growth in AI and cybersecurity and all that. And with the film and gaming industries, I wonder what doesn’t come next. I think AI has so much potential, but it also scares me a bit, to be honest. Like, things are going so fast and who knows what kind of power that gives a few people, right? Right! Exactly. Which reminds me, did you watch that new AI movie that's out? I heard it's pretty thought-provoking. No, not yet. You’ll have to tell me about it then. But honestly, I find some of these AI films terrifying for that exact reason. Oh, truly so! And yet, they're also really fascinating because they help us think about the potential consequences. Agreed. And speaking of films, anyone know any good recommendations for British films from around the 80s or 90s? I'm on a bit of a nostalgia kick.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that online date I had today? The poor guy thought Watford was somewhere in Manchester! I couldn't believe his confusion. Right! And here I am telling people Wilmslow is just a quick train ride from Manchester and they're like 'What's Wilmslow? Is that even a place?' Honestly, I grew up near Winchester and people still can't pronounce it. It's always Winche-ster for them. It's funny, though. I've just had these bizarre dates with guys who think 'accessibility' just means having a step up to their front door. Tell me about it. I had this guy who insisted we meet at a certain pub, which he thought was accessible - until he arrived and was greeted with a staircase. And these people travel from London thinking they've got it all figured out. Oh yes, because it's all about having the 'London experience' right? Speaking of which, did you hear about the new politics? What? There's something new in politics? A surge in right wing parties using 'London folk' stereotypes in their campaigns, really trying to demonize people from the city, and all that racist rhetoric. It's like it's the 1980s all over again. Yeah, and the really disturbing thing is that people are actually buying it. We need to talk to people, actually listen to their worries and educate them about this type of rhetoric. Exactly. It's scary how easily we let fear and ignorance cloud our judgment. And it’s everywhere. Even in casual conversations, people drop these prejudices without realizing how damaging they are. You could even say it’s like almost every conversation in this very room. Do you think if we got a screen up here we could project some educational content? Maybe a series of short clips explaining the history of this kind of rhetoric and... Don't get ahead of yourself, love. We’d probably just get into more arguments. How about we just talk about it here, and actually listen to each other? Great idea. So, back to the fun stuff what are we up to next? Well, I'm actually hoping to get a project going in London, but funding is always an issue. Just keep applying, right? Don’t let one 'no' discourage you. Oh, and I've just finished a great project at the office.

Ah, welcome to our little nest. I hope you've had a pleasant journey here from London. Yes, thank you for having us. It's lovely to finally meet you in person rather than just over video calls! You both look very busy with work – do you find it challenging to make time for hobbies or interests? Well, my job as an English Language Instructor keeps me pretty busy, but I always try to squeeze in some time for reading or learning a bit about another language. Speaking of languages, did you hear about that new app for learning languages through music? I'm planning to try it out. Yeah, I've seen ads for it too. How's your study going by the way? Was it tough finishing graduate school during lockdown? It was quite challenging, but I managed okay. I did miss out on some of the usual university experiences though – creative writing workshops, film screenings, that sort of thing. But now I'm free to focus on my studies and share them with you guys! That's great. I'm looking forward to it. I've been meaning to ask – is your flat mostly furnished or did you buy most of it yourselves? We've slowly furnished it over time. We even found some great, affordable pieces on a local furniture market. Ah, love local markets. I found a beautiful vintage bike there for a good price last year. Bikes remind me of the Raleigh I had back in my 20s. These modern ones are quite fancy with their gears and all! I've always preferred my old-fashioned pushbike. I don't understand all these gears people rave about. It’s all a matter of preference, of course. Speaking of preferences, have you ever tried getting a bike rebuilt or customized? There's a small shop near here that's really good and reasonable. That's a great tip. I'll look into it. You know, I often think about how much things cost now. Bikes, houses – it's all so expensive. I worry about young people trying to make a start in life today. That's definitely true. We could use some better financial support systems, couldn’t we? Absolutely. It can be pretty daunting, especially when you're just starting out. Exactly! But, it’s not just about money. Things seem more expensive now, but there are also more opportunities.

Yo, mate, did you seen any of that latest social media's online shenanigans? I mean, talk about drama! Oh, you're talking about that unreal video on YouTube right? Yeah, I saw it too. It’s just, the way this generation is consumed by these online questions and answers kind of makes me wonder if we’re losing something genuine in the physical world. I couldn't agree more! But at the same time, I couldn't imagine not being able to Google my work queries during meetings. Technology is a two-edged sword, innit? Yeah, but sometimes you get lazy because of it. Like at work today, I was supposed to calculate something, but then I instinctively pulled out my phone to look up an app for it instead of just working through it from scratch. It’s almost like we're losing our problem-solving skills. Exactly! My dad, he's an old-school engineer, man. He didn’t have any of that in his time, and he still turned out good. And it's funny because it also applies to cooking - like those apps that guide you through a recipe. Sure, it's helpful, but it robs you of the joy of discovery, you know? Not to mention the unexpected quirks that happen when you don’t follow the script. I was cooking up a storm at the weekends, experimenting with new recipes, and you’re right, there's something amazing about working through the process, perhaps messing it up a bit, but then fixing it yourself. It feels much more rewarding than if you just followed a recipe without thinking much about it. And cooking and working are similar in that way - both are crafts that benefit from thought and creativity. Absolutely! It's like, we've got all these tools and resources at our fingertips, but we're not using the flexibility and creativity those same tools could offer if we were more focused on learning. Instead, we’re just using them for convenience. It’s like we’re forgetting how to be self-sufficient. True, but changing the world takes time. We could sit here and bemoan the internet or advanced tech all day, but it's also done incredible things for health and well-being. Like, when I was studying, so much of my health advice came from online resources because my university didn't have a great health center.

Oh, did I tell you last night's shift was a whirlwind? No, what happened? Well, we had a patient with a suspected pneumonia. It was just one of those cases where every piece of equipment on the ward was needed at once. You know, one minute I'd be fetching the blood gas machine, the next, I'd have to assist with a respiratory assessment. I've got similar keeps coming up at work, actually. Sometimes it feels like I need an extra pair of hands. Definitely! I've been training to get a certificate in first aid just cos it's useful for my line of work. Ah, that's brilliant! Nurses are always in need of people who have those skills. Speaking of work, I just had a meeting with a new client. They wanted a similar type of health-related document. It was a bit of a challenge, but I really enjoyed it. For me, it's usually a mixed bag with patients. Some days are great, and others... well, they just test your patience. I think the secret is finding the good things to make it all worth it. Like, when you manage to get someone's favorite meal in, or just having a chat that makes them feel listened to. You're so right about that. Alright, I'm shifting gears. Go on then. So the lads at my work are planning a end of year party. I don't know what I'm going to wear though. Oh, the age-old question! Just wear something comfortable and classic. You can never go wrong with that. Or a nice changing dress. You can add some accessories and change it up. Ah, I hadn't thought of that. I like it. Either way, it's always a bit of a stress having to choose what to wear. Again, agreed. Speaking of stress, I've just been trying to plan for next week, and it's not going smoothly. Always a challenge when you've got multiple care plans to juggle. I know that feeling. I feel like my greatest challenge is always trying to get my clients to communicate what they're actually needing from me. That can be a challenge, can't it? Definitely. And then there are the 'if only I had the magic wand' moments. We all have those. Oh, speaking of magic wands, I had plans to try and convince my boss to spend a little more on our holiday party.
